آخر.etymology: Elative/active-participle formation آخِر (ʾāḫir, 'last, final part; end') from the Semitic root ء-خ-ر (ʾ-ḫ-r, 'to come after, be behind, delay').

آذى.etymology: Form IV causative verb آذَى (ʾāḏā, from underlying *ʾaʾḏaya, 'to cause harm, hurt, or annoyance') on the pattern أَفْعَلَ (ʾafʿala) from أَذِيَ (ʾaḏiya, 'to suffer harm'), doubly weak root ء-ذ-ي (ʾ-ḏ-y).

history.meaning: harm -> to inflict harm or distress

آذى.notes: In spoken Jordanian, imperfective forms preserve or re-insert the initial hamza stem (ما بدي أأذيها, 'I don't want to hurt her'; عم يأذوا البنات).

آرمة.etymology: Levantine borrowing from Italian arma ('coat of arms, emblem, shop crest'), which came to denote a painted shopfront signboard across the eastern Mediterranean.

history.meaning: coat of arms; emblem; shop sign

آسف.etymology: Active participle آسِف (ʾāsif, 'regretful, sorry') from the verb أَسِفَ (ʾasifa, 'to grieve, feel regret') on the triliteral root ء-س-ف (ʾ-s-f).

آمن.etymology: Active participle آمِن (ʾāmin, 'safe, secure, free from fear') from أَمِنَ (ʾamina, 'to be safe, feel secure'), derived from the Proto-Semitic root ء-م-ن (ʾ-m-n, 'firmness, trust, safety').

آه.etymology: Primary expressive interjection آه (ʾāh), used across Classical and Levantine Arabic as an exclamation of realization ('oh!, ah!') and in Levantine speech as the everyday affirmative ('yes, yeah').

آها.etymology: Expressive exclamation آهَا (ʾāhā, 'aha!, I see!'), an extended emphatic form of آه marking sudden realization or comprehension.

آي.etymology: Natural expressive interjection آي (ʾāy, 'ouch!, ow!') voiced upon sudden pain, heat, or a minor bump.

أبد.etymology: Rooted in the Arabic triliteral أ-ب-د (ʾ-b-d), which signifies permanence, endless duration, and timelessness. In Classical Arabic, أَبَد (ʾabad) denotes unending future time, and in Jordanian speech it commonly appears in the prepositional phrase للأبد.

أبدا.etymology: Adverbial accusative أَبَدًا (ʾabadan, 'ever, forever; [with negation] never, not at all') from the noun أَبَد (ʾabad, 'endless time, eternity'), root ء-ب-د (ʾ-b-d).

أبداً.etymology: Formed as the accusative adverbial tanwīn (-an) of أَبَد (ʾabad), built on the triliteral root أ-ب-د (ʾ-b-d, eternity). While Classical Arabic uses أَبَداً both affirmatively and negatively, modern Levantine speakers use it predominantly to reinforce negation as 'not at all' or 'never'.

أبدع.etymology: Constructed on Form IV (أَفْعَلَ, ʾafʿala) from the triliteral root ب-د-ع (b-d-ʿ), meaning to originate, innovate, or produce something unprecedented. In both Modern Standard Arabic and everyday Jordanian conversation, أبدع praises someone for excelling or doing remarkable creative work.

أبعد.etymology: Form IV causative verb أَبْعَدَ (ʾabʿada, 'to remove to a distance, push away') on the pattern أَفْعَلَ (ʾafʿala) from بَعُدَ (baʿuda, 'to be far, distant'), Semitic triliteral root ب-ع-د (b-ʿ-d).

morphemes.meaning: Form IV causative verb ('put at a distance')

history.meaning: to be far -> to send or push away
to push away, keep away; (imperative ابعدي) step back!

rootFamily.gloss: to move away, stay clear (Form VIII)

أبعد.notes: In Jordanian speech, transitive 'push her away' uses أَبْعَدْهَا or Form II بَعَّدْهَا, while intransitive imperative ابعدي عني! ('stay away / back off from me!') aligns with Form I.

أبيض.etymology: Primary colour adjective on the pattern أَفْعَل (afʿal, feminine بَيْضَاء bayḍāʾ > Levantine بيضا) from root ب-ي-ض (b-y-ḍ, 'whiteness, brightness; egg').

أجنبي.etymology: Derived via the nisba adjectival suffix -ī (-ي) from أَجْنَب (ʾajnab, outsider or stranger), belonging to the root ج-ن-ب (j-n-b, side or flank). Originally referring to someone standing off to the side or outside the kin group, it became the standard term for 'foreign' across Levantine Arabic.

أجّر.etymology: Form II verb أَجَّرَ (ʾajjara, 'to rent out, let for hire'), denominative from أَجْر (ʾajr, 'reward, wage, hire') on the Semitic root ء-ج-ر (ʾ-j-r).

history.meaning: to rent out; let on lease

أجّل.etymology: Form II verb أَجَّلَ (ʾajjala, 'to postpone, defer to a later term'), derived from أَجَل (ʾajal, 'appointed time, fixed term') on the root ء-ج-ل (ʾ-j-l).

أحد.etymology: Derived from the Semitic root أ-ح-د denoting oneness; Sunday is literally the first day of the week in Arabic reckoning.

أحرف.etymology: Broken plural on the pattern أَفْعُل (ʾafʿul) of حَرْف (ḥarf, edge, border, letter), built on the root ح-ر-ف (ḥ-r-f). Originally signifying an edge or boundary in Classical Arabic, the plural أحرف designates individual alphabetic characters in both standard and Jordanian usage.

أحسن.etymology: Elative adjective on the pattern أَفْعَل (ʾafʿal) from the triliteral root ح-س-ن (ḥ-s-n, beauty, goodness, excellence). Across Jordanian Arabic, أحسن serves as the primary comparative and superlative ('better / best') for both quality and physical well-being.

أحلى.etymology: Defective elative adjective (أَفْعَل) built on the root ح-ل-و (ḥ-l-w, sweetness, charm, beauty). Extending beyond literal sugar sweetness, everyday Jordanian speakers use أحلى to praise anything prettier, kinder, or more enjoyable.

أحمر.etymology: Primary color adjective أَحْمَر (ʾaḥmar, feminine حَمْرَاء > Levantine حمرا) on the pattern أَفْعَل from the root ح-م-ر (ḥ-m-r, 'redness, ruddy hue').

أحيانا.etymology: Adverbial accusative أَحْيَانًا (ʾaḥyānan, 'at times, sometimes') of أَحْيَان (ʾaḥyān), the broken plural of حِين (ḥīn, 'time, period, moment'), root ح-ي-ن (ḥ-y-n).

أخ.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *'aḫ- ('brother'), one of the core biradical kinship nouns across Semitic languages.
أخ.notes: Before possessive suffixes or in construct, the long stem vowel resurfaces (أخوي 'my brother', أخوك 'your brother'), and the dual is أخوين ('two brothers').

أخد.etymology: Levantine reflex (with regular shift of interdental ذ ḏ to stop د d) of Classical Arabic أَخَذَ (ʾaḫaḏa, 'to take'), inherited from Proto-Semitic *ʾaḫaḏ-.

أخضر.etymology: Primary colour adjective on the pattern أَفْعَل (afʿal, feminine خَضْرَاء > Levantine خضرا) from Semitic root خ-ض-ر (ḫ-ḍ-r, 'fresh green growth, herbs, vegetables').

أخير.etymology: From Classical Arabic أَخِير (ʾaḫīr, 'last, final, latter'), faʿīl adjective from the Semitic root ء-خ-ر (ʾ-ḫ-r, 'to come after, be behind').

أخيراً.etymology: Built on the adjective أَخِير (ʾaxīr, last/final) with the adverbial accusative ending -an (-اً), tracing back to the root أ-خ-ر (ʾ-x-r, behind, after, or delayed). Everyday Jordanian speech preserves this Literary Arabic adverbial form verbatim to express relief or culmination.

أدار.etymology: Hollow-root Form IV verb (أَفْعَلَ) from د-و-ر (d-w-r, to turn, revolve, or circulate), where Classical أَدْوَرَ contracted to أَدَارَ (ʾadāra). Moving from the physical sense of turning a wheel or steering, it came to mean directing, managing, or running an enterprise in educated Jordanian speech.

أدفى.etymology: Levantine elative أَدْفَى (ʾadfā, 'warmer, warmest') from Classical أَدْفَأ (ʾadfaʾ) via regular loss of final hamza, from the root د-ف-ء (d-f-ʾ, 'warmth, shelter').

أدلة.etymology: Broken plural on the pattern أَفْعِلَة (ʾafʿila) of دَلِيل (dalīl, guide, sign, proof), formed from the geminate root د-ل-ل (d-l-l, to point out or guide). Used consistently across legal, academic, and everyday Jordanian speech, أدلة refers to proofs or supporting clues.

أذكياء.etymology: Diptote broken plural (أَفْعِلَاء, ʾafʿilāʾ) of ذَكِيّ (ðakiyy, clever, sharp-witted) on the root ذ-ك-و / ذ-ك-ي (ð-k-w, keenness, blazing brightness). Retaining its Classical Arabic form in educated Jordanian speech, أذكياء describes clever or quick-minded people.

أذن.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *ʾuḏn- ('ear'), a core anatomical noun shared across all branches of Semitic (root ء-ذ-ن).

أربع.etymology: Cardinal numeral stem tracing to the pan-Semitic root ر-ب-ع (r-b-ʿ, four, cf. Hebrew אַרְבַּע), formed with a prosthetic glottal stop as أَرْبَع (ʾarbaʿ). Under Arabic numeral polarity, this unmarked form precedes feminine counted nouns in both Standard and Jordanian usage.

أربعة.etymology: Marked cardinal numeral أَرْبَعَة (ʾarbaʿa) built on the Semitic root ر-ب-ع (r-b-ʿ, four) with the feminine ending -a (-ة). In Arabic syntax it counts masculine nouns and also serves in Jordanian speech as the standalone counting form and clock hour ('four o'clock').

أربعطعش.etymology: Levantine compound numeral contracted from Classical أَرْبَعَةَ عَشَرَ (ʾarbaʿata ʿašara, 'four-teen'), with pharyngeal-triggered emphasis producing the characteristic -ṭaʿš teen suffix.

أربعين.etymology: Oblique/generalized spoken form of Classical أَرْبَعُونَ / أَرْبَعِينَ (ʾarbaʿīna, 'forty'), decade numeral formed with the plural suffix -īn from أَرْبَع (ʾarbaʿ, 'four').

أرجوك.etymology: Polite expression from Classical Arabic أَرْجُوكَ (ʾarjūka, 'I beseech/ask you'), 1st-person imperfect of رَجَا (rajā, 'to hope, ask earnestly', root ر-ج-و) with 2ms suffix -ka.

أرز.etymology: Early Mediterranean agricultural loanword entering Classical Arabic as أَرُزّ / رُزّ (ʾaruzz / ruzz) from Ancient Greek ὄρυζα (óryza) or an Old Iranian/Indo-Aryan trade route (ultimately Sanskrit vrīhí-). While formal writing uses أرز, everyday Jordanian speech overwhelmingly prefers رز.

morphemes.meaning: from Greek óryza / Iranian rice trade term

أرض.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *ʾarṣ̂- ('earth, land, ground'), one of the most ancient feminine nouns in the Semitic lexicon (root ء-ر-ض).

أرضي.etymology: Relational (nisba) adjective أَرْضِيّ (ʾarḍiyy, 'terrestrial, ground-level, ground-floor') derived from أَرْض (ʾarḍ, 'ground, earth') with the suffix -ِيّ (-iyy).

أرضية.etymology: Feminine substantive أَرْضِيَّة (ʾarḍiyya, 'flooring, floor surface, ground base') formed from the relational adjective أَرْضِيّ (ʾarḍiyy).

أرق.etymology: Elative adjective أَرَقّ (ʾaraqq, 'thinner, gentler, more delicate') on the pattern أَفْعَل from the geminate root ر-ق-ق (r-q-q, 'thinness, fineness, tenderness').

أزرق.etymology: Color adjective on the pattern أَفْعَل (ʾafʿal, feminine زَرْقَاء zarqāʾ) from the root ز-ر-ق (z-r-q, blue, pale-eyed, gleaming). Originally applied in Classical Arabic to bright blue eyes or clear water, أزرق is the everyday Jordanian term for blue.

أزعج.etymology: Form IV causative verb أَزْعَجَ (ʾazʿaja, 'to unsettle, disturb, bother') from the root ز-ع-ج (z-ʿ-j, 'to disquiet, rouse from rest').

أزمة.etymology: Noun أَزْمَة (ʾazma, 'tightness, strait, crisis') from أَزَمَ (ʾazama, 'to constrict, bite tightly, become severe'); in Jordanian Arabic it also specializes as 'traffic jam, bottleneck'.

أساس.etymology: Formed on the noun pattern fa'aal from the triliteral root أ-س-س meaning to lay a foundation or establish.

أسبوع.etymology: Formed on the pattern أُفْعُول (ʾufʿūl) from the numeral root س-ب-ع (s-b-ʿ, 'seven'), naming the seven-day week.

أستاذ.etymology: Classical Arabic أُسْتَاذ (ʾustāḏ, 'master craftsman, teacher, tutor; polite title sir/Mr'), borrowed from Middle Persian awestād ('master, skilled artisan').

أستاذك.etymology: Inflected form combining أُسْتَاذ (ʾustāð, 'master, teacher, professor')—an early borrowing from Middle Persian ostād ('master craftsman, teacher')—with the 2nd-person masculine singular possessive suffix -ak ('your'). Wait: because it includes the bound pronoun, it denotes 'your male teacher' in Jordanian speech.

أسفل.etymology: Formed on the elative pattern أَفْعَل (ʾafʿal) from the root س-ف-ل (s-f-l, lowness, bottom, or descent). Functioning syntactically as a locative noun and semi-preposition in construct phrases, it remains common in Jordanian Arabic alongside colloquial تحت.

أسوأ.etymology: Elative adjective أَسْوَأ (ʾaswaʾ, 'worse, worst') on the pattern أَفْعَل from سَاءَ (sāʾa, 'to be bad, evil'), root س-و-ء (s-w-ʾ).

أسود.etymology: Primary color adjective on the pattern أَفْعَل (ʾafʿal, feminine سَوْدَاء sawdāʾ) from the hollow root س-و-د (s-w-d, blackness, darkness, chieftainship). Used identically in Modern Standard and spoken Jordanian Arabic, أسود describes black objects, coffee, or hair.

أشرف.etymology: Form IV verb أَشْرَفَ (ʾašrafa, 'to look down from an elevation; oversee, supervise') from شَرَف (šaraf, 'high ground, eminence'), root ش-ر-ف (š-r-f).

أشوفكم.etymology: Colloquial Levantine 1st-person singular subjunctive/cohortative verb (أَشُوف) on the hollow root ش-و-ف (š-w-f, to look, see, originally 'to polish or look down from a height'), suffixed with the 2nd-person plural object pronoun -kum ('you all'). It serves as a warm Jordanian farewell ('see you').

history.meaning: let me see you / see you all

أشياء.etymology: Irregular diptote broken plural of شَيْء (šayʾ, 'thing') on the root ش-ي-أ (š-y-ʾ, to will, something willed into existence). Widely retained in educated Jordanian speech alongside colloquial إشي / أغراض, أشياء refers to tangible items or abstract matters.

أشّر.etymology: Form II verb أَشَّرَ (ʾaššara, 'to make a sign, point, wave, mark') from the root ء-ش-ر (ʾ-š-r, 'marking, pointing, gesturing').

أصبح.etymology: Form IV verb أَصْبَحَ (ʾaṣbaḥa, 'to enter upon the morning; wake at dawn; become') derived from صُبْح (ṣubḥ, 'morning, daybreak'), root ص-ب-ح (ṣ-b-ḥ).

history.meaning: to enter morning; wake in the morning; become

أصدقاء.etymology: Diptote broken plural on the pattern أَفْعِلَاء (ʾafʿilāʾ) of صَدِيق (ṣadīq, 'true friend'), derived from the root ص-د-ق (ṣ-d-q, truth, sincerity, loyalty). Standard in educated Jordanian conversation alongside colloquial صحاب, it emphasizes genuine friendship.

أصغر.etymology: Elative adjective أَصْغَر (ʾaṣġar, 'smaller, smallest; younger, youngest') on the pattern أَفْعَل from صَغُرَ (ṣaġura, 'to be small'), root ص-غ-ر (ṣ-ġ-r).

أصفر.etymology: Primary colour adjective on the pattern أَفْعَل (afʿal, feminine صَفْرَاء > Levantine صفرا) from root ص-ف-ر (ṣ-f-r, 'yellow, golden-pale, gleaming brass').

أصل.etymology: Masculine noun on the pattern فَعْل (faʿl) from the root أ-ص-ل (ʾ-ṣ-l), denoting a tree root, foundation, or lineage. In everyday Jordanian Arabic, it covers ancestry and authenticity as well as the fixed expression من أصل ('out of a total of').

أصلا.etymology: Adverbial accusative أَصْلًا (ʾaṣlan, 'originally, fundamentally, in the first place') from أَصْل (ʾaṣl, 'root, foundation, origin'), root ء-ص-ل (ʾ-ṣ-l).

history.meaning: at root; originally; in the first place

أصلي.etymology: Relational (nisba) adjective أَصْلِيّ (ʾaṣliyy, 'original, authentic, genuine') formed from أَصْل (ʾaṣl, 'root, origin') + -ِيّ (-iyy), root ء-ص-ل.

أصيل.etymology: Adjective أَصِيل ('genuine, authentic, deep-rooted') on the pattern فَعِيل from أَصْل ('root, origin, foundation', root ء-ص-ل): literally 'firmly rooted in its true nature'.

أضاف.etymology: Form IV causative verb أَضَافَ (ʾaḍāfa, 'to add, join, append', originally 'to incline or attach one thing beside another') from the hollow root ض-ي-ف (ḍ-y-f).

أطول.etymology: Elative adjective أَطْوَل (ʾaṭwal, 'taller, longest, longer') on the pattern أَفْعَل from طَالَ (ṭāla, 'to be long, tall'), root ط-و-ل (ṭ-w-l).

أطيب.etymology: Elative (comparative/superlative) adjective on the pattern أَفْعَل (ʾafʿal) from the hollow root ط-ي-ب (ṭ-y-b, goodness, pleasantness, fragrance). While Classical Arabic uses أَطْيَب primarily for 'better' or 'more fragrant', Levantine Arabic favors طيب for 'tasty', making أطيب the quintessential compliment for food.

أعاد.etymology: Form IV causative verb built on the hollow root ع-و-د meaning to return, shifting the sense to bringing back or repeating an action.

أعطى.etymology: Form IV verb أَعْطَى (ʾaʿṭā, 'to give, grant, hand over') from the root ع-ط-و (ʿ-ṭ-w, 'to reach for, take in the hand, offer').

أغرب.etymology: Elative adjective أَغْرَب (ʾaġrab, 'stranger, strangest') on the pattern أَفْعَل from غَرِيب (ġarīb, 'strange, unfamiliar, foreign'), root غ-ر-ب (ġ-r-b).

أغلب.etymology: Elative adjective أَغْلَب (ʾaġlab, 'predominant, most, majority') on the pattern أَفْعَل from غَلَبَ (ġalaba, 'to prevail, overcome'), root غ-ل-ب (ġ-l-b).

أغنية.etymology: Derived on the pattern أُفْعولة (ufʿūla) from the root غ-ن-ي (gh-n-y), whose Form II verb غَنَّى (ghannā) means 'to sing, chant melodiously'.

أقدم.etymology: Constructed on the elative pattern af'al from the root ق-د-م denoting antiquity, precedence, and oldness.

أقرأ.etymology: First-person singular imperfect/subjunctive verb (أَفْعَل) from the triliteral root ق-ر-أ (q-r-ʾ, to recite, gather, read), cognate with Syriac qərā and Hebrew קָרָא. In Jordanian Arabic, أقرأ appears after modal words like بدي ('I want to read') or بحب ('I like to read').

أقل.etymology: Elative adjective أَقَلّ (ʾaqall, 'less, fewer, least') on the pattern أَفْعَل from the geminate root ق-ل-ل (q-l-l, 'to be few, small in quantity').

أكتر.etymology: Levantine reflex (with regular shift of interdental ث ṯ to stop ت t) of Classical Arabic أَكْثَر (ʾakṯar, 'more, most'), elative of كَثِير (kaṯīr, 'many, much'), root ك-ث-ر.

أكل.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *ʾakal- ('to eat, consume'), one of the most conserved primary verbs across all Semitic languages (root ء-ك-ل).

أكيد.etymology: Qualitative adjective on the pattern فَعِيل (faʿīl) from the root أ-ك-د (ʾ-k-d, to confirm, make firm, assure), itself an orthographic variant of earlier و-ك-د (w-k-d). Functioning both adjectivally ('certain') and adverbially ('definitely / of course'), أكيد is constant in Jordanian conversation.

أكْل.etymology: Primary verbal noun (maṣdar) on the pattern فَعْل (faʿl) from the pan-Semitic root أ-ك-ل (ʾ-k-l, to eat or consume), cognate with Hebrew אָכַל and Aramaic ʾăḵal. In spoken Jordanian Arabic, it serves as the everyday collective noun for 'food' and 'meals'.

ألف.etymology: Inherited across Classical and colloquial Arabic from Proto-Semitic *ʾalp- ('one thousand'), root ء-ل-ف (ʾ-l-f), originally tied in Northwest and Central Semitic to 'ox / herd / large clan division' (whence also the first letter of the Phoenician/Arabic alphabet, ألف).
ألف.notes: Used hyperbolically across Arabic greetings and idioms: ألف مبروك! ('a thousand congratulations!'), قلتلك ألف مرة ('I told you a thousand times'), and بحسب إلها ألف حساب.

ألقى.etymology: Form IV verb أَلْقَى (ʾalqā, 'to cast, throw, direct [a glance or speech]') from the root ل-ق-ي (l-q-y, 'to meet, encounter, place before').

ألو.etymology: Standard telephone greeting أَلُو (ʾalō), borrowed via French allô from English hallo / hello in the late 19th-century spread of telephony.

أم.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *ʾimm- ('mother'), an ancient nursery and kinship noun universal across the Semitic family (root ء-م-م).

أمامي.etymology: Relational (nisba) adjective أَمَامِيّ (ʾamāmiyy, 'front, forward, anterior') formed from أَمَام (ʾamāma, 'in front of'), root ء-م-م (ʾ-m-m, 'to go before, lead').

أمان.etymology: Verbal/abstract noun أَمَان (ʾamān, 'safety, security, protection, peace of mind') from أَمِنَ (ʾamina, 'to be safe'), root ء-م-ن (ʾ-m-n).

أمانة.etymology: Noun أَمَانَة (ʾamāna, 'trustworthiness; something entrusted for safekeeping; civic municipality') from أَمُنَ (ʾamuna, 'to be faithful, trustworthy'), root ء-م-ن.

history.meaning: trust; deposit held in safekeeping; stewardship

أمر.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *ʾamār- ('to say, command, make known'), yielding Classical Arabic أَمْر (ʾamr, 'command, order; matter, affair'), root ء-م-ر.

أمين.etymology: Stative adjective on the pattern فَعِيل (faʿīl) from the root أ-م-ن (ʾ-m-n, safety, trust, faithfulness), sharing its Semitic heritage with the root of 'amen'. In Jordanian Arabic, أمين describes both trustworthy people and safe, secure custody.

أنا.etymology: Ancient pan-Semitic 1st-person singular independent pronoun descended from Proto-Semitic *ʾanā, cognate with Hebrew אֲנִי (ʾănī), Aramaic ʾănā, and Akkadian anāku. Preserved almost unchanged across every Arabic register, أنا marks speaker emphasis or nominal sentences in Jordan.

أنجز.etymology: Form IV causative verb أَنْجَزَ (ʾanjaza, 'to bring to completion, accomplish, fulfil') on the pattern أَفْعَلَ (ʾafʿala) from the root ن-ج-ز (n-j-z, 'to conclude, carry out, be complete'). Originally linked in Classical Arabic to fulfilling a promise or finishing an expedition cleanly.

history.meaning: to be concluded -> to accomplish, execute

أنف.etymology: Ancient Proto-Semitic body-part noun أَنْف ('nose; proud promontory') from `*ʾanp-`, preserving the original medial `-n-` that assimilated to `-pp-` in Northwest Semitic.

أنقذ.etymology: Form IV causative verb أَنْقَذَ (ʾanqaḏa, 'to rescue, save, deliver from danger') from نَقَذَ (naqaḏa, 'to escape, be safe'), root ن-ق-ذ (n-q-ḏ).

أها.etymology: Spontaneous vocalic exclamation common across Levantine dialects, closely aligned with آها and widespread Semitic affirmative particles.

أهدى.etymology: Levantine elative أَهْدَى (ʾahdā, 'quieter, calmer, calmest') from Classical أَهْدَأ (ʾahdaʾ) via regular loss of final glottal stop, from هَدَأَ (hadaʾa, 'to be calm, quiet'), root ه-د-ء.

أهل.etymology: From Classical Arabic أَهْل (ʾahl, 'kin, household, people of a place, worthy inhabitants'), inherited from Proto-Semitic *ʾahl- ('tent, household, family', cognate with Hebrew ʾōhel 'tent').

أهلا.etymology: Accusative greeting أَهْلًا (ʾahlan, 'welcome!, hello!'), elliptically shortened from the classical hospitality formula حَلَلْتَ أَهْلًا وَنَزَلْتَ سَهْلًا ('you have come among family and stepped onto smooth ground'), from أَهْل ('family, kin', root ء-ه-ل).

أهلاً.etymology: Elliptical accusative greeting from أَهْل (ʾahl, family, kin, people) on the root أ-ه-ل (ʾ-h-l), historically short for حَلَلْتَ أَهْلاً ('you have arrived among family'). Across Jordan and the Levant, أهلاً (often paired with وسهلاً) is the warm standard welcome.

أهم.etymology: Elative (comparative/superlative) adjective أَهَمّ (ʾahamm, underlying *ʾahmamu with regular geminate contraction) on the pattern أَفْعَل (ʾafʿal) from the geminate root ه-م-م (h-m-m, verb هَمَّ hamma, 'to concern, weigh on the mind, be of consequence').

history.meaning: to concern -> more/most pressing or important

أهم.notes: Constructed directly before an indefinite singular noun ('the most important thing': أهم إشي in Jordanian, أهم شيء in MSA) or a definite plural (أهم القيم).

أو.etymology: Coordinating conjunction أَوْ (ʾaw, 'or'), inherited from Proto-Semitic *ʾaw ('or').

أوبس.etymology: Modern conversational interjection borrowed from English oops!, used playfully after a minor slip or spill.

history.meaning: exclamation after a small mistake or spill

أوسط.etymology: Elative adjective on the pattern أَفْعَل (ʾafʿal, feminine وُسْطَى wusṭā) formed from the root و-س-ط (w-s-ṭ, center, middle, mediation). In modern Jordanian Arabic it appears in geographic, musical, and anatomical terms such as الشرق الأوسط and النغمة الوسطى.

أوطى.etymology: Elative pattern أَفْعَل (ʾafʿal) formed from the weak-final adjective وَاطِئ / واطي (wāṭiʾ / wāṭi, 'low'), from the root و-ط-ء (w-ṭ-ʾ, 'to tread down, make low or level'). In Levantine Arabic the final glottal stop disappeared completely, yielding the invariable comparative ʾawṭa ('lower, lowest').

أوعى.etymology: Grammaticalized warning particle originating from an imperative/elative of the root و-ع-ي (w-ʿ-y, to be aware, heed, pay attention), related to Classical وَعَى ('to heed'). In Jordanian and Levantine speech, أوعى (and suffixed أوعك/أوعي) functions as an urgent negative admonition ('watch out / don't ever!').

أوف.etymology: Expressive exclamation أُوف (ʾūf, 'oof!, ugh!, phew!') voicing fatigue, relief, or dismay; closely related to the Classical interjection أُفّ (ʾuff, 'fie!, ugh!').

أوكتاف.etymology: Musical terminology loanword borrowed from French octave ('interval of eight diatonic degrees'), from Latin octāva ('eighth').

history.meaning: musical interval of eight scale steps

أول.etymology: Elative-pattern ordinal أَوَّل (ʾawwal, 'first, foremost, beginning'), derived from the root أ-و-ل / و-أ-ل ('to precede, be foremost; return to origin').

أولى.etymology: Feminine elative (فُعْلَى, fuʿlā) corresponding to masculine أَوَّل (ʾawwal, 'first') from the root أ-و-ل (ʾ-w-l, precedence, beginning, returning). Used in both standard and Jordanian Arabic, أولى modifies feminine singular and non-human plural nouns ('first').

أوه.etymology: Natural expressive exclamation أُوه (ʾōh, 'oh!') marking mild surprise, sympathy, or sudden realization.

أي.etymology: Interrogative and indefinite determiner descended from Proto-Semitic *ʾayy- ('which?, what?, any', cf. Hebrew אֵי־ and Aramaic ʾay-). Appearing invariantly before singular or plural nouns in Jordanian Arabic, أي asks 'which?' or expresses 'any' in negative and conditional clauses.

أيار.etymology: Levantine and Mesopotamian solar calendar month name for May, borrowed from Aramaic/Syriac ʾIyyār (אִיָּר), itself tracing to Akkadian Ayāru ('blossoming, rosette'). Throughout Jordan, Syria, and Lebanon, أيار is the standard everyday name for the fifth month of the year.

morphemes.meaning: from Syriac ʾIyyār < Akkadian Ayāru (blossom month)

أيمتى.etymology: Levantine interrogative adverb أَيْمَتَى / إِيمْتَى (ʾēmtā, 'when?'), compounded from أَيّ (ʾayy, 'which [time]') + مَتَى (matā, 'when?', from Proto-Semitic *matay).

أيوا.etymology: Warm Levantine and Egyptian affirmative particle أَيْوَا / أَيْوَه (ʾaywa, 'yes!, that\'s right!'), contracted from the Classical oath phrase أَيْ وَاللّٰهِ (ʾay wallāhi, 'yes, by God!').

إبريق.etymology: Early borrowing into Classical Arabic from Middle Persian *ābrēz / ābrēg* ('water-pourer', from *āb* 'water' + *rēxtan* 'to pour').
إبريق.notes: Names a spouted teapot, kettle, or pitcher (plural أباريق).

إبط.etymology: Classical Arabic anatomical noun إِبْط (ʾibṭ, 'armpit, underarm'), from the Semitic root ء-ب-ط (ʾ-b-ṭ).

إجا.etymology: Levantine verb إِجَا (ʾijā, 'to come'), reshaped from Classical Arabic جَاءَ (jāʾa, root ج-ي-ء) by loss of final hamza and addition of a prosthetic initial vowel on analogy with weak-final verbs.

إحدعش.etymology: Contracted Levantine compound from Classical Arabic أحد عشر (ahada 'ashar), fusing the unit and ten into a single stressed word.

إحنا.etymology: Spoken Levantine first-person plural pronoun إِحْنَا (ʾiḥnā, 'we'), developed from Classical Arabic نَحْنُ (naḥnu, Proto-Semitic *niḥnū / *ʾanḥnū) with loss of initial n- and generalized -nā ending.

إذا.etymology: Conditional and temporal conjunction إِذَا (ʾiḏā, 'when, if'), built on the Proto-Semitic demonstrative/temporal base *ʾiḏ- ('then, when').

إذن.etymology: Verbal noun إِذْن (ʾiḏn, 'permission, leave, authorization') from أَذِنَ (ʾaḏina, 'to give ear, listen to, allow'), derived from the Semitic ear/hearing root ء-ذ-ن (ʾ-ḏ-n).

إزعاج.etymology: Form IV verbal noun (maṣdar) إِزْعَاج (ʾizʿāj, 'disturbance, bother, annoyance') of أَزْعَجَ (ʾazʿaja, 'to disturb, unsettle'), root ز-ع-ج (z-ʿ-j).

إسفنجة.etymology: Singulative noun إِسْفَنْجَة ('a sponge') from collective إِسْفَنْج, borrowed in antiquity from Greek σπόγγος / σφόγγος ('sea sponge')—the same Mediterranean source behind English 'sponge'.

cognates.meaning: cleaning sponge, from the same Greek source

إسفنجي.etymology: Nisba adjective derived by suffixing -i to إسفنج, itself borrowed into Arabic from Ancient Greek spongos via Aramaic.

إشارة.etymology: Form IV verbal noun إِشَارَة (ʾišāra, 'pointing, gesture, signal') from أَشَارَ (ʾašāra, 'to point, indicate'), built on the hollow root ش-و-ر (š-w-r, 'to show, display, counsel'). Semantically widened in modern Arabic to cover traffic signals, railway signals, and stage cues.

إشعار.etymology: Form IV verbal noun إِشْعَار (ʾišʿār, 'notification, notice, making known') from أَشْعَرَ (ʾašʿara, 'to inform, notify'), root ش-ع-ر (š-ʿ-r, 'to perceive, feel, know').

إشي.etymology: Jordanian and Palestinian spoken noun إِشِي (ʾiši, 'thing, something, anything'), evolved from Classical شَيْء (šayʾ, 'thing', root ش-ي-ء) with a prosthetic vowel and reinforced by the interrogative phrase أَيُّ شَيْءٍ ('what thing? / anything').

إصبع.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *ʾiṣbaʿ- ('finger, toe'), preserved in Classical Arabic as إِصْبَع (ʾiṣbaʿ), root ص-ب-ع (ṣ-b-ʿ).

إطار.etymology: From Classical Arabic إِطَار (ʾiṭār, 'hoop, ring, border, frame around something'), noun of instrument/enclosure on the pattern فِعَال from أَطَرَ (ʾaṭara, 'to bend around, encircle', root ء-ط-ر).

إطلالة.etymology: Form IV instance/verbal noun إِطْلَالَة (ʾiṭlāla, 'overlook, scenic view, appearance from above') from أَطَلَّ (ʾaṭalla, 'to look down upon, overlook'), root ط-ل-ل (ṭ-l-l).

history.meaning: looking out from above; view; outlook

إعادة.etymology: Form IV verbal noun إِعَادَة (ʾiʿāda, 'repeating, returning, run-through') from أَعَادَ (ʾaʿāda, 'to repeat, restore'), built on the hollow root ع-و-د (ʿ-w-d, 'to return, do again'). The compensatory ta marbuta (-a) marks the hollow Form IV masdar pattern إِفَالَة.

إعارة.etymology: Verbal noun of Form IV أعار formed on the root ع-و-ر, expressing the act of lending something temporarily.

إقامة.etymology: Feminine Form IV verbal noun (إِفْعَالَة, ʾifʿāla) from the hollow root ق-و-م (q-w-m, standing, remaining, residing), where the weak medial consonant reduces and takes the feminine marker -a. Both formal and spoken Jordanian Arabic use إقامة for a hotel stay as well as legal residency.

إل.etymology: Spoken Levantine dative/possessive preposition stem (إل- il-, hosting pronoun suffixes: إلي 'to/for me', إلك 'to/for you', إلنا 'for us', إلهم 'to them'), developed from Classical Arabic لِـ / لَـ (li- / la-, 'to, for') reinforced by a prosthetic vowel i- (influenced by إِلَى ʾilā, 'toward') to form an independent stressed syllable.

morphemes.meaning: to, for, belonging to (< Classical لِـ / إِلَى)

history.meaning: to me / to you / for us
to/for + pronoun; dative and possessive marker

rootFamily.gloss: to, for (proclitic form before nouns: للبنات)

إل.notes: Strictly Levantine/Iraqi colloquial with pronoun suffixes (MSA uses لي، لك، لنا); also expresses possession ('mine / belongs to me': هاد الكتاب إلي) and indirect objects after verbs.

إلا.etymology: Compound exception particle إِلَّا (ʾillā, 'except, unless; [in time-telling] minutes to the hour'), formed from conditional إِنْ (ʾin, 'if') + negative لَا (lā, 'not').

إلى.etymology: Directional preposition إِلَى (ʾilā, 'to, toward, until'), inherited from Proto-Semitic *ʾilay ('toward, unto').

إم.etymology: Spoken Levantine form إِمّ (ʾimm, 'mother, mum') with characteristic high front vowel i, preserving the Proto-Semitic vocalism *ʾimm- alongside Classical Arabic أُمّ (ʾumm).

إن.etymology: Classical and Levantine particle covering both conditional إِنْ (ʾin, 'if', as in إِنْ شَاءَ اللّٰهُ 'God willing') and the complementizer إِنَّ / أَنَّ ('that, indeed'), inherited from Proto-Semitic *ʾin / *ʾanna.

إنت.etymology: Levantine 2nd-person masculine singular pronoun evolved from Classical أَنْتَ (ʾanta, Proto-Semitic *ʾantā), raising the initial vowel from a- to i- and dropping the final short -a. In Jordan, إنت (ʾinte / ʾinta) contrasts in vowel with feminine إنتي (ʾinti).

إنتو.etymology: Spoken Levantine second-person plural pronoun إِنْتُو (ʾintū, 'you all'), evolved from Classical Arabic أَنْتُمْ (ʾantum, Proto-Semitic *ʾantum) with shift of the plural ending -um to -ū.

إنتي.etymology: Spoken Levantine second-person feminine singular pronoun إِنْتِي (ʾintī, 'you'), from Classical أَنْتِ (ʾanti), retaining the Proto-Semitic long final vowel *ʾantī.

إنش.etymology: Modern measurement loanword borrowed directly from English 'inch' (ultimately Old English ynce < Latin uncia 'one-twelfth part'). Treated as a masculine countable noun in Jordan, إنش is used chiefly for television screens, monitors, tires, and pipe diameters.

إنك.etymology: Clause-introducing complementizer fusing the Classical subordinating particle إِنَّ / أَنَّ (ʾinna / ʾanna, 'that, indeed') with the 2nd-person masculine singular bound pronoun -ak ('you'). In Jordanian speech, إنك introduces reported clauses whose subject is 'you (m.)'.

إنكم.etymology: Inflected complementizer combining the subordinating particle إِنَّ / أَنَّ ('that') with the 2nd-person plural enclitic pronoun -kum ('you all'). Spoken Jordanian Arabic requires pronoun attachment onto إنّ whenever a 'that'-clause begins with a pronominal subject.

إنو.etymology: Colloquial complementizer evolved from Classical Arabic أَنَّهُ / إِنَّهُ (ʾannahu / ʾinnahu, 'that it is'), combining the subordinating particle إِنَّ with a frozen 3rd-person masculine pronoun suffix. In Jordanian Arabic, إنو serves as the default invariable conjunction 'that' before all clauses.

إي.etymology: Classical and Levantine affirmative particle إِي (ʾī, 'yes, yea, indeed'), attested in Classical Arabic before oaths (إِي وَرَبِّي 'yes, by my Lord') and used standalone in everyday Levantine speech.

إيا.etymology: Ancient Semitic pronominal object carrier إِيَّا (ʾiyyā-), cognate with Hebrew אֶת־ (ʾēt-) and Aramaic yāṯ, which never stands bare and always carries a bound pronoun suffix. Jordanian Arabic retains إيا- extensively whenever a verb takes two object pronouns, as in أعطيك إياها.

history.meaning: object pronoun carrier after double-object verbs

إيانا.etymology: Detached accusative pronoun combining the ancient Semitic object-carrier إِيَّا- (ʾiyyā-) with the 1st-person plural suffix -nā ('us'). In Jordanian speech it survives both in elevated double-object constructions and in traditional blessings paired with وإياكم.

إياه.etymology: Detached direct-object pronoun إِيَّاهُ (ʾiyyāhu, 'him, it'), composed of the pronominal object base إِيَّا- (ʾiyyā-) + third-person masculine singular suffix -هُ (-hu).

إيجار.etymology: Form IV verbal noun إِيجَار (ʾījār < *ʾiʾjār, 'rent, lease, letting out') from آجَرَ (ʾājara, 'to let for hire'), root ء-ج-ر (ʾ-j-r).

إيد.etymology: Spoken Levantine noun إِيد (ʾīd, 'hand, handle'), reshaped with a long stem vowel from Classical Arabic يَد (yad, Proto-Semitic *yad-) by leveling from the dual/broken-plural stem أَيْدٍ (ʾaydin).

إيقاع.etymology: Form IV verbal noun إِيقَاع ('rhythm, cadence') from the root و-ق-ع ('fall, land in beats'): literally 'letting beats fall in measured time', established since al-Kindi and al-Farabi as the core Arabic term for musical rhythm.

إيمتى.etymology: Levantine interrogative adverb إِيمْتَى (ʾēmtā, 'when?'), compounded from أَيّ (ʾayy, 'which [time]') + مَتَى (matā, 'when?', from Proto-Semitic *matay).

ابتسامة.etymology: Feminine Form VIII verbal noun (اِفْتِعَالَة, iftiʿāla) derived from the triliteral root ب-س-م (b-s-m, to smile gently without laughing aloud). Unlike ضحكة ('laugh'), ابتسامة preserves the Classical semantic nuance of a quiet, warm smile in everyday Levantine speech.

ابتسم.etymology: Form VIII verb اِبْتَسَمَ (ibtasama, 'to smile') from بَسَمَ (basama, 'to part the lips in a gentle smile'), root ب-س-م (b-s-m).

ابن.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *bin- ('son'), with a prosthetic vowel in Classical Arabic اِبْن (ibn), root ب-ن-ي (b-n-y, 'to build').

اتبع.etymology: Form VIII reflexive-transitive verb built on the root ت-ب-ع (to follow), with assimilation of the root taa' into the infix -t-.

اتجاه.etymology: Form VIII verbal noun اِتِّجَاه (ittijāh, 'facing toward, direction, orientation'), from اِتَّجَهَ (ittajaha < *iwtajaha) from وَجْه (wajh, 'face, front'), root و-ج-ه (w-j-h).

اتسكّر.etymology: Colloquial Levantine Form V passive/reflexive verb it-sakkar ('to close itself, be locked up, shut for the day') formed by prefixing the spoken reflexive marker it- (Classical ta-) onto Form II سكّر ('to close, bolt'). The root س-ك-ر (s-k-r, 'to dam, block, shut') traces back to Semitic roots for stopping up water channels.

اتصل.etymology: Form VIII verb اِتَّصَلَ (ittaṣala < *iwtaṣala, 'to be joined, connected; get in touch, telephone') with assimilation of initial w- to -t-, from وَصَلَ (waṣala, 'to join, arrive'), root و-ص-ل.

اتطلّع.etymology: Levantine Form V reflex of تَطَلَّعَ (taṭallaʿa) from the root ط-ل-ع (ṭ-l-ʿ, to rise, appear, look out), where the initial prefix ta- assimilates to it- (اِتْـ) in spoken Arabic. In Jordan, اتطلّع is the standard verb for looking attentively or gazing at something.

history.meaning: to gaze intently, look out at

اتفاق.etymology: Form VIII verbal noun (maṣdar) اِتِّفَاق (ittifāq, 'coming into harmony, agreement, deal') of اِتَّفَقَ (ittafaqa, underlying *iwtafaqa, with regular total assimilation of initial radical و to the Form VIII infix -t- -> -tt-), from the root و-ف-ق (w-f-q, 'suitability, concord').

morphemes.meaning: Form VIII reciprocal verbal noun (*iwtifāq > ittifāq)

اتفاق.notes: Watch the disguised root: learners looking up اتفاق or اتفق must look under و-ف-ق (not ا-ت-ف), because the original و assimilated into the doubled تّ!

اتفق.etymology: Form VIII verb اِتَّفَقَ (ittafaqa < *iwtafaqa, 'to agree, concur, come to an accord') from وَفِقَ (wafiqa, 'to be fitting, harmonious'), root و-ف-ق (w-f-q).

history.meaning: to agree; come to an agreement

اتلغى.etymology: Spoken Levantine mediopassive Form VII/VIII-style verb (اتْفَعَلَ) built from لَغَى / أَلْغَى on the defective root ل-غ-و (l-ġ-w, idle talk, nullification, cancelling). While Classical Arabic prefers أُلْغِيَ, colloquial Jordanian systematically forms passives with the prefix it-/in-, yielding اتلغى.

morphemes.meaning: Levantine passive prefix it- + weak-final stem

اتنعش.etymology: Spoken Levantine compound numeral اِتْنَعْش (itnaʿš, 'twelve'), contracted from Classical اِثْنَا عَشَرَ (iṯnā ʿašara, 'two-teen') with regular shift of interdental ṯ to t.

اثنين.etymology: Oblique dual numeral stem built on the pan-Semitic root ث-ن-ي (θ-n-y, to fold, double, repeat), descended from Classical اِثْنَيْنِ (iθnayni, oblique of iθnāni). Levantine dialects generalized the oblique -ēn ending and typically pronounce the initial consonant as /t/ (tnēn).

اجتمع.etymology: Form VIII reflexive-reciprocal verb (اِفْتَعَلَ, iftaʿala) from the root ج-م-ع (j-m-ʿ, gathering, assembling, uniting). Passing straight from Classical Arabic into modern spoken Jordanian, it denotes both informal family gatherings and formal meetings.

احتاج.etymology: Form VIII verb (افتعل) from the root ح-و-ج (h-w-j), associated with need, want, and necessity.
احتاج.notes: In everyday Jordanian conversation, speakers often use the active participle محتاج ('needing, in need of') alongside بده.

history.meaning: to need, want, be in need of

احترم.etymology: Form VIII verb اِحْتَرَمَ (iḥtarama, 'to revere, honor, respect') derived from the Semitic root ح-ر-م (ḥ-r-m, 'sacredness, inviolability').

احتفل.etymology: Form VIII verb اِحْتَفَلَ (iḥtafala, 'to gather in a festive crowd, celebrate') from حَفَلَ (ḥafala, 'to assemble, teem'), root ح-ف-ل (ḥ-f-l).

history.meaning: to assemble in a crowd; celebrate

احتياط.etymology: Form VIII verbal noun اِحْتِيَاط (iḥtiyāṭ, 'precaution, safeguard; reserve, spare item') from اِحْتَاطَ (iḥtāṭa, 'to surround, guard, take precaution'), root ح-و-ط (ḥ-w-ṭ).

اختار.etymology: Form VIII verb اِخْتَارَ (iḫtāra, 'to choose, select, prefer') derived from خَيْر (ḫayr, 'good, best'), root خ-ي-ر (ḫ-y-r).

اختبار.etymology: Masdar of Form VIII اختبر on the ifti'aal pattern from the root خ-ب-ر, meaning knowledge gained through trial or experience.

اختبر.etymology: Rooted in خ-ب-ر (experience, knowledge), this Form VIII verb denotes putting something to the proof or examining it.

اختصار.etymology: Verbal noun of Form VIII اختصر built from the root خ-ص-ر, originally meaning to trim the waist or abridge a path or text.

اختيار.etymology: Form VIII verbal noun اِخْتِيَار (iḫtiyār, 'choice, selection, free will') of اِخْتَارَ (iḫtāra, 'to choose'), root خ-ي-ر (ḫ-y-r).

ادخل.etymology: Masculine singular imperative (اُفْعُلْ) of دَخَلَ ('to enter, go inside') formed from the triliteral root د-خ-ل (d-x-l, entrance, interior). Used interchangeably across formal and spoken Jordanian Arabic, ادخل often pairs with polite تفضل when welcoming guests indoors.

اذا.etymology: Conditional conjunction descended from Classical إِذَا (ʾiðā, 'when, if'), cognate with Semitic temporal-conditional *ʾið- (cf. Hebrew אָז). Written frequently without hamza in informal text, اذا (pronounced ʾiza in urban Jordanian) introduces real and likely conditions.

ارتاح.etymology: Form VIII verb اِرْتَاحَ (irtāḥa, 'to rest, relax, feel at ease') from رَاحَة (rāḥa, 'rest, ease, relief'), root ر-و-ح (r-w-ḥ, 'breeze, breath, repose').

ارتبك.etymology: Form VIII mediopassive verb اِرْتَبَكَ (irtabaka, 'to become entangled, confused, flustered') from رَبَكَ (rabaka, 'to mix, entangle'), root ر-ب-ك (r-b-k).

history.meaning: to become entangled; get flustered or confused

ارتعب.etymology: Form VIII mediopassive verb اِرْتَعَبَ (irtaʿaba, 'to be terrified, startled, panic') from رَعَبَ (raʿaba, 'to frighten, fill with dread'), root ر-ع-ب (r-ʿ-b).

history.meaning: to be frightened; panic; be startled

ارتفع.etymology: Form VIII mediopassive verb اِرْتَفَعَ (irtafaʿa, 'to rise, ascend, increase in height or level') from رَفَعَ (rafaʿa, 'to lift, raise'), root ر-ف-ع (r-f-ʿ).

history.meaning: to rise; be raised; go up

ارجع.etymology: Masculine singular imperative (اِفْعِلْ) of رَجَعَ ('to return, go back') on the root ر-ج-ع (r-j-ʿ, returning, reverting). In everyday Jordanian speech, ارجع commands someone to come back physically or repeat an action.

ارجعوا.etymology: Plural imperative (اِفْعِلُوا) of رَجَعَ ('to return') on the root ر-ج-ع (r-j-ʿ), adding the masculine/common plural suffix -ū (-وا) with silent orthographic alif al-wiqāya. Jordanian speakers use ارجعوا to tell a group to return or step back.

ارفعي.etymology: Feminine singular imperative (اِفْعَلِي) of رَفَعَ ('to raise, lift up') from the triliteral root ر-ف-ع (r-f-ʿ, elevation, lifting), marked by the 2nd-person feminine singular ending -ī (-ي). It directs a female listener to raise an object, voice, or curtain.

استأذن.etymology: Form X requestative verb اِسْتَأْذَنَ (istaʾḏana, 'to seek permission, ask leave to enter or depart') on the pattern اِسْتَفْعَلَ (istafʿala, the canonical Semitic 'seeking X' stem) built on إِذْن (ʾiḏn, 'permission, leave', tied to أُذُن, 'ear / lending an ear'), root ء-ذ-ن (ʾ-ḏ-n).

history.meaning: to ask permission; politely excuse oneself to leave

rootFamily.gloss: permission (عن إذنك = 'excuse me / by your leave')

استأذن.notes: Textbook example of Form X's requestative meaning (like استغفر 'seek forgiveness' and استفسر 'seek explanation'); polite أستأذن! alone means 'I'll take my leave now!'.

استأهل.etymology: Form X verb اِسْتَأْهَلَ (istaʾhala > spoken Levantine بستاهل bistāhal, 'to deserve, be worthy of'), denominative from أَهْل (ʾahl, 'worthy, fit for; family'), root ء-ه-ل.

history.meaning: to merit; be worthy of; deserve

استاهل.etymology: Spoken Levantine Form X verb اِسْتَاهَل (istāhal, 'to deserve, merit'), leveled from Classical اِسْتَأْهَلَ (istaʾhala, 'to deem oneself/another worthy') from أَهْل (ʾahl, 'worthy, fit'), root ء-ه-ل.

استراحة.etymology: Form X verbal noun (maṣdar) اِسْتِرَاحَة (istirāḥa, 'seeking or taking rest, break, intermission') of اِسْتَرَاحَ (istarāḥa, 'to find relief, rest'), built on the Semitic hollow root ر-و-ح (r-w-ḥ, 'breeze, breath, spaciousness, ease').
استراحة.notes: In Jordanian schools, الاستراحة (alongside الفرصة) is school recess/break time, while تاخدي استراحة means 'take a breather'.

استعجل.etymology: Form X verb اِسْتَعْجَلَ (istaʿjala, 'to hurry, rush, seek haste') from عَجِلَ (ʿajila, 'to hasten, be quick'), root ع-ج-ل (ʿ-j-l).

استعمل.etymology: Form X verb اِسْتَعْمَلَ (istaʿmala, 'to put to work, use, employ') from عَمِلَ (ʿamila, 'to work, make, do'), root ع-م-ل (ʿ-m-l).

history.meaning: to use; employ; put to work

استقبال.etymology: Form X verbal noun اِسْتِقْبَال (istiqbāl, 'going forward to meet; reception, welcome; front desk') from اِسْتَقْبَلَ (istaqbala), root ق-ب-ل (q-b-l).

استقبل.etymology: Form X verb اِسْتَقْبَلَ (istaqbala, 'to face, go to meet, welcome, receive guests') from the Semitic root ق-ب-ل (q-b-l, 'front; facing; accepting').

استلم.etymology: Form VIII verb اِسْتَلَمَ (istalama, 'to receive, take delivery of, take over a post'), originally in Classical Arabic 'to touch or greet the stone (سِلْم)' from root س-ل-م (s-l-m).

history.meaning: to touch; receive in hand; take charge of

استنتاج.etymology: Formed on the Form X masdar pattern istif'aal from the root ن-ت-ج (to produce, bring forth), signifying drawing out a conclusion.

استنوالسه.etymology: Fused colloquial phrase joining the plural imperative استنوا ('wait!', from Form X verb استنى on root أ-ن-ي 'to wait/take one's time') and the temporal adverb لسه ('not yet / still', contracted from لِلسَّاعَة li-s-sāʿa 'up to this hour'). Recorded without a word space, it expresses 'hold on, not yet!'.

استنى.etymology: Levantine Form X verb evolved from Classical اِسْتَأْنَى (istaʾnā, 'to take one's time, wait patiently') on the root أ-ن-ي (ʾ-n-y, patience, unhurriedness), simplifying the medial glottal stop to geminate -nn- (istanna). In Jordanian Arabic it is the everyday verb for 'to wait'.

history.meaning: to wait patiently, take one's time

استني.etymology: Feminine singular imperative of استنى ('to wait', from Classical اِسْتَأْنَى on root أ-ن-ي 'patience'), marked by the 2nd-person feminine suffix -ī (-ي). Everyday Jordanian speakers use استني when asking a woman or girl to hold on or wait.

استوديو.etymology: International cultural loanword from Italian studio ('study, artist's workshop', ultimately Latin studium), borrowed into Arabic via French and English in the twentieth century. Treated as a masculine noun in Jordanian Arabic, it refers to art/music studios as well as studio apartments.

morphemes.meaning: Italian/French/English loanword for workshop or apartment

استوعب.etymology: Form X verb اِسْتَوْعَبَ (istawʿaba, 'to take in completely, contain the whole of something; mentally absorb or comprehend') on the pattern اِسْتَفْعَلَ (istafʿala) from the initial-weak root و-ع-ب (w-ʿ-b, 'to gather wholly into a spacious container').

morphemes.meaning: Form X derivational prefix (taking in completely)

history.meaning: to contain completely, take in root and branch
to grasp mentally, process, wrap one's head around; accommodate

استوعب.notes: Preserves the radical و intact in Form X (استوعب), though in the verbal noun استيعاب (-iw- > -ī-) it vocalizes into long ي.

استوى.etymology: Doubly weak Form VIII verb (اِفْتَعَلَ) from the root س-و-ي (s-w-y, to be equal, even, mature, or complete). From the Classical sense of reaching maturity or full readiness, Jordanian Arabic developed its signature culinary meaning: 'to be cooked through' or 'to ripen'.

history.meaning: to become even, mature, thoroughly cooked
to cook through, be done (food), ripen

اسم.etymology: An ancient Proto-Semitic basic noun (*šim- 'name'), written in Arabic with an initial prosthetic vowel (همزة الوصل) before the two root consonants س-م.
اسم.notes: Cognates appear across every branch of Semitic, making اسم one of the oldest everyday words in Arabic.

اسمعوا.etymology: Plural imperative (اِفْعَلُوا) of سَمِعَ ('to hear, listen') built on the pan-Semitic root س-م-ع (s-m-ʿ, cognate with Hebrew שָׁמַע). Taking the plural ending -ū (-وا), اسمعوا is commonly used in Jordan to gather a group's attention before an announcement.

اسند.etymology: Masculine singular imperative (اُفْعُلْ / اِفْعِلْ) of سَنَدَ ('to lean against, prop up, support') on the root س-ن-د (s-n-d, support, backing). Used in practical Jordanian speech when propping up ladders, boards, or open doors.

اشتاق.etymology: Form VIII verb اِشْتَاقَ (ištāqa, 'to yearn, long for, miss someone') from شَوْق (šawq, 'longing, yearning'), root ش-و-ق (š-w-q).

اشترى.etymology: Form VIII verb اِشْتَرَى (ištarā, 'to buy, purchase') from شَرَى (šarā, 'to trade, exchange, buy/sell'), root ش-ر-ي (š-r-y).

اشتغل.etymology: Form VIII verb اِشْتَغَلَ (ištaġala, 'to be busy, work, run/operate') from شُغْل (šuġl, 'work, occupation'), root ش-غ-ل (š-ġ-l).

اشي.etymology: Colloquial Levantine masculine noun evolved from Classical شَيْء (šayʾ, 'thing') on the root ش-ي-أ (š-y-ʾ) via vowel epenthesis and glide resolution (šayʾ > ʾiši). Functioning as both 'thing' and indefinite 'something', اشي is one of the highest-frequency words in Jordanian Arabic.

اصفر.etymology: Color adjective on the pattern أَفْعَل (ʾafʿal, feminine صَفْرَاء ṣafrāʾ) built on the root ص-ف-ر (ṣ-f-r, yellowness, saffron hue, emptiness). Identical across Standard and spoken Jordanian Arabic, اصفر describes lemons, autumn leaves, and bright fabrics.

اضطر.etymology: Form VIII verb اِضْطَرَّ (iḍṭarra, 'to compel; [in passive/spoken] be forced, have to'), where the Form VIII infix -t- assimilates in emphasis to -ṭ- after root-initial ض (ḍ), from root ض-ر-ر (ḍ-r-r, 'necessity, pressure').

history.meaning: to compel; be forced or obliged to

اطمن.etymology: Spoken Levantine verb اِطَّمَّن (iṭṭamman, 'to feel reassured, check on someone'), reshaped from Classical quadriliteral Form IV اِطْمَأَنَّ (iṭmaʾanna, 'to be tranquil, calm, reassured'), root ط-م-أ-ن.

اطنعش.etymology: Spoken Levantine compound numeral اِطْنَعْش (iṭnaʿš, 'twelve'), contracted from Classical اِثْنَا عَشَرَ (iṯnā ʿašara, 'two-teen') with emphatic ṭ induced by pharyngeal ʿayn.

اطنعشر.etymology: Levantine compound numeral evolving from Classical Arabic اثنا عشر (ithnaa 'ashar), with emphatic assimilation of the t and retention of final r before nouns.

اطوي.etymology: Imperative (اِفْعِلْ / اِفْعِلِي) of طَوَى ('to fold, roll up, tuck') on the doubly weak root ط-و-ي (ṭ-w-y). In Jordanian households, اطوي is used when folding laundry, bedsheets, paper, or large maps.

اعتذر.etymology: Form VIII verb اِعْتَذَرَ (iʿtaḏara, 'to offer an excuse, apologize') from عُذْر (ʿuḏr, 'excuse, pardon'), root ع-ذ-ر (ʿ-ḏ-r).

اعتمد.etymology: Form VIII verb اِعْتَمَدَ (iʿtamada, 'to lean upon, rely on, count on') from عَمَدَ (ʿamada, 'to support, prop up with a pillar [عَمُود]'), root ع-م-د (ʿ-m-d).

history.meaning: to lean upon; rely on; depend on

افتتاح.etymology: Form VIII verbal noun اِفْتِتَاح (iftitāḥ, 'inauguration, grand opening, commencement') from اِفْتَتَحَ (iftataḥa, 'to open ceremonially'), root ف-ت-ح (f-t-ḥ).

افتح.etymology: Masculine singular imperative (اِفْعَلْ) of فَتَحَ ('to open, unlock, begin') on the pan-Semitic root ف-ت-ح (f-t-ḥ, cognate with Hebrew פָּתַח). Retaining its Classical form, افتح is used constantly in Jordan for doors, windows, jars, and shops.

افتكر.etymology: Form VIII reflexive/cognitive verb اِفْتَكَرَ (iftakara, 'to reflect inwardly, call to mind; in Levantine and Egyptian speech, to think, suppose, or remember') on the pattern اِفْتَعَلَ (iftaʿala) from the triliteral root ف-ك-ر (f-k-r, 'thought, reflection').
افتكر.notes: In conversational questions like بتفتكري سمعتنا؟ ('do you reckon/think she heard us?'), افتكر expresses tentative supposition.

اقرأي.etymology: Feminine singular imperative of قَرَأَ ('to read, recite') on the root ق-ر-أ (q-r-ʾ), keeping the alif seat for the hamza before the feminine suffix -ī (-ي) as an orthographic variant of اقرئي. Common in instructional and literary Jordanian Arabic.

اقرئي.etymology: Standard orthographic feminine singular imperative of قَرَأَ ('to read') from the root ق-ر-أ (q-r-ʾ), seating the medial hamza on a dotless yāʾ (ئ) because of the following long /ī/ vowel (-ي). It alternates in spelling with اقرأي.

اقرئيها.etymology: Composite feminine imperative combining اِقْرَئِي ('read!' f.sg., root ق-ر-أ q-r-ʾ) with the 3rd-person feminine singular direct-object pronoun -hā (-ها, 'it/her'). It commands a female listener to read a grammatically feminine noun such as رسالة or قصة.

اقلبي.etymology: Feminine singular imperative (اِفْعِلِي) of قَلَبَ ('to turn over, invert, flip') on the root ق-ل-ب (q-l-b, turning, changing, heart). Marked with the feminine ending -ī (-ي), it is used in Jordanian kitchens and daily tasks for flipping bread, pancakes, or pages.

الأبيض.etymology: Definite form combining the article الـ (al-) with أَبْيَض (ʾabyaḍ, 'white') on the hollow root ب-ي-ض (b-y-ḍ, whiteness, egg, brightness). In Jordan, الأبيض describes white Amman limestone architecture, clean linens, and bright surfaces.

الأحد.etymology: Short for يَوْم الأَحَد ('day one / the first day'), built from the Semitic numeral root ء-ح-د ('one') on the stem أَحَد. Alongside الإثنين ('Monday, day two'), الثلاثاء ('Tuesday, day three'), الأربعاء ('Wednesday, day four'), and الخميس ('Thursday, day five'), it preserves the ancient Near Eastern numbered-day week.

الأحمر.etymology: Definite color adjective prefixing الـ (al-) to أَحْمَر (ʾaḥmar, 'red') on the root ح-م-ر (ḥ-m-r, redness, ruddy complexion). Preserved uniformly from Classical Arabic across Jordanian speech, الأحمر modifies masculine definite nouns.

الأخضر.etymology: Definite masculine adjective joining the article الـ (al-) to أَخْضَر (ʾaxḍar, 'green') from the root خ-ض-ر (x-ḍ-r, greenness, lush vegetation). In Jordan it modifies fresh produce, foliage, traffic lights, and tea.

الأدلة.etymology: Definite broken plural adding الـ (al-) to أَدِلَّة (ʾadilla, pl. of دَلِيل 'proof/guide') on the geminate root د-ل-ل (d-l-l, pointing out, demonstrating). Common across formal and conversational Jordanian Arabic, الأدلة designates accumulated proofs or clues.

الأربعا.etymology: Spoken Levantine form of يَوْم الْأَرْبِعَاء (yawm al-ʾarbiʿāʾ, 'the fourth day'), derived from the Semitic numeral root ر-ب-ع (r-b-ʿ, 'four').

الأربعة.etymology: Definite numeral joining the article الـ (al-) with أَرْبَعَة (ʾarbaʿa, 'four') from the Semitic root ر-ب-ع (r-b-ʿ). Placed appositionally after a definite plural noun in Jordanian Arabic, الأربعة specifies 'the four' of that group.

الأسلوب.etymology: Definite masculine noun prefixing الـ (al-) to أُسْلُوب (ʾuslūb, 'way, manner, literary style'), derived on the pattern أُفْعُول from the root س-ل-ب (s-l-b, stripping, path, line). In Jordan, الأسلوب refers to someone's personal manner of speaking as well as artistic or writing style.

الأصلية.etymology: Definite feminine nisba adjective formed from الـ + أَصْل (ʾaṣl, root/origin) + -iyya (-ية) on the root أ-ص-ل (ʾ-ṣ-l). Widely used in Jordanian markets and offices, الأصلية distinguishes authentic goods or primary documents from imitations or copies.

الأولى.etymology: Definite feminine ordinal combining the article الـ (al-) with أُولَى (ʾūlā, feminine counterpart of أَوَّل 'first') from the root أ-و-ل (ʾ-w-l, precedence, beginning). In Jordanian Arabic it modifies definite feminine nouns like المرة الأولى ('the first time') or الدرجة الأولى.

الإبرة.etymology: Definite feminine noun prefixing الـ (al-) to إِبْرَة (ʾibra, 'needle, sting'), built on the root أ-ب-ر (ʾ-b-r, to prick, pollinate, slander). Across Jordan, الإبرة covers sewing needles, compass needles, and modern medical hypodermic injections.

الاثنين.etymology: Definite form of اِثْنَيْن ('two', root ث-ن-ي θ-n-y), meaning literally 'the second [day]' after Sunday (الأحد 'the first'). Across Jordan and the Levant, يوم الاثنين (often pronounced yōm it-tnēn) is the standard weekday name for Monday as well as 'both / the two'.

الارض.etymology: Definite form of the pan-Semitic feminine noun أَرْض (ʾarḍ, 'earth, ground, floor', cognate with Hebrew אֶרֶץ and Aramaic ʾarʿā), written here without the initial hamza seat. Grammatically feminine despite lacking -a, الارض denotes the planet, soil, land, or indoor floor in Jordanian Arabic.

الاستقبال.etymology: Definite Form X verbal noun (اِسْتِفْعَال, istifʿāl) built on the root ق-ب-ل (q-b-l, to face, meet, accept), prefixed with الـ (al-). Literally 'going out to meet someone', الاستقبال serves in Jordanian hotels, clinics, and homes for reception, welcoming guests, or a front desk.

البسكوت.etymology: Definite collective loanword prefixing الـ (al-) to بَسْكُوت (baskōt), borrowed via Italian biscotto or French biscuit ('twice-baked', from Latin bis coctus). Treated as a masculine collective noun in Jordanian Arabic, البسكوت refers to cookies, tea biscuits, and wafers.

البطاقات.etymology: Definite feminine sound plural (-āt, -ات) of بِطَاقَة (biṭāqa, 'slip of paper, card, tag'), derived from the root ب-ط-ق (b-ṭ-q) and historically tied to medieval Byzantine Greek πιττάκιον (pittákion, 'writing tablet/label'). In Jordan, البطاقات refers to postcards, ID cards, or tickets.

morphemes.meaning: slip, tag, card (early Greek pittákion contact)

history.meaning: the slips of paper, tags, cards

البطاقة.etymology: Definite feminine singular noun combining الـ (al-) with بِطَاقَة (biṭāqa, 'card, slip, label'), analyzed under root ب-ط-ق (b-ṭ-q) with medieval borrowing from Greek πιττάκιον (pittákion, 'note, tablet'). Modern Jordanian usage covers ID cards, bank cards, and greeting or postcards.

البوابة.etymology: Definite feminine intensive noun combining الـ (al-) with بَوَّابَة (bawwāba, 'large gate, portal') on the hollow root ب-و-ب (b-w-b, door, entrance, gate), itself cognate with Aramaic bāḇā. Augmenting باب ('door') via the pattern فَعَّالَة, البوابة denotes a grand entrance or campus gate.

البوصلة.etymology: Definite maritime loanword prefixing الـ (al-) to بُوصَلَة (būṣala, 'magnetic compass'), borrowed into Arabic from Italian bussola ('little box', from Late Latin buxis 'boxwood container'). Treated as feminine across Jordan, البوصلة denotes both a physical compass and a metaphorical sense of direction.

التالت.etymology: Spoken Levantine definite ordinal combining الـ (il-) with تالت (tālet), evolved from Classical ثَالِث (θāliθ, 'third') on the root ث-ل-ث (θ-l-θ, three). Reflecting the regular urban Jordanian shift of interdental /θ/ to /t/, التالت is the everyday spoken form of الثالث.

التعليق.etymology: Definite Form II verbal noun (تَفْعِيل, tafʿīl) joining الـ (al-) with تَعْلِيق (taʿlīq, 'hanging, appending, commenting') from the root ع-ل-ق (ʿ-l-q, attaching, suspending). Extending from marginal annotations hung onto a manuscript, التعليق now commonly means a spoken remark or online comment.

التعليمات.etymology: Definite feminine sound plural (-āt, -ات) of تَعْلِيم (taʿlīm, 'teaching, instruction'), Form II verbal noun on the root ع-ل-م (ʿ-l-m, knowledge, teaching). Across Jordan, التعليمات denotes official guidelines, safety directives, or product instructions.

morphemes.meaning: Form II verbal noun + feminine plural

التقى.etymology: Defective Form VIII reciprocal verb from the root ل-ق-ي (to encounter), expressing mutual meeting or intersection.

التلاتا.etymology: Spoken Levantine reflex (with regular shift of ṯ to t and loss of final hamza) of Classical يَوْمُ الثُّلَاثَاءِ (al-ṯulāṯāʾ, 'Tuesday', literally 'the third day [of the week]'), root ث-ل-ث (ṯ-l-ṯ, 'three').

التلصص.etymology: Definite Form V verbal noun (تَفَعُّل, tafaʿʿul) built from تَلَصَّصَ ('to act like a thief, lurk, spy') on the geminate root ل-ص-ص (l-ṣ-ṣ, thief/robber, traditionally linked to Greek λῃστής lēistḗs). Meaning stealthy peeking or eavesdropping, التلصص retains this vivid sense in Jordanian Arabic.

التنتيناحكيلنا.etymology: Merged textual compound joining التنتين ('two' f., from root ث-ن-ي θ-n-y with urban θ > t, used for two o'clock because ساعة is feminine) and احكيلنا ('tell us!', imperative of حكى on root ح-ك-ي + dative لـ + -نا). Resulting from an omitted space in dialogue transcription, each part remains everyday Jordanian speech.

التنين.etymology: Spoken Levantine reflex (with regular shift of ṯ to t) of Classical يَوْمُ الِاثْنَيْنِ (al-iṯnayn, 'Monday', literally 'the second day [of the week]'), from اِثْنَانِ ('two', root ث-ن-ي).

التنينالساعة.etymology: Unspaced transcription compound of التنين ('Monday', colloquial form of الاثنين from root ث-ن-ي θ-n-y with θ > t) and الساعة ('the hour / o'clock', root س-و-ع s-w-ʿ). Spoken together fluidly when scheduling days and times in Jordan.

التوت.etymology: Definite collective botanical noun combining الـ (al-) with تُوت (tūt, 'mulberry, berry'), an ancient Near Eastern/Semitic fruit term cognate with Aramaic tūṯā and Syriac tūṯē (and borrowed into Persian as tūt). In Jordan, التوت refers especially to white and black mulberries as well as berries in general.

الثالث.etymology: Standard definite ordinal combining the article الـ (al-) with ثَالِث (θāliθ, 'third') on the root ث-ل-ث (θ-l-θ, three). Retaining the classical interdental /θ/ in formal, rural Jordanian, and careful educated speech, الثالث contrasts with urban colloquial التالت.

الثانية.etymology: Definite feminine noun and ordinal formed from الـ (al-) + ثَانِيَة (θāniya, 'second [in order or time]') on the root ث-ن-ي (θ-n-y, two, second). Adapting medieval astronomical subdivisions of the hour (corresponding to Latin secunda 'second division'), الثانية means both 'the second (f.)' and 'the second (unit of time)'.

history.meaning: the second (time unit or feminine ordinal)

الثانيين.etymology: Combining the definite prefix al- with thānīyīn, this masculine sound plural adjective derives from the Classical root ث-ن-ي (th-n-y, 'to fold, double, repeat'). In Jordanian Arabic, the interdental shifts to a stop or sibilant depending on dialect while retaining its sense of 'the others'.

الثقيل.etymology: Rooted in the triconsonantal base ث-ق-ل (th-q-l, 'to be heavy, weighty'), this faʿīl-pattern adjective carries the definite prefix al-. Everyday Levantine speakers apply it literally to physical weight as well as figuratively to tedious tasks or serious personalities.

الثمانية.etymology: Formed from the Proto-Semitic numeral stem for 'eight', Classical Arabic al-thamāniya preserves the feminine-marked cardinal used for telling time and counting. Colloquial Jordanian speech frequently reduces the medial vowel to tamānye while keeping the full written form in formal contexts.

الجمعة.etymology: Meaning literally 'the gathering', al-jumʿa stems from the root ج-م-ع (j-m-ʿ, 'to gather, assemble'). Early Islamic usage replaced the pre-Islamic day name al-ʿarūba because the community convened for Friday congregational prayer, a sense preserved throughout modern Jordan.

الجوانب.etymology: Broken plural of jānib on the fawāʿil template, al-jawānib traces back to the root ج-ن-ب (j-n-b, 'side, flank'). Modern speakers in Jordan employ it both concretely for physical edges and abstractly when weighing different aspects of an issue.

الجوز.etymology: Arabic jawz ('walnut') is an early borrowing from Middle Persian gōz ('nut, walnut'), entering Classical lexicons long before Islam and later spawning botanical terms across the Levant. In Jordanian kitchens, al-jawz refers primarily to walnuts used in sweets and salads.

الجيران.etymology: Pluralized on the fiʿlān pattern from jār ('neighbor'), al-jīrān goes back to the hollow root ج-و-ر (j-w-r, 'to seek protection, dwell beside'). The underlying glide w surfaces as long ī in the plural, a regular Classical pattern still universal across Jordan.

الحجار.etymology: Broken plural al-ḥijār (from ḥajar, 'stone') descends from the Semitic root ح-ج-ر (ḥ-j-r), cognate with Aramaic ḥagrā. In Jordanian spoken Arabic, il-ḥjār is the everyday collective plural for rocks and masonry blocks, slightly shorter than the literary plural al-ḥijāra.

الحجارة.etymology: As the fiʿāla broken plural of ḥajar, al-ḥijāra builds on the Semitic root ح-ج-ر (ḥ-j-r, 'stone, rock'). It remains standard across formal prose and everyday Levantine speech alike when referring to cut building stones or piles of rubble.

الحجر.etymology: Tracing directly to Proto-Semitic *ḥigr- ('stone, enclosure'), al-ḥajar represents the faʿal singular noun of the root ح-ج-ر (ḥ-j-r). Throughout Jordan it denotes both a single rock and quarried white limestone used in architecture.

الحديدة.etymology: Singulative feminine noun formed by adding -a to ḥadīd ('iron'), itself from the root ح-د-د (ḥ-d-d, 'sharp, keen') because iron was prized for sharp blades. In colloquial Jordanian, il-ḥadīde refers to any individual piece, rod, or bar of iron.

history.meaning: a piece of iron, iron blade

الحلو.etymology: Substantivized from the root ح-ل-و (ḥ-l-w, 'to be sweet, pleasant'), al-ḥulw (colloquial il-ḥilu) functions both as the adjective 'sweet, nice' and as a collective noun meaning 'sweets, dessert'. Jordanian hosts commonly offer il-ḥilu after meals or celebratory occasions.

الحمد.etymology: Verbal noun (maṣdar) of ḥamida ('to praise, thank'), al-ḥamd comes from the root ح-م-د (ḥ-m-d), cognate with Old South Arabian and Sabaic ḥmd. Ubiquitous across the Arab world, it anchors daily Jordanian expressions like al-ḥamdu lillāh.

الحمرا.etymology: Colloquial spelling of al-ḥamrāʾ, the feminine singular color adjective built on the faʿlāʾ template from the root ح-م-ر (ḥ-m-r, 'red'). Levantine Arabic regularly drops the final glottal stop, yielding il-ḥamra as reflected in this informal orthography.

الخبز.etymology: Derived from the root خ-ب-ز (kh-b-z, 'to bake'), al-khubz is the primary Arabic noun for bread, related to Geʿez ḫəbəzt. In Jordanian Arabic il-khubiz denotes staple flatbreads such as khubz ʿarabī and shrak served with nearly every meal.

الخرايط.etymology: Orthographically reflecting Levantine pronunciation of al-kharāʾiṭ, this broken plural of kharīṭa ('map') stems from خ-ر-ط (kh-r-ṭ, 'to strip, sketch') and was semantically influenced by Greek khártēs ('sheet of papyrus'). Modern Jordanians use il-kharāyiṭ daily for paper charts and GPS apps.

morphemes.meaning: broken plural pattern with glide shift

الخشب.etymology: Collective noun al-khashab goes back to the root خ-ش-ب (kh-sh-b, 'to roughen, hew timber'), yielding singular khashaba for a single plank. Across Jordan and the wider Levant, il-khashab covers raw lumber, firewood, and wooden furniture materials.

الخميس.etymology: Short for يَوْم الْخَمِيس (yawm al-ḫamīs, 'the fifth day'), built on pattern فَعِيل from the Semitic numeral root خ-م-س (ḫ-m-s, 'five').

الخير.etymology: Built on the hollow root خ-ي-ر (kh-y-r, 'to be good, choose'), al-khayr signifies moral good, prosperity, and blessing. In Jordanian Arabic il-khēr anchors countless polite greetings such as ṣabāḥ il-khēr and wishes of abundance.

الخيط.etymology: Going back to the root خ-ي-ط (kh-y-ṭ, 'to sew, stitch'), al-khayṭ ('the thread') shares its Semitic heritage with Aramaic ḥūṭā and Hebrew ḥūṭ. Spoken Jordanian shifts the diphthong to a long vowel in il-khēṭ for sewing thread, string, or thin wire.

الذهب.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *ḏahab- ('gold'), cognate with Hebrew zāhāḇ and Aramaic dahăḇā, al-dhahab belongs to the root ذ-ه-ب (dh-h-b). In Jordanian colloquial speech the initial interdental commonly becomes a dental stop, pronounced id-dahab.

الرئيسية.etymology: Feminine nisba adjective derived from raʾīs ('chief, head'), itself built on the Semitic root ر-أ-س (r-ʾ-s, 'head'). Affixed with al- and the feminine ending -iyya, al-raʾīsiyya modifies feminine nouns across formal and spoken Jordanian Arabic to mean 'main' or 'primary'.

الرسالة.etymology: Stemming from the root ر-س-ل (r-s-l, 'to send a messenger, dispatch'), al-risāla originally meant an oral dispatch or written epistle. Today in Jordan it seamlessly covers paper letters, academic theses, and mobile text messages.

الرسمة.etymology: Instance noun (ism al-marra) of rasm on the faʿla template, al-rasma derives from ر-س-م (r-s-m, 'to trace, mark, sketch'). Whereas rasm names the act or art of drawing, il-rasme in Jordanian Arabic denotes a single concrete illustration, sketch, or diagram.

history.meaning: a single drawing, mark, or sketch

الزاهية.etymology: Feminine active participle of zahā ('to shine, flourish, glow') from the root ز-ه-و (z-h-w), al-zāhiya combines the definite article with the feminine ending -a. Both literary and Jordanian Arabic pair it with colors, flowers, and fabrics to describe vivid brightness.

الزاوية.etymology: Active-participle noun from the root ز-و-ي (z-w-y, 'to tuck away, gather into a corner'), al-zāwiya denoted both geometric angles and secluded Sufi lodges in classical usage. In Jordanian everyday speech iz-zāwye refers to room corners and street intersections.

الزوايا.etymology: Broken plural of zāwiya on the faʿāyā/faʿāʾil template, al-zawāyā traces to the root ز-و-ي (z-w-y, 'corner, recess'). Its feminine grammatical agreement reflects Arabic plural rules for non-human nouns, preserved identically across Jordanian speech.

morphemes.meaning: broken plural pattern for weak-final nouns

الزيت.etymology: Cognate with Aramaic zaytā and Hebrew zayit ('olive, olive oil'), Arabic al-zayt is a shared Northwest Semitic agricultural term from ز-ي-ت (z-y-t). In Jordan iz-zēt by default means olive oil unless another cooking oil is specified.

الساحة.etymology: Hollow-root noun from س-و-ح (s-w-ḥ, 'open courtyard, wide ground'), al-sāḥa originally named the broad open space before or within a dwelling. Modern Jordanian Arabic applies is-sāḥa to public squares, schoolyards, and political or cultural arenas.

الساحةمكتوبة.etymology: This token is an unspaced compound artifact combining the definite noun الساحة (al-sāḥa, 'the square', root س-و-ح) and the feminine passive participle مكتوبة (maktūba, 'written', root ك-ت-ب). In normal Jordanian and Standard Arabic orthography the two words are always written separately.

السبت.etymology: Borrowed early into Arabic from Hebrew shabbāṯ / Aramaic shabbəṯā ('day of rest'), al-sabt was assimilated into the native root س-ب-ت (s-b-t, 'to cease, rest'). Throughout Jordan is-sabt denotes Saturday, the start of the weekend or end of the week.

morphemes.meaning: from Aramaic shabbəṯā / Hebrew shabbāṯ ('Sabbath, rest')

السفلي.etymology: Formed by adding the nisba suffix -ī to sufl ('bottom, lowest part'), al-suflī comes from the Semitic root س-ف-ل (s-f-l, 'to be low'). In Jordanian speech speakers either keep is-suflī in architectural phrases or substitute il-taḥtānī in casual talk.

الشاب.etymology: Active participle of the geminate verb shabba ('to grow up, become youthful'), al-shābb descends from the root ش-ب-ب (sh-b-b). In Jordanian usage ish-shabb is a polite everyday word for any young man or fellow.

الشباك.etymology: Intensive pattern faʿʿāl from the root ش-ب-ك (sh-b-k, 'to interlace, weave'), al-shubbāk originally named a latticework grille or mashrabiya screen. Over centuries across the Levant, ish-shubbāk shifted seamlessly to mean any glass window.

الشتا.etymology: Colloquial spelling of al-shitāʾ with regular loss of the final glottal stop, this noun springs from the Semitic root ش-ت-و (sh-t-w, 'winter, rain'). Across Jordan ish-shita denotes both the winter season and rainfall itself.

الشجر.etymology: Collective noun al-shajar comes from the root ش-ج-ر (sh-j-r, 'to branch out, intertwine'), giving rise to singulative shajara for one tree. In Jordanian dialect ish-shajar collectively refers to trees, groves, and orchard foliage.

الشرف.etymology: Meaning originally 'elevation, high ground', al-sharaf derives from the root ش-ر-ف (sh-r-f, 'to overlook, be lofty'). Metaphorical extension into nobility, dignity, and social honor occurred already in pre-Islamic poetry and persists in polite Jordanian expressions.

الشمال.etymology: Rooted in Proto-Semitic *śimʾāl- ('left hand, north'), al-shamāl reflects ancient orientation facing the rising sun where the north lay to one's left. Colloquially in Jordan, speakers distinguish ish-shamāl ('the north') from is-shmāl ('left side').

الشمع.etymology: Derived from the root ش-م-ع (sh-m-ʿ), Arabic al-shamʿ denotes both raw beeswax and finished wax candles, with cognate forms in Aramaic shāmāʿā. Jordanian speakers pronounce it ish-shamiʿ when talking about lighting candles or wax sealing.

الصبح.etymology: Built on the triconsonantal root ص-ب-ح (ṣ-b-ḥ, 'to dawn, shine brightly'), al-ṣubḥ refers to early morning light and dawn. In Jordanian Arabic iṣ-ṣubiḥ works adverbially without a preposition to mean 'in the morning'.

الصدف.etymology: Collective noun from the root ص-د-ف (ṣ-d-f), al-ṣadaf names seashells, oyster shells, and mother-of-pearl, giving individual singulative ṣadafa. Jordanian artisans also prize iṣ-ṣadaf for traditional inlaid woodwork boxes.

الصغير.etymology: Faʿīl adjective built on the Semitic root ص-غ-ر (ṣ-gh-r, 'smallness, youth'), al-ṣaghīr parallels Hebrew ṣāʿīr ('little, young'). Spoken Jordanian regularly softens it to iṣ-ṣghīr when describing small size or a younger sibling.

الصغيرة.etymology: Attaching the feminine ending -a to al-ṣaghīr produces al-ṣaghīra from the root ص-غ-ر (ṣ-gh-r, 'small, young'). It agrees with feminine or non-human plural nouns across both Standard Arabic and Jordanian colloquial speech.

الصفيح.etymology: Stemming from the root ص-ف-ح (ṣ-f-ḥ, 'to flatten, beat thin into plates'), al-ṣafīḥ historically described flat metal slabs or broad sword blades. In modern Levantine and Jordanian usage iṣ-ṣafīḥ denotes sheet metal and tinplate.

الصيفي.etymology: Nisba relational adjective formed from ṣayf ('summer') with the suffix -ī, al-ṣayfī traces back to the hollow root ص-ي-ف (ṣ-y-f). Across Jordan iṣ-ṣēfī describes seasonal clothes, university semesters, and warm weather.

الطابق.etymology: Formed on the fāʿil template from ط-ب-ق (ṭ-b-q, 'to cover, lay one layer upon another'), al-ṭābiq originally signified a flat lid, tray, or structural layer. In urban Jordanian Arabic iṭ-ṭābiʾ/iṭ-ṭābiq is the standard noun for a building floor or story.

history.meaning: the floor, story of a building

الطاولة.etymology: Arabic ṭāwila ('table') entered via Mediterranean trade from Italian tavola (ultimately Latin tabula, 'board, plank'), later harmonized with the native root ط-و-ل ('long'). Across Jordan iṭ-ṭāwle denotes dining tables, desks, and backgammon.

morphemes.meaning: from Italian tavola / Latin tabula ('table, board')

الطرف.etymology: Going back to the root ط-ر-ف (ṭ-r-f, 'extremity, edge, tip'), al-ṭaraf designates an edge, border, or side in an agreement. Jordanian speech uses iṭ-ṭaraf both physically for table corners and figuratively for parties in a dispute.

الطعجة.etymology: Colloquial Levantine instance noun from the dialectal root ط-ع-ج (ṭ-ʿ-j, 'to bend, dent, crease'), likely an expressive or phonological variant related to عوج/طعن. In Jordanian Arabic iṭ-ṭaʿje specifically means a dent in sheet metal or a crease in paper.

الظل.etymology: Geminate noun from Proto-Semitic *ẓill- ('shadow, shade'), cognate with Hebrew ṣēl and Akkadian ṣillu, al-ẓill preserves its classical sense in both Standard and Jordanian Arabic. Colloquially in Jordan, speakers often pronounce it iẓ-ẓull or if-fayy interchangeably.

العلبة.etymology: Coming from the root ع-ل-ب (ʿ-l-b), al-ʿulba originally designated a leather-covered wooden vessel for milking camels or storing small items. In modern Jordan il-ʿilbe refers broadly to tin cans, cardboard boxes, and plastic food containers.

العيد.etymology: Adapted via Syriac ʿīdā ('feast, festival') and linked semantically to the hollow root ع-و-د (ʿ-w-d, 'to return annually'), al-ʿīd has long stood for any recurring holiday or religious feast. Across Jordan il-ʿīd refers especially to Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha.

morphemes.meaning: from Syriac ʿīdā, assimilated to root ع-و-د ('returning feast')

الغدا.etymology: Colloquial spelling of Classical al-ghadāʾ ('morning or midday meal'), derived from the root غ-د-و (gh-d-w, 'early morning'). Dropping the final glottal stop yields il-ghada in Jordanian Arabic, where it universally refers to lunch, the day's main meal.

الغرف.etymology: Broken plural of ghurfa ('upper room, chamber') on the fuʿal pattern, al-ghuraf comes from غ-ر-ف (gh-r-f, 'to scoop, elevate'). In Classical usage it meant loft chambers, whereas modern Jordanian il-ghuraf simply means any interior rooms.

الغطا.etymology: Written without the final hamza to reflect spoken Levantine il-ghaṭa, this noun comes from Classical al-ghiṭāʾ and the root غ-ط-و (gh-ṭ-w, 'to cover, conceal'). Jordanians use it for pot lids, bottle caps, and bed blankets.

الفانوس.etymology: Adopted into Arabic via Aramaic or Late Greek phānós ('torch, bright lantern'), al-fānūs became iconic across Egypt and the Levant for festive Ramadan lanterns. In Jordan il-fānūs refers to decorative lanterns as well as old oil lamps.

الفحم.etymology: Inheriting the Semitic root ف-ح-م (f-ḥ-m, 'black, charred'), cognate with Hebrew peḥām and Aramaic paḥmā, al-faḥm names charcoal and mineral coal. Across Jordan il-faḥim is indispensable for weekend barbecues and shisha preparation.

الفوقاني.etymology: Colloquial Levantine adjective attaching the -ānī suffix to the spatial adverb fawq ('above', root ف-و-ق). This productive -ānī pattern creates directional pairs in Jordanian speech such as il-fōʾānī ('the upper one') versus it-taḥtānī ('the lower one').

القديم.etymology: Faʿīl adjective from the Semitic root ق-د-م (q-d-m, 'to precede, come before in time or space'), al-qadīm parallels Hebrew qāḏūm ('ancient'). In Jordanian Arabic il-ʾadīm/il-qadīm describes anything old, vintage, or worn from use.

القديمة.etymology: Feminine counterpart of al-qadīm formed with -a on the root ق-د-م (q-d-m, 'preceding, ancient'). Both written and spoken Jordanian Arabic use il-ʾadīme/il-qadīme with feminine singulars and non-human plural nouns alike.

القصدير.etymology: Early Arabic al-qaṣdīr ('tin') was borrowed from Ancient Greek kassíteros ('tin') via trade routes, shifting k to emphatic q. While originally naming the metal tin, modern Jordanians almost universally mean kitchen aluminum foil when saying il-qaṣdīr.

القماش.etymology: Descending from the root ق-م-ش (q-m-sh, 'to gather scraps or furnishings'), al-qumāsh came in medieval Arabic to mean woven textiles and drapery goods. In Jordan il-ʾmāsh/il-qmāsh is the standard collective word for cloth and fabric.

الكتان.etymology: Borrowed into Classical Arabic from Aramaic kittānā ('linen, flax'), cognate with Akkadian kitû and ultimately Sumerian gada, al-kattān has designated both the flax plant and woven linen for millennia. Jordanians also encounter it in bizzir il-kittān ('flaxseed').

الكتب.etymology: Fuʿul broken plural of kitāb ('book'), al-kutub traces back to the root ك-ت-ب (k-t-b, 'to stitch together, write'). In Jordanian Arabic the short vowels often assimilate to il-kutub or il-kutib in rapid speech.

الكراسي.etymology: Broken plural of kursī ('chair'), al-karāsī derives from an ancient Semitic loan ultimately from Aramaic kursəyā and Sumerian gu-za ('throne, seat'), analyzed under root ك-ر-س. Today il-karāsī is universal across Jordan for all kinds of chairs and seats.

الكرت.etymology: Loaned into Levantine and Egyptian Arabic from French carte or English card (both via Latin charta), al-kart became an everyday noun across urban Jordan. Speakers use il-kart for bank cards, transit passes, business cards, and prepaid phone vouchers.

الكريمية.etymology: Modern culinary nisba adjective formed from the European loan krīmā ('cream', via French crème / Italian crema) plus the feminine ending -iyya. Restaurant menus and home cooks in Jordan regularly use il-krīmiyye to describe creamy soups, sauces, and pastries.

الكنز.etymology: Early Arabic adopted kanz ('treasure, hoard') from Middle Persian ganj ('treasury, storehouse'), integrating it into the verb kanaza ('to bury treasure'). In Jordan il-kanz appears in folktales as well as figurative praise for valuable knowledge or loyal friends.
