الكنزمين.etymology: This apparent token combines the definite noun الكنز (al-kanz, 'the treasure', originally from Middle Persian ganj) with an unclear or corrupted suffix -mīn, likely resulting from a transcription splice with مين ('who') or similar surrounding words rather than an attested Arabic lexical item.

morphemes.meaning: likely merged interrogative 'who' or transcription suffix

history.meaning: treasure (base noun prior to transcription blend)

الله.etymology: Classical contraction of the definite article الـ (al-) and إِلٰه (ʾilāh, deity), built on the ancient Semitic root أ-ل-ه (ʾ-l-h) cognate with Aramaic ʾAlāhā and Hebrew ʾElōah. Beyond its theological meaning, الله anchors countless everyday Jordanian idioms of gratitude, relief, and blessing.

history.meaning: God (core of daily blessings and exclamations)

اللوز.etymology: Shared across Semitic languages (cf. Aramaic lūzā, Hebrew lūz), al-lawz represents the collective Arabic noun for almonds from the root ل-و-ز (l-w-z). Beyond toasted almonds on mansaf, modern Jordanian youth slang uses il-lōz ('the almonds') to mean 'awesome, top-notch'.

اللي.etymology: Colloquial relative pronoun illī (also spelled اللي) developed through phonetic leveling of Classical alladhī, allatī, and alladhīna into a single invariant form across dialects. Indispensable in Jordanian Arabic, it links relative clauses regardless of gender or number.

morphemes.meaning: leveled relative element from Classical alladhī/allatī

الماطر.etymology: Active participle formed on the fāʿil pattern from م-ط-ر (m-ṭ-r, 'to rain'), al-māṭir carries the definite article al- and qualifies masculine nouns. Both weather forecasts and everyday Jordanian speech use il-māṭir for rainy days and skies.

المتقاعد.etymology: Form VI active participle of taqāʿada ('to sit back, retire from active duty') from the root ق-ع-د (q-ʿ-d, 'to sit'), al-mutaqāʿid became standard Modern Arabic for a retiree or pensioner. Jordanians employ il-mutaqāʿid both as an adjective and as a masculine noun.

المحارم.etymology: Plural of maḥrama ('kerchief, cloth'), al-maḥārim derives from the root ح-ر-م (ḥ-r-m, 'forbidden, sacred, private'), originally referring to a veiled or personal handkerchief. In Jordan today il-maḥārim almost exclusively denotes paper facial tissues and napkins.

المدهون.etymology: Passive participle built on the mafʿūl template from د-ه-ن (d-h-n, 'to anoint, oil, paint'), al-madhūn shifted from 'oiled' in classical prose to 'painted' in modern crafts. Jordanian speakers use il-madhūn for freshly painted walls, doors, or buttered pastries.

المربعة.etymology: Form II passive participle with feminine ending -a from ر-ب-ع (r-b-ʿ, 'four'), al-murabbaʿa literally means 'made four-sided'. Across Levantine and Jordanian Arabic il-mrabbaʿa describes square rooms, plates, or checked patterns.

المرتبة.etymology: Stemming from the Form II verb rattaba ('to arrange, put in order', root ر-ت-ب), the feminine passive participle al-murattaba qualifies tidy spaces, neat appearance, or well-organized people. In Jordan il-mrattabe is also a high compliment meaning classy or well-mannered.

المرسومة.etymology: Feminine passive participle of rasama ('to draw, trace') on the mafʿūla pattern, al-marsūma traces back to the root ر-س-م (r-s-m). Modern Jordanians apply il-marsūme to sketched illustrations, tattooed designs, or drawn plans.

المس.etymology: Borrowed directly from English 'Miss', il-miss entered Jordanian school culture during the twentieth century alongside bilingual instruction. Pupils across Jordan routinely address female schoolteachers as il-miss or simply miss.

history.meaning: title for an unmarried woman or female teacher

المسطح.etymology: Form II passive participle of saṭṭaḥa ('to flatten, level out') from the root س-ط-ح (s-ṭ-ḥ, 'surface, roof'), al-musaṭṭaḥ serves as an adjective meaning 'flat, planar'. Jordanians use il-msaṭṭaḥ for flat roofs, screens, and dishes.

المسطحة.etymology: Feminine singular of al-musaṭṭaḥ formed by suffixing -a onto the Form II passive participle of س-ط-ح (s-ṭ-ḥ, 'flat surface'). It agrees with feminine nouns and inanimate plurals across both Standard Arabic and Jordanian colloquial usage.

المطبخ.etymology: Noun of place (ism al-makān) on the mafʿal pattern from ط-ب-خ (ṭ-b-kh, 'to cook, slaughter'), al-maṭbakh literally means 'the place of cooking'. Its form and pronunciation il-maṭbakh remain virtually identical from Classical Arabic to everyday Jordanian speech.

المطبوعة.etymology: Rooted in ط-ب-ع (ṭ-b-ʿ, 'to stamp, impress, print'), al-maṭbūʿa is the feminine passive participle of ṭabaʿa. Originally describing stamped seals or minted coins, it evolved with the printing press into 'printed' and now covers laser-printed documents in Jordan.

المفتوحة.etymology: Built from the root ف-ت-ح (f-t-ḥ, 'to open, unlock') on the feminine passive participle pattern mafʿūla, al-maftūḥa contrasts directly with maghlūqa/msakkara. Jordanians apply il-maftūḥa both to open doors and to open-minded attitudes or open-ended invitations.

المفضل.etymology: Form II passive participle of faḍḍala ('to prefer, favor') from the root ف-ض-ل (f-ḍ-l, 'merit, excess, favor'), al-mufaḍḍal means 'the preferred, favorite'. Both Modern Standard and Jordanian Arabic pair il-mufaḍḍal with meals, colors, and pastimes.

المكتوب.etymology: Passive participle of kataba ('to write', root ك-ت-ب), al-maktūb became a standalone noun meaning 'written letter' or 'destiny, what is decreed'. In Jordanian speech il-maktūb refers warmly both to a mailed letter and to fate.

history.meaning: that which is written, letter, fate

المكتوبة.etymology: Feminine inflection of al-maktūb formed on the mafʿūla pattern from the Semitic root ك-ت-ب (k-t-b, 'to write'). In Jordan il-maktūbe describes handwritten notes, printed policies, and feminine subjects tied to writing.

الملصق.etymology: Form IV passive participle of alṣaqa ('to glue, affix') from the root ل-ص-ق (l-ṣ-q, 'to adhere, stick'), al-mulṣaq evolved in Modern Arabic into a noun for posters, labels, and adhesive stickers. In Jordan it frequently alternates with the English loan istīkar.

الملفوف.etymology: Substantivized from the passive participle of laffa ('to wrap, roll up', root ل-ف-ف), al-malfūf literally means 'the wrapped-up one' because of its tightly layered leaves. Throughout Jordan il-malfūf names both the vegetable cabbage and stuffed cabbage rolls.

المليانة.etymology: Feminine faʿlāna-pattern adjective derived from the root م-ل-أ (m-l-ʾ, 'to fill'), replacing Classical al-malʾāna by regularizing the final hamza into glide y. Across Jordanian Arabic il-malyāne is the standard everyday word for 'full'.

النجمة.etymology: Singulative feminine noun formed from the collective najm ('stars'), al-najma comes from the root ن-ج-م (n-j-m, 'to rise, appear as a celestial body'). In Jordanian Arabic in-nijme refers both to a star in the sky and a five-star rating or film star.

النحاس.etymology: Cognate with Hebrew nəḥōšeṯ and Aramaic nəḥāshā ('bronze, copper'), al-nuḥās goes back to the Semitic root ن-ح-س (n-ḥ-s). In Jordanian households in-nḥās denotes copper cookware, brass trays, and copper wiring.

النحاسية.etymology: Formed by adding the feminine nisba suffix -iyya to nuḥās ('copper, brass', root ن-ح-س), al-nuḥāsiyya describes objects cast or hammered from copper alloys. Jordanian artisans in Amman still market hand-engraved copper trays under this label.

النحل.etymology: Collective noun al-naḥl comes from the root ن-ح-ل (n-ḥ-l), whose individual singulative is naḥla ('one bee'). Throughout Jordan and the Levant in-naḥil designates honeybees collectively in beekeeping and rural sayings.

النص.etymology: Colloquial reduction of Classical al-niṣf ('the half', root ن-ص-ف), produced by dropping the final labiodental f and geminating the ṣ in everyday speech. Across Jordan in-nuṣṣ serves as both 'half' in fractions and 'the middle' of a place or time.

الهامش.etymology: Active participle noun from ه-م-ش (h-m-sh, 'to gather around the edges, bite lightly'), al-hāmish came to designate the blank margin of a manuscript page where glosses were written. Modern Jordanians use il-hāmish both for book margins and metaphorical sidelines.

الواجهة.etymology: Built on the hollow-initial root و-ج-ه (w-j-h, 'face, front') with the fāʿila template, al-wājiha names the front-facing exterior of a building or display. In contemporary Jordanian Arabic it covers stone facades, shopfronts, and software user interfaces.

الواضح.etymology: Active participle of waḍaḥa ('to become clear, plain') from the root و-ض-ح (w-ḍ-ḥ, 'clarity, brightness'), al-wāḍiḥ functions across registers as 'the clear, obvious one'. Jordanians frequently open observations with il-wāḍiḥ inno ('evidently').

الورق.etymology: Rooted in و-ر-ق (w-r-q, 'foliage, leaf'), al-waraq originally meant tree leaves before extending by analogy to sheets of papyrus, parchment, and paper. In Jordanian speech il-waraʾ/il-waraq also names grape leaves (waraʾ dawālī) and playing cards.

الورقة.etymology: Singulative feminine noun derived from collective waraq ('leaves, paper', root و-ر-ق) by appending -a. Whether referring to a single leaf on a tree, an official form, or a banknote, il-waraʾa/il-waraqa is standard across Jordan.

history.meaning: a single leaf or sheet of paper
the leaf, sheet of paper, document

الورقي.etymology: Relational nisba adjective combining waraq ('paper', root و-ر-ق) with the definite prefix al- and suffix -ī. In contemporary Jordanian usage il-waraʾī/il-waraqī contrasts print books, cash, and paper bags against digital or plastic equivalents.

الوصفة.etymology: Instance noun built from the initial-weak root و-ص-ف (w-ṣ-f, 'to describe, prescribe'), losing its initial w in the verbal noun ṣifa while preserving it in waṣfa. Jordanian speakers use il-waṣfe equally for medical prescriptions and cooking recipes.

الياسمين.etymology: Early borrowing into Arabic from Middle Persian yāsaman / yāsamīn (jasmine), prefixed with the definite article الـ (al-). Deeply woven into Levantine courtyard culture and Amman street names, it entered European languages (English 'jasmine', Spanish 'jazmín') through medieval Arabic.

اليسار.etymology: Euphemistically derived from the root ي-س-ر (y-s-r, 'ease, prosperity, auspiciousness'), al-yasār was historically adopted in Arabic to avoid ill-omened words for the left side. In everyday Jordanian Arabic il-yasār alternates with ish-shmāl when giving directions.

اليمين.etymology: Inheriting Proto-Semitic *yamīn- ('right hand, south'), cognate with Hebrew yāmīn and Akkadian imnu, al-yamīn ties the right side to blessing and oath-taking under ي-م-ن (y-m-n). Across Jordan il-yamīn serves in street directions, politics, and sworn oaths.

اليوم.etymology: Directly preserving Proto-Semitic *yawm- ('day'), cognate with Hebrew yōm and Aramaic yōmā, al-yawm contracts its diphthong to il-yōm in spoken Levantine dialects. Across Jordan it denotes both the noun 'the day' and the time adverb 'today'.

امتص.etymology: Geminate Form VIII verb constructed on the root م-ص-ص (to suck, sip), meaning to draw in liquid or scent.

امد.etymology: First-person singular imperfect verb amudd (spelled unhamzated as امد) from the geminate root م-د-د (m-d-d, 'to stretch, extend'). Used after modal auxiliaries in Jordanian Arabic, baddī amidd means 'I want to reach out' or 'lay down' (a carpet, cable, or hand).

امشوا.etymology: Plural imperative of مشى derived from the defective root م-ش-ي, retaining the classical final -uu plural marker.

انباع.etymology: Colloquial Form VII passive formed by prefixing in- to the hollow verb باع from root ب-ي-ع, replacing Classical internal passive بِيعَ.

انبسط.etymology: Form VII verb (اِنْفَعَلَ, infaʿala) from the triliteral root ب-س-ط (b-s-ṭ, to spread out, open, make cheerful). Moving from the physical idea of a face or heart opening wide with ease, انبسط became the hallmark Levantine verb for 'to be happy' or 'have a great time'.

history.meaning: to spread out, feel at ease, be cheerful
to be happy, delighted, enjoy oneself

انتباه.etymology: Form VIII verbal noun (maṣdar) اِنْتِبَاه (intibāh, 'waking up from sleep, alertness, paying heed') of اِنْتَبَهَ (intabaha, pattern اِفْتَعَلَ), built on the triliteral root ن-ب-ه (n-b-h, 'to wake, rouse, notice').

history.meaning: to awaken from sleep -> wakefulness, vigilance

انتباه.notes: Used across MSA and educated Levantine speech; begins with hamzat al-waṣl (الانتباه), while its imperative انتبه / انتبهي! means 'watch out! / pay attention!'.

انتبه.etymology: Form VIII verb اِنْتَبَهَ (intabaha, 'to wake up, become alert, notice, pay attention') from نَبِهَ (nabiha, 'to be perceptive, awake'), root ن-ب-ه (n-b-h).

history.meaning: to become alert; pay attention; watch out

انتشر.etymology: Form VIII verb (اِفْتَعَلَ, iftaʿala) formed on the root ن-ش-ر (n-š-r, to unfold, scatter, diffuse, publish). Across both Classical and Levantine Arabic, انتشر describes scents, news, people, or phenomena dispersing widely.

history.meaning: to spread out, disperse, become widespread

انتظام.etymology: Verbal noun of Form VIII انتظم built on the root ن-ظ-م (to string pearls, arrange in order).

انتقال.etymology: Masculine Form VIII verbal noun (اِفْتِعَال, iftiʿāl) from the root ن-ق-ل (n-q-l, moving, transferring, shifting from place to place). Used in modern Jordanian Arabic for physical relocation as well as musical, narrative, or career transitions.

انتهى.etymology: Form VIII mediopassive verb اِنْتَهَى (intahā, 'to reach the end, come to a close, be finished') from نَهَى (nahā, 'to reach a limit; forbid'), root ن-ه-ي (n-h-y).

history.meaning: to reach an end; finish; conclude

انتو.etymology: Levantine second-person plural independent pronoun simplified from Classical أنتم by dropping final -m and lengthening the vowel.

انتوا.etymology: Orthographic variant of انتو adding a silent alif by analogy with third-person plural verbs.

انحرق.etymology: Form VII mediopassive verb derived from the root ح-ر-ق (to burn), expressing an involuntary or spontaneous burning event.

انحط.etymology: Form VII passive/intransitive verb اِنْحَطَّ (inḥaṭṭa, 'to be put down, be placed, descend') from حَطَّ (ḥaṭṭa, 'to put down, set down'), root ح-ط-ط (ḥ-ṭ-ṭ).

history.meaning: to be set down; be placed

انحل.etymology: Form VII reflexive-passive verb اِنْحَلَّ (inḥalla) derived with the passive prefix in- from the geminate root ح-ل-ل (ḥ-l-l, 'to untie, loosen, dissolve'). Across both Classical and Levantine Arabic, it expresses either a physical knot/substance loosening in liquid or an abstract problem resolving.

انحلّ.etymology: Geminate Form VII verb (اِنْفَعَلَ, infaʿala) from the root ح-ل-ل (ḥ-l-l, to untie, loosen, dissolve, resolve). In Jordanian Arabic, انحلّ covers both concrete untying and figurative resolution of disputes or logistical snags.

انحنى.etymology: Defective Form VII verb (اِنْفَعَلَ, infaʿala) built on the root ح-ن-ي (ḥ-n-y, to bend, curve, incline). Retained across formal and educated Jordanian Arabic, انحنى describes both physical bending and bowing on stage or in respect.

انخبز.etymology: Form VII passive verb انْخَبَزَ (inḵabaza, 'to be baked') derived from خَبَزَ (ḵabaza, 'to bake bread'), root خ-ب-ز (ḵ-b-z, 'bread-making'). Form VII productively supplies everyday passives in Jordanian Arabic where Classical Arabic prefers internal vowel passives (خُبِزَ).

اندفع.etymology: Form VII verb اِنْدَفَعَ (indafaʿa, 'to rush forward; [in Levantine] to be paid') formed with the detransitivizing prefix in- from دَفَعَ (dafaʿa, 'to push; pay'), root د-ف-ع (d-f-ʿ).

history.meaning: to be pushed forward; be paid

اندمج.etymology: Form VII verb اِنْدَمَجَ (indamaja, 'to become merged, fused, or integrated') built from the triliteral root د-م-ج (d-m-j, 'to enter firmly, fit closely, combine'). In modern spoken and standard Arabic it covers both physical blending of inks or pigments and social mingling.

انساب.etymology: Hollow Form VII verb (اِنْفَعَلَ) from the root س-ي-ب (s-y-b, to flow freely, glide, run smoothly without obstruction). Literary and elevated Jordanian usage applies انساب vividly to water, light, hair, or flowing musical phrases.

انسحب.etymology: Form VII mediopassive verb اِنْسَحَبَ (insaḥaba, 'to be pulled back, withdraw, retreat') from سَحَبَ (saḥaba, 'to pull, drag, draw'), root س-ح-ب (s-ḥ-b).

انشال.etymology: Form VII passive constructed by prefixing in- to the hollow colloquial verb شال (root ش-ي-ل).

انطوى.etymology: Doubly weak Form VII verb (اِنْفَعَلَ) from the root ط-و-ي (ṭ-w-y, to fold, roll up, tuck away). Serving as the medio-passive counterpart to طوى ('to fold'), it appears in Jordanian Arabic for foldable furniture, paper, and rolled goods.

history.meaning: to be folded, rolled up, tucked in

انعقد.etymology: Form VII medio-passive اِنْعَقَدَ (inʿaqada, 'to become knotted, tied, or convened') from the root ع-ق-د (ʿ-q-d, 'to tie, bind, knot'). While formal prose uses it for meetings convening, everyday Levantine speech preserves its concrete physical sense of cords tangling into knots.

انفتح.etymology: Form VII anticausative/passive verb اِنْفَتَحَ (infataḥa, 'to come open, be opened') from فَتَحَ (fataḥa, 'to open'), root ف-ت-ح (f-t-ḥ).

history.meaning: to open by itself; be opened

انفلت.etymology: Form VII verb اِنْفَلَتَ (infalata, 'to break loose, slip free, escape') built from the triliteral root ف-ل-ت (f-l-t, 'to escape, slip out of grasp'). In Jordanian speech it describes any clip, knot, or object unexpectedly slipping away from its fastening.

انقرأ.etymology: Colloquial Levantine Form VII passive verb (اِنْفَعَلَ) built from قَرَأَ on the root ق-ر-أ (q-r-ʾ, to read or recite), replacing Classical passive قُرِئَ. In Jordanian Arabic, انقرأ expresses both eventive passive ('was read') and potentiality ('is legible/readable').

انقطع.etymology: Form VII mediopassive verb اِنْقَطَعَ (inqaṭaʿa, 'to be cut off, snap, be interrupted') from قَطَعَ (qaṭaʿa, 'to cut, sever'), root ق-ط-ع (q-ṭ-ʿ).

history.meaning: to be cut off; snap; cease

انكتب.etymology: Form VII passive verb اِنْكَتَبَ (inkataba, 'to be written, get inscribed') from كَتَبَ (kataba, 'to write'), root ك-ت-ب (k-t-b).

انكسر.etymology: Form VII anticausative/passive verb اِنْكَسَرَ (inkasara, 'to break, snap, shatter') from كَسَرَ (kasara, 'to break'), root ك-س-ر (k-s-r).

انلف.etymology: Levantine Form VII passive verb اِنْلَفّ (inlaff, 'to be wrapped, get packed or rolled') from لَفَّ (laffa, 'to wrap, fold, turn'), root ل-ف-ف (l-f-f).

انمزع.etymology: Levantine Form VII anticausative/passive verb اِنْمَزَع (inmazaʿ, 'to tear, get ripped') from مَزَعَ (mazaʿa, 'to tear, pluck, rend'), root م-ز-ع (m-z-ʿ).

اه.etymology: Informal unhamzated spelling (اه, pronounced ʾā / āh) of the Levantine affirmative particle آه ('yes, yeah'), evolved from the primary Semitic vocalic interjection آه (ʾāh, expressing acknowledgment or realization) into the standard everyday spoken affirmative across Jordan, Palestine, Syria, Lebanon, and Egypt.
اه.notes: Colloquial Jordanian register: اه is casual 'yeah' among friends and family, whereas نَعَم (naʿam) is more formal/polite (or used to say 'pardon? / yes?' when called).

اهتم.etymology: Form VIII verb اِهْتَمَّ (ihtamma, 'to be concerned, take care of, pay heed to') from هَمَّ (hamma, 'to concern, occupy the mind'), root ه-م-م (h-m-m).

history.meaning: to be concerned; care for; look after

او.etymology: Unpointed spelling of أو, the standard coordinating conjunction expressing alternation.

اوه.etymology: Expressive vocal interjection used across Jordanian Arabic to signal sudden surprise or realization.

ايدي.etymology: Colloquial Levantine noun إيد (from Classical يد, root ي-د) suffixed with the first-person possessive -i.

ب.etymology: Inseparable proclitic preposition بِـ (bi-, 'in, at, with, by'), inherited from Proto-Semitic *bi- ('in, with, by').

بأربعة.etymology: Prepositional phrase combining instrumental بـ (with, for) with the cardinal number أربعة (root ر-ب-ع).

بإبهام.etymology: Combines the preposition بـ (with) and إبهام (thumb), derived from root ب-ه-م.

بإيدي.etymology: Preposition بـ attached to إيد (hand) and the first-person singular possessive suffix -i.

باب.etymology: An ancient Semitic word for 'door, gate, entrance' (already attested in Akkadian *bābu* and Aramaic *bābā*).
باب.notes: Yields the derived feminine noun بوابة ('outer gate, portal') for the iron courtyard entrance.

بابونج.etymology: Classical Arabic botanical and medical term بَابُونَج ('chamomile'), borrowed during the Abbasid pharmacological era from Middle Persian bābūnag (modern Persian بابونه bābūneh) and treasured across Levantine households as a calming evening tea.

باربع.etymology: Attaches the preposition بـ to أربع, the shorter construct numeral used before feminine nouns.

بارد.etymology: Active participle adjective بَارِد (bārid, 'cold, cool, chilly') from بَرَدَ (barada, 'to be cold'), root ب-ر-د (b-r-d).

بارك.etymology: Form III verb بَارَكَ (bāraka, 'to bless, invoke blessing upon; congratulate'), derived from the Semitic root ب-ر-ك (b-r-k, 'blessing; kneeling').

باص.etymology: Modern transport loanword borrowed from English bus (itself clipped from Latin omnibus, 'for all').

باع.etymology: Hollow Form I verb بَاعَ (bāʿa, 'to sell, strike a bargain') from the root ب-ي-ع (b-y-ʿ), originally referring to stretching out the arm (بَاع) to clasp hands when sealing a commercial transaction.

باقي.etymology: Active participle بَاقٍ / البَاقِي (bāqī, 'remaining; the rest, the remainder, monetary change') from بَقِيَ (baqiya, 'to remain, stay'), root ب-ق-ي (b-q-y).

بال.etymology: Classical and Levantine noun بَال (bāl, 'mind, attention, heart, state'), used in core idioms such as دير بالك ('take care') and طول بالك ('be patient'), root ب-و-ل (b-w-l).

بالإيد.etymology: Fuses prepositional بـ, definite article الـ, and the colloquial noun إيد (hand).

بالتساوي.etymology: Adverbial compound uniting بـ with the definite Form VI masdar التساوي (root س-و-ي).

بالجامعة.etymology: Locative phrase linking بـ (at, in) to الجامعة (university, from root ج-م-ع meaning to gather).

بالحبر.etymology: Prepositional combination of بـ (in, with) and definite الحبر (ink, root ح-ب-ر).

بالدرجة.etymology: Joins preposition بـ with definite الدرجة (degree, rank, step, from root د-ر-ج).

بالرسم.etymology: Unites بـ (in, at) with the definite noun الرسم (drawing, from root ر-س-م).

بالزاوية.etymology: Locative phrase pairing بـ (in, at) with definite الزاوية (corner, angle, root ز-و-ي).

بالزبط.etymology: Spoken Levantine adverb بِالزَّبْط (bi-z-zabṭ, 'exactly, spot-on'), reflecting the urban/sibilant pronunciation of Classical بِالضَّبْطِ (bi-l-ḍabṭ, 'with precision'), from ضَبَطَ ('to hold fast, regulate accurately', root ض-ب-ط).

بالساحة.etymology: Combines locative بـ with definite الساحة (courtyard, square, root س-و-ح).

بالشمع.etymology: Pairs instrumental بـ (with) with definite الشمع (wax, candle, root ش-م-ع).

بالضبط.etymology: Standard adverbial phrase pairing بـ with definite الضبط (precision, root ض-ب-ط), also spelled بالزبط.

بالعلبة.etymology: Locative expression merging بـ (in) with definite العلبة (box, tin, root ع-ل-ب).

بالغلط.etymology: Manner adverb combining بـ (by) and definite الغلط (mistake, error, root غ-ل-ط).

بالفحم.etymology: Instrumental phrase uniting بـ (with) and definite الفحم (charcoal, root ف-ح-م).

بالك.etymology: Noun بال (mind, attention, from hollow root ب-و-ل) plus the 2ms possessive suffix -ak.

باللوبي.etymology: Hybrid expression joining the Arabic preposition بـ and definite الـ to the English loanword lobby.

بالمرة.etymology: Colloquial adverbial phrase composed of preposition بـ (bi-, 'by/in') + definite noun المَرَّة (al-marra, 'the time/once', root م-ر-ر), developing the sense 'at one go, completely, (not) at all'.

بالنص.etymology: Levantine adverbial phrase uniting بـ (in) with definite النص, shortened from Classical النصف (root ن-ص-ف).

بامان.etymology: Adverbial expression combining بـ (with, in) with أمان (safety, peace, root أ-م-ن).

بان.etymology: Hollow Form I verb بَانَ (bāna, 'to become clear, appear, stand out'), built on the root ب-ي-ن (b-y-n, 'separation, clarity, interval'). In Levantine Arabic it functions widely as a stative verb meaning 'to look, seem, show up' (بيبان حلو 'it looks nice').

باهت.etymology: Active participle from the root ب-ه-ت meaning to fade, grow dim, or lose brightness.

بايد.etymology: Preposition بـ prefixed to إيد (hand, handle), the Levantine reflex of Classical يد.

بايديكي.etymology: Combines بـ (with), dual إيدين (hands), and the 2fs possessive suffix -ki.

ببطء.etymology: Manner adverbial linking بـ (with) to the noun بطء (slowness, root ب-ط-أ).

ببلاش.etymology: Levantine and Egyptian adverb بِبَلَاش (bi-balāš, 'for free, at no cost'), contracted from بِـ (bi-, 'with/for') + بِلَا شَيْءٍ (bilā šayʾin, 'without anything, for nothing').

ببين.etymology: Present-tense verb prefixing the Levantine b- marker to يبيّن (to appear, seem, root ب-ي-ن).

بتأشر.etymology: Present continuous form attaching bit- (2ms/3fs) to Form II أشّر (to point, signal, root أ-ش-ر).

بتبلش.etymology: Levantine 3fs/2ms present verb with bit- prefixed to بلّش (to start, likely from Aramaic/Syriac roots).

بترخي.etymology: Levantine b-imperfect 3fs/2ms verb from رخي (root ر-خ-و, to slacken or soften).

بتشبه.etymology: Present indicative verb pairing بتـ (3fs/2ms) with شبه (root ش-ب-ه, likeness).

بتصب.etymology: Geminate Form I verb صبّ (root ص-ب-ب) inflected for 3fs/2ms present with بتـ.

بتعرف.etymology: Core Jordanian present form from عرف (root ع-ر-ف, to know) with prefix بتـ.

بتفتح.etymology: Imperfect Form I verb built on فتح (root ف-ت-ح, to open) carrying indicative بتـ.

بتلف.etymology: Geminate root ل-ف-ف (to turn, wrap) in 2ms/3fs Levantine present tense with بتـ.

بتولا.etymology: Modern Arabic botanical borrowing بَتُولا (batūlā) from Latin betula ('birch tree'), itself of Gaulish Celtic origin (*betw-). Adopted into Arabic woodworking and botanical terminology for pale northern birch timber.

بثانية.etymology: Temporal prepositional phrase merging بـ (in) with ثانية (second, root ث-ن-ي).

بجراب.etymology: Dialectal phrase linking بـ (in) to جراب (sock, pouch, ultimately Persian/Classical جُورَب).

بجعة.etymology: Singulative noun بَجَعَة (bajaʿa, 'swan; pelican') formed with the suffix -ة (-a) from the Classical collective بَجَع (bajaʿ, 'pelicans, large waterbirds'), root ب-ج-ع (b-j-ʿ).

بجيبي.etymology: Possessive phrase uniting بـ (in), جيب (pocket, root ج-ي-ب), and 1sg -i.

بحبر.etymology: Instrumental expression combining بـ (with, in) and حبر (ink, root ح-ب-ر).

بحتاج.etymology: Indicative Form VIII verb from احتاج (hollow root ح-و-ج, need) with present بـ.

بحث.etymology: Masdar and noun of action from the triliteral root ب-ح-ث, originally meaning to scratch or dig the earth in search of something.

بحر.etymology: Classical Arabic noun بَحْر ('sea, great river', plural بِحَار / بُحُور) from the Semitic root ب-ح-ر ('wide cleft expanse of water'), used metaphorically in classical poetry for boundless generosity and for poetic meters.

بحري.etymology: Nisba relational adjective بَحْرِيّ (baḥriyy) derived with the suffix -iyy from بَحْر (baḥr, 'sea'), root ب-ح-ر (b-ḥ-r). The adverbial accusative بَحْرِيًّا (baḥriyyan) adds the -an ending to mean 'nautically' or 'marinely'.

بحطها.etymology: Compound verb form uniting بحط (I/he puts, root ح-ط-ط) and 3fs object suffix -ha.

بخار.etymology: Masculine noun on the pattern فُعَال (fuʿāl) from the root ب-خ-ر (b-x-r, vapor, mist, incense). Both Classical and everyday Jordanian Arabic use بخار for steam from cooking pots, bathwater, or garment steamers.

بخفة.etymology: Manner adverb combining بـ (with) and خفة (lightness, agility, root خ-ف-ف).

بخيط.etymology: Prepositional combination of بـ (with) and خيط (thread, string, root خ-ي-ط).

بد.etymology: Signature Levantine modal pseudo-verb grammaticalized from Classical بِوُدِّ (bi-wuddi, 'in the wish/desire of'), derived from the geminate root و-د-د (w-d-d, love, wish, desire). Rather than taking verbal prefixes, بد takes pronominal suffixes (بدي، بدك، بده) to express 'want' or 'need'.

history.meaning: in the wish of, by desire of
to want, need, be about to

بدأ.etymology: Form I verb بَدَأَ (badaʾa, 'to begin, start, originate'), from the Semitic root ب-د-ء (b-d-ʾ, 'beginning, first doing').

بداية.etymology: Noun بِدَايَة ('beginning, opening') from the root ب-د-ء / ب-د-ي ('begin, start first'), paired naturally with نِهَايَة ('ending').

بدري.etymology: Classical adverbial derived from root ب-د-ر (to hasten, come early), everyday in Jordanian.

بدل.etymology: Noun and preposition بَدَل (badal, 'substitute, replacement; instead of, in place of') from بَدَلَ (badala, 'to exchange, replace'), root ب-د-ل (b-d-l).

بده.etymology: Signature Levantine volitional pseudo-verb بِدُّه (biddo, 'he wants, needs'; 1sg بِدِّي biddī), grammaticalized and contracted from Classical Arabic بِوُدِّهِ (bi-wuddihi, 'in his wish/desire'), from وُدّ ('love, wish, desire', root و-د-د).

history.meaning: in his wish; by his desire

بدهم.etymology: Volitional pseudo-verb fusing بدّ (wish, root و-د-د) with the 3pl suffix -hum.

بدون.etymology: Privative preposition merging بـ (with) and دون (aside from, short of, root د-و-ن).

بدي.etymology: Colloquial Levantine reflex of Classical Arabic بدأ (bada'a) from root ب-د-أ, in which the final glottal stop weakened and shifted the stem into the defective pattern.

بدّل.etymology: Form II verb بَدَّلَ (baddala, 'to exchange, alternate, replace') on the intensive-causative pattern فَعَّلَ (faʿʿala) from the root ب-د-ل (b-d-l, 'substitute, exchange'). In everyday Jordanian Arabic it serves both for changing clothes and alternating items in sequence.

برا.etymology: Spatial adverb descended from برّا (outside, root ب-ر-ر denoting open desert or outside).

برافو.etymology: International exclamation borrowed into Levantine Arabic from Italian bravo! ('well done!', originally adjective 'brave, capable, skilled', via French/Italian cultural contact).

برتقال.etymology: Collective noun بُرْتُقَال (burtuqāl, 'sweet oranges'), borrowed via Ottoman Turkish portakal and Italian portogallo after the country Portugal, whose maritime traders popularized sweet Chinese oranges across the Mediterranean.

برج.etymology: Architectural noun borrowed in late antiquity from Greek pyrgos (tower) via Aramaic.

برد.etymology: Form I verb بَرَدَ (barada, 'to become cold, cool down'), inherited from the Semitic root ب-ر-د (b-r-d, 'coldness, hail, cooling').

بردقان.etymology: Jordanian and Levantine colloquial noun بَرْدَقَان (bardaqān, 'oranges'), adapted by voicing /t/ > /d/ and /l/ > /n/ from standard بُرْتُقَال (burtuqāl). The fruit was named after Portugal (Portuguese navigators helped spread sweet Asian oranges into the Mediterranean in the 16th century).

morphemes.meaning: country name reanalysed as fruit name

برش.etymology: Verbal noun بَرْش (barš, 'grating, rasping; grated zest') from بَرَشَ (baraša, 'to scrape, grate, shred'), root ب-ر-ش (b-r-š), widely used in Levantine cooking for grated cheese and citrus zest.

برغي.etymology: Levantine and Iraqi noun بُرْغِي (burġī, 'screw, bolt'), borrowed from Ottoman Turkish burgu ('auger, gimlet, screw', derived from the Turkic verb bur- 'to twist, bore').

برفع.etymology: First/third person present tense of رفع (root ر-ف-ع, to raise) with b- prefix.

برق.etymology: Inherited Proto-Semitic noun بَرْق ('lightning') from the root ب-ر-ق ('flash, gleam, shine brightly').

برقية.etymology: Modern Arabic coinage بَرْقِيَّة (barqiyya, 'telegram, cable'), formed as a feminine nisba noun from بَرْق (barq, 'lightning, electric flash'), root ب-ر-ق (b-r-q). Coined in the 19th-century Arab press and postal services to translate European 'telegram' via electric 'lightning' signals.

برنامج.etymology: Early Arabic borrowing بَرْنَامَج (barnāmaj) from Middle Persian barnāmag ('plan, list, register', composed of bar 'on' + nāmag 'book, writing'). Re-borrowed into modern Arabic usage for theatre/concert programmes, schedules, and software.

بروفة.etymology: Arabic theatrical and musical loanword بْرُوفَة (brōva, 'rehearsal, trial run, tailor's fitting'), borrowed in the 19th–20th centuries from Italian prova ('test, trial, rehearsal'), from Late Latin proba ('proof, test') < probare ('to test, approve').

بريد.etymology: Classical Arabic بَرِيد (barīd, 'postal courier, mail service'), borrowed in antiquity via Syriac/Middle Persian from Late Latin verēdus / Byzantine Greek βέρηδος ('post-horse, state relay horse').

بريدي.etymology: Relational nisba adjective derived from بَرِيد (barīd, mail/courier), an early Arabic borrowing linked to Late Latin verēdus ('post horse') or Persian burīda-dumb ('docked-tail courier mule'). In Jordanian usage, بطاقة بريدية is the standard term for a postcard.

morphemes.meaning: post, mail (early loan from Latin/Persian courier terms)

بس.etymology: Spoken Levantine, Egyptian, and Gulf particle بَسّ (bass, 'only, just; enough!; but'), borrowed from Persian بَس (bas, 'enough, sufficient, only').

بساحتنا.etymology: Locative phrase uniting بـ (in), ساحة (courtyard, root س-و-ح), and 1pl -na.

بساحتي.etymology: Attaches locative بـ and 1sg possessive -i to the noun ساحة (open yard).

بسافر.etymology: Form III present verb combining b- prefix with سافر (root س-ف-ر, to journey).

بسطة.etymology: Noun بَسْطَة (basṭa, 'flat expanse, stair landing; open vendor stall') from بَسَطَ (basaṭa, 'to spread out flat'), root ب-س-ط (b-s-ṭ).

history.meaning: spread-out surface; stair landing; market stall

بسكوت.etymology: Culinary loanword entering Arabic from Italian biscotto / French biscuit (twice-baked).

بسيط.etymology: Adjective بَسِيط (basīṭ, 'spread out, uncompounded, simple, minor') on the pattern فَعِيل from بَسَطَ (basaṭa, 'to spread out flat, make plain'), root ب-س-ط (b-s-ṭ).

بشارع.etymology: Unites preposition بـ (in, on) with شارع (street, from root ش-ر-ع).

بشكل.etymology: Adverbial expression merging بـ (in) with شكل (shape, manner, root ش-ك-ل).

بصل.etymology: Collective masculine noun on the root ب-ص-ل (b-ṣ-l, onion), cognate with Hebrew בָּצָל (bāṣāl) and Aramaic beṣlā across the Semitic family. Like other Arabic botanical collectives, بصل denotes onions in general while singulative بصلة marks a single bulb.

بصوت.etymology: Pairs instrumental بـ (with, in) with صوت (voice, sound, root ص-و-ت).

بطاقات.etymology: Sound feminine plural of بطاقة (card, ticket), originally borrowed via Aramaic/Greek pittakion.

بطاقة.etymology: Singular feminine noun traced via Syriac and Classical Arabic بِطَاقَة to Greek pittakion (label, tablet).

بطال.etymology: Intensive adjective بَطَّال (baṭṭāl, 'idle, worthless, bad; [in Levantine مش بطال] not bad!') on the pattern فَعَّال from بَطَلَ (baṭala, 'to become null, idle, vain'), root ب-ط-ل (b-ط-l).

بطانة.etymology: Noun بِطَانَة (biṭāna, 'inner lining of a coat or mechanism; felt bushing') derived from بَطْن (baṭn, 'interior, inside, belly'), root ب-ط-ن (b-ṭ-n).

بطاولة.etymology: Combines بـ (on, at) with طاولة (table, borrowed from Italian tavola).

بطل.etymology: Levantine Form II verb بَطَّلَ (baṭṭal, 'to stop doing, quit, cut out'; in Classical Arabic 'to render void, abolish') on the pattern فَعَّلَ (faʿʿala) from Form I بَطَلَ (baṭala, 'to become null, cease, be in vain'), Semitic root ب-ط-ل (b-ṭ-l, 'idleness, cessation, vanity').

history.meaning: to become void -> to annul, discontinue
to stop, quit, no longer do (+ imperfective verb or noun)

بطل.notes: Watch the unvocalized homograph: verb بَطَّل (baṭṭal, 'stopped / quit': بطلي حركاتك! 'cut out your antics!', بطلت أحكي معها 'I stopped talking to her') vs noun بَطَل (baṭal, 'hero / champion', from a distinct semantic branch of ب-ط-ل)!

بطلة.etymology: Feminine noun بَطَلَة (baṭala, 'heroine, female champion') from بَطَل (baṭal, 'hero, brave warrior, champion') on the root ب-ط-ل (b-ṭ-l, 'valor, bravery').

بطيء.etymology: Adjective بَطِيء (baṭīʾ, 'slow, tardy, unhurried') on the pattern فَعِيل from بَطُؤَ (baṭuʾa, 'to be slow'), root ب-ط-ء (b-ṭ-ʾ).

بطّل.etymology: Form II verb بَطَّلَ (baṭṭala, 'to invalidate, cease, stop doing something') from بَطَلَ (baṭala, 'to become void, cease'), root ب-ط-ل (b-ṭ-l).

بعت.etymology: Spoken Levantine reflex (with regular shift of interdental ث ṯ to dental stop ت t) of Classical Arabic بَعَثَ (baʿaṯa, 'to send, dispatch'), root ب-ع-ث (b-ʿ-ṯ).

بعد.etymology: Preposition and adverb بَعْدَ (baʿda, 'after, later, still'), inherited from the Proto-Semitic spatial/temporal root ب-ع-د (b-ʿ-d, 'distance, behind, after').

بعدين.etymology: Spoken Levantine temporal adverb بَعْدِين (baʿdēn, 'then, afterwards, later'), formed as an adverbial dual/extension from بَعْد (baʿd, 'after'), root ب-ع-د.

بعرف.etymology: First-person or 3ms present of عرف (root ع-ر-ف, to know) with colloquial prefix بـ.

بعض.etymology: Noun and reciprocal pronoun بَعْض (baʿḍ, 'part, portion, some; [after plural verbs] each other, one another'), from the root ب-ع-ض (b-ʿ-ḍ, 'to divide into parts').

بعيد.etymology: Adjective بَعِيد (baʿīd, 'far, distant, remote') on the pattern فَعِيل from بَعُدَ (baʿuda, 'to be distant'), root ب-ع-د (b-ʿ-d).

بغرفة.etymology: Spatial prepositional phrase uniting بـ (in) with غرفة (room, root غ-ر-ف).

بغطا.etymology: Unites instrumental بـ (with) with غطا, the Levantine reflex of غطاء (cover, root غ-ط-و).

بـ.etymology: Proclitic Semitic preposition bi- written separately with tatweel before detached nouns or foreign words.

بفاجئ.etymology: Form III present tense from فاجأ (root ف-ج-أ, to come suddenly upon) prefixed with b-.

بقاع.etymology: Locative phrase merging بـ (in, at) with قاع (bottom, floor, hollow root ق-و-ع).

بقافية.etymology: Attaches بـ (with) to قافية (rhyme, from root ق-ف-و meaning to follow behind).

بقدونس.etymology: Mediterranean culinary loanword entering Levantine Arabic from Medieval Greek μακεδονήσιον (makedonḗsion, 'Macedonian herb'), often via Ottoman or Syriac-Romance channels as maqdūnis / baqdūnis. Across Jordan and the Levant, it is a kitchen staple in tabbouleh, falafel, and tahini dishes.

بقلم.etymology: Instrumental phrase joining بـ (with) and قلم (pen, borrowed in antiquity from Greek kalamos).

بقماش.etymology: Prepositional combination pairing instrumental بـ (with) and قماش (woven cloth, fabric, from root ق-م-ش).

بكرا.etymology: Spoken Levantine and Egyptian temporal adverb بُكْرَا (bukrā, 'tomorrow'), from the Classical adverbial accusative بُكْرَةً (bukratan, 'early in the morning, at daybreak'), root ب-ك-ر (b-k-r).

بكرة.etymology: Levantine and Egyptian temporal adverb ('tomorrow') continuing Classical Arabic بُكْرَة (bukra, 'early morning, daybreak'), built on the Semitic root ب-ك-ر (b-k-r, 'to rise early, be first'), via the common cross-linguistic shift 'early [next] morning' -> 'tomorrow' (cf. Spanish mañana, German morgen).

cognates.meaning: morning (from the same Semitic root b-k-r)

بكرة.notes: Replaces MSA غداً (ġadan) in all Levantine and Egyptian conversation; بعد بكرة means 'the day after tomorrow'.

بكلف.etymology: Form II present verb from كلّف (root ك-ل-ف, to cost or charge) with b- marker.

بكى.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *bakay- ('to weep, cry'), yielding Classical Arabic بَكَى (bakā), root ب-ك-ي (b-k-y).

بكير.etymology: Signature Levantine adverb بِكِّير (bikkīr, 'early'), an intensive formation on the pattern فِعِّيل from the root ب-ك-ر (b-k-r, 'early morning, setting out at dawn').

بلا.etymology: Compound preposition بِلَا (bilā, 'without; let\'s skip / no...'), formed from the proclitic preposition بِـ (bi-) + negative particle لَا (lā).

بلاستيك.etymology: Modern loanword from English plastic (from French plastique, from Latin plasticus < Ancient Greek πλαστικός plastikós, 'fit for moulding', from πλάσσω plássō 'to mould').

بلاط.etymology: Collective Arabic noun بَلَاط (balāṭ, 'paving stones, floor tiles, palace pavement'), an early borrowing from Late Latin palatium ('palace') or Aramaic/Greek plax/palation, influenced by Arabic root ب-ل-ط ('flat, paved'). From its architectural use came Spanish/Portuguese azulejo-adjacent masonry terms and modern 'floor tiles'.

بلاطة.etymology: Feminine singulative noun from collective بَلَاط (balāṭ, stone paving/tiles), traditionally analyzed under the root ب-ل-ط (b-l-ṭ) with likely early contact with Greek πλατύς / Latin palātium ('flat slab, paved palace floor'). In Jordanian architecture, بلاطة refers to a floor tile or stone flagstone.

بلد.etymology: Classical Arabic بَلَد (balad, 'town, city, settlement, country'), referring in Jordanian usage especially to downtown (وسط البلد), root ب-ل-د (b-l-d).

بلدي.etymology: Relational (nisba) adjective بَلَدِيّ (baladiyy, 'local, native, home-grown, traditional') formed from بَلَد (balad, 'country, local land') + -ِيّ (-iyy).

بلدية.etymology: Feminine noun بَلَدِيَّة (baladiyya, 'municipality, city council, town hall'), coined in the 19th-century Ottoman and Arab civic reforms from بَلَدِيّ (baladiyy, 'municipal, civic').

بلش.etymology: Characteristic Levantine Form II verb بَلَّشَ (ballaš, 'to begin, start, get stuck into'), developed in Syrian/Levantine Arabic from بَلِشَ / اِبْتَلَشَ ('to become entangled or embroiled in an affair', cf. بَلْشَة 'predicament, involvement', influenced by Aramaic b-l-š 'to search into, engage with' and semantic overlap with بَاشَرَ 'to initiate').

history.meaning: to become engaged or entangled in a matter
to start, begin (both transitive and intransitive)

rootFamily.gloss: to get stuck/bogged down with trouble (Levantine)

بلش.notes: Quintessential Levantine marker (replacing MSA بَدَأَ badaʾa): هي اللي بلشت means 'she started it!', and بلشت الحصة means 'class has started'.

بلكونة.etymology: Loanword entering Levantine Arabic from Italian balcone (or French balcon), adapted to the Arabic feminine noun ending -a/-e.

بلكي.etymology: Borrowed into Levantine Arabic from Ottoman Turkish belki (perhaps), itself derived from Persian balke and ultimately Arabic بل كي.

بلوط.etymology: Classical Arabic بَلُّوط (ballūṭ, 'oak tree, acorn'), borrowed in antiquity from Aramaic בַּלּוּטָא / ܒܠܘܛܐ (ballūṭā, 'oak, acorn').

بلوك.etymology: Modern loanword adopted from English block or French bloc into Levantine urban vocabulary to count city blocks and masonry units.

بلّش.etymology: Signature Levantine Form II verb بَلَّش (ballaš, 'to begin, start'), historically derived as a denominative from بَلَاش ('for free, from nothing/scratch') or influenced by Aramaic.

بلّغ.etymology: Form II causative verb بَلَّغَ (ballaġa, 'to cause to reach; convey a message, notify, report') from بَلَغَ (balaġa, 'to reach, attain'), root ب-ل-غ (b-l-ġ).

بمكان.etymology: Combines locative بـ (in) with مكان (place, noun of place from root ك-و-ن).

بناية.etymology: Verbal and concrete noun بِنَايَة (bināya, 'building, structure, edifice') from بَنَى (banā, 'to build, construct'), root ب-ن-ي (b-n-y).

بنت.etymology: Inherited across Classical and colloquial Arabic from Proto-Semitic *bint- ('daughter, girl'), feminine counterpart of ابْن (ibn, 'son') built on the ancient biconsonantal/triliteral kinship root ب-ن-و / ب-ن-ي (b-n-y) + the archaic Semitic feminine suffix -t.
بنت.notes: Whereas MSA distinguishes فتاة ('girl, young woman') from بنت / ابنة ('daughter'), Levantine Arabic uses بنت (pl. بنات) for both 'girl' and 'daughter'.

بند.etymology: Classical and Modern Arabic بَنْد (band, 'clause, article of a contract, item; banner'), borrowed from Persian بَنْد (band, 'tie, joint, binding, numbered article').

بندورة.etymology: Levantine borrowing بَنْدُورَة ('tomato') from Italian pomodoro (literally pomo d'oro, 'golden apple'), adapted into Eastern Mediterranean Arabic when New World tomatoes arrived via Italian port trade in the 18th–19th centuries.

بنشر.etymology: Spoken quadriliteral verb بَنْشَر (banšar, 'to get a flat tire, break down'), denominalized from the early 20th-century automotive borrowing بَنْشَر (banšar) from English puncture.

بنفسكم.etymology: Reflexive phrase pairing بـ (by), نفس (self, soul, root ن-ف-س), and 2pl suffix -kum.

بنفع.etymology: Present tense of نفع (root ن-ف-ع, to be useful) used impersonally in Jordanian questions.

بنمشي.etymology: First-person plural present verb prefixing bin- to defective مشى (root م-ش-ي, to walk).

بنى.etymology: Pan-Semitic Form I defective verb (فَعَلَ) from the root ب-ن-ي (b-n-y, to build, construct, establish), cognate with Hebrew בָּנָה (bānā) and Aramaic bənā. Unchanged in core form and meaning, بنى is the everyday Jordanian verb for constructing buildings or establishing projects.

بني.etymology: Relational (nisba) color adjective بُنِّيّ (bunniyy, 'brown, coffee-colored') derived from بُنّ (bunn, 'coffee beans, roasted coffee').

بهيك.etymology: Levantine expression joining بـ (in) to هيك (thus, such), contracted from هذا + ك.

بوابة.etymology: Augmented feminine noun بَوَّابَة ('main gate, arched portal', plural بَوَّابَات) derived on the intensive pattern فَعَّالَة from بَاب ('door', root ب-و-ب), naming a grand courtyard or street entrance larger than an ordinary room door.

بوابتنا.etymology: Fuses بوابة (wide gate, intensive form from باب, root ب-و-ب) with 1pl possessive -na.

بوصلة.etymology: Borrowed into Arabic from Italian bussola (little box for a magnetic needle).

بياع.etymology: Occupational noun بَيَّاع (bayyāʿ, 'seller, vendor, shopkeeper') on the intensive/agentive pattern فَعَّال from بَاعَ (bāʿa, 'to sell'), root ب-ي-ع (b-y-ʿ).

بيانو.etymology: Modern musical loanword adopted from Italian piano (short for pianoforte).

بيت.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *bayt- ('house, dwelling'), related to the verbal root ب-ي-ت ('to spend the night').
بيت.notes: The same Semitic word gave rise to the Phoenician letter name *bēt* ('house'), ancestor of Greek beta (Β). In Amman, بيت names both a family home and a traditional courtyard house.

بيخبز.etymology: Variant orthography of بخبز attaching bi- to خبز (root خ-ب-ز, to bake).

بير.etymology: Spoken and lightened Classical form بِير (bīr, 'water well') of بِئْر (biʾr) via compensatory lengthening after loss of the glottal stop, inherited from Proto-Semitic *biʾr- ('well, cistern').

بيز.etymology: Modern musical loanword بِيز (bēz, 'bass instrument, bass line'), borrowed from English 'bass' (with final voicing -s > -z typical in Arabic musical borrowings, parallel to جاز 'jazz'). English 'bass' comes from Old French bas / Late Latin bassus ('low').

بيض.etymology: Collective noun بَيْض (bayḍ, 'eggs'; singulative بَيْضَة bayḍa), inherited from Proto-Semitic *bayḍ- ('egg; whiteness'), root ب-ي-ض (b-y-ḍ).

بيضات.etymology: Countable feminine plural of بيضة (single egg, root ب-ي-ض meaning whiteness).

بيضحكوا.etymology: Third-person plural present verb built on ضحك (root ض-ح-ك, to laugh).

بيع.etymology: Form I verbal noun بَيْع (bayʿ, 'selling, sale') from بَاعَ (bāʿa, 'to sell'), root ب-ي-ع (b-y-ʿ).

بيعني.etymology: Present indicative of defective عنى (root ع-ن-ي, to mean, signify) with bi- prefix.

بين.etymology: Locative preposition بَيْنَ (bayna, 'between, among'), inherited from Proto-Semitic *bayn- ('interval, space between'), root ب-ي-ن (b-y-n).

بينما.etymology: Subordinating temporal conjunction compounding بين (between, root ب-ي-ن) with ما.

بيّن.etymology: Form II verb بَيَّنَ (bayyana, 'to make clear, show; [in Levantine] to appear, seem, show off') from بَانَ (bāna, 'to become clear, apparent'), root ب-ي-ن (b-y-n).

بَعَد.etymology: Form I verb بَعَدَ / بَعُدَ (baʿada, 'to step back, move away, become distant') from the Semitic spatial root ب-ع-د (b-ʿ-d, 'distance, remoteness').

history.meaning: to be distant; move away; step back

بُعد.etymology: Verbal/abstract noun بُعْد (buʿd, 'distance, remoteness, dimension') on the pattern فُعْل from the root ب-ع-د (b-ʿ-d).

تأخّر.etymology: Form V reflexive verb تَأَخَّرَ (taʾaḫḫara, 'to fall behind, be delayed, be late') from أَخَّرَ (ʾaḫḫara, 'to delay, put back'), root ء-خ-ر (ʾ-ḫ-r).

history.meaning: to lag behind; be delayed; be late

تأكد.etymology: Form V reflexive verb (تَفَعَّلَ, tafaʿʿala) formed from the root أ-ك-د (ʾ-k-d, to tighten, confirm, assure). Paired with the preposition من, تأكد is ubiquitous in Jordanian Arabic for verifying facts, checking doors or locks, and making certain.

تأكّد.etymology: Form V reflexive verb تَأَكَّدَ (taʾakkada, 'to become certain, make sure, verify') from أَكَّدَ (ʾakkada, 'to confirm, assure'), root ء-ك-د (ʾ-k-d).

history.meaning: to become certain; verify; make sure

تابلت.etymology: Modern digital loanword borrowed from English tablet ('portable touchscreen tablet computer').

تارت.etymology: Culinary loanword borrowed from French tarte / English tart ('open shortcrust pastry shell filled with fruit or custard').

تاريخ.etymology: Verbal noun (تَفْعِيل) of Form II أَرَّخَ (ʾarraḫa, 'to date a letter or chronicle'), linked to the Semitic moon/month word *warḫ- (compare Hebrew yārēaḥ 'moon', yereḥ 'month'): fixing an event by month and day.

تاريخي.etymology: Nisba adjective formed by adding -ī (-ي) to تَارِيخ (tārīx, date/history), the Form II verbal noun of أ-ر-خ (ʾ-r-x, to date or chronicle, related to Semitic terms for 'moon/month'). In modern Levantine Arabic, تاريخي modifies heritage sites, squares, and memorable events.

تاسع.etymology: Ordinal adjective تَاسِع (tāsiʿ, 'ninth') formed on the active-participle pattern فَاعِل from تِسْعَة (tisʿa, 'nine'), root ت-س-ع (t-s-ʿ).

تاكسي.etymology: International loanword borrowed from French/English taxi (shortened from taximètre, 'taximeter cab').

تالت.etymology: Colloquial Levantine ordinal تالت (tālit, 'third'), with regular shift of interdental ث ṯ to stop ت t from Classical ثَالِث (ṯāliṯ) on the pattern فَاعِل from ثَلَاثَة ('three'), root ث-ل-ث.

تام.etymology: Active participle on the faa'il pattern from the geminate root ت-م-م (to be complete, finished), with contraction of the identical radicals.

تاني.etymology: Spoken Levantine reflex (with regular shift of ث ṯ to ت t) of Classical ثَانٍ / الثَّانِي (ṯānī, 'second; another, other') on the ordinal pattern فَاعِل from root ث-ن-ي (ṯ-n-y, 'two; doubling').

تبديل.etymology: Verbal noun (masdar) of Form II بدّل from the root ب-د-ل meaning exchange or substitution.

تبدّل.etymology: Form V mediopassive verb تَبَدَّلَ (tabaddala, 'to be exchanged, get swapped, change') from بَدَّلَ (baddala, 'to change, replace'), root ب-د-ل (b-d-l).

history.meaning: to be replaced; get swapped; change

تبريد.etymology: Derived on the Form II verbal-noun pattern تَفْعِيل (tafʿīl) from ب-ر-د (b-r-d, cold, chill, hail). Functioning as the action noun of برّد ('to cool down'), it is standard across Jordan for culinary cooling as well as air-conditioning and refrigeration.

تبع.etymology: Signature Levantine genitive exponent derived from root ت-ب-ع (following, belonging to).

تبعت.etymology: Feminine singular form of the Levantine possessive linker تبع agreeing with feminine nouns.

تبعي.etymology: Combines the Levantine possessive marker تبع with the 1sg pronominal suffix -i.

تبلّل.etymology: Form V mediopassive verb تَبَلَّلَ (taballala, 'to get wet, become soaked') from بَلَّلَ (ballala, 'to wet, moisten'), root ب-ل-ل (b-l-l).

history.meaning: to become wet; get damp or soaked

تجاري.etymology: Relational (nisba) adjective تِجَارِيّ (tijāriyy, 'commercial, mercantile, trade-') from تِجَارَة (tijāra, 'commerce, trade'), root ت-ج-ر (t-j-r).

تجربة.etymology: Form II verbal noun تَجْرِبَة (tajriba, 'trial, test, experiment, experience') from جَرَّبَ (jarraba, 'to test, try out'), root ج-ر-ب (j-r-b).

تجريدي.etymology: Nisba adjective تَجْرِيدِيّ (tajrīdiyy) derived from تَجْرِيد (tajrīd, 'stripping away, abstraction'), the Form II verbal noun of ج-ر-د (j-r-d, 'to strip bare'). In modern Arabic aesthetics, it translates European 'abstract' in art and philosophy.

تجيبري.etymology: Colloquial variant spelling of تجبري (2fs imperfect of جبر, root ج-ب-ر, to compel) reflecting epenthetic vowel.

تحت.etymology: Inherited Semitic spatial preposition and adverb from root ت-ح-ت denoting beneath or under.

تحتاني.etymology: Levantine relational adjective تَحْتَانِيّ (taḥtānī, 'bottom, lower, downstairs'), formed from تَحْت (taḥt, 'under, below') with the augmented relational suffix -َانِيّ (-ānī, shared with Aramaic -ānāyā).

تحته.etymology: Preposition تحت suffixed with the 3ms object pronoun -u/-o (under it/him).

تحتها.etymology: Spatial preposition تحت joined to the 3fs pronominal suffix -ha (under her/it).

تحدى.etymology: Form V verb تَحَدَّى (taḥaddā, 'to challenge, defy, vie with someone for mastery') on the pattern تَفَعَّلَ (tafaʿʿala) from the defective root ح-د-و / ح-د-ي (ḥ-d-y, Classical تَحَدَّاهُ, 'to compete with someone, summon to a contest', famously used of the Qurʾanic inimitability challenge).

history.meaning: to vie with, challenge an opponent to match a feat

تحدى.notes: Transitive in both MSA and Jordanian: عم بتتحديني؟ ('are you challenging/defying me right now?') attaches the 1sg object suffix -ني directly.

تحرس.etymology: Subjunctive 3fs/2ms verb from حرس (root ح-ر-س, to guard or keep watch).

تحرك.etymology: Form V mediopassive/intransitive verb تَحَرَّكَ (taḥarraka, 'to be set in motion, move oneself, stir') on the pattern تَفَعَّلَ (tafaʿʿala), paired with transitive Form II حَرَّكَ ('to move something'), from the triliteral root ح-ر-ك (ḥ-r-k, 'motion, movement').

history.meaning: to set in motion -> to move, stir
to move, get going, take action

تحرك.notes: Imperative تحركي! / يلا نتحرك! means both literally 'move!' and practically 'let's head out / take action!'.

تحرّك.etymology: Form V mediopassive verb تَحَرَّكَ (taḥarraka, 'to move, stir, shift') from حَرَّكَ (ḥarraka, 'to set in motion, move'), root ح-ر-ك (ḥ-r-k).

history.meaning: to move (intransitive); be set in motion

تحضير.etymology: Form II verbal noun تَحْضِير (taḥḍīr, 'making present, preparing') from حضّر (ḥaḍḍara), root ح-ض-ر (ḥ-ḍ-r, 'to be present, attend'). Literally meaning 'bringing something into readiness', it is the everyday word for prep work in kitchens and events.

تحفة.etymology: From Classical Arabic تُحْفَة (tuḥfa, 'rare gift, prized curiosity, masterpiece'), root ت-ح-ف (t-ḥ-f, reshaped by metanalysis from وَحَفَ/أَتْحَفَ 'to present with a rare gift'). Across Levantine speech, calling anything 'tuhfe' is warm praise for fine craft or beauty.

تحكم.etymology: Form V reflexive/intensive verb تَحَكَّمَ (taḥakkama, 'to exercise arbitrary control, dominate, boss around') on the pattern تَفَعَّلَ (tafaʿʿala) from the Semitic root ح-ك-م (ḥ-k-m, 'to restrain, judge, rule', tied to حَكَمَة, the curb-bit of a horse's bridle).

history.meaning: to pass judgment at will, hold sway
to control, boss around (with بـ or في)

rootFamily.gloss: (verbal noun) control; جهاز تحكم = remote control

تحكم.notes: Shared across MSA and Jordanian speech; construes with في or بـ for controlling people (بتتحكمي فينا, 'you're bossing us around').

تحمل.etymology: Form V reflexive/patientive verb تَحَمَّلَ (taḥammala, 'to take a heavy load upon oneself, endure patiently, bear') on the pattern تَفَعَّلَ (tafaʿʿala), paired with Form II حَمَّلَ ('to load onto someone'), from the Semitic root ح-م-ل (ḥ-m-l, 'to carry, bear').

morphemes.meaning: Form V verb (shouldering a burden oneself)

history.meaning: to load up one's camel, take on a burden, endure
to endure, put up with, take on (responsibility)

تحمل.notes: Used across registers both for enduring mistreatment (مش قادرة أتحمل, 'I can't take it anymore') and assuming responsibility (نتحمل المسؤولية).

تحمّل.etymology: Form V reflexive-intensive verb تَحَمَّلَ (taḥammala, 'to take upon oneself, bear, endure') from حَمَلَ (ḥamala, 'to carry, bear'), Semitic root ح-م-ل (ḥ-m-l).

تحويل.etymology: Form II verbal noun تَحْوِيل (taḥwīl, 'turning, conversion, transfer, diversion') from حَوَّلَ (ḥawwala, 'to transform, transfer'), root ح-و-ل (ḥ-w-l).

تحويلة.etymology: Feminine noun تَحْوِيلَة (taḥwīla, 'turnoff, detour, branch track, call transfer'), an instance-noun derivative of Form II verbal noun تَحْوِيل (taḥwīl, 'turning, diverting') from حَوَّلَ (ḥawwala, root ح-و-ل 'to turn, shift, change').

تحية.etymology: Form II verbal noun تَحِيَّة (taḥiyya, 'greeting, salutation, salute, toast') from حَيَّا (ḥayyā, originally 'to say حَيَّاكَ اللّٰهُ [may God preserve your life]'), root ح-ي-ي (ḥ-y-y, 'life').

تخانق.etymology: Form VI reciprocal verb تَخَانَقَ (taḫānaqa, 'to quarrel, argue heatedly'), literally 'to seize one another by the throat', from خَنَقَ (ḫanaqa, 'to throttle, choke'), root خ-ن-ق (ḫ-n-q).

تخبي.etymology: Form II subjunctive verb from خبّى (root خ-ب-أ, to conceal) for 3fs or 2ms.

تخبّى.etymology: Spoken Levantine Form V reflexive verb تَخَبَّى (tḫabbā, 'to hide oneself, take cover'), from Classical تَخَبَّأَ (taḫabbaʾa) with regular loss of final hamza, root خ-ب-ء (ḫ-b-ʾ).

تخت.etymology: Everyday Levantine noun تَخْت (taḫt, 'bed, bedstead; raised platform'), borrowed from Persian تَخْت (taxt, 'throne, raised wooden platform, couch, bedstead').

تخمر.etymology: Verbal form built on خمر (root خ-م-ر, leavening/fermentation), used for dough rising or tea steeping.

تخيّل.etymology: Form V verb تَخَيَّلَ (taḫayyala, 'to imagine, fancy, picture in the mind') from خَيَال (ḫayāl, 'image, vision, imagination'), root خ-ي-ل (ḫ-y-l).

تدرّب.etymology: Form V reflexive verb (تَفَعَّلَ, tafaʿʿala) built on the root د-ر-ب (d-r-b, path, habit, familiarity, skill). Originally carrying the sense of becoming accustomed to a mountain pass or route, it developed the modern meaning 'to train, practice, or rehearse' (usually with على).

تدفئة.etymology: Form II verbal noun تَدْفِئَة (tadfiʾa, 'warming, heating') from دَفَّأَ (daffaʾa, 'to make warm, heat'), root د-ف-ء (d-f-ʾ, 'warmth').

تذكار.etymology: From Classical Arabic تَذْكَار (taḏkār, 'reminder, memorial, keepsake'), verbal noun pattern تَفْعَال from ذَكَرَ (ḏakara, 'to remember, recall', root ذ-ك-ر).

تذكرة.etymology: Verbal noun of Form II ذَكَّرَ ('to remind'), built on the root ذ-ك-ر ('remember, mention') with the pattern تَفْعِلَة: originally 'a written reminder or memorandum', whence Ottoman and modern Arabic specialized it to a travel or admission 'ticket'.

تذكّر.etymology: Form V verb تَذَكَّرَ (taḏakkara, 'to remember, recall, bear in mind') from ذَكَّرَ (ḏakkara, 'to remind'), derived from the Proto-Semitic root ذ-ك-ر (*ḏ-k-r, 'to remember, mention').

تذوق.etymology: Form V masdar derived from the hollow root ذ-و-ق (to taste), denoting deliberate tasting or refined appreciation.

تراث.etymology: Classical Arabic تُرَاث (turāṯ, 'heritage, inheritance'), formed with regular initial w -> t assimilation (*wurāṯ > turāṯ) from root و-ر-ث (w-r-ṯ, 'to inherit').

تراثي.etymology: Relational (nisba) adjective تُرَاثِيّ (turāṯiyy, 'heritage, traditional, historic') from تُرَاث (turāṯ < *wurāṯ, 'inheritance, cultural heritage'), from وَرِثَ ('to inherit', root و-ر-ث).

ترتيب.etymology: Form II verbal noun تَرْتِيب (tartīb, 'putting in order, arrangement, tidiness') from رَتَّبَ (rattaba, 'to arrange, order, tidy'), root ر-ت-ب (r-t-b).

ترحيب.etymology: Central to hospitality phrasing, ترحيب is the Form II maṣdar (تَفْعِيل) from ر-ح-ب (r-ḥ-b, spaciousness, openness, generosity), the same root behind مَرْحَبًا. Expressing the idea of making room generously for a guest, ترحيب sits at the heart of Jordanian hospitality vocabulary.

ترحيبي.etymology: Relational (nisba) adjective تَرْحِيبِيّ (tarḥībiyy, 'welcoming, introductory') derived from تَرْحِيب (tarḥīb, 'welcoming, saying marḥaban'), verbal noun of Form II رَحَّبَ (raḥḥaba), root ر-ح-ب (r-ḥ-b, 'spaciousness, generosity').

ترقّى.etymology: Form V verb تَرَقَّى (taraqqā, 'to ascend step by step, advance, get promoted') from رَقِيَ (raqiya, 'to climb, ascend'), root ر-ق-ي (r-q-y).

history.meaning: to rise by degrees; be promoted

ترك.etymology: Form I verb تَرَكَ (taraka, 'to leave, let be, leave behind'), root ت-ر-ك (t-r-k).

history.meaning: to leave; let alone; leave behind

ترميم.etymology: Architectural usage of ترميم comes from the Form II verbal noun (تَفْعِيل) of ر-م-م (r-m-m, to mend, repair decayed bone or masonry). From Classical usage for mending worn walls, ترميم became the technical and everyday Jordanian term for architectural and heritage restoration.

تستنى.etymology: Levantine Form X verb استنى (from تأنّى, root أ-ن-ي, to wait patiently) in 2ms/3fs.

تسعة.etymology: Ancient Semitic cardinal numeral from the root ت-س-ع meaning nine.

تسعطعش.etymology: Fused Levantine compound numeral descending from Classical Arabic تسعة عشر (tis'ata 'ashar), retaining the emphatic t from 'ashar.

تسعطعشر.etymology: Spoken Levantine construct compound numeral تِسَعْطَعْشَر (tisaʿṭaʿšar, 'nineteen' before a counted noun), contracted from Classical تِسْعَةَ عَشَرَ (tisʿata ʿašara, 'nine-teen') with pharyngeal-induced emphasis of t to ṭ.

تشرّف.etymology: Form V verb تَشَرَّفَ (tašarrafa, 'to be honored; [in تَشَرَّفْنَا] we are honored / pleased to meet you') from شَرَّفَ (šarrafa, 'to honor'), root ش-ر-ف (š-r-f, 'elevation, nobility, honor').

تشطيب.etymology: Form II masdar on the taf'iil pattern from the root ش-ط-ب (to cross out, bring to completion), broadened in modern Arabic to finishing touches.

تشييك.etymology: Colloquial Form II verbal noun تَشْيِيك (tašyīk, 'checking, inspection, going over a list'), formed natively on the Arabic تَفْعِيل pattern from the modern denominal verb شيّك ('to check'), borrowed from English 'check'. Shows how productive Arabic root-and-pattern morphology integrates loanwords.

تصالح.etymology: Form VI reciprocal verb تَصَالَحَ (taṣālaḥa, 'to make peace with one another, reconcile') from صُلْح (ṣulḥ, 'peace, reconciliation'), root ص-ل-ح (ṣ-l-ḥ).

تصرف.etymology: Form V reflexive verb تَصَرَّفَ (taṣarrafa, 'to turn freely in handling affairs, act on one's own, behave') on the pattern تَفَعَّلَ (tafaʿʿala) from Form II صَرَّفَ ('to turn, circulate, inflect, dispatch'), triliteral root ص-ر-ف (ṣ-r-f, 'to turn away, shift, exchange').

history.meaning: to move freely, manage affairs at one's discretion
to behave, act; to handle a situation

rootFamily.gloss: behaviors, actions (plural of verbal noun تصرف)

تصرف.notes: Used both for manner of behavior (تصرفي بطبيعتك, 'act naturally') and alone as an urgent imperative (تصرفي!, 'do something / figure out how to handle it!').

تصليح.etymology: Form II verbal noun تَصْلِيح (taṣlīḥ, 'repairing, fixing, restoration') from صَلَّحَ (ṣallaḥa, 'to mend, repair'), root ص-ل-ح (ṣ-l-ḥ, 'sound, upright, in good working order'). Standard across everyday Arabic for repairing tracks, appliances, and instruments.

history.meaning: to be right -> to mend -> repair

تصميم.etymology: Built on the Form II maṣdar pattern تَفْعِيل (tafʿīl) from geminate ص-م-م (ṣ-m-m, firmness, resolve, determination). While earlier Arabic emphasized firm intention ('resolving upon something'), modern Arabic expanded تصميم to mean architectural, graphic, and interior design.

تضل.etymology: Dialectal subjunctive of ضلّ (from ظلّ, root ظ-ل-ل, to remain) with emphatic stop shift.

تطلع.etymology: Spoken Levantine Form V verb تْطَلَّع (tṭallaʿ, 'to look at, gaze upon'), from Classical تَطَلَّعَ (taṭallaʿa, 'to crane the neck to look, gaze toward'), root ط-ل-ع (ṭ-l-ʿ).

history.meaning: to look out toward; gaze closely

تطلعوا.etymology: Second-person plural subjunctive of طلع (root ط-ل-ع, to go up/out) ending in -uu.

تطور.etymology: Form V verbal noun تَطَوُّر (taṭawwur, 'development, progress, stage-by-stage evolution') from تَطَوَّرَ (taṭawwara, 'to develop through successive stages [أَطْوَار]'), root ط-و-ر (ṭ-w-r).

تعال.etymology: Suppletive imperative verb تَعَالَ (taʿāla, f. تَعَالَيْ, pl. تَعَالَوْا, 'come!'), originally the Form VI imperative of عَلَا (ʿalā, 'to rise, ascend'), meaning literally 'come up here!', root ع-ل-و (ʿ-l-w).

تعالوا.etymology: Plural imperative of the defective suppletive verb تعال (root ع-ل-و, literally rise up/come here).

تعبان.etymology: Colloquial adjective تَعْبَان (taʿbān, 'tired, fatigued') on the intensive/experiential pattern فَعْلَان (faʿlān, like جوعان 'hungry') from تَعِبَ (taʿiba, 'to grow tired'), root ت-ع-ب (t-ʿ-b).

تعبّى.etymology: Spoken Levantine Form V reflexive verb (تَفَعَّلَ) from the defective/hamzated root ع-ب-أ / ع-ب-ي (ʿ-b-ʾ, to pack, load, fill). Shifting the original final hamza into a weak -y/-ā stem, تعبّى acts as the intransitive counterpart to عبّى ('to fill').

تعديل.etymology: Form II verbal noun تَعْدِيل (taʿdīl, 'straightening, adjustment, modification, edit') from عَدَّلَ (ʿaddala, 'to make straight, adjust evenly'), root ع-د-ل (ʿ-d-l).

تعريشة.etymology: Form II instance/concrete noun تَعْرِيشَة (taʿrīša, 'garden trellis, vine arbor, pergola') from عَرَّشَ (ʿarraša, 'to train a vine over a wooden trellis [عَرِيش]'), root ع-ر-ش (ʿ-r-š).

تعرّف.etymology: Form V verb تَعَرَّفَ (taʿarrafa, 'to become acquainted with, get to know, meet') from عَرَفَ (ʿarafa, 'to know, recognize'), root ع-ر-ف (ʿ-r-f).

history.meaning: to get to know; become acquainted

تعليقة.etymology: Feminine noun تَعْلِيقَة (taʿlīqa, 'hook, hanger, peg, hanging ornament'), instance-noun formation on تَفْعِيلَة from Form II عَلَّقَ (ʿallaqa, 'to hang, suspend'), root ع-ل-ق (ʿ-l-q, 'to cling, hang, attach').

تعليم.etymology: Masdar of Form II علّم derived from the root ع-ل-م (to know), with its feminine plural تعليمات specialized for directions and instructions.

تعلّق.etymology: Form V reflexive-passive verb تَعَلَّقَ (taʿallaqa, 'to hang onto, be suspended') built with t- prefix onto Form II علّق (ʿallaqa, 'to hang'), from the root ع-ل-ق (ʿ-l-q, 'to adhere, hang'). It supplies the intransitive 'will hang' corresponding to transitive 'to hang up'.

تعلّم.etymology: Form V reflexive verb تَعَلَّمَ (taʿallama, 'to learn, study') from عَلَّمَ (ʿallama, 'to teach'), root ع-ل-م (ʿ-l-m, 'knowledge').

تعيين.etymology: Form II verbal noun تَعْيِين (taʿyīn, 'specifying, designation, appointment to a post') from عَيَّنَ (ʿayyana, 'to single out, appoint'), denominative from عَيْن ('eye; specific individual'), root ع-ي-ن.

تغدّى.etymology: Form V defective verb تَغَدَّى (taġaddā, 'to eat lunch, dine at midday') from غَدَاء (ġadāʾ, 'midday meal'), root غ-د-و (ġ-d-w, 'morning, early day'). Historically غداء originally meant an early-morning meal before shifting to the main midday lunch.

history.meaning: to go early -> morning/midday meal -> to have lunch

تغليف.etymology: Form II verbal noun تَغْلِيف (taġlīf, 'wrapping, casing, packaging') from غَلَّفَ (ġallafa, 'to encase, wrap'), root غ-ل-ف (ġ-l-f, 'cover, sheath').

تغيّر.etymology: Form V reflexive verb تَغَيَّرَ (taġayyara, 'to undergo change, alter') derived from Form II غَيَّرَ (ġayyara, 'to alter something'), root غ-ي-ر (ġ-y-r, 'other, different'). In Jordanian speech it contrasts cleanly with transitive غيّر whenever plans or weather shift on their own.

تفاجأ.etymology: Modern Standard and Levantine Form VI mediopassive verb تَفَاجَأَ (tafājaʾa, Levantine tfājaʾ, 'to be caught off guard, be surprised') on the pattern تَفَاعَلَ (tafāʿala), formed as the reflexive/patientive counterpart to Form III فَاجَأَ (fājaʾa, 'to surprise someone'), final-hamza root ف-ج-ء (f-j-ʾ).

morphemes.meaning: Form VI mediopassive of Form III فَاجَأَ

history.meaning: to be surprised, be caught unawares (with بـ / من)

تفاجأ.notes: Traditional Classical purists preferred passive فُوجِئَ ('was surprised'), while modern MSA and all Levantine speakers overwhelmingly use active-looking تَفَاجَأ.

تفاح.etymology: Collective noun تُفَّاح (tuffāḥ, 'apples'; singulative تُفَّاحَة), a Northwest/Central Semitic fruit name (cognate with Hebrew תַּפּוּחַ tappūaḥ) traditionally connected to the root ن-ف-ح / ف-و-ح ('to diffuse a sweet fragrance').

تفتح.etymology: Subjunctive 3fs/2ms form of فتح (root ف-ت-ح, to open) used after modals like عشان/لازم.

تفتحوا.etymology: Second-person plural subjunctive/jussive of فتح (root ف-ت-ح, to open) marked with plural suffix -uu.

تفتيش.etymology: Form II verbal noun تَفْتِيش (taftīš, 'searching, inspection, examination') from فَتَّشَ (fattaša, 'to search carefully, inspect'), root ف-ت-ش (f-t-š).

تفرّج.etymology: Form V verb تَفَرَّجَ (tafarraja, 'to watch, look on at a view or spectacle'), originally 'to dispel worry [فَرَج] by going out to view something pleasant', from root ف-ر-ج (f-r-j, 'opening, relief from grief').

history.meaning: to find relief by viewing; watch; look on

تفضلي.etymology: Polite feminine singular Form V imperative from فضّل (root ف-ض-ل, favour, grace), inviting or offering.

تفضّل.etymology: Form V hospitality verb تَفَضَّلَ (tafaḍḍala, 'to be so kind as to; [imperative تَفَضَّلْ] please come in, have a seat, go ahead, here you are'), from فَضْل (faḍl, 'grace, kindness, favor'), root ف-ض-ل (f-ḍ-l).

history.meaning: to confer a favor; deign; 'please go ahead'

تفقّد.etymology: Form V verb تَفَقَّدَ (tafaqqada, 'to check on, inspect, look for what may be missing') from فَقَدَ (faqada, 'to lose, miss'), root ف-ق-د (f-q-d).

history.meaning: to seek out; inspect; check on

تفكير.etymology: Form II verbal noun تَفْكِير (tafkīr, 'thinking, thought, reflection') from فَكَّرَ (fakkara, 'to think, ponder'), root ف-ك-ر (f-k-r).

تقديم.etymology: Form II verbal noun تَقْدِيم (taqdīm, 'bringing forward, offering, serving guests, presentation') from قَدَّمَ (qaddama, 'to present, serve'), root ق-د-م (q-d-m).

تقدّم.etymology: Form V reflexive/mediopassive verb تَقَدَّمَ (taqaddama, 'to step forward, advance, progress; be served') from قَدَّمَ (qaddama, 'to bring forward, serve'), root ق-د-م (q-d-m).

history.meaning: to step forward; advance; be served

تقريبا.etymology: Built from the Form II masdar تقريب (bringing near, root ق-ر-ب) with the adverbial tanwiin al-fath ending -an.

تقرير.etymology: Form II verbal noun تَقْرِير (taqrīr, 'setting down, establishing, official report') from قَرَّرَ (qarrara, 'to settle, decide, report'), from قَرَّ (qarra, 'to rest, be fixed', root ق-ر-ر).

تقسيم.etymology: Form II verbal noun (maṣdar) تَقْسِيم (taqsīm, 'dividing into shares, distribution, allocation') on the pattern تَفْعِيل (tafʿīl) of قَسَّمَ (qassama, 'to divide up, apportion'), from the Semitic triliteral root ق-س-م (q-s-m, 'to divide, allot').

history.meaning: division, distribution, room/group assignment; musical improvisation

تقسيم.notes: Shared across MSA and Levantine; in Arab music, تقسيم (pl. تقاسيم) also denotes a solo modal improvisation.

تقطيع.etymology: Culinary noun تقطيع represents the Form II action noun (تَفْعِيل) from ق-ط-ع (q-ṭ-ʿ, cutting, severing, dividing). Forming the action noun of قطّع ('to cut into pieces'), it is standard in Jordanian kitchens, especially in the compound لوح تقطيع ('cutting board').

تقيل.etymology: Jordanian and urban Levantine adjective تقيل (tqīl, 'heavy'), showing the regular shift of interdental ث ṯ to stop ت t from Classical Arabic ثَقِيل (ṯaqīl, pattern فَعِيل) from ثَقُلَ (ṯaqula), root ث-ق-ل.

تقيلة.etymology: Feminine adjective on fa'iila from ثقيل (root ث-ق-ل), showing the urban Levantine stop shift th > t.

تقييم.etymology: Form II verbal noun تَقْيِيم (taqyīm, 'valuation, assessment, rating, review') from قَيَّمَ (qayyama, 'to evaluate, appraise'), denominative from قِيمَة (qīma, 'value, worth'), root ق-و-م (q-w-m).

تقّل.etymology: Levantine Form II causative verb تَقَّل (taqqal, 'to make heavy, weigh down'), reflecting Classical ثَقَّلَ (ṯaqqala) with regular urban Jordanian shift of interdental ث (ṯ) to stop ت (t), from the root ث-ق-ل (ṯ-q-l, 'weight, heaviness').

تلات.etymology: Construct numeral from Semitic root ث-ل-ث used before counted plurals, with urban shift th > t.

تلاتة.etymology: Standalone Levantine cardinal three descended from Classical ثَلَاثَة via th > t dental stop shift.

تلاتين.etymology: Colloquial decimal numeral corresponding to Classical ثَلَاثِين (root ث-ل-ث) with plural -iin ending.

تلاجة.etymology: Spoken Levantine reflex (with shift of ث ṯ to ت t) of ثَلَّاجَة (ṯallāja, 'icebox, refrigerator'), an instrumental/appliance noun on the pattern فَعَّالَة derived from ثَلْج (ṯalj, 'snow, ice'), root ث-ل-ج.

تلة.etymology: Singulative noun تَلَّة ('a hill') from collective تَلّ ('mound, hillock'), rooted in ت-ل-ل and shared across ancient Mesopotamian and Levantine topography (familiar in archaeology as 'tell', a layered settlement mound).

cognates.meaning: Middle Eastern archaeological mound, borrowed from Arabic تَلّ

تلت.etymology: Colloquial Levantine reflex of Classical Arabic ثُلْث (ṯulṯ, 'one third') and construct numeral ثَلَاث (ṯalāṯ, 'three'), showing the regular urban/rural shift of interdental ث (ṯ) to stop ت (t).

تلج.etymology: Levantine pronunciation تَلْج (talj, 'ice; snow') of Classical Arabic ثَلْج (ṯalj), inherited from Proto-Semitic `*ṯalg-` ('snow,winter ice') with regular urban Levantine shift of interdental ث (ṯ) to ت (t).

تلخبط.etymology: Colloquial quadriliteral reflexive verb تْلَخْبَط (tlaḵbaṭ, 'to get mixed up, become confused'), derived by prefixing t(a)- onto لَخْبَط (laḵbaṭ, 'to jumble, scramble'). Likely an expressive blend of خَبَطَ ('to strike/flounder') and خَلَطَ ('to mix').

history.meaning: to mix up -> to get confused

تلطيخة.etymology: Instance noun formed on the Form II pattern taf'iila from the root ل-ط-خ meaning to stain, daub, or smear.

تلفون.etymology: Modern technological loanword from French téléphone / English telephone (coined from Greek tēle 'far' + phōnē 'voice'). Integrated as a masculine noun in Jordanian Arabic, it also forms the common prepositional contraction عالتلفون ('on the phone').

تلميع.etymology: Form II verbal noun تَلْمِيع (talmīʿ, 'polishing, buffing, making shine') from لَمَّعَ (lammaʿa, 'to polish, burnish'), from لَمَعَ ('to shine, gleam'), root ل-م-ع (l-m-ʿ).

تليفون.etymology: Modern international loanword borrowed via French téléphone / English telephone (coined from Greek τῆλε 'far' + φωνή 'voice, sound').

history.meaning: apparatus for transmitting speech over distance

تم.etymology: Everyday Levantine noun تُمّ / تِمّ (tumm / timm, 'mouth, opening, spout'), evolved in Syro-Levantine Arabic from Classical فَم (fam, 'mouth') via labial assimilation or merger with ثُمّ ('orifice, mouth').

تمام.etymology: Verbal/abstract noun تَمَام (tamām, 'completeness, perfection; [in spoken Arabic] fine, all set, spot-on!') from تَمَّ (tamma, 'to be complete, finished'), root ت-م-م (t-m-m).

تماما.etymology: Adverbial accusative formed from تمام (completeness, root ت-م-م) with classical tanwin -an.

تماماً.etymology: Adverbial accusative (-an, -اً) of تَمَام (tamām, completeness, perfection), derived from the geminate root ت-م-م (t-m-m, to be whole or complete). Jordanian speakers routinely use تماماً to express total agreement or exact precision.

تمانية.etymology: Everyday Levantine numeral تمانية (tamānye, 'eight'), reflecting the regular shift of interdental ث ṯ to stop ت t from Classical ثَمَانِيَة (ṯamāniya), inherited from Proto-Semitic *ṯamāniy-, root ث-م-ن.

تمانين.etymology: Spoken Levantine reflex (with shift of ث ṯ to ت t) of Classical ثَمَانُونَ / ثَمَانِينَ (ṯamānīna, 'eighty'), decade numeral formed from ثَمَانٍ ('eight'), root ث-م-ن.

تمايل.etymology: Form VI verb تَمَايَلَ (tamāyala, 'to sway from side to side') derived from the hollow root م-ي-ل (m-y-l, 'to lean, incline'). The Form VI pattern تَفَاعَلَ (tafāʿala) gives the basic tilting motion a back-and-forth, rhythmic quality ideal for trees or hanging lanterns.

تمرن.etymology: Form V reflexive verb تَمَرَّنَ (tamarrana, 'to practice, train, exercise') from مَرَّنَ (marrana, 'to accustom, train, make supple'), root م-ر-ن (m-r-n).

تمرين.etymology: Form II verbal noun تَمْرِين (tamrīn, 'training, drilling, practice') from مرّن (marrana, 'to train, make supple'), root م-ر-ن (m-r-n, 'to be supple, accustomed'). In everyday Arabic it covers physical exercise, musical rehearsals, and school drills.

تمنى.etymology: Form V verb تَمَنَّى (tamannā, 'to wish for, desire, long for') on the pattern تَفَعَّلَ (tafaʿʿala) from the Semitic defective root م-ن-ي (m-n-y, originally 'to count out, apportion destiny; form a wish in the mind').
تمنى.notes: In MSA تمنى governs أن + subjunctive or لَوْ, whereas spoken Jordanian drops أن directly before the verb (كل بنت بتتمنى تكون مكانها, 'every girl wishes to be in her shoes').

تمنية.etymology: Levantine numeral descending from Classical Arabic ثمانية (thamaaniya) via the regular urban shift of thaa' to taa'.

تمنّى.etymology: Form V verb تَمَنَّى (tamannā, 'to wish, desire, hope for') derived from مُنْيَة (munya, 'wish, desire'), root م-ن-ي (m-n-y).

تمّ.etymology: Geminate Form I verb (فَعَّ) from the root ت-م-م (t-m-m, to be complete, accomplished, fulfilled). Paired with a verbal noun subject such as الموافقة or التوقيع, تمّ serves as a formal and semi-formal periphrastic passive in Jordanian administrative speech.

history.meaning: to be completed, come to pass

تناغم.etymology: Form VI verbal noun تَنَاغُم (tanāġum, 'mutual harmony, chiming together in tune') from the root ن-غ-م (n-ġ-m, 'musical tone, hum, melody'). Formed on تَفَاعُل, it expresses multiple voices, colours, or objects moving in pleasing unison.

تنبيه.etymology: Form II verbal noun تَنْبِيه (tanbīh, 'alerting, notice, reminder, warning') from نَبَّهَ (nabbaha, 'to awaken, draw someone's attention'), root ن-ب-ه (n-b-h, 'to notice, be alert, wake'). Used for posted notices, urgent warnings, and reminders.

history.meaning: to be aware -> to alert -> notice, reminder

تنفّس.etymology: Form V verb تَنَفَّسَ (tanaffasa, 'to breathe, draw breath') from نَفَس (nafas, 'breath'), inherited from the Proto-Semitic root ن-ف-س (*n-p-š, 'breath, soul, life').

تنين.etymology: Urban Jordanian numeral two evolved from Classical اِثْنَيْن (root ث-ن-ي) with th > t and ay > ee.

توأم.etymology: Classical Arabic تَوْأَم (tawʾam, 'twin'), inherited from Proto-Semitic *tawʾam- ('twin'), root ت-ء-م / و-ء-م.

توت.etymology: From Classical Arabic تُوت (tūt, 'mulberry, berry'), an early Near Eastern cultural word related to Aramaic תּוּתָא (tūṯā) and Middle Persian tūt.

توتّر.etymology: Form V verb تَوَتَّرَ (tawattara, 'to become taut, strained; get nervous, tense up'), denominative from وَتَر (watar, 'bowstring, lute string, tendon'), root و-ت-ر (w-t-r).

history.meaning: to be stretched taut like a string; become tense

توست.etymology: Modern culinary loanword borrowed from English toast ('sliced bread browned by radiant heat').

توصيل.etymology: Form II verbal noun تَوْصِيل (tawṣīl, 'delivering, conveying, connecting') from وَصَّلَ (waṣṣala, 'to deliver, connect'), root و-ص-ل (w-ṣ-l).

توفيق.etymology: Form II verbal noun تَوْفِيق (tawfīq, 'granting success, harmonious alignment, good fortune') from وَفَّقَ (waffaqa, 'to make successful, reconcile'), root و-ف-ق (w-f-q).

توفّى.etymology: Form V verb تَوَفَّى (tawaffā, passive تُوُفِّيَ > spoken Levantine توفى twaffā, 'to pass away, die'), originally meaning 'to receive one\'s full allotted span of life', from وَفَى ('to be complete, fulfill'), root و-ف-ي (w-f-y).

history.meaning: to fulfill one's allotted span; pass away

توقيع.etymology: Form II verbal noun تَوْقِيع (tawqīʿ, 'signature, endorsement; setting down a seal or mark') from وَقَّعَ (waqqaʿa, 'to sign, register'), root و-ق-ع (w-q-ʿ).

history.meaning: affixing a seal or mark; signature
