توقّع.etymology: Form V verb (تَفَعَّلَ, tafaʿʿala) built on the root و-ق-ع (w-q-ʿ, falling, occurring, happening). From the sense of anticipating what is about to fall or transpire, توقّع became the primary verb for 'to expect' or 'anticipate' across Jordanian Arabic.

تيتا.etymology: Affectionate Levantine kinship noun تِيتَا (tētā, 'grandma, grandmother'), formed by nursery reduplication in child speech.

ثابت.etymology: Active participle adjective ثَابِت (ṯābit, 'firm, steady, fixed, stable') from ثَبَتَ (ṯabata, 'to stand firm'), root ث-ب-ت (ṯ-b-t).

ثانية.etymology: Feminine noun from ordinal ثانية (second division of a minute, root ث-ن-ي), preserving th in educated speech.

ثبت.etymology: Form I verb ثَبَتَ (ṯabata, 'to stand firm, hold still, remain steady') from the Semitic root ث-ب-ت (ṯ-b-t, 'firmness, steadfastness').

ثبّت.etymology: Form II causative verb ثَبَّتَ (ṯabbata, 'to fasten, fix firmly in place, stabilize') from ثَبَتَ (ṯabata, 'to stand firm'), root ث-ب-ت (ṯ-b-t).

history.meaning: to fasten; fix firmly in place

ثروة.etymology: Classical abstract noun from root ث-ر-و signifying abundance, riches, and lasting fortune.

ثقيل.etymology: Standard-register adjective on fa'iil from root ث-ق-ل (weight), retaining interdental th alongside rural dialects.

ثلاثة.etymology: Formal or Bedouin/rural Jordanian numeral retaining interdental ث from the Semitic root ث-ل-ث.

ثلاثين.etymology: Plural-marked decade numeral built on ث-ل-ث, preserving classical ث in careful or rural speech.

ثمانية.etymology: Cardinal numeral eight derived from Semitic root ث-م-ن, retaining interdental ث in standard register.

ثمنطعش.etymology: Compound Levantine numeral contracted from Classical Arabic ثمانية عشر (thamaaniyata 'ashar) with pharyngealized t from عشر.

ثنائي.etymology: Nisba formation (ثُنَائِيّ, θunāʾiyy) built from the distributive numeral ثُنَاء (θunāʾ, two by two) on the root ث-ن-ي (θ-n-y, two, fold, double). Used as both an adjective ('dual, two-part') and a musical noun for a duo or duet in Jordanian cultural life.

جاب.etymology: Spoken Arabic hollow verb جَاب (jāb, 'to bring'), formed by univerbation and contraction of Classical Arabic جَاءَ بِـ (jāʾa bi-, 'to come with -> to bring'), from root ج-ي-ء + preposition بِـ.

جار.etymology: Classical Arabic جَار (jār, 'neighbor, one living next door under mutual protection'), from the root ج-و-ر (j-w-r, 'proximity, neighborhood, sanctuary').

جاف.etymology: Active participle adjective جَافّ (jāff, 'dry, arid') from the geminate verb جَفَّ (jaffa, 'to become dry'), root ج-ف-ف (j-f-f).

جاكيت.etymology: Clothing loanword borrowed from French jaquette / English jacket.

جامد.etymology: Active participle adjective جَامِد (jāmid, 'solid, firm, stiff, frozen') from جَمَدَ (jamada, 'to congeal, solidify, freeze'), root ج-م-د (j-m-d).

جامعة.etymology: Feminine noun جَامِعَة (jāmiʿa, 'university; league, gathering body'), originally the feminine active participle of جَمَعَ (jamaʿa, 'to gather, bring together') on the root ج-م-ع (j-m-c). Short for المدرسة الجامعة ('the all-encompassing school') or a translation-calque of Latin universitas ('the whole body').

جانبي.etymology: Relational (nisba) adjective جَانِبِيّ (jānibiyy, 'side, lateral') derived from جَانِب (jānib, 'side, flank'), root ج-ن-ب (j-n-b).

جاهز.etymology: Active participle adjective جَاهِز (jāhiz, 'ready, prepared, equipped') from the root ج-ه-ز (j-h-z, 'fitting out, preparing').

جاي.etymology: Spoken Levantine active participle جَاي (jāy, 'coming, arriving; next [week/time]'), from Classical جَاءٍ (jāʾin), active participle of جَاءَ (jāʾa, 'to come'), root ج-ي-ء.

جايب.etymology: Active participle (فَاعِل, fāʿil) of the Levantine hollow verb جاب (jāb, 'to bring'), itself a historical fusion of Classical جَاءَ بِـ (jāʾa bi-, 'to come with') under root ج-ي-أ (j-y-ʾ). Jordanian Arabic strongly favors جايب over a finite verb to express 'bringing' or 'having brought'.

جبان.etymology: Adjective جَبَان (jabān, 'cowardly, timid, faint-hearted') on the pattern فَعَال from جَبُنَ (jabuna, 'to be timid, shrink back'), root ج-ب-ن (j-b-n).

جبت.etymology: Colloquial 1sg/2ms past verb from جاب (root ج-ي-ب), contracted historically from Classical جَاءَ بِـ (came with).

جبل.etymology: Inherited Semitic noun جَبَل ('mountain') from the triliteral root ج-ب-ل ('to form, mould, rise as a massif'). In Amman, جبل also designates the city's historic neighbourhoods perched across rolling limestone hills (such as Jabal Amman and Jabal al-Weibdeh).

جبلي.etymology: Relational (nisba) adjective جَبَلِيّ (jabaliyy, 'mountain-, mountainous, highland') derived from جَبَل (jabal, 'mountain'), root ج-ب-ل (j-b-l).

جبنة.etymology: Singulative and mass noun جُبْنَة (jubna, 'cheese') from Classical collective جُبْن (jubn, 'cheese'), inherited from Proto-Semitic *gubn- ('curdled milk, cheese'), root ج-ب-ن (j-b-n, 'to curdle, coagulate').

جبين.etymology: Inherited Semitic body-part noun جَبِين ('forehead, brow') on the pattern فَعِيل from the root ج-ب-ن, originally denoting the prominent upper brow ridge on either side of the forehead.

جد.etymology: Conversational adverb and noun from root ج-د-د meaning earnestness, seriousness, or truth.

جدة.etymology: Feminine noun derived from the geminate root ج-د-د meaning ancestor, fortune, or greatness.

جدول.etymology: Classical Arabic جَدْوَل (jadwal, 'little stream, irrigation rill; by extension, a ruled column in a manuscript, chart, timetable, schedule'), root ج-د-و-ل / ج-د-ل.

جديد.etymology: Adjective جَدِيد (jadīd, 'new, fresh, recent') on the pattern فَعِيل from جَدَّ (jadda, 'to be new'), root ج-د-د (j-d-d).

جذع.etymology: Triliteral noun from the root ج-ذ-ع denoting a tree trunk or main stem.

جربي.etymology: Feminine singular Form II imperative of جرّب (root ج-ر-ب, to test, sample, or try out).

جرس.etymology: Classical Arabic جَرَس (jaras, 'bell, chime'), originally denoting a low ringing sound or chime, from the root ج-ر-س (j-r-s).

جريء.etymology: Adjective جَرِيء (jarīʾ, 'bold, daring, outspoken') on the pattern فَعِيل from جَرُؤَ (jaruʾa, 'to be bold, dare'), root ج-ر-ء (j-r-ʾ).

جريدة.etymology: Originally Classical Arabic جَرِيدَة (jarīda, 'stripped palm-branch stalk' used as a writing tally or dispatch roll), from root ج-ر-د ('to strip leaves/bark'); adopted in the 19th century for 'newspaper'.

جرّب.etymology: Form II verb جَرَّبَ (jarraba, 'to test, try out, try on, experiment') from the root ج-ر-ب (j-r-b, 'putting to the test').

جزء.etymology: Inherited noun on fu'l from the root ج-ز-ء signifying a portion, fraction, or section of a whole.

جزدان.etymology: Loanword entering Levantine Arabic via Ottoman Turkish cüzdan (pocketbook, folder), compounded from Arabic جزء (part, section) and Persian -dan (container).

جزر.etymology: Collective noun جَزَر ('carrots', singulative جَزَرَة), borrowed in early Islamic agricultural trade from Middle Persian gazar (modern Persian گزر gazar) when purple, yellow, and orange root carrots spread westward from the Iranian plateau across the Levant.

جسر.etymology: Classical Arabic جِسْر (jisr, 'bridge, causeway, beam'), shared with Aramaic גִּשְׁרָא (gišrā) and Akkadian gišru ('log bridge, beam'), root ج-س-ر (j-s-r).

جفاف.etymology: Abstract/verbal noun جَفَاف (jafāf, 'dryness, aridity, drought') on the pattern فَعَال from جَفَّ (jaffa, 'to become dry'), root ج-ف-ف (j-f-f).

جلد.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *gild- ('skin, hide, leather'), yielding Classical Arabic جِلْد (jild), root ج-ل-د (j-l-d).

جلدة.etymology: Singulative noun جِلْدَة (jilda, 'a piece of leather or hide; in craftsmanship, a leather, felt, or rubber washer/bushing') from جِلْد (jild, 'leather, skin'), root ج-ل-د.

جماعة.etymology: Collective feminine noun built on root ج-م-ع (to gather), widely used in vocative address in Jordan.

جمال.etymology: Abstract noun جَمَال (jamāl, 'beauty, grace, comeliness') from جَمُلَ (jamula, 'to be beautiful, handsome'), root ج-م-ل (j-m-l).

جمع.etymology: Form I verb جَمَعَ (jamaʿa, 'to gather, collect, bring together, add') from the Semitic root ج-م-ع (j-m-ʿ, 'gathering, uniting').

جمعة.etymology: Feminine noun on the pattern فُعْلَة (fuʿla) from the triliteral root ج-م-ع (j-m-ʿ, gathering, assembling). Named يَوْم الجُمُعَة ('the day of congregation') in early Islamic and Classical Arabic, it became the standard feminine weekday name for Friday across Jordan.

جملة.etymology: Noun جُمْلَة (jumla, 'sum, aggregate, whole; grammatical sentence or clause') from جَمَلَ (jamala, 'to gather into a whole, sum up'), root ج-م-ل (j-m-l).

جنب.etymology: Locative preposition derived from Classical جَانِب (side, root ج-ن-ب) by vowel shortening in dialect.

جنوب.etymology: Classical Arabic جَنُوب (janūb, 'south; south wind'), derived from the root ج-ن-ب (j-n-b, 'side, quarter of the sky').

جنون.etymology: Abstract noun on the fu'uul pattern from the geminate root ج-ن-ن (to veil, cover, or possess the mind).

جنينة.etymology: Diminutive of جَنَّة (janna, 'garden, orchard'), from the triliteral root ج-ن-ن (j-n-n) expressing covering and dense foliage shading the ground. Standard Levantine word for a courtyard or home garden.

جنّن.etymology: Form II causative verb جَنَّنَ (jannana, 'to drive mad, dazzle, captivate') from the root ج-ن-ن (j-n-n, 'to cover, hide, possess, craze'). In Levantine speech, the 3rd-person imperfect بيجنن (bijannin, literally 'it drives one crazy') is an everyday hyperbole meaning 'amazing, gorgeous, delicious'.

history.meaning: to be mad -> to drive crazy

جهة.etymology: Noun جِهَة (jiha < *wijha, 'side, direction, facing quarter'), formed with regular loss of root-initial w- from وَجْه (wajh, 'face, front'), root و-ج-ه (w-j-h).

جهّز.etymology: Form II verb جَهَّزَ (jahhaza, 'to prepare, equip, make ready'), denominative from جَهَاز (jahāz, 'equipment, outfit, gear'), root ج-ه-ز (j-h-z).

جو.etymology: Continues Classical Arabic جَوّ (jaww, 'the open air between sky and earth, interior expanse') from the geminate/hollow root ج-و-و (j-w-w); extended in modern Arabic to meteorological 'weather' and the emotional 'atmosphere / vibe' of a group.

rootFamily.gloss: inside (Levantine adverb from the same root)

جو.notes: Versatile in everyday Jordanian: الجو حلو ('the weather is nice'), نغير جو ('have a change of scenery/fun'), and مش جوي ('not my vibe / not my thing').

جوا.etymology: Spatial adverb and preposition from Classical جَوّ (interior, midst, root ج-و-و) meaning inside.

جواب.etymology: From Classical Arabic جَوَاب (jawāb, 'reply, response, answer'), verbal noun of أَجَابَ (ʾajāba, 'to answer, respond'), hollow root ج-و-ب (j-w-b, originally 'to traverse, respond back').

جوز.etymology: Classical Arabic collective noun جَوْز ('walnuts; walnut timber'), borrowed early from Middle Persian gōz ('walnut') and prized across Damascus and Amman for fine inlaid furniture and piano cabinetry (خشب جوز).

cognates.meaning: walnut, from the same Iranian source

جوعان.etymology: Adjective جَوْعَان (jawʿān > Levantine جوعان jūʿān, 'hungry') on the bodily-state pattern فَعْلَان from جَاعَ (jāʿa, 'to feel hunger'), root ج-و-ع (j-w-ʿ).

جيب.etymology: Inherited from Classical Arabic جَيْب (jayb, 'collar opening, bosom, pocket'), derived from the hollow root ج-ي-ب (j-y-b) originally referring to cutting an opening in a garment. Across Levantine Arabic it became the standard noun for a sewn trouser or coat pocket.

جيبة.etymology: Levantine singulative noun جَيْبَة (jēbe, 'pocket') from Classical جَيْب (jayb, 'bosom opening of a garment, pocket'), root ج-ي-ب (j-y-b).

جَنْب.etymology: Masculine noun جَنْب (janb, 'side, flank, edge') from the Semitic root ج-ن-ب (j-n-b, 'side, flank, ward off'). In Arabic, the noun 'side' also grammaticalized into the everyday preposition جنب ('beside, next to').

حابب.etymology: Spoken Levantine active participle حَابِب (ḥābib, feminine حَابَّة ḥābbe, 'liking, wanting, fond of'), formed by reshaping the contracted Classical geminate active participle حَابّ (ḥābb) onto the transparent uncontracted triliteral pattern فَاعِل (fāʿil) from the Semitic root ح-ب-ب (ḥ-b-b, 'love, affection').

morphemes.meaning: uncontracted Levantine active participle (m. حَابِب, f. حَابَّة)

history.meaning: would like to, wanting, liking right now

حابب.notes: Polite, softer alternative to بدي ('I want') in Jordanian conversation: حابة أحكي معك means 'I'd like to talk with you', and كنت حابة means 'I would have loved to'.

حاجب.etymology: Active participle noun حَاجِب (ḥājib, 'eyebrow; screen, chamberlain'), literally 'that which screens or shades the eye', from حَجَبَ (ḥajaba, 'to veil, screen, shield'), root ح-ج-ب (ḥ-j-b).

حادثة.etymology: Feminine active-participle noun حَادِثَة (ḥādiṯa, 'occurrence, incident, mishap', literally 'something newly happening') from حَدَثَ (ḥadaṯa, 'to happen, occur'), Semitic root ح-د-ث (ḥ-d-ṯ).

حارة.etymology: Urban noun حَارَة (ḥāra, 'neighborhood, residential quarter, lane, alley'), derived from the root ح-و-ر / ح-ي-ر ('enclosed quarter, cluster of dwellings').

history.meaning: quarter of a city; neighborhood; lane

حاسب.etymology: Form III associative verb حَاسَبَ (ḥāsaba, 'to settle accounts with someone, call to account, hold answerable') on the pattern فَاعَلَ (fāʿala) from the Semitic triliteral root ح-س-ب (ḥ-s-b, 'to count, reckon, tally').

history.meaning: to audit or reckon accounts with another
to hold accountable, make someone pay (also 'to pay a bill')

حاسب.notes: In Jordanian speech, رح نحاسبهم means 'we will hold them accountable', while at a café حاسب means 'to pay the check' and حاسبي! means 'watch out / careful!'.

حاسس.etymology: Spoken Levantine active participle حَاسِس (ḥāsis, 'feeling, sensing'), formed with regular dialectal uncontracted geminate stem from Classical حَاسّ (ḥāss), active participle of حَسَّ (ḥassa, 'to feel'), root ح-س-س.

حاسيتها.etymology: Feminine active participle حاسة (feeling, root ح-س-س) suffixed with an epenthetic y and 3fs -ha.

حاسّ.etymology: Active participle (فَاعِل, fāʿil) of the geminate verb حسّ (ḥass, 'to feel or sense') on the root ح-س-س (ḥ-s-s, perception, sensation). Rather than using the present tense verb, Jordanian speakers almost exclusively use حاسّ / حاسة for current physical or emotional feelings.

حاضر.etymology: Active participle (فَاعِل, fāʿil) from the root ح-ض-ر (ḥ-ḍ-r, to be present, attend, stand ready). Evolving from 'present and attentive', حاضر became a polite, warm Jordanian interjection meaning 'yes, right away' or 'at your service'.

morphemes.meaning: active participle used as polite interjection

history.meaning: yes, right away, consider it done!

حاطط.etymology: Spoken Levantine active participle حَاطِط (ḥāṭiṭ, 'putting, having placed or packed'), formed with uncontracted geminate stem from Classical حَاطّ (ḥāṭṭ), active participle of حَطَّ (ḥaṭṭa, 'to put, set down'), root ح-ط-ط.

حافة.etymology: From Classical Arabic حَافَّة (ḥāffa, 'rim, edge, border, brink'), from حَفَّ (ḥaffa, 'to surround, border, edge'), geminate root ح-ف-ف (ḥ-f-f).

حال.etymology: Classical Arabic حَال (ḥāl, 'condition, state, circumstance; [in Levantine with pronoun suffixes] oneself') from حَالَ (ḥāla, 'to turn, shift, change state'), root ح-و-ل (ḥ-w-l).

حالة.etymology: Feminine noun from the hollow root ح-و-ل (to turn, change state), referring to a condition or situation.

حاليا.etymology: Adverbial accusative حَالِيًّا (ḥāliyyan, 'at present, currently, for now') from the relational adjective حَالِيّ (ḥāliyy, 'present, current'), derived from حَال ('present state', root ح-و-ل).

حامض.etymology: Active participle functioning as an adjective from the root ح-م-ض meaning to be sour or acidic.

حامل.etymology: Active participle noun حَامِل (ḥāmil, 'carrier, bearer; music stand, holder, rack') from حَمَلَ (ḥamala, 'to carry, bear, hold up'), root ح-م-ل (ḥ-m-l).

حاول.etymology: Form III verb حَاوَلَ (ḥāwala, 'to try, attempt, endeavor') from the root ح-و-ل (ḥ-w-l, 'shifting, seeking a way or means [حِيلَة]').

history.meaning: to seek a way; attempt; try

حب.etymology: Form I (and Classical Form IV أَحَبَّ) geminate verb حَبَّ (ḥabba, 'to love, like, hold dear'), inherited from the Proto-Semitic root ح-ب-ب (*ḥ-b-b, 'to love, cherish').

حبة.etymology: Singulative noun حَبَّة (ḥabba, 'a single grain, seed, berry, pill; a single piece or item') from collective حَبّ (ḥabb, 'grain, seed, kernels'), root ح-ب-ب (ḥ-b-b).

حبر.etymology: Classical Arabic noun from root ح-ب-ر (associated with adorning or writing) denoting writing ink.

حبس.etymology: Form I verb حَبَسَ (ḥabasa, 'to hold back, confine, detain, trap'), from the Semitic root ح-ب-س (ḥ-b-s, cognate with Hebrew חָבַשׁ ḥāḇaš 'to bind, confine').

حبل.etymology: Common Semitic noun حَبْل (ḥabl, 'rope, cord'), cognate with Hebrew ḥeḇel ('cord, measuring line'), Aramaic ḥaḇlā, and Akkadian eblu. Derived from the root ح-ب-ل (ḥ-b-l, 'to bind, snare'), it is one of the oldest everyday Arabic words for cordage.

حبيب.etymology: Adjective and affectionate noun حَبِيب (ḥabīb, 'beloved, dear, darling') on the pattern فَعِيل from حَبَّ (ḥabba, 'to love'), root ح-ب-ب (ḥ-b-b).

حبيبتيفي.etymology: Orthographic fusion of حبيبتي (my darling, root ح-ب-ب) and the preposition في (in).

حبّ.etymology: Colloquial Form I reflex of Classical Form IV أَحَبَّ (ʾaḥabba) and Form I حَبَّ on the geminate root ح-ب-ب (ḥ-b-b, love, affection, preference). In Jordanian speech, حبّ handles both deep affection ('to love') and polite everyday offers via بتحب ('would you like?').

حتى.etymology: Classical particle and conjunction حَتَّى preserved unchanged in Levantine Arabic to mark limits or inclusion.

حجار.etymology: Broken plural pattern fi'aal/fa'aal of حجر (stone, root ح-ج-ر), standard in colloquial Jordanian.

حجر.etymology: Semitic concrete noun from root ح-ج-ر meaning stone or rock, identical in Classical and Levantine Arabic.

حجري.etymology: Relational (nisba) adjective حَجَرِيّ (ḥajariyy, 'made of stone, stony') derived from حَجَر (ḥajar, 'stone') + -ِيّ (-iyy), root ح-ج-ر.

حجز.etymology: Form I verbal noun حَجْز (ḥajz, 'holding back, setting aside, booking, reservation') from حَجَزَ (ḥajaza, 'to separate, hold back, reserve'), root ح-ج-ز (ḥ-j-z).

حد.etymology: Geminate noun from root ح-د-د meaning edge, limit, or boundary, used literally and figuratively.

حدا.etymology: Indefinite pronoun evolved from Classical أَحَد (one, someone, root أ-ح-د) via initial vowel loss.

حدعش.etymology: Spoken Levantine compound numeral حْدَعْش (ḥdaʿš, 'eleven'), contracted from Classical أَحَدَ عَشَرَ (ʾaḥada ʿašara, 'one-teen') via aphesis of initial ʾa- and reduction of -ʿašar to -ʿš.

حديث.etymology: Adjective حَدِيث (ḥadīṯ, 'new, recent, modern') on the pattern فَعِيل from حَدَثَ (ḥadaṯa, 'to happen newly, be young/new'), inherited from Proto-Semitic *ḥadaṯ- ('new'), root ح-د-ث.

حديد.etymology: Material noun from root ح-د-د (originally meaning sharp or edged) denoting the metal iron.

حديقة.etymology: From Classical Arabic حَدِيقَة (ḥadīqa, 'walled garden, orchard, park'), originally 'an enclosed piece of greenery' from حَدَقَ (ḥadaqa, 'to surround, enclose'), root ح-د-ق (ḥ-d-q).

حذاء.etymology: Classical Arabic حِذَاء ('shoe, footwear', plural أَحْذِيَة) from the root ح-ذ-و ('place sole-to-sole, cut leather to match the foot's outline'), originally naming a strapped leather sandal cut to the exact measure of its wearer.

حذوة.etymology: Feminine noun حَذْوَة (ḥaḏwa, 'horseshoe') from the root ح-ذ-و (ḥ-ḏ-w, 'to fit footwear, cut to match'), the same root that yields حِذَاء (ḥiḏāʾ, 'shoe'). In Arabic usage, حذوة specifically refers to the iron shoe nailed onto a horse's hoof.

حرارة.etymology: Abstract noun حَرَارَة (ḥarāra, 'heat, warmth, temperature') on the pattern فَعَالَة from حَرَّ (ḥarra, 'to be hot, warm'), inherited from Proto-Semitic *ḥarār- ('to burn, be hot'), root ح-ر-ر.

حرام.etymology: In Levantine household usage, حْرَام (ḥrām, 'woolen bed blanket'), shortened from Classical إِحْرَام (iḥrām, 'seamless woolen wrap or cloak'); homographic with Classical حَرَام (ḥarām, 'forbidden, sacred; a pity!'), both from the Semitic root ح-ر-م (ḥ-r-m).

حرامي.etymology: Derived from حرام (forbidden, unlawful, root ح-ر-م) with the nisba suffix -i, literally one who engages in unlawful taking.

حرف.etymology: Classical Arabic حَرْف (ḥarf, 'sharp edge, border, rim; letter of the alphabet, grammatical particle'), from the root ح-ر-ف (ḥ-r-f, 'edge, turning aside').

history.meaning: edge; border; letter of the alphabet

حرفة.etymology: From Classical Arabic حِرْفَة (ḥirfa, 'craft, trade, occupation, handiwork'), pattern فِعْلَة from حَرَفَ (ḥarafa, 'to turn to, earn a livelihood'), root ح-ر-ف (ḥ-r-f).

حرق.etymology: Form I verb حَرَقَ (ḥaraqa, 'to burn, scorch, scald') from the root ح-ر-ق (ḥ-r-q, 'fire, burn, rub friction'). In everyday kitchen speech, بتحرق ('it burns') describes food or pans that are piping hot.

حرك.etymology: Form II transitive verb حَرَّكَ (ḥarraka, 'to move, stir, set in motion, wiggle') from حَرُكَ (ḥaruka, 'to be in motion'), root ح-ر-ك (ḥ-r-k).

history.meaning: to set in motion; move; stir

حركة.etymology: Continues Classical Arabic حَرَكَة (ḥaraka, 'movement, motion, vowel mark') on the pattern فَعَلَة (faʿala) from the triliteral root ح-ر-ك (ḥ-r-k, 'to move, stir').

history.meaning: move, gesture; in colloquial plural حَرَكَات, 'antics, stunts, attitude'

حركة.notes: In Jordanian teen and family talk, بلا هالحركات or بطلي حركاتك means 'cut out those stunts / mind games / attitude!'.

حرّك.etymology: Causative Form II verb (فَعَّلَ, faʿʿala) built from the triliteral root ح-ر-ك (ḥ-r-k, motion, movement, stirring). Used identically across Classical and Levantine Arabic, حرّك means 'to set in motion' and is the standard kitchen verb for stirring pots and sauces.

history.meaning: to move, stir, set in motion

حزر.etymology: Form I verb حَزَرَ (ḥazara, 'to estimate, conjecture, guess'), root ح-ز-ر (ḥ-z-r).

حس.etymology: Form I (and Form IV أَحَسَّ) geminate verb حَسَّ (ḥassa, 'to feel, sense, perceive'), from the Semitic root ح-س-س (ḥ-s-s, 'feeling, perception, faint sound').

حساب.etymology: Verbal and concrete noun حِسَاب (ḥisāb, 'reckoning, calculation, bill, account') from حَسَبَ (ḥasaba, 'to count, reckon, compute'), root ح-س-ب (ḥ-s-b).

حساباتي.etymology: Sound feminine plural حسابات (calculations, root ح-س-ب) with the 1sg possessive suffix -i.

حسب.etymology: Form I verb حَسَبَ (ḥasaba, 'to count, calculate, reckon') and حَسِبَ (ḥasiba, 'to suppose, deem') inherited from Proto-Semitic root ح-س-ب (ḥ-s-b, 'counting, reckoning, esteeming').

history.meaning: to number, compute, take into account
to count, calculate; in حسب حساب, to reckon cautiously with

حسب.notes: Idiomatic gem: الكل بحسب إلها ألف حساب ('everyone counts a thousand accounts for her') means everyone walks on eggshells around her and thinks twice before crossing her.

حسن.etymology: Abstract masculine noun حُسْن (ḥusn, 'goodness, beauty, excellence') from حَسُنَ (ḥasuna, 'to be good, handsome, fine'), root ح-س-ن (ḥ-s-n). Preserved especially in formal and semi-formal phrases such as لحسن الحظ ('fortunately').

حسّس.etymology: Form II causative verb حَسَّسَ (ḥassasa, 'to cause someone to feel, touch gently') from حَسَّ (ḥassa, 'to feel, perceive'), Semitic root ح-س-س (ḥ-s-s).

حصان.etymology: From Classical Arabic حِصَان (ḥiṣān, 'stallion, noble horse'), derived from the root ح-ص-ن (ḥ-ṣ-n, 'to be strong, fortified, inaccessible'). Originally naming a prized, well-guarded stallion, it became the standard everyday singular word for 'horse' across spoken Levantine Arabic.

حضرة.etymology: Feminine noun on the pattern فَعْلَة (faʿla) from the root ح-ض-ر (ḥ-ḍ-r, presence, attendance). Literally meaning 'presence', Classical and Ottoman-era administrative usage elevated حضرة into an honorific title ('Your/Esteemed Presence') that remains common in Jordanian polite address (حضرتك).

حضرتك.etymology: Polite second-person honorific pronoun حَضْرَتُكَ (ḥaḍratuka > Levantine ḥaḍritak [m.] / ḥaḍirtik [f.], 'you, sir/ma\'am'), literally 'your presence', from حَضْرَة (ḥaḍra, 'presence, dignity', root ح-ض-ر) + possessive suffix -كَ (-ka).

حط.etymology: Form I geminate verb حَطَّ (ḥaṭṭa, 'to put down, place, set, lower'), from the root ح-ط-ط (ḥ-ṭ-ṭ).

حطّ.etymology: Geminate Form I verb (فَعَّ) from the root ح-ط-ط (ḥ-ṭ-ṭ, to set down, unload, lower). Narrowing from the Classical sense of setting down a camel's load, حطّ replaced وضع as the primary everyday verb for 'to put' or 'place' across Jordan and the Levant.

حظ.etymology: From Classical Arabic حَظّ (ḥaẓẓ, 'share, lot, portion, good fortune, luck'), geminate root ح-ظ-ظ (ḥ-ẓ-ẓ, 'to be fortunate, allotted a share').

حفة.etymology: Dialectal pronunciation of Classical حَافَّة (rim, edge, border) from the geminate root ح-ف-ف.

حفته.etymology: Noun حفة (edge, root ح-ف-ف) in construct state with the 3ms possessive pronoun -o/-hu.

حفر.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *ḥapar- ('to dig, excavate'), yielding Classical Arabic حَفَرَ (ḥafara, 'to dig, carve, wear a groove in'), root ح-ف-ر (ḥ-f-r).

حفرتوا.etymology: Second-person plural past verb from حفر (root ح-ف-ر, to dig) carrying the dialectal suffix -tu.

حفظ.etymology: Form I verbal noun حِفْظ (ḥifẓ, 'safekeeping, preservation, guarding, learning by heart') from حَفِظَ (ḥafiẓa, 'to guard, keep safe, preserve'), root ح-ف-ظ (ḥ-f-ẓ).

حفلة.etymology: Instance and concrete noun حَفْلَة (ḥafla, 'gathering, celebration, party, concert') from حَفَلَ (ḥafala, 'to gather in a crowd, assemble'), root ح-ف-ل (ḥ-f-l).

حفيد.etymology: Kinship noun حَفِيد (ḥafīd, 'grandson, grandchild') on the pattern فَعِيل from حَفَدَ (ḥafada, 'to walk briskly in service, attend upon elders in the household'), root ح-ف-د (ḥ-f-d).

حق.etymology: Classical Arabic حَقّ (ḥaqq, 'truth, right, just claim, due price') from حَقَّ (ḥaqqa, 'to be true, right, binding'), from the Proto-Semitic root ح-ق-ق (*ḥ-q-q, 'to cut/inscribe a law, be rightful').

حققت.etymology: Form II 3fs past verb from حقّق (root ح-ق-ق, to realize or verify) with feminine -at.

حقيقة.etymology: Feminine noun حَقِيقَة (ḥaqīqa, 'truth, reality, fact') on the pattern فَعِيلَة from حَقَّ (ḥaqqa, 'to be true, real, established'), root ح-ق-ق (ḥ-q-q).

حقيقي.etymology: Relational (nisba) adjective حَقِيقِيّ (ḥaqīqiyy, 'real, true, genuine, authentic') derived from حَقِيقَة (ḥaqīqa, 'truth, reality'), root ح-ق-ق.

حك.etymology: Form I geminate verb حَكَّ (ḥakka, 'to rub, scrape, scratch; itch'), inherited from Proto-Semitic *ḥakak- ('to scratch, rub'), root ح-ك-ك (ḥ-k-k).

حكالي.etymology: Contracts the past verb حكى (root ح-ك-ي, to tell) with the dative prepositional clitic لي (to me).

حكم.etymology: Form I verb حَكَمَ (ḥakama, 'to pass judgment, rule, restrain') inherited from Proto-Semitic root ح-ك-م (ḥ-k-m, 'wisdom, arbitration, restraint').

history.meaning: to judge (with على, 'to judge someone'), rule

حكم.notes: Takes على for judging people or appearances (لا تحكمي عالناس بسرعة, 'don't judge people quickly').

حكى.etymology: Form I verb حَكَى (ḥakā, 'to relate, recount, narrate; [in Levantine] to speak, talk, tell'), from the root ح-ك-ي (ḥ-k-y).

حكي.etymology: Verbal noun حَكْي (ḥaky > Levantine حَكِي ḥakī, 'talk, speech, words') from حَكَى (ḥakā, 'to speak, tell'), root ح-ك-ي (ḥ-k-y).

حكيم.etymology: Adjective حَكِيم (ḥakīm, 'wise, judicious, sensible; sage') on the pattern فَعِيل from حَكُمَ (ḥakuma, 'to be wise, exercise sound judgment'), inherited from Proto-Semitic *ḥakam- ('to be wise'), root ح-ك-م.

حل.etymology: Geminate Form I verb built on the root ح-ل-ل, carrying the core meaning of loosening, untying, and by extension resolving a problem.

حلق.etymology: Continues Classical Arabic anatomical noun حَلْق (ḥalq, 'throat, pharynx, gullet') on the pattern فَعْل (faʿl) from the Semitic triliteral root ح-ل-ق (ḥ-l-q, 'ring, circular throat passage; also to shave smooth').

history.meaning: throat; colloquially inside of the mouth/throat

حلق.notes: In MSA التهاب الحلق means 'sore throat', while in Jordanian idioms جوا حلقك ('inside your throat/mouth') intensifies commands to keep quiet.

حلقة.etymology: Noun حَلْقَة / حَلَقَة (ḥalqa, 'ring, circular link, metal washer; circle of people; series episode') from the root ح-ل-ق (ḥ-l-q, 'circle, ring').

حلم.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *ḥulm- ('dream, vision in sleep'), yielding Classical Arabic حُلْم (ḥulm), root ح-ل-م (ḥ-l-m).

حلموا.etymology: Past tense 3pl conjugation built on حلم (root ح-ل-م, to dream) with plural suffix -uu.

حلو.etymology: Common adjective descended from root ح-ل-و signifying sweetness in taste as well as pleasantness or beauty.

حلي.etymology: Stative defective Form I verb (فَعِلَ) from the root ح-ل-و (ḥ-l-w, sweetness, pleasantness, beauty), sharing its root with حلو ('sweet'). In Levantine Arabic, حلي describes fruit ripening to sweetness, onions caramelizing, or situations growing pleasanter.

حليب.etymology: From the Proto-Semitic dairy root ح-ل-ب (*ḥ-l-b, 'to milk'), formed on the pattern فَعيل ('freshly milked milk').
حليب.notes: Whereas Classical لبن meant fresh milk, in Levantine Arabic حليب means fresh milk while لبن denotes yoghurt.

حمام.etymology: Noun حَمَّام (ḥammām, 'bath, bathhouse, bathroom') on the pattern فَعَّال from the Proto-Semitic root ح-م-م (*ḥ-m-m, 'to be hot, heat water').

حماية.etymology: Form I verbal noun حِمَايَة (ḥimāya, 'protection, safeguarding, defense') from حَمَى (ḥamā, 'to protect, guard, defend'), root ح-م-ي (ḥ-m-y).

حمد.etymology: Form I verbal noun حَمْد (ḥamd, 'praise, commendation, thankfulness', as in الحَمْدُ لِلّٰهِ 'praise be to God / thank goodness') from حَمِدَ (ḥamida, 'to praise, thank'), root ح-م-د (ḥ-m-d).

حمر.etymology: Broken plural colour adjective on the pattern fu'ul/fu'l from root ح-م-ر (redness).

حمض.etymology: Built on the triliteral root ح-م-ض (sourness, acidity), denoting the process of becoming sour or fermenting.

حمل.etymology: Form I verb حَمَلَ (ḥamala, 'to carry, bear, lift, hold up'), inherited from the Semitic root ح-م-ل (ḥ-m-l, 'carrying, bearing a load').

حملة.etymology: Noun of instance from the root ح-م-ل (to carry, launch an attack or effort), specialized for organized drives and expeditions.

حمّى.etymology: Form II transitive verb حَمَّى (ḥammā, 'to heat up, warm an oven or dish') derived from the root ح-م-ي / ح-م-م (ḥ-m-y, 'hot, feverish, glowing'). Pairs with Form I حَمِيَ ('to become hot').

history.meaning: to grow hot -> to heat up

حواجبك.etymology: Broken plural حواجب (from sg. حاجب, root ح-ج-ب meaning arch/shield above the eye) plus 2ms -ak.

حوالي.etymology: Spatial preposition stemming from the hollow root ح-و-ل (to surround, turn around), related to Classical Arabic حول.

حوالين.etymology: Levantine spatial preposition evolved from Classical حَوْلَ (root ح-و-ل) plus the dual-like ending -ayn.

حوض.etymology: From Classical Arabic حَوْض (ḥawḍ, 'cistern, watering trough, basin'), from the hollow root ح-و-ض (ḥ-w-ḍ, 'to collect water'). Found throughout traditional Arab courtyard architecture to name the central carved stone water basin.

حوّل.etymology: Form II causative verb حَوَّلَ (ḥawwala, 'to turn, shift, convert, transform, transfer') from حَالَ (ḥāla, 'to change state, shift'), root ح-و-ل (ḥ-w-l).

حي.etymology: Classical Arabic حَيّ (ḥayy, 'kinship group, encampment, urban quarter, neighborhood district'), derived from the Semitic root ح-ي-ي (ḥ-y-y, 'life, living community').

حياة.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *ḥayy-at- ('life'), spelled in Classical orthography as حَيَوٰة / حَيَاة (ḥayāh), root ح-ي-ي (ḥ-y-y).

حيط.etymology: Spoken Levantine noun حَيْط (ḥēṭ, 'wall'; plural حِيطَان ḥīṭān), contracted from Classical حَائِط (ḥāʾiṭ, 'enclosing wall'), originally the active participle of حَاطَ (ḥāṭa, 'to surround, enclose, guard'), root ح-و-ط.

حَجَز.etymology: Form I verb حَجَزَ (ḥajaza, 'to hold back, set aside, book, reserve; vocalized to distinguish the verb from the noun حَجْز'), root ح-ج-ز (ḥ-j-z).

history.meaning: to hold back; set aside; reserve

حَمْل.etymology: Form I verbal noun حَمْل (ḥaml, 'carrying, bearing, load') from حَمَلَ (ḥamala, 'to carry, lift'), root ح-م-ل (ḥ-m-l). Distinct in vocalization from حِمْل ('burden/cargo'), though both derive from the same root.

حَيّ.etymology: Adjective حَيّ (ḥayy, 'alive, living, live; vocalized with shadda to distinguish it from the homographic noun حَيّ "quarter"'), inherited from Proto-Semitic *ḥayy- ('alive, living'), root ح-ي-ي.

حِفِظ.etymology: Form I verb حَفِظَ (ḥafiẓa > Levantine حِفِظ ḥifiẓ, 'to keep safe, preserve, hold onto, memorize; vocalized to distinguish the verb from the verbal noun حِفْظ'), root ح-ف-ظ (ḥ-f-ẓ).

history.meaning: to guard; keep safe; preserve; memorize

حِلِم.etymology: Form I verb حَلَمَ (ḥalama > Levantine حِلِم ḥilim, 'to dream; vocalized to distinguish the verb from the noun حُلْم "dream"'), inherited from Proto-Semitic *ḥalam- ('to dream'), root ح-ل-م.

خارجي.etymology: Relational (nisba) adjective خَارِجِيّ (ḫārijiyy, 'outer, exterior, outside') derived from خَارِج (ḫārij, 'outside, exterior', active participle of خَرَجَ 'to go out'), root خ-ر-ج (ḫ-r-j).

خاص.etymology: Active participle adjective خَاصّ (ḫāṣṣ, 'special, private, particular, exclusive') from the geminate verb خَصَّ (ḫaṣṣa, 'to single out, belong specifically to'), root خ-ص-ص (ḫ-ṣ-ṣ).

خاف.etymology: Hollow Form I stative verb خَافَ (ḫāfa < *ḫawifa, 'to fear, be afraid, worry'), from the root خ-و-ف (ḫ-w-f, 'fear, dread').

خانوم.etymology: Borrowed into Levantine Arabic from Ottoman Turkish hanım (lady, madam), originally a feminine title derived from Turko-Mongol khan.

خايف.etymology: Spoken Levantine active participle (خَايِف ḫāyif, 'afraid, scared'), regular colloquial continuation of Classical Arabic خَائِف (ḫāʾif) on the pattern فَاعِل (fāʿil) of the hollow verb خَافَ (ḫāfa, 'to fear, be afraid'), root خ-و-ف (ḫ-w-f), with medial hamza (ئ) shifting to palatal glide ي (y).
خايف.notes: Takes من before what one fears (خايفة منها) or a subjunctive clause for 'worried lest...' (خايفة تفضحنا, 'I'm afraid she'll expose us').

خباز.etymology: Occupational noun خَبَّاز (ḫabbāz, 'baker') on the professional pattern فَعَّال from خَبَزَ (ḫabaza, 'to bake bread'), root خ-ب-ز (ḫ-b-z).

خبر.etymology: Classical Arabic خَبَر (ḫabar, 'news, report, tidings, piece of information') from the root خ-ب-ر (ḫ-b-r, 'knowing by experience, informing').

خبز.etymology: From the triliteral root خ-ب-ز (kh-b-z, 'to bake bread'), common across Arabic and Ethiopian Semitic.
خبز.notes: Fresh morning خبز is a staple of every Jordanian breakfast table.

خبط.etymology: Form I verb خَبَطَ (ḫabaṭa, 'to strike, beat, knock or bump into'), inherited from the Semitic root خ-ب-ط (ḫ-b-ṭ, 'beating, striking').

خبوا.etymology: Plural imperative of Form II خبّى (from root خ-ب-أ, to conceal), dropping final glottal stop.

خبّاز.etymology: Intensive occupational noun built on the classic pattern فَعَّال (faʿʿāl) from the root خ-ب-ز (x-b-z, to bake bread). Denoting someone who repeatedly or professionally performs an action, خبّاز remains the standard word across Jordan for a baker.

خبّر.etymology: Form II verb خَبَّرَ (ḫabbara, 'to inform, tell, report news to someone') from خَبَر (ḫabar, 'news, report'), root خ-ب-ر (ḫ-b-r).

خبّى.etymology: Spoken Levantine Form II verb خَبَّى (ḫabbā, 'to hide, conceal, put away safely'), from Classical خَبَّأَ (ḫabbaʾa) via regular loss of final glottal stop, root خ-ب-ء (ḫ-b-ʾ).

ختم.etymology: Classical Arabic خَتْم (ḫatm, 'seal, stamp, signet impression'), from the Semitic root خ-ت-م (ḫ-t-m, 'to seal, stamp, conclude'), ultimately an ancient borrowing from Egyptian ḫtm ('seal, signet ring; to seal').

خجل.etymology: Form I stative verb خَجِلَ (ḫajila, 'to feel shy, be bashful or embarrassed'), from the root خ-ج-ل (ḫ-j-l, 'shyness, bashfulness').

history.meaning: to feel shy; be abashed or embarrassed

خدش.etymology: Verbal noun and concrete noun from triliteral root خ-د-ش denoting scraping, grazing, or scratching.

خدع.etymology: Form I verb خَدَعَ (ḫadaʿa, 'to deceive, trick, fool, mislead'), from the root خ-د-ع (ḫ-d-ʿ, 'concealing, deceiving').

خدعة.etymology: Feminine instance noun on the pattern فُعْلَة (fuʿla) derived from the root خ-د-ع (x-d-ʿ, to deceive, conceal, outwit). In everyday Jordanian speech, خدعة refers equally to a clever magic/optical trick and a dishonest scheme.

خدم.etymology: Form I verb خَدَمَ (ḫadama, 'to serve, attend upon, work in service'), from the root خ-د-م (ḫ-d-m).

خدمة.etymology: Noun خِدْمَة (ḫidma, 'service, attendance, helpful turn') from خَدَمَ (ḫadama, 'to serve'), root خ-د-م (ḫ-d-m).

خدوها.etymology: Imperative plural خذوا (root أ-خ-ذ, to take, with loss of initial hamza) plus 3fs object -ha.

خرب.etymology: Form I stative/intransitive verb خَرِبَ (ḫariba, 'to fall into ruin; [in Levantine] to break down, stop working, spoil'), from the Proto-Semitic root خ-ر-ب (*ḫ-r-b, 'ruin, desolation').

history.meaning: to fall into ruin; break down

خربان.etymology: Adjective formed on the fa'laan pattern from the root خ-ر-ب (to be ruined or out of order), standard across Levantine speech.

خربطة.etymology: Colloquial Levantine feminine noun خَرْبَطَة (ḵarbaṭa, 'mix-up, mess, jumble, confusion'), verbal noun of the quadriliteral verb خَرْبَطَ (ḵarbaṭa, 'to scramble, mess up'). Expressive colloquial formation likely blending خَرَبَ ('to ruin') and لَخْبَطَ / خَبَطَ ('to mix/jumble').

خردوات.etymology: Plural noun خُرْدَوَات (ḫurdawāt, 'hardware, small metal wares, sundries'), borrowed via Ottoman Turkish hırdavat from Persian خُرْدَه (xurda, 'small piece, fragment, retail item') with the Arabic feminine plural ending -āt.

history.meaning: small items; retail hardware and sundries

خريطة.etymology: Classical borrowing related to Latin charta / Greek khartes (papyrus sheet), integrated into root خ-ر-ط.

خريف.etymology: Derived on pattern فَعِيل from root خ-ر-ف (ḫ-r-f, 'to pluck ripe fruit from trees'): originally the autumn fruit-picking and harvest season.

خرّب.etymology: Form II causative verb خَرَّبَ (ḫarraba, 'to ruin, wreck, break [something]') from خَرِبَ (ḫariba, 'to break down, fall into ruin'), root خ-ر-ب (ḫ-r-b).

خزانة.etymology: Noun of place/instrument خِزَانَة (ḫizāna, 'cupboard, closet, wardrobe, cabinet; treasury') from خَزَنَ (ḫazana, 'to store, lay up for safekeeping'), root خ-ز-ن (ḫ-z-n).

خزف.etymology: Classical Arabic خَزَف (ḫazaf, 'pottery, earthenware, glazed ceramic or porcelain'), cognate with Aramaic חַסְפָּא (ḥaspā) and Akkadian ḫaṣbu ('pottery, terra cotta'), root خ-ز-ف.

خزين.etymology: Noun خَزِين (ḫazīn, 'stored provisions, pantry stock, larder') on the passive-sense pattern فَعِيل ('that which is stored away') from خَزَنَ (ḫazana, 'to store'), root خ-ز-ن (ḫ-z-n).

خسارة.etymology: From Classical Arabic خَسَارَة (ḫasāra, 'loss, damage, regret'), verbal noun of خَسِرَ (ḫasira, 'to lose, suffer loss'), Semitic root خ-س-ر (ḫ-s-r).

خسر.etymology: Form I verb خَسِرَ (ḫasira, 'to suffer loss, lose a stake or possession, go astray') on the pattern فَعِلَ (faʿila) from Proto-Semitic root خ-س-ر (ḫ-s-r, 'diminution, shortage, loss').

history.meaning: to incur loss in trade or life, forfeit
to lose (a game, friend, status, or everything — NOT misplacing an object)

خسر.notes: Learner distinction: خسر means forfeiting a match, money, reputation, or friendship (تخسر كل إشي), whereas misplacing physical keys or a phone in Jordanian is ضيّع (ḍayyaʿ).

خشب.etymology: Inherited Semitic collective noun on the root خ-ش-ب denoting timber, lumber, or wood.

خشبي.etymology: Nisba relational adjective formed by suffixing -ī (-ي) to خَشَب (xašab, wood, timber), from the root خ-ش-ب (x-š-b, rough-hewn timber). Widely used in Jordanian Arabic to describe furniture, utensils, and architectural trim made of wood.

خصم.etymology: Verbal noun خَصْم (ḫaṣm, 'deduction, price discount; adversary') from خَصَمَ (ḫaṣama, 'to deduct from an account; contend with'), root خ-ص-م (ḫ-ṣ-m).

خصوص.etymology: Verbal noun خُصُوص (ḫuṣūṣ, 'particularity, specialness; [in بِخُصُوص] regarding, concerning') from خَصَّ (ḫaṣṣa, 'to single out, concern specifically'), root خ-ص-ص (ḫ-ṣ-ṣ).

خصوصاً.etymology: Adverbial accusative (-an, -اً) of خُصُوص (xuṣūṣ, particularity, specialness), a verbal noun built on the geminate root خ-ص-ص (x-ṣ-ṣ, to single out, distinguish). Retained intact from Classical prose, خصوصاً is the everyday Jordanian adverb for 'especially'.

خضار.etymology: Collective noun خُضَار (ḫuḍār, 'greens, fresh vegetables') derived from the Semitic root خ-ض-ر (ḫ-ḍ-r, 'greenness, fresh herbs and vegetation').

خط.etymology: Geminate noun from root خ-ط-ط (to trace or furrow), serving for drawn lines, routes, and handwriting.

خطاب.etymology: Verbal and concrete noun خِطَاب (ḫiṭāb, 'speech, public address, formal letter') from خَاطَبَ (ḫāṭaba, 'to address, speak to'), root خ-ط-ب (ḫ-ṭ-b).

خطة.etymology: Noun خُطَّة (ḫuṭṭa, 'plan, course of action, laid-out design'), originally a plot of land or course marked out with lines, from خَطَّ (ḫaṭṭa, 'to trace lines'), root خ-ط-ط (ḫ-ṭ-ṭ).

خطط.etymology: Form II denominative/intensive verb خَطَّطَ (ḫaṭṭaṭa, 'to draw lines, mark out boundaries, map out a plan') on the pattern فَعَّلَ (faʿʿala) from خَطّ (ḫaṭṭ, 'line, furrow, script'), geminate Semitic root خ-ط-ط (ḫ-ṭ-ṭ).

morphemes.meaning: carve or draw a line, mark out
Form II verb ('sketch out lines -> plan')

history.meaning: line -> to streak with lines, lay out urban plots

خطط.notes: Uncontracted in Form II because the middle radical is geminated (خَطَّطَ), unlike Form I خَطَّ ('to write/draw a line').

خطوة.etymology: Instance noun (ism marra) formed on root خ-ط-و denoting a single stride, pace, or step.

خطوط.etymology: Broken plural on the fu'uul pattern built from خط (line, root خ-ط-ط).

خطّط.etymology: Form II verb خَطَّطَ (ḫaṭṭaṭa, 'to draw lines, lay out a design, plan') from خَطّ (ḫaṭṭ, 'line'), root خ-ط-ط (ḫ-ṭ-ṭ).

history.meaning: to mark with lines; design; plan

خف.etymology: Form I geminate verb خَفَّ (ḫaffa, 'to be light in weight, become lighter, ease off, subside'), from the Semitic root خ-ف-ف (ḫ-f-f, 'lightness').

history.meaning: to be light; lessen; ease off

خفة.etymology: Feminine abstract noun خِفَّة (ḵiffa, 'lightness, deftness, gentleness') from خَفَّ (ḵaffa, 'to be light in weight'), geminate root خ-ف-ف (ḵ-f-f). With بـ, بخفة means 'lightly, gently, deftly'.

خفق.etymology: Form I verb خَفَقَ (ḫafaqa, 'to beat, throb, flutter; in cooking, to whisk or whip eggs and cream until light'), root خ-ف-ق (ḫ-f-q).

خفنا.etymology: First-person plural past tense of hollow verb خاف (root خ-و-ف, to fear), shortening medial vowel before -na.

خفيف.etymology: Adjective خَفِيف (ḫafīf, 'light in weight, mild, gentle, nimble') on the pattern فَعِيل from خَفَّ (ḫaffa, 'to be light'), root خ-ف-ف (ḫ-f-f).

خفيفة.etymology: Feminine singular adjective on fa'iila from the geminate root خ-ف-ف (lightness, agility).

خفّف.etymology: Form II causative verb خَفَّفَ (ḫaffafa, 'to lighten, reduce, tone down, soften') from خَفَّ (ḫaffa, 'to be light'), root خ-ف-ف (ḫ-f-f).

خل.etymology: Collective noun خَلّ ('vinegar') from the geminate Semitic root خ-ل-ل ('turn sour, ferment acidly'), naming wine or cider soured into household vinegar.

خلاف.etymology: Form III verbal noun خِلَاف (ḫilāf, 'disagreement, difference, variance, dispute') from خَالَفَ (ḫālafa, 'to differ with, go contrary to'), root خ-ل-ف (ḫ-l-f).

خلال.etymology: From Classical Arabic خِلَالَ (ḫilāla, 'through, amidst, during the interval of'), originally plural/verbal noun from خَلَّ (ḫalla, 'to pierce, pass between', root خ-ل-ل).

خلت.etymology: Third-person feminine singular past of Form II خلّى (root خ-ل-و, to leave or allow), dropping weak final radical.

خلص.etymology: Discourse interjection grammaticalized from the past verb خَلَصَ ('it ended / is finished') on the root خ-ل-ص (x-l-ṣ, to be pure, clear, finished). Functioning almost like a Swiss-army particle in Jordan, خلص signals 'enough!', 'okay, settled', or 'never mind'.

history.meaning: to become clear, end, be done

خلطة.etymology: Feminine noun خَلْطَة (ḵalṭa, 'mixture, blend, glaze, concoction'), an instance noun from خَلَطَ (ḵalaṭa, 'to mix, blend'), root خ-ل-ط (ḵ-l-ṭ). Standard in Levantine cooking for dough mixes, spice blends, and sugar glazes.

خلفي.etymology: Relational (nisba) adjective خَلْفِيّ (ḫalfiyy, 'back, rear, posterior') formed from خَلْف (ḫalfa, 'behind, at the back of'), root خ-ل-ف (ḫ-l-ف).

خلوا.etymology: Plural imperative of colloquial Form II خلّى (root خ-ل-و) used for letting or leaving something in place.

خلى.etymology: Form II causative verb خَلَّى (ḫallā, 'to leave alone, vacate, let go, allow, keep') on the pattern فَعَّلَ (faʿʿala) from Form I خَلَا (ḫalā, 'to be empty, free, secluded'), defective triliteral root خ-ل-و (ḫ-l-w).

morphemes.meaning: Form II verb ('leave free -> let, keep, make')

history.meaning: to be empty -> to release, leave alone
to let, allow, make, keep (hortative خَلِّينَا = 'let's...')

rootFamily.gloss: to abandon, give up (Form V, with عن)

خلى.notes: One of the highest-frequency verbs in spoken Jordanian: الله يخليكي ('may God keep you safe / please!'), خليني أحكي ('let me speak'), and خليكم بحالكم ('mind your own business').

خليط.etymology: Fa'iil pattern noun from the root خ-ل-ط (to mix, blend), denoting a blended substance or batter.

خلينا.etymology: Hortative construction pairing the imperative خلّي (allow, root خ-ل-و) with 1pl object -na.

خليني.etymology: Combines the imperative خلّي (root خ-ل-و) with 1sg object pronoun -ni (me) to mean let me.

خلّص.etymology: Form II verb خَلَّصَ (ḫallaṣa, 'to extricate, clear; [in Levantine] to finish, complete') from خَلَصَ (ḫalaṣa, 'to become pure, clear, finished'), root خ-ل-ص (ḫ-l-ṣ).

history.meaning: to clear; bring to completion; finish

خلّى.etymology: Form II verb خَلَّى (ḫallā, 'to leave alone, vacate; [in Levantine] to let, allow, keep') from خَلَا (ḫalā, 'to be empty, free'), root خ-ل-و (ḫ-l-w).

خمس.etymology: Construct cardinal numeral five from Semitic root خ-م-س used before counted plural nouns.

خمسة.etymology: Standalone cardinal numeral five built on the pan-Semitic root خ-م-س with feminine ending -a.

خمستعشر.etymology: Spoken Levantine construct compound numeral خَمْسْتَعْشَر (ḫamstaʿšar, 'fifteen' before a counted noun), contracted from Classical خَمْسَةَ عَشَرَ (ḫamsata ʿašara, 'five-teen').

خمسطعش.etymology: Contracted compound numeral from Classical Arabic خمسة عشر (khamsata 'ashar), exhibiting pharyngealization of t from عشر.

خمسين.etymology: Oblique/generalized spoken form of Classical خَمْسُونَ / خَمْسِينَ (ḫamsīna, 'fifty'), decade numeral formed with the plural suffix -īn from خَمْس ('five'), root خ-م-س.

خميل.etymology: Colloquial Levantine adjective descended from root خ-م-ل (thick pile or dense nap of fabric).

خوف.etymology: Form II causative verb خَوَّفَ (ḫawwafa, 'to frighten, scare, startle') on the pattern فَعَّلَ (faʿʿala) from the hollow root خ-و-ف (ḫ-w-f, Form I خَافَ ḫāfa, 'to fear'), retaining the consonantal medial glide -ww- under gemination.

morphemes.meaning: Form II causative verb ('cause to fear')

history.meaning: to fear -> to instill fear, intimidate

خوف.notes: Notice how unvocalized خوف spells both the noun خَوْف (ḫawf, 'fear') and the Form II causative verb خَوَّف (ḫawwaf, 'scared/startled': خوفتيني! 'you startled me!').

خيال.etymology: Classical Arabic خَيَال (ḫayāl, 'apparition, silhouette, cast shadow; imagination, fancy') from خَالَ (ḫāla, 'to suppose, imagine'), root خ-ي-ل (ḫ-y-l).

خير.etymology: Classical Arabic خَيْر (ḫayr, 'good, goodness, blessing, well-being'), central to everyday greetings such as صباح الخير ('good morning') and تصبحوا على خير ('good night'), root خ-ي-ر (ḫ-y-r).

خيط.etymology: Concrete noun from root خ-ي-ط (to sew or stitch) denoting thread, string, or twine.

خَبَز.etymology: Form I verb خَبَزَ (ḫabaza, 'to bake bread or pastry; vocalized with fatḥas to distinguish the verb from خُبْز "bread" and خَبْز "baking"'), root خ-ب-ز (ḫ-b-z).

خَبْز.etymology: Form I verbal noun خَبْز (ḫabz, 'act of baking; vocalized with fatḥa-sukūn to distinguish it from خُبْز ḫubz "bread"') from خَبَزَ (ḫabaza, 'to bake'), root خ-ب-ز.

خِلِص.etymology: Spoken Levantine Form I intransitive verb خِلِص (ḫiliṣ, 'to run out, be finished, come to an end'), from Classical خَلَصَ (ḫalaṣa, 'to become clear, reach completion'), root خ-ل-ص (ḫ-l-ṣ).

history.meaning: to reach the end; become clear

دائرة.etymology: Feminine active participle substantive دَائِرَة (dāʾira, 'circle, ring; administrative department, bureau') from دَارَ (dāra, 'to go around, revolve'), root د-و-ر (d-w-r).

دائم.etymology: Active participle adjective دَائِم (dāʾim, 'lasting, permanent, continual') from دَامَ (dāma, 'to last, endure, continue'), root د-و-م (d-w-m).

داخل.etymology: Active participle دَاخِل (dāḫil, 'entering, going in, inner') of Form I دَخَلَ (daḫala, 'to enter'), root د-خ-ل (d-ḫ-l).

داخلي.etymology: Nisba adjective formed by adding -ī (-ي) to دَاخِل (dāxil, inside/interior), the active participle of the root د-خ-ل (d-x-l, to enter). In Jordanian usage, داخلي describes indoor spaces, interior design, and domestic travel.

دار.etymology: Hollow verb دَارَ (dāra, 'to turn, go around; [in Levantine, merging with Form IV أَدَارَ ʾadāra] to run, manage a place, or direct attention in دير بالك "take care"'), root د-و-ر (d-w-r).

دافع.etymology: Active participle دَافِع (dāfiʿ, 'pushing; paying, having paid; motive') from دَفَعَ (dafaʿa, 'to push; pay'), root د-ف-ع (d-f-ʿ).

دافي.etymology: Active participle from root د-ف-أ (warmth) with classical final hamza dropped in Jordanian.

داق.etymology: Everyday Levantine hollow verb داق (dāq, 'to taste'), showing the regular urban shift of interdental ذ ḏ to dental stop د d from Classical ذَاقَ (ḏāqa, 'to taste, sample'), root ذ-و-ق (ḏ-w-q).

دان.etymology: Spoken Levantine feminine noun دَان (dān, 'ear'), reduced from earlier إِذْن / أُذُن (ʾuḏun, 'ear') via syncope of the initial vowel and *ḏ > d shift (retained in dual دِينَيْن 'two ears'). Traces back to Proto-Semitic *ʾuḏn- ('ear').

دايم.etymology: Spoken Levantine reflex of Classical دَائِم (dāʾim, lasting, perpetual), the active participle of the hollow root د-و-م (d-w-m, to last or continue), where the medial hamza glides to -y-. In Jordanian markets and cafés, زبون دايم means a loyal regular patron.

دايما.etymology: Spoken Levantine form دَايْمًا (dāyman, 'always') with palatal glide y for the Classical medial hamza in دَائِمًا (dāʾiman, 'continually, always'), adverbial accusative of دَائِم (root د-و-م).

دايماً.etymology: Spoken Levantine reflex (dāyman) of the Classical Arabic adverbial accusative دَائِمًا (dāʾiman, 'continually, always'), built on the active participle دَائِم (dāʾim, 'lasting, enduring') from the hollow root د-و-م (d-w-m, 'to last, continue'), showing regular colloquial replacement of medial hamza (ئ) with palatal glide ي (y).
دايماً.notes: Spelled دائماً in formal MSA writing and دايماً in colloquial Levantine transcripts to reflect spoken dāyman.

دبق.etymology: Colloquial stative adjective built from the root د-ب-ق, classically associated with birdlime and sticky sap.

دبوس.etymology: Classical and Levantine noun دَبُّوس (dabbūs, 'pin, tack, metal pivot pin; originally a rounded iron mace'), formed on the instrument pattern فَعُّول from root د-ب-س (d-b-s).

history.meaning: knobbed mace; metal pin; pivot pin

دخل.etymology: Form I verb دَخَلَ (daḫala, 'to enter, come in, go inside'), from the Semitic root د-خ-ل (d-ḫ-l, 'entering, interior').

دخلة.etymology: Feminine noun of place/instance from the root د-خ-ل (to enter), specialized in Levantine city speech for a side alley or turn-off.

دخول.etymology: From Classical Arabic دُخُول (duḫūl, 'entering, entrance, admission'), regular Form I verbal noun on pattern فُعُول from دَخَلَ (daḫala, 'to enter'), root د-خ-ل (d-ḫ-l).

دخيلك.etymology: Warm Levantine entreaty دَخِيلَك (daḫīlak, 'please!, I beg you!'), literally '[I am] your sanctuary-seeker (دَخِيل)', referring to the ancient Arabian custom of entering (دَخَلَ) a host\'s tent to claim protection, root د-خ-ل.

history.meaning: your sanctuary-guest; 'I appeal to your protection!'

دخّل.etymology: Form II causative verb دَخَّلَ (daḫḫala, 'to bring inside, let in, insert') from دَخَلَ (daḫala, 'to enter'), root د-خ-ل (d-ḫ-l).

history.meaning: to cause to enter; bring inside

درابزين.etymology: Levantine architectural loanword دَرَابْزِين (darābzīn, 'balustrade, railing') borrowed via Ottoman Turkish trabzan / Persian darābzīn from Byzantine Greek τραπέζιον (trapézion, literally 'little table, rail bar'). Long naturalized across Jordan, Syria, and Lebanon for balcony and stair railings.

درج.etymology: From the root د-ر-ج (d-r-j, 'to step, advance gradually'), used collectively for a flight of stairs—or with different vowels (دُرج) for a desk drawer.
درج.notes: Amman's hillsides are famous for public stone staircases (أدراج) linking upper and lower streets.

درجة.etymology: Noun دَرَجَة (daraja, 'step, stair, rung; degree, grade') from دَرَجَ (daraja, 'to walk step by step, advance by degrees'), root د-ر-ج (d-r-j).

دردش.etymology: Colloquial Levantine and Egyptian quadriliteral verb دَرْدَشَ (dardaš, 'to chat casually, shoot the breeze') on the pattern فَعْلَلَ (faʿlala, root د-ر-د-ش), formed either as an expressive reduplicative stem for light, rambling talk or through Ottoman/Persian conversational contact (often linked to Persian dard-e dil, 'pouring out one's heart').

history.meaning: to talk intimately or lightly at leisure
to chat casually (in person or online)

دردش.notes: Warm colloquial register (contrasting with formal تحدث / تحاور), though its verbal noun دردشة was adopted across modern Arab tech interfaces to translate 'online chat'.

درس.etymology: Verbal and concrete noun دَرْس (dars, 'studying; lesson, class') from دَرَسَ (darasa, 'to study, read repeatedly'), cognate with Aramaic דְּרַשׁ (daraš, 'to expound, study'), root د-ر-س (d-r-s).

درفة.etymology: Levantine and Egyptian architectural noun دَرْفَة (darfa, 'single hinged leaf or panel of a double window, shutter, or door'), from Classical دَرْف (darf, 'side, wing, protective screen'), root د-ر-ف (d-r-f).

history.meaning: side wing; hinged shutter or door leaf

دزينة.etymology: Levantine market noun دَزِّينَة (dazzīne, 'dozen, set of twelve'), borrowed from Italian dozzina ('dozen', ultimately from Latin duodecim 'twelve').

دس.etymology: Geminate Form I verb دَسَّ (dassa, 'to thrust in secretly, tuck away, slip inside'), Semitic root د-س-س (d-s-s).

دعا.etymology: Form I verb دَعَا (daʿā, 'to call, invite; pray for someone, wish someone well') from the Semitic root د-ع-و (d-ʿ-w, 'calling, invoking').

دعم.etymology: Triliteral Form I verb from the root د-ع-م, originally meaning to prop up a leaning wall and figuratively to back or endorse.

دعوة.etymology: From Classical Arabic دَعْوَة (daʿwa, 'call, summons, invitation'), instance noun from دَعَا (daʿā, 'to call, invite'), Semitic root د-ع-و (d-ʿ-w).

دغري.etymology: Spatial and temporal adverb borrowed from Ottoman Turkish doğru (straight, direct, right away).

دفا.etymology: Spoken and lightened Classical noun دَفَا (dafā, 'warmth') from Classical دِفْء / دَفَاء (difʾ / dafāʾ, 'warmth, shelter from cold') via regular loss of final glottal stop, root د-ف-ء (d-f-ʾ).

دفاية.etymology: Appliance noun دَفَّايَة (daffāye, 'heater, radiator, stove') on the instrumental pattern فَعَّالَة from دَفَّى < دَفَّأَ (daffaʾa, 'to warm, heat'), root د-ف-ء (d-f-ʾ).

دفتر.etymology: Borrowed via Persian *daftar* from Ancient Greek διφθέρα (diphthéra, 'prepared hide, parchment, ledger').
دفتر.notes: Entered Classical Arabic early for an account register or ledger—just like Tariq's paper reception book.

دفع.etymology: Form I verb دَفَعَ (dafaʿa, 'to push, propel, ward off; hand over a sum, pay'), from the Semitic root د-ف-ع (d-f-ʿ).

دفن.etymology: Form I verb دَفَنَ (dafana, 'to bury, conceal in the earth'), from the Semitic root د-ف-ن (d-f-n, 'burying, covering over').

history.meaning: to bury; cover in the ground

دفّى.etymology: Form II factitive verb built on the root د-ف-أ (warmth), dropping the final hamza in Levantine pronunciation.

دق.etymology: Geminate Form I verb from root د-ق-ق denoting knocking, tapping, striking, or ringing.

دقة.etymology: Covers both the instance noun دَقَّة (daqqa, 'a single knock, beat, or clock chime') and the abstract noun دِقَّة (diqqa, 'fineness, accuracy, precision, punctuality'), from the geminate root د-ق-ق (d-q-q).

history.meaning: single knock or chime; precision, exactness

دقيقة.etymology: Feminine noun دَقِيقَة (daqīqa, 'minute [of time or arc]'), literally 'a fine or small part' (paralleled by Medieval Latin pars minuta prima, 'first small division of the hour'), from دَقِيق (daqīq, 'fine, minute'), root د-ق-ق.

history.meaning: minute particle; minute (sixtieth of an hour)

دقّ.etymology: Geminate Form I verb (فَعَّ) from the root د-ق-ق (d-q-q, to crush, pound, strike lightly, tap). While Classical Arabic uses دَقَّ for pounding grain or knocking, Levantine Arabic extended it to tapping keys, knocking on doors, and ringing someone on the phone.

دقّق.etymology: Denominative Form II verb from the geminate root د-ق-ق (fine, minute), expressing careful attention to small details.

دكان.etymology: Classical Arabic دُكَّان (dukkān, 'raised platform or bench; shop, store'), borrowed in antiquity via Aramaic דֻּכָּנָא (dukkānā) from Akkadian dukkannu / Sumerian dug-gan ('platform, counter').

دكتور.etymology: International academic and medical title borrowed from European doctor (Latin docere, to teach).

دكتورك.etymology: Combines the loanword دكتور (doctor) with the 2ms possessive suffix -ak.

دلف.etymology: Verbal and concrete noun دَلْف (dalf, 'roof leak, dripping of rainwater through a ceiling') from دَلَفَ (dalafa, 'to trickle, leak through a roof'), cognate with Aramaic דְּלַף / ܕܠܦ (dalap̄, 'to drip, leak'), root د-ل-ف (d-l-f).

دليل.etymology: Nouns on fa'iil from root د-ل-ل (to point, guide), meaning either a guide/directory or a clue/proof.

دم.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *dam- ('blood'), one of the core biradical anatomical nouns across all Semitic languages, yielding Classical Arabic دَم (dam).

دمر.etymology: Form II intensive/causative verb دَمَّرَ (dammara, 'to destroy utterly, lay waste, ruin') on the pattern فَعَّلَ (faʿʿala) from Form I دَمَرَ (damara, 'to perish, face ruin'), triliteral root د-م-ر (d-m-r).

history.meaning: to destroy, ruin (a building, reputation, or life)

دمر.notes: Used literally in news Arabic and hyperbolically in Levantine drama: رح أدمرك ('I will ruin you!') and أنا مدمرة ('I'm emotionally wrecked').

دمعة.etymology: Feminine singulative noun on the pattern فَعْلَة (faʿla) from the Semitic root د-م-ع (d-m-ʿ, tear, weeping), cognate with Hebrew דִּמְעָה (dimʿā) and Aramaic demʿəṯā. Singulative دمعة denotes a single teardrop, with broken plural دموع used for tears in general.

دمّع.etymology: Form II verb دَمَّعَ (dammaʿa, 'to shed tears, well up with tears') derived from دَمْع (damʿ, 'tears'), Proto-Semitic *damʿ- ('tear'), root د-م-ع (d-m-ʿ).

دندن.etymology: Expressive reduplicated quadriliteral verb دَنْدَنَ (dandana, 'to hum a tune softly, murmur, buzz'), formed onomatopoeically on the root د-ن-د-ن (d-n-d-n).

دندنة.etymology: Quadriliteral verbal noun دَنْدَنَة (dandana, 'soft humming of a melody, gentle strumming or murmuring') from دَنْدَنَ (dandana, 'to hum'), root د-ن-د-ن.

دنيا.etymology: Feminine elative substantive دُنْيَا (dunyā, 'this world, earthly life; [in Levantine] the world and weather outside'), originally feminine of أَدْنَى (ʾadnā, 'nearer, closer', i.e. '[the] nearer life'), from دَنَا ('to be near'), root د-ن-و (d-n-w).

دهان.etymology: Verbal and material noun دِهَان (dihān, 'paint, oil coating, pigment; act of painting') from دَهَنَ (dahana, 'to oil, anoint, coat with paint'), root د-ه-ن (d-h-n).

دهب.etymology: Spoken Jordanian and Levantine pronunciation and spelling دَهَب (dahab, 'gold') of Classical ذَهَب (ḏahab), showing the urban Levantine sound change of interdental /ḏ/ > stop /d/. Inherited from Proto-Semitic *ḏahab- ('gold').

دهبي.etymology: Levantine relational nisba adjective دهبي (dahabi, 'golden'), showing the regular shift of interdental ذ ḏ to stop د d from Classical ذَهَبِيّ (ḏahabiyy) built on ذَهَب ('gold', Proto-Semitic *ḏahab-), root ذ-ه-ب.

دهن.etymology: Form I verb دَهَنَ (dahana, 'to anoint, oil, coat, paint walls or woodwork'), from the Semitic root د-ه-ن (d-h-n, 'oil, grease, coating').

دهنة.etymology: Instance noun derived from the root د-ه-ن (oil, ointment, to anoint or spread), denoting a single light application.

دو.etymology: Musical solfège syllable دُو (dō, 'the note C'), borrowed from Italian/French do (which replaced earlier ut in European solfège).

history.meaning: first note of the diatonic scale (C)

دواسة.etymology: Instrumental noun دَوَّاسَة (dawwāsa, 'foot pedal, piano pedal, treadle, doormat') on the pattern فَعَّالَة from دَاسَ (dāsa, 'to tread, step on, press with the foot'), root د-و-س (d-w-s).

دوام.etymology: Verbal noun دَوَام (dawām, 'continuance, permanence; regular working hours, work shift') from دَامَ (dāma, 'to last, continue, endure'), root د-و-م (d-w-m).

دور.etymology: Verbal and concrete noun دَوْر (dawr, 'rotation, cycle, turn; role or part; story/floor of a building') from دَارَ (dāra, 'to turn, revolve'), root د-و-ر (d-w-r).

دوزان.etymology: Levantine and Egyptian musical term دُوزَان (dūzān, 'tuning of a stringed or keyboard instrument'), borrowed from Ottoman Turkish düzen ('order, harmony, musical tuning', from Turkic düz- 'to arrange, put in order').

دوزن.etymology: Levantine quadriliteral verb دَوْزَن (dawzan, 'to tune a musical instrument'), denominalized from دُوزَان (dūzān, 'musical tuning', from Ottoman Turkish düzen).

دوش.etymology: Household noun دُوش (dūš, 'bath shower'), borrowed from French douche ('shower', itself from Italian doccia 'water conduit, spout').

دوّر.etymology: Form II verb دَوَّرَ (dawwara, 'to turn round, make revolve; [with عَلَى] to go around looking for, search for') from دَارَ (dāra, 'to turn, go around'), root د-و-ر (d-w-r).

history.meaning: to turn round; search for (with على)

دير.etymology: Imperative of Form IV أدار / colloquial دار (hollow root د-و-ر, to turn), especially in idiom دير بالك.

دينار.etymology: Classical Arabic دِينَار (dīnār, 'gold coin; modern currency unit of Jordan and several Arab countries'), borrowed in antiquity via Aramaic/Syriac ܕܝܢܪܐ (dīnārā) and Greek δηνάριον from Latin dēnārius ('coin of ten asses').

ذاق.etymology: Hollow Form I verb from the root ذ-و-ق meaning to sample or perceive flavour.

ذان.etymology: Colloquial Jordanian and Levantine noun ذَان / دَان (ḏān / dān, 'ear'), back-formed as a long-vowel singular from the Classical broken plural آذَان (ʾāḏān, 'ears', plural of أُذُن ʾuḏun), root ء-ذ-ن.

ذقنه.etymology: Anatomical noun ذقن (chin, beard, root ذ-ق-ن) suffixed with the 3ms possessive -u/-o.

ذكرى.etymology: Feminine noun ذِكْرَى (ḏikrā, 'memory, remembrance, recollection, commemoration') formed with the feminine suffix -َى (-ā) on the pattern فِعْلَى from ذَكَرَ (ḏakara, 'to remember, mention'), root ذ-ك-ر.

ذكي.etymology: Adjective ذَكِيّ (ḏakiyy, 'smart, clever, quick-witted') on the pattern فَعِيل from ذَكَا (ḏakā, 'to blaze brightly [of fire], give off a sharp scent, be acute in mind'), root ذ-ك-و (ḏ-k-w).

ذكيةوشوفوا.etymology: Accidental spacing merge of ذكية (clever, root ذ-ك-و), conjunction و (and), and plural imperative شوفوا (look).

ذكّر.etymology: Form II causative verb ذَكَّرَ (ḏakkara, 'to remind, cause to remember') from ذَكَرَ (ḏakara, 'to remember'), inherited from Proto-Semitic *ḏakar-, root ذ-ك-ر.

ذهب.etymology: From Classical Arabic ذَهَب (ḏahab, 'gold'), inherited from Proto-Semitic *ḏahab- (cognate with Hebrew זָהָב zāhāḇ, Aramaic דַּהֲבָא dahăḇā). In Jordanian speech ذ shifts to d (dahab).

ذهبي.etymology: Nisba adjective derived by adding -i to ذهب (gold, root ذ-ه-ب).

ذواق.etymology: Intensive agent noun ذَوَّاق (ḏawwāq, 'taste-tester, connoisseur, person of refined palate') on the pattern فَعَّال from ذَاقَ (ḏāqa, 'to taste'), root ذ-و-ق (ḏ-w-q).

ذوق.etymology: Form I verbal noun ذَوْق (ḏawq, 'sense of taste; good taste, tact, grace, kindness', as in كلك ذوق 'you are all kindness') from ذَاقَ (ḏāqa, 'to taste'), root ذ-و-ق (ḏ-w-q).

ذوّب.etymology: Form II causative verb formed on the hollow root ذ-و-ب (to melt or dissolve).

رئيسي.etymology: Relational (nisba) adjective رَئِيسِيّ (raʾīsiyy, 'main, principal, chief, primary') derived from رَئِيس (raʾīs, 'chief, head'), from رَأْس (raʾs, 'head'), root ر-ء-س (r-ʾ-s).

رائع.etymology: Active participle adjective رَائِع (rāʾiʿ, 'wonderful, splendid, admirable, striking') from رَاعَ (rāʿa, 'to strike with awe, dazzle, thrill with admiration'), root ر-و-ع (r-w-ʿ).

رابح.etymology: Active participle on the faa'il pattern from the root ر-ب-ح denoting profit, gain, or victory.

رابع.etymology: Ordinal adjective رَابِع (rābiʿ, 'fourth') formed on the pattern فَاعِل from أَرْبَعَة (ʾarbaʿa, 'four'), root ر-ب-ع (r-b-ʿ).

راتب.etymology: From the triliteral root ر-ت-ب (r-t-b), expressing steadiness, order, and fixed arrangement. As an active participle راتب describes something regular and enduring, whence a fixed periodic salary.
راتب.notes: Used across modern Arabic for a regular monthly wage alongside مرتب.

راجع.etymology: Active participle رَاجِع (rājiʿ, 'returning, coming back') from رَجَعَ (rajaʿa, 'to return'), root ر-ج-ع (r-j-ʿ).

راح.etymology: Hollow Form I verb on the root ر-و-ح (originally to go in the evening), the primary verb for going in Jordan.

راحة.etymology: Noun رَاحَة (rāḥa, 'rest, repose, comfort, ease') from the Semitic root ر-و-ح (r-w-ḥ, 'refreshing breeze, breath, relief from toil').

راحت.etymology: Third-person feminine singular past of راح (root ر-و-ح) marked by -at.

راس.etymology: Spoken and lightened Classical form رَاس (rās, 'head, top, summit') of رَأْس (raʾs) via compensatory lengthening after loss of medial glottal stop, inherited from Proto-Semitic *raʾš- ('head'), root ر-ء-س.

راسم.etymology: Agent noun on the faa'il pattern from the root ر-س-م meaning to trace, sketch, or draw.

راضي.etymology: Active participle رَاضٍ / الرَّاضِي (rāḍī, 'satisfied, content, willing; [with مش] unwilling, refusing to budge') from رَضِيَ (raḍiya, 'to be pleased, consent'), root ر-ض-و / ر-ض-ي.

راقب.etymology: Form III verb رَاقَبَ (rāqaba, 'to watch closely, observe, monitor, keep an eye on') from رَقَبَ (raqaba, 'to watch, look out'), connected to رَقَبَة ('neck, stretched to look out'), root ر-ق-ب (r-q-b).

راقص.etymology: Active participle adjective رَاقِص (rāqiṣ, 'dancing, lilting') from رَقَصَ (raqaṣa, 'to dance, leap rhythmicaly'), root ر-ق-ص (r-q-ṣ).

راكض.etymology: Active participle formed on the faa'il pattern from the root ر-ك-ض (to run, gallop), serving as a progressive predicate in Levantine Arabic.

رامي.etymology: Traditional Arabic masculine given name derived from the active participle رَامِي (rāmī, 'thrower, archer') of the defective root ر-م-ي (r-m-y, to throw or shoot an arrow). Common throughout Jordan and the Levant, it historically evoked skill in archery and aim.

morphemes.meaning: active participle used as personal name

رايح.etymology: Spoken Levantine active participle رَايِح (rāyiḥ, 'going, heading to') with palatal glide y for the Classical medial hamza in رَائِح (rāʾiḥ), active participle of رَاحَ ('to go'), root ر-و-ح.

رب.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *rabb- ('great, chief, master, lord'), yielding Classical Arabic رَبّ (rabb, 'Lord, master'), root ر-ب-ب (r-b-b).

رباعي.etymology: Relational adjective رُبَاعِيّ (rubāʿiyy, 'fourfold, composed of four') built on the distributive stem رُبَاع (rubāʿ) from the root ر-ب-ع (r-b-ʿ, 'four'). In music and geometry it expresses anything performed by four parts or four hands.

ربط.etymology: Classical and spoken Arabic Form I verb رَبَطَ (rabaṭa, 'to tie, bind, connect'), root ر-ب-ط (r-b-ṭ, 'to bind fast'). It serves equally for tying knots in rope, fastening parcels, and linking concepts.

ربع.etymology: Fractional noun رُبْع (rubʿ, 'one-fourth, quarter; fifteen minutes of an hour') formed on the fractional pattern فُعْل from the numeral root ر-ب-ع (r-b-ʿ, 'four').

ربى.etymology: Form II causative verb رَبَّى (rabbā, 'to rear, nurture, bring up a child, educate') on the pattern فَعَّلَ (faʿʿala) from رَبَا (rabā, 'to grow up, increase'), defective root ر-ب-و (r-b-w).

history.meaning: to grow -> to rear, raise, educate
to raise children; (colloquially) to teach someone manners / a lesson

ربى.notes: In confrontational Jordanian speech, والله لربّيها / لازم نربيهم means 'we have to teach them a lesson' (implying their parents failed to teach them manners).

ربيع.etymology: From the root ر-ب-ع (r-b-ʿ), connected with resting in lush pasture and spring rains that revive grazing land; hence the spring season across Arabic dialects.

ربيعي.etymology: Nisba adjective derived from ربيع (springtime, root ر-ب-ع) with the relational suffix -i.

رتّب.etymology: Form II verb رَتَّبَ (rattaba, 'to arrange, put in order, tidy') from رَتَبَ (rataba, 'to stand firm and upright in rank'), root ر-ت-ب (r-t-b).

history.meaning: to arrange; put in order; tidy

رجا.etymology: Form I verb رَجَا (rajā, 'to hope for, entreat, ask earnestly', used in the polite request أَرْجُوك ʾarjūk 'please! / I beg you'), from the root ر-ج-و (r-j-w).

رجال.etymology: Spoken Levantine singular noun رِجَّال (rijjāl, 'man'), reshaped on the intensive pattern فِعَّال from Classical Arabic رَجُل (rajul, 'man', originally 'man on foot', plural رِجَال rijāl), root ر-ج-ل.

رجالي.etymology: Relational (nisba) adjective رِجَالِيّ (rijāliyy, 'men\'s, for men') formed from the broken plural رِجَال (rijāl, 'men', plural of رَجُل), root ر-ج-ل (r-j-l).

رجع.etymology: Form I verb رَجَعَ (rajaʿa, 'to return, come back, go back'), from the root ر-ج-ع (r-j-ʿ).

رجعة.etymology: Instance noun (ism marra) رَجْعَة (rajʿa, 'a return, return trip, coming back') from رَجَعَ (rajaʿa, 'to return'), root ر-ج-ع (r-j-ʿ).

رجف.etymology: Form I verb رَجَفَ (rajafa, 'to tremble, shake, shiver, quake'), from the Semitic root ر-ج-ف (r-j-f, 'quaking, trembling').

رجل.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *rigl- ('foot, leg'), yielding Classical Arabic رِجْل (rijl), a core feminine paired body-part noun, root ر-ج-ل (r-j-l).

رجّع.etymology: Form II causative verb رَجَّعَ (rajjaʿa, 'to bring back, return [something], restore') from رَجَعَ (rajaʿa, 'to come back'), root ر-ج-ع (r-j-ʿ).

history.meaning: to cause to return; bring back; give back

رح.etymology: Future-tense particle grammaticalized from the active participle رايح / verb راح (going to).

رحلة.etymology: Noun رِحْلَة (riḥla, 'trip, journey, travel') from رَحَلَ (raḥala, 'to saddle a mount, set out on a journey'), root ر-ح-ل (r-ḥ-l).

رحم.etymology: Form I verb رَحِمَ (raḥima, 'to have mercy, compassion on'), inherited from the Proto-Semitic root ر-ح-م (*r-ḥ-m, 'womb; tender mercy, compassion').

رحمة.etymology: Feminine abstract noun from the root ر-ح-م denoting compassion, womb-kinship, and mercy.

رحّب.etymology: Form II denominative verb (فَعَّلَ, faʿʿala) formed from مَرْحَبًا / رَحْب on the root ر-ح-ب (r-ḥ-b, spaciousness, generosity). Pairing with the preposition بـ (or فـ in spoken Jordanian), رحّب means 'to greet warmly' and 'make someone feel welcome'.

رخامة.etymology: Singulative noun رُخَامَة (ruḫāma, 'a slab of marble; in Levantine households, the kitchen countertop') from the Classical collective رُخَام (ruḫām, 'marble'), root ر-خ-م (r-ḫ-m).

رخوة.etymology: Feminine adjective formed from root ر-خ-و signifying slackness, looseness, or softness.

رخّى.etymology: Spoken Levantine Form II verb رَخَّى (raḫḫā, 'to loosen, slacken, ease tension'), corresponding to Classical Form IV أَرْخَى (ʾarḫā) from رَخُوَ (raḫuwa, 'to be soft, loose, slack'), root ر-خ-و (r-ḫ-w).

رد.etymology: Form I geminate verb رَدَّ (radda, 'to send back, turn back; reply, answer a call or question'), from the Semitic root ر-د-د (r-d-d, 'returning, replying').

history.meaning: to return; send back; answer, reply

رسالة.etymology: Derived on pattern فِعَالَة from root ر-س-ل (r-s-l, 'to send forth a messenger or dispatch'): anything sent, from a handwritten letter to a recorded voice message.

رسام.etymology: Intensive occupational noun رَسَّام (rassām, 'painter, illustrator, draughtsman') on pattern فَعَّال from رَسَمَ (rasama, 'to trace, draw, sketch'), root ر-س-م (r-s-m).

رسم.etymology: Form I verb رَسَمَ (rasama, 'to trace, mark out, draw, sketch'), cognate with Aramaic רְשַׁם (rəšam, 'to inscribe, trace, draw'), root ر-س-م (r-s-m).

history.meaning: to trace; mark out; draw; sketch

رسمة.etymology: Instance noun with ta marbuta built on root ر-س-م (to trace, sketch, draw).

رسمي.etymology: Relational (nisba) adjective رَسْمِيّ (rasmiyy, 'official, formal, prescribed') derived from رَسْم (rasm, 'prescribed mark, established rule or canon'), root ر-س-م (r-s-m).

رسميا.etymology: Adverbial accusative رَسْمِيًّا (rasmiyyan, 'officially, formally') from the relational adjective رَسْمِيّ (rasmiyy, 'official'), root ر-س-م (r-s-m).

رسّام.etymology: Intensive occupational noun on the pattern فَعَّال (faʿʿāl) from the triliteral root ر-س-م (r-s-m, to trace, sketch, draw, design). Denoting a specialist who draws or paints, رسّام covers visual artists, illustrators, and technical draftsmen or mapmakers.

رش.etymology: Form I geminate verb رَشَّ (rašša, 'to sprinkle, splash, spray water or fine powder'), inherited from the Semitic root ر-ش-ش (r-š-š, 'sprinkling, light rain').

رشة.etymology: Instance noun رَشَّة (rašša, 'a sprinkle, light spray, or culinary pinch [of salt/spice]') from رَشَّ (rašša, 'to sprinkle, spray'), root ر-ش-ش (r-š-š).

رشفة.etymology: Instance noun رَشْفَة (rašfa, 'a sip, small draught') from رَشَفَ (rašafa, 'to sip gently with the lips'), root ر-ش-ف (r-š-f).

رصاص.etymology: Noun from root ر-ص-ص denoting lead metal and, by modern extension, graphite pencil lead.

رصيف.etymology: Noun رَصِيف (raṣīf, 'paved stone causeway, sidewalk, pavement, railway platform, quay') on the passive-sense pattern فَعِيل ('that which is fitted tightly stone-to-stone') from رَصَفَ (raṣafa, 'to lay stones closely together'), root ر-ص-ف (r-ṣ-ف).

رطب.etymology: Adjective رَطْب (raṭb, 'moist, damp, wet, fresh') from رَطُبَ (raṭuba, 'to be moist, tender, fresh'), inherited from Proto-Semitic *raṭb- ('moist, green'), root ر-ط-ب.

رطوبة.etymology: Abstract noun on the fu'uula pattern derived from root ر-ط-ب (moisture, dampness).

رغيف.etymology: Masculine noun on the pattern فَعِيل (faʿīl) from the root ر-غ-ف (r-ġ-f, to knead or shape dough into a round cake). Throughout Jordan and the Levant, رغيف (pl. أرغفة / رغفان) denotes a single flat round loaf of bread.

morphemes.meaning: shaping dough into a round loaf

رف.etymology: Classical Arabic رَفّ (raff, 'wall shelf, ledge, bracket', plural رُفُوف rufūf), from the geminate root ر-ف-ف (r-f-f).

رفض.etymology: Form I triliteral verb from the root ر-ف-ض meaning to cast aside, refuse, or decline.

رفع.etymology: Form I verb from the triliteral root ر-ف-ع meaning to lift, hoist, or elevate.

رفيع.etymology: Adjective رَفِيع (rafīʿ, 'high in rank; fine in thread or texture, thin, slender') on the pattern فَعِيل from رَفُعَ (rafuʿa, 'to be elevated, fine, slender'), root ر-ف-ع (r-f-ʿ).

رقاقة.etymology: Feminine noun رُقَاقَة (ruqāqa, 'thin flake, crisp wafer, flat bread sheet') from the adjective رَقِيق (raqīq, 'thin, delicate'), root ر-ق-ق (r-q-q, 'thin, fine'). Its broken plural رَقَائِق (raqāʾiq) is used for almond flakes, pastry sheets, and cereal flakes.

history.meaning: to be thin -> thin sheet, flake

رقم.etymology: Classical noun from root ر-ق-م (originally marking or inscribing numerals on cloth or stone).

رقيق.etymology: Adjective رَقِيق (raqīq, 'thin, fine, delicate, tender') on the pattern فَعِيل from رَقَّ (raqqa, 'to be thin, delicate, gentle'), inherited from Proto-Semitic *raqīq- ('thin'), root ر-ق-ق.

رقّم.etymology: Form II denominative verb رَقَّمَ (raqqama, 'to number, mark with numerals') derived from رَقْم (raqm, 'number, mark'), root ر-ق-م (r-q-m, 'to stripe, mark, write'). Its passive participle مرقّم (mraqqam) means 'numbered'.

ركب.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *rakib- ('to mount, ride, sit upon'), yielding Classical Arabic رَكِبَ (rakiba, 'to ride, board a vehicle; fit upon'), root ر-ك-ب (r-k-b).

history.meaning: to mount; ride; fit in place

ركبة.etymology: Anatomical noun رُكْبَة (rukba, 'knee', plural رُكَب rukab), inherited from Proto-Semitic *birk- / *rukb-at- ('knee', with consonant metathesis in Arabic), root ر-ك-ب.

ركض.etymology: Form I verbal noun رَكْض (rakḍ, 'running, sprinting, galloping') from رَكَضَ (rakaḍa, 'to run, urge a mount with the foot'), root ر-ك-ض (r-k-ḍ).

ركضة.etymology: Instance noun (ism marra) رَكْضَة (rakḍa, 'a run, sprint, quick dash') from رَكَضَ (rakaḍa, 'to run'), root ر-ك-ض (r-k-ḍ).

ركّب.etymology: Form II causative verb رَكَّبَ (rakkaba, 'to mount, fit together, assemble, install') from رَكِبَ (rakiba, 'to mount, sit upon'), root ر-ك-ب (r-k-b).

رمادي.etymology: Relational (nisba) color adjective رَمَادِيّ (ramādiyy, 'ash-colored, grey') derived from رَمَاد (ramād, 'ashes') + -ِيّ (-iyy), root ر-م-د (r-m-d).

رمز.etymology: Noun from the root ر-م-ز denoting a discreet sign, hint, or emblem.

رمش.etymology: Triliteral verb built on the root ر-م-ش referring to eyelashes and the quick blinking or squinting of the eyes.

رمل.etymology: Pan-Semitic collective noun from root ر-م-ل denoting sand and fine desert grit.

رمى.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *ramay- ('to throw, cast, shoot'), yielding Classical Arabic رَمَى (ramā, 'to throw, toss, fling'), root ر-م-ي (r-m-y).

رن.etymology: Form I geminate verb رَنَّ (ranna, 'to ring, chime, resound, twang'), inherited from the Semitic expressive root ر-ن-ن (r-n-n, 'ringing, resounding voice or tone').

رنة.etymology: Instance noun (ism marra) رَنَّة (ranna, 'a single ring, chime, or resonant tone') from رَنَّ (ranna, 'to ring'), root ر-ن-ن (r-n-n).

رنين.etymology: Fa'iil pattern verbal noun from the geminate root ر-ن-ن denoting a resonant sound, ring, or chime.

رنّ.etymology: Sound-symbolic geminate Form I verb (فَعَّ) from the root ر-ن-ن (r-n-n, to resound, ring, twang, echo). Originally describing the ringing twang of a bowstring or resonant voice in Classical poetry, رنّ is now the everyday Jordanian verb for bells, timers, and ringing phones.

رهيب.etymology: Adjective رَهِيب (rahīb, 'awe-inspiring, formidable; in everyday Levantine speech, terrific, amazing, intense') on the pattern فَعِيل from رَهِبَ (rahiba, 'to stand in awe, fear'), root ر-ه-ب (r-h-b).

روعة.etymology: Derived from the hollow root ر-و-ع (to inspire awe or wonder), shifting in modern Arabic from fear/awe to admiration and excellence.

روّح.etymology: Form II verb (فَعَّلَ, faʿʿala) from the hollow root ر-و-ح (r-w-ḥ, evening breeze, going in the evening). While Classical رَوَّحَ meant returning livestock or travelers at dusk, Levantine Arabic generalized روّح to mean 'to go home' at any hour of the day.

history.meaning: to return in the evening, bring back

روّق.etymology: Form II verb رَوَّقَ (rawwaqa, 'to clarify a liquid; in Levantine, to calm down, relax, clear one\'s mind') from رَاقَ (rāqa, 'to become clear, pure, serene'), root ر-و-ق (r-w-q).

history.meaning: to clarify; make serene; calm down
