طوّل.etymology: From Classical Arabic طَوَّلَ (ṭawwala, 'to lengthen, prolong, take a long time'), Form II intensive/causative of طَالَ (ṭāla, 'to be long'). Used in the Levantine idiom طَوِّل بَالَك (ṭawwil bālak, literally 'lengthen your mind/patience', i.e., 'be patient, take it easy').

morphemes.meaning: causative: to make long or take a long time

طيار.etymology: Intensive adjective on the fa''aal pattern from the hollow root ط-ي-ر (to fly), expressing quick evaporation or flight.

طيب.etymology: From Classical Arabic طَيِّب (ṭayyib, 'good, pleasant, sweet, kind-hearted, wholesome'), on the intensive stative pattern فَيْعِل (fayʿil) from طَابَ (ṭāba, 'to be good, pleasant, fragrant, agreeable'), from Proto-Semitic *ṭāb- ('good, sweet'). Also used conversationally as 'alright, well then'.

طية.etymology: Instance noun built on the root ط-و-ي (to fold or roll up), naming a single crease or folded flap.

طير.etymology: Collective and singular noun from the hollow root ط-ي-ر denoting winged birds as a class or single bird.

طيران.etymology: From Classical Arabic طَيَرَان (ṭayarān, 'flying, flight'), the standard فَعلان (faʿalān) verbal noun denoting motion from the hollow root ط-ي-ر (ṭ-y-r, 'to fly'). In modern Arabic it covers both literal flight through the air and commercial aviation.

طين.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *ṭīn- ('wet earth, potter's clay, mud'), preserved unchanged across Aramaic and Classical Arabic طِين (ṭīn).

طيّر.etymology: Form II causative verb طَيَّرَ (ṭayyara, 'to cause to fly, blow away, launch into the air') from the root ط-ي-ر (ṭ-y-r, 'to fly'). In Levantine Arabic it replaces Classical Form IV أطار in everyday speech for wind blowing objects away or children flying kites.

طَلّ.etymology: From Classical Arabic طَلَّ / أَطَلَّ (ṭalla / ʾaṭalla, 'to look out from above, overlook, peer out, appear'), geminate verb from the root ط-ل-ل (ṭ-l-l, 'looking out over, elevated view; light dew').

history.meaning: to look out, peer, overlook from a height, appear

morphemes.meaning: overlooking from a height, peering out

ظل.etymology: From Classical Arabic ظِلّ (ẓill, 'shade, shadow'), Semitic root ظ-ل-ل (ẓ-l-l), cognate with Hebrew צֵל (ṣēl).

ظلم.etymology: Verbal noun ظُلْم (ẓulm, 'injustice, oppression, wronging') of Classical Arabic ظَلَمَ (ẓalama, originally 'to put a thing in the wrong place, transgress proper bounds'), from the Semitic root ظ-ل-م (ẓ-l-m, intertwined with ظَلَام, 'darkness').
ظلم.notes: Moral keyword across all registers of Arabic; the active/passive pair ظالم ('wrongdoer') vs مظلوم ('one wronged') structures debates over bullying throughout *AlRawabi School*.

ظن.etymology: From Classical Arabic ظَنَّ (ẓanna, 'to think, suppose, conjecture, deem'), geminate verb of cognition from the root ظ-ن-ن (ẓ-n-n, 'thinking, supposing').

ظهر.etymology: From Classical Arabic ظُهْر (ẓuhr, 'midday, noon') and ظَهْر (ẓahr, 'back, rear, surface'), from the Proto-Semitic root *ẓ-h-r ('back; midday; to become visible').

عائلي.etymology: Nisba adjective عَائِلِيّ (ʿāʾiliyy, 'family [adj.], familial, domestic') formed from عَائِلَة (ʿāʾila, 'family, household'), from عَالَ (ʿāla, 'to support, sustain dependents').

عاجل.etymology: Active participle adjective عَاجِل (ʿājil, 'urgent, immediate, pressing, hasty') from عَجِلَ (ʿajila, 'to hurry, hasten'), root ع-ج-ل (ʿ-j-l, 'speed, haste'). Contrasts with آجل ('deferred, later') and labels urgent dispatches and news.

عاجي.etymology: Derived from Arabic عَاج (ʿāj, 'ivory, elephant tusk') plus the nisba adjective suffix -ِيّ (-iyy).

عاد.etymology: From Classical Arabic عَادَ (ʿāda, 'to return, come back, do again, repeat'), hollow verb from the root ع-و-د (ʿ-w-d, 'returning, repeating').

عادة.etymology: From Classical Arabic عَادَة (ʿāda, 'habit, custom, usual practice'), from عَادَ (ʿāda, 'to return, do repeatedly'), because a habit is an action one returns to repeatedly.

morphemes.meaning: that which is returned to repeatedly

عادي.etymology: Nisba adjective عَادِيّ (ʿādiyy, 'customary, ordinary, regular, normal; [of nuts/snacks] plain, unsalted'), formed from عَادَة (ʿāda, 'custom, habit').

عارضة.etymology: From Classical Arabic عَارِضَة (ʿāriḍa, 'horizontal beam, lintel, crossbar, rung, rafter'), feminine active participle of عَرَضَ (ʿaraḍa, 'to lie across, present itself horizontally').

عارف.etymology: Active participle (فَاعِل, fāʿil) of عَرَفَ ('to know, recognize') on the triliteral root ع-ر-ف (ʿ-r-f, knowledge, acquaintance). In Jordanian and broader Levantine grammar, عارف / عارفة functions as the standard present-tense expression for 'I/you/he/she knows', outnumbering finite بعرف in many contexts.

عازف.etymology: Active participle (فَاعِل) of Arabic عَزَفَ (ʿazafa, 'to play a musical instrument'), root ع-ز-ف (ʿ-z-f).

عاش.etymology: From Classical Arabic عَاشَ (ʿāša, 'to live, be alive, subsist'), hollow verb from the root ع-ي-ش (ʿ-y-š, 'life, living, livelihood').

عاصفة.etymology: Feminine active participle عَاصِفَة ('storm, gale', plural عَوَاصِف) from the root ع-ص-ف ('blow fiercely, sweep away chaff'), substantivized from رِيح عَاصِفَة ('tempestuous wind').

عاطفة.etymology: From Classical Arabic عَاطِفَة (ʿāṭifa, 'affection, sympathy, emotion, sentiment, tender feeling'), feminine active participle used as a noun from عَطَفَ (ʿaṭafa, 'to incline towards, bend with tenderness and compassion').

history.meaning: inclination of affection, sympathy, emotion, feeling

morphemes.meaning: bending, inclining with affection or sympathy

عاطل.etymology: From Classical Arabic عَاطِل (ʿāṭil, 'unadorned [originally of a woman without jewellery], idle, unemployed, devoid of good; [in Levantine] bad, spoiled, out of order'), active participle of عَطِلَ (ʿaṭila, 'to be devoid of ornament or work, lie idle').

morphemes.meaning: being unadorned, idle, out of work or order
in an idle or defective state

عاقل.etymology: From Classical Arabic عَاقِل (ʿāqil, 'possessing reason, sensible, wise, well-behaved'), active participle of عَقَلَ (ʿaqala, 'to understand, reason', originally 'to hobble a camel with a cord so it does not stray').

عالق.etymology: From Classical Arabic عَالِق (ʿāliq, 'clinging, hanging, caught, stuck, jammed'), active participle of عَلِقَ (ʿaliqa, 'to cling to, catch on, get stuck').

morphemes.meaning: in a state of clinging or being stuck

عالكامل.etymology: Adverbial phrase contracting على (on), الـ (the), and كامل (complete, root ك-م-ل).

عالي.etymology: Defective active participle of علا (root ع-ل-و, to rise high), designating elevated height or loud volume.

عام.etymology: From Classical Arabic عَامّ (ʿāmm, 'general, universal, public, common, main'), active participle of عَمَّ (ʿamma, 'to encompass all, be general or universal').

عامل.etymology: From Classical Arabic عَامِل (ʿāmil, 'worker, labourer, maker, agent, factor'), active participle of عَمِلَ (ʿamila, 'to work, do, make').

عبر.etymology: From Classical Arabic عَبَرَ (ʿabara, 'to cross over [a river, road, or border], pass through, traverse'), from the Proto-Semitic root *ʿ-b-r ('to cross over, pass beyond').

history.meaning: to cross over, pass across, traverse

عبقري.etymology: From Classical Arabic عَبْقَرِيّ (ʿabqariyy, 'matchless, brilliant, genius'), originally meaning 'inhabitant of ʿAbqar' — a legendary desert valley in pre-Islamic Arabian lore believed to be haunted by inspiring jinn where poets and artisans gained extraordinary skill.

عبّى.etymology: Spoken Arabic reflex of Classical Arabic عَبَّأَ (ʿabbaʾa, 'to pack, fill up, load, prepare, mobilize'), Form II from the root ع-ب-ء (ʿ-b-ʾ, 'load, packing'), reshaped as a final-weak verb عَبَّى (ʿabbā) through loss of final hamza.

history.meaning: to fill up, pack full, load, prepare

morphemes.meaning: intensive: to fill or pack completely

عتبة.etymology: From Classical Arabic عَتَبَة (ʿataba, 'threshold, doorstep, lintel, stair step'), from the root ع-ت-ب (ʿ-t-b, 'step, threshold; stepping across').

history.meaning: threshold of a door, doorstep, step

عتمة.etymology: From Classical Arabic عَتْمَة (ʿatma, 'darkness of the first third of the night after twilight has faded; gloom, dark'), from عَتَمَ (ʿatama, 'to grow dark, delay into the night').

عتيق.etymology: From Classical Arabic عَتِيق (ʿatīq, 'ancient, old, antique, vintage, noble, emancipated'), on the pattern فَعِيل (faʿīl) from عَتَقَ (ʿataqa, 'to grow old and matured [of wine or buildings]; to become free').

morphemes.meaning: growing old and seasoned; freedom, nobility

عجل.etymology: From Classical Arabic عَجَل (ʿajal, collective of عَجَلَة ʿajala, 'wheel, cartwheel, handwheel, pulley'), from the root ع-ج-ل (ʿ-j-l, 'to hasten, roll swiftly, speed along').

عجن.etymology: From Classical Arabic عَجَنَ (ʿajana, 'to knead dough with the hands, work into a paste'), from the root ع-ج-ن (ʿ-j-n, 'kneading, pressing dough').

history.meaning: to knead dough, press into a mass

morphemes.meaning: kneading dough, working into a paste

عجين.etymology: Collective masculine noun on the pattern فَعِيل (faʿīl) from the root ع-ج-ن (ʿ-j-n, to knead flour into dough), cognate with Aramaic ʿəḡan. Referring to dough or batter in bulk, عجين pairs with the feminine singulative عجينة for a single batch or piece of dough.

عجينة.etymology: Culinary noun built on root ع-ج-ن (to knead flour and water into dough) with feminine -a.

عد.etymology: From Classical Arabic عَدَّ (ʿadda, 'to count, enumerate'), Semitic root ع-د-د (ʿ-d-d), cognate with Aramaic עֲדָה.

عدا.etymology: Originally a defective verb from ع-د-و meaning to pass beyond or omit, grammaticalized as an exception preposition.

عدة.etymology: From Classical Arabic عُدَّة (ʿudda, 'equipment, gear, tools, toolkit, readiness, provision'), from أَعَدَّ (ʾaʿadda, 'to prepare, make ready, equip'), from the geminate root ع-د-د (ʿ-d-d, 'counting, preparing, reckoning').

history.meaning: equipment, tools, outfit, state of readiness

عدس.etymology: Inherited Semitic collective noun عَدَس ('lentils'), cultivated across the Fertile Crescent since the Neolithic and celebrated in Levantine kitchens for golden شوربة عدس ('lentil soup').

history.meaning: lentils (also the origin of عَدَسَة 'optical lens', shaped like a lentil)

عدسة.etymology: Singulative noun عَدَسَة ('a single lentil; optical lens') from collective عَدَس ('lentils'). Medieval Arab opticians—most famously Ibn al-Haytham (Alhazen) in Kitāb al-Manāẓir—named convex glass lenses عدسة because their biconvex curvature resembles a lentil seed; Latin translators calqued this directly as lens ('lentil'), giving English 'lens'!

cognates.meaning: from Latin lens ('lentil'), matching Arabic عدسة

عدوا.etymology: Past tense 3pl (and 2pl imperative) of geminate عدّ (root ع-د-د, to count or tally).

عدي.etymology: Feminine singular imperative of عدّ (root ع-د-د, to count) taking the 2fs ending -i.

عدّ.etymology: Geminate Form I verb (فَعَّ) from the root ع-د-د (ʿ-d-d, number, counting, reckoning). Preserved from Classical Arabic into every register of Jordanian speech, عدّ means 'to count' items or money, as well as 'to consider/regard' in formal phrasing.

عرض.etymology: From Classical Arabic عَرْض (ʿarḍ, 'breadth, width; presentation, display, offer, show'), verbal noun of عَرَضَ (ʿaraḍa, 'to present, display, show, lie across').

morphemes.meaning: width; act of presenting or offering

عرف.etymology: From Classical Arabic عَرَفَ (ʿarafa, 'to know, recognize, perceive, be acquainted with'), from the root ع-ر-ف (ʿ-r-f, 'knowing, recognizing, discerning by signs or scent').

history.meaning: to know, recognize, be acquainted with

عرق.etymology: From Classical Arabic عِرْق (ʿirq, 'root of a plant, stem, vein, blood vessel, lineage') and عَرَق (ʿaraq, 'sweat, perspiration; distilled spirit [arrack]'), from the root ع-ر-ق (ʿ-r-q).

morphemes.meaning: root, vein, branching vessel; exuding moisture

عريض.etymology: From Classical Arabic عَرِيض (ʿarīḍ, 'wide, broad, extensive'), on the adjectival pattern فَعِيل (faʿīl) from عَرُضَ (ʿaruḍa, 'to be wide, broad').

عزف.etymology: From Classical Arabic عَزْف (ʿazf, 'playing musical instruments, making music; originally the whistling sound of desert winds or jinn'), verbal noun of عَزَفَ (ʿazafa, 'to play music, strum or blow an instrument').

history.meaning: playing of musical instruments; whistling sound

عزم.etymology: Form I verb (فَعَلَ) from the triliteral root ع-ز-م (ʿ-z-m, firm resolve, determination, pressing invitation). Shifting from the Classical meaning 'to resolve firmly' or 'entreat someone earnestly', عزم became the quintessential Jordanian verb for hosting or inviting someone to a meal or coffee.

history.meaning: to invite (for food, coffee, or event)

عزيز.etymology: Adjective on the pattern فَعِيل (faʿīl) from the geminate root ع-ز-ز (ʿ-z-z, strength, honor, rarity, preciousness). From the Classical sense of 'rare and honored', عزيز (pl. أعزاء) became the universal Arabic term for 'dear' in greetings, letters, and affectionate speech.

عسل.etymology: Native Arabic noun from the root ع-س-ل ('-s-l), naming bee honey and prized since pre-Islamic poetry for sweetness and healing.
عسل.notes: Served across Jordan at breakfast alongside warm bread, olive oil, or tea.

عشا.etymology: Spoken Arabic reflex of Classical Arabic عَشَاء (ʿašāʾ, 'evening meal, dinner, supper'), from the root ع-ش-و (ʿ-š-w, 'evening, nightfall'), with regular vernacular loss of final hamza.

morphemes.meaning: evening, nightfall, dining in the evening

عشان.etymology: Ubiquitous Levantine causal/purpose conjunction contracted from على شأن (on account of, for the matter of).

عشاني.etymology: Conjunction عشان (contracted from على شأن) suffixed with the 1sg pronominal object -i.

عشب.etymology: From Classical Arabic عُشْب (ʿušb, 'fresh green grass, herbage, herbs, pasture plants'), collective noun from the Proto-Semitic root *ʿ-ś-b ('green grass, herbs').

عشر.etymology: Construct cardinal numeral from Semitic root ع-ش-ر used directly before counted plural nouns.

عشرة.etymology: Standalone feminine-marked cardinal ten from the pan-Semitic numeral root ع-ش-ر.

عشرين.etymology: Pluralized form of عشر (ten, root ع-ش-ر) formed with -iin to express the numeral twenty.

عصابة.etymology: Continues Classical Arabic عِصَابَة (ʿiṣāba, originally 'cloth fillet or headband tied tightly round the brow', extended already in Classical Arabic to 'tightly bound band of men, faction, gang') on the pattern فِعَالَة (fiʿāla) from the root ع-ص-ب (ʿ-ṣ-b, 'to bind tightly, twist, wrap').

history.meaning: headband, bandage; tightly knit band or troop

rootFamily.gloss: nerve, sinew; (Form II) to get angry

عصابة.notes: Notice how the root ع-ص-ب ('tightly stretched cord/sinew') connects عصابة ('tightly bound gang'), أعصاب ('nerves'), and Levantine عصب ('to lose one's temper').

عصب.etymology: Levantine Form II intransitive verb عَصَّبَ (ʿaṣṣab, 'to tense up one's nerves, lose one's temper, get angry') on the pattern فَعَّلَ (faʿʿala), denominative in modern colloquial Arabic from أَعْصَاب / عَصَب (ʿaṣab, 'sinews, nerves'; Classical Form II meant 'to bind a headband tightly'), root ع-ص-ب (ʿ-ṣ-b).

morphemes.meaning: Form II denominative verb ('get one's nerves taut')

history.meaning: sinew, tendon / to bind tightly round the head
to get angry, flare up, lose one's cool

rootFamily.gloss: angry, mad right now (Levantine active ptcp. mʿaṣṣib)

عصب.notes: Everyday Jordanian equivalent of MSA غَضِبَ (ġaḍiba); construes with على for getting mad at someone (عصبت عليّ, 'she got mad at me').

عصر.etymology: From Classical Arabic عَصْر (ʿaṣr, 'late afternoon; age, era, epoch; pressing/squeezing [fruit]'), from the root ع-ص-ر (ʿ-ṣ-r, 'to press out juice; time of day when the sun declines').

history.meaning: late afternoon; epoch, era; pressing out juice

morphemes.meaning: time of late afternoon; act of pressing

عصرية.etymology: Feminine nisba noun عَصْرِيَّة (ʿaṣriyya, 'late afternoon time, afternoon gathering or stroll'), derived from عَصْر (ʿaṣr, 'late afternoon').

عصفور.etymology: From Classical Arabic عُصْفُور (ʿuṣfūr, 'sparrow, small songbird'), a quadriliteral noun connected to Proto-Semitic *ʿiṣpūr- / *ṣippūr- ('small bird, sparrow', originally 'chirper / whistler').

عصير.etymology: From Classical Arabic عَصِير (ʿaṣīr, 'juice, pressed must'), on the pattern فَعِيل (faʿīl, passive sense 'that which is pressed or squeezed out') from عَصَرَ (ʿaṣara, 'to press, squeeze fruit').

عضلة.etymology: From Classical Arabic عَضَلَة (ʿaḍala, 'muscle'), singulative of عَضَل (ʿaḍal, 'muscles, muscular tissue'), from the root ع-ض-ل (ʿ-ḍ-l, 'to be muscular, firm, tightly bound').

history.meaning: a muscle (originally compared in shape to a small mouse, عَضَل)

عضلة.notes: Like Latin musculus ('little mouse'), classical Arab anatomists noted the visual comparison between a flexing muscle and a mouse (عَضَل).

عطلة.etymology: From Classical Arabic عُطْلَة (ʿuṭla, 'cessation of work, leisure, holiday, day off, vacation'), from عَطِلَ (ʿaṭila, 'to be free of work, idle, unemployed').

morphemes.meaning: being free of work or ornament, cessation of activity

عظيم.etymology: From Classical Arabic عَظِيم (ʿaẓīm, 'great, mighty, magnificent, splendid, vast'), on the adjectival pattern فَعِيل (faʿīl) from عَظُمَ (ʿaẓuma, 'to be great, large, mighty'), related to عَظْم (ʿaẓm, 'bone, bodily frame').

عفش.etymology: From post-Classical and Levantine/Egyptian Arabic عَفْش (ʿafš, 'household furniture, baggage, belongings, stuff'), from عَفَشَ (ʿafaša, 'to gather together household goods, collect odds and ends').

عفوا.etymology: From Classical Arabic عَفْوًا (ʿafwan, 'pardon me, excuse me; you're welcome'), adverbial accusative of عَفْو (ʿafw, 'pardon, forgiveness, effacing a fault; spontaneous favour without obligation'), from عَفَا (ʿafā, 'to efface, pardon, remit').

history.meaning: [I ask] pardon / [granted] without obligation; excuse me, you're welcome

عفواً.etymology: Adverbial accusative (-an, -اً) of عَفْو (ʿafw, pardon, erasure, forgiveness) on the defective root ع-ف-و (ʿ-f-w, to efface, forgive). Functioning as a polite ellipsis for 'I ask pardon', عفواً serves across Jordan as both 'excuse me' and 'you're welcome'.

عقار.etymology: From Classical Arabic عَقَار (ʿaqār, 'immovable property, landed estate, real estate, palm groves and buildings'), from the root ع-ق-ر (ʿ-q-r, 'base, fixed foundation of a house or land').

history.meaning: immovable property, real estate, landed property

morphemes.meaning: fixed base, immovable root of property

عقد.etymology: From Classical Arabic عَقْد (ʿaqd, 'knot, tying; contract, lease, covenant; arch or vault'), verbal noun of عَقَدَ (ʿaqada, 'to tie a knot, bind fast, conclude a contract').

history.meaning: knot; binding agreement, contract, lease; arch

morphemes.meaning: tying a knot, binding fast, concluding an agreement
act of binding or a bound contract

عقدة.etymology: From Classical Arabic عُقْدَة (ʿuqda, 'knot, tie, bond'), derived from the root ع-ق-د (ʿ-q-d, 'to knot, bind, conclude an agreement'), cognate with Hebrew עָקַד (ʿāqaḏ, 'to bind'). Its plural عُقَد (ʿuqad) covers both physical knots in cordage and complex knots in plots or problems.

عكاز.etymology: Masculine noun عُكَّاز (ʿukkāz, 'walking stick, staff, crutch'; also feminine عُكَّازَة) from the root ع-ك-ز (ʿ-k-z, 'to lean on a staff'). Originally an iron-tipped walking staff used by travellers and shepherds, now also a hiker's stick or medical crutch.

history.meaning: to lean on a staff -> walking stick, crutch

علامة.etymology: From Classical Arabic عَلَامَة (ʿalāma, 'mark, sign, token, badge; grade/score'), from the root ع-ل-م (ʿ-l-m, 'mark, sign, knowledge', originally 'distinguishing landmark in the desert').

morphemes.meaning: sign or mark by which something is known

علبة.etymology: Traditional container noun from root ع-ل-ب denoting a small box, tin, or lidded canister.

علطول.etymology: Univerbated colloquial spelling of عَلَى طُول (ʿalā ṭūl, literally 'upon length'), used across Levantine and Egyptian Arabic to mean 'straight ahead', 'right away / immediately', or 'all the time / continuously'.

history.meaning: along the length; continuously, straight away

علق.etymology: From Classical Arabic عَلِقَ (ʿaliqa, 'to hang from, cling to, catch on, get stuck or jammed'), from the root ع-ل-ق (ʿ-l-q, 'clinging, hanging, adhering').

history.meaning: to cling, catch on, get stuck, adhere

علوي.etymology: From Classical Arabic عُلْوِيّ / عَلَوِيّ (ʿulwiyy, 'upper, top, overhead, elevated'), nisba adjective from عُلْو (ʿulw, 'upper part, height, top'), from the root ع-ل-و (ʿ-l-w).

على.etymology: Fundamental Semitic preposition عَلَى expressing contact above, direction toward, or obligation.

علي.etymology: From Classical Arabic عَلِيَ (ʿaliya, 'to rise, ascend, become high or louder'), Form I stative/inchoative verb from the root ع-ل-و (ʿ-l-w, 'height, elevation').

history.meaning: to rise, climb higher, become elevated

علية.etymology: From Classical Arabic عُلِّيَّة (ʿulliyya, 'upper room, rooftop chamber, attic, loft'), from the root ع-ل-و (ʿ-l-w, 'height, being above'), with ancient Semitic parallels.

عليها.etymology: Preposition على (taking stem 'alay- before pronouns) combined with 3fs suffix -ha.

علّق.etymology: From Classical Arabic عَلَّقَ (ʿallaqa, 'to hang up, suspend, attach; to comment upon'), Form II causative of عَلِقَ (ʿaliqa, 'to cling, hang'); in spoken Arabic, also 'to get stuck/jammed (of a button, lock, or screen)'.

morphemes.meaning: causative: to suspend or cause to hang

علّم.etymology: From Classical Arabic عَلَّمَ (ʿallama, 'to teach, instruct; to mark, put a sign upon'), Form II causative of عَلِمَ (ʿalima, 'to know') and denominative from عَلَم / عَلَامَة ('mark, sign').

history.meaning: to cause to know, teach, instruct; to mark

morphemes.meaning: causative: to cause someone to know, teach

عم.etymology: Levantine progressive aspect particle عَم (ʿam, 'currently doing [-ing]'), grammaticalized by phonetic erosion from عَمَّال (ʿammāl, intensive active adjective meaning 'actively working at, busily engaged in doing'), from the root ع-م-ل (ʿ-م-l, 'to work, do').

history.meaning: actively engaged in doing, busily working at

عم.notes: The full form عمّال (ʿammāl) is still used as a progressive marker in Egyptian and some rural Levantine dialects.

عمة.etymology: Feminine of عَمّ (ʿamm, 'paternal uncle'), from ancient Semitic kinship root ع-م-م (ʿ-m-m, 'father's kin, paternal clan').

عمتي.etymology: Kinship noun عمة (paternal aunt, feminine of عمّ, root ع-م-م) with 1sg possessive -i.

عمر.etymology: From Classical Arabic عُمْر / عُمُر (ʿumr / ʿumur, 'life, lifetime, age, span of life'), from the root ع-م-ر (ʿ-m-r, 'to live long, inhabit, thrive, build').

عمرك.etymology: Noun عمر (age, lifetime, root ع-م-ر) plus 2ms -ak, also functioning idiomatically as have you ever.

عمره.etymology: Combines عمر (lifespan, age, root ع-م-ر) with the 3ms possessive clitic -o/-hu.

عمرها.etymology: Noun عمر (lifetime, root ع-م-ر) plus 3fs -ha, used with negation for she has never.

عمل.etymology: From Classical Arabic عَمِلَ (ʿamila, 'to do, make, work, act') and its verbal noun عَمَل (ʿamal, 'work, deed, action'), from the Semitic root ع-م-ل (ʿ-m-l, 'working, labouring, making').

history.meaning: to do, make, work; work, action

morphemes.part: فَعِلَ / فَعَل (Form I verb and verbal noun)

عملي.etymology: Derived from Arabic عَمَل (ʿamal, 'work, action') plus the nisba suffix -ِيّ (-iyy), root ع-م-ل (ʿ-m-l).

عمود.etymology: From Classical Arabic عَمُود (ʿamūd, 'column, pillar, post, pole, upright shaft'), from عَمَدَ (ʿamada, 'to prop up, support, intend'), from Proto-Semitic *ʿammūd- ('pillar, column').

morphemes.meaning: supporting, propping up with a pillar

عميق.etymology: From Classical Arabic عَمِيق (ʿamīq, 'deep, profound'), on the adjectival pattern فَعِيل (faʿīl) from عَمُقَ (ʿamuqa, 'to be deep'), from Proto-Semitic *ʿamūq- / *ʿamīq- ('deep').

عمّ.etymology: From Classical Arabic عَمّ (ʿamm, 'paternal uncle, father's brother; polite title of respect for an older man'), inherited from Proto-Semitic *ʿamm- ('paternal uncle, father's kinsmen, people').

عن.etymology: From Classical Arabic عَنْ (ʿan, 'from, away from, about, concerning, off'), classical preposition of separation, source, and topic.

عناد.etymology: From Classical Arabic عِنَاد (ʿinād, 'stubbornness, obstinacy, willful resistance'), Form III verbal noun of عَانَدَ (ʿānada, 'to oppose stubbornly, resist') and عَنَدَ (ʿanada, 'to swerve aside, be headstrong and refractory').

عنجد.etymology: Conversational Jordanian adverb fusing عن (about, in) and جد (earnestness, root ج-د-د).

عند.etymology: Classical spatial and possessive preposition عِنْدَ denoting proximity or having something at hand.

عندي.etymology: Preposition عند (at, with) suffixed with 1sg pronoun -i to express possession (I have).

عنوان.etymology: From Classical Arabic عُنْوَان / عِنْوَان (ʿunwān / ʿinwān, 'title of a book, heading, superscription, sign; [modern] postal or street address'), from عَنَّ / عَنْوَنَ ('to appear in front, place a title upon a letter or book').

morphemes.meaning: placing a title, heading, or address

عنيد.etymology: From Classical Arabic عَنِيد (ʿanīd, 'stubborn, obstinate, headstrong, unyielding'), on the adjectival pattern فَعِيل (faʿīl) from عَنَدَ (ʿanada, 'to be obstinate, turn aside willfully').

عودة.etymology: Feminine verbal noun عَوْدَة (ʿawda, 'return, coming back') from the hollow verb عَادَ (ʿāda, 'to return, come back'), root ع-و-د (ʿ-w-d). Common in welcoming expressions upon someone's arrival home.

عيب.etymology: From Classical Arabic عَيْب (ʿayb, 'fault, defect, blemish, flaw; shame, disgraceful or rude act'), from عَابَ (ʿāba, 'to be defective, marred; to find fault with'). Used as an interjection ('shame!, how rude!').

عيلة.etymology: Spoken Arabic reflex of Classical Arabic عَائِلَة (ʿāʾila, 'family, household, dependents'), with regular vernacular shift of medial -āʾi- to -ay- / -ē- (عَيْلَة ʿayla / ʿēla), from the root ع-و-ل (ʿ-w-l, 'to sustain, support dependents').

عيلتي.etymology: Levantine عيلة (contraction of Classical عَائِلَة, family, root ع-و-ل) plus 1sg possessive -i.

عين.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *'ayn- ('eye; natural water spring'), grammatically feminine.
عين.notes: Gives rise to warm Levantine expressions of affection and delight such as يا عيني ('oh my!', literally 'oh my eye') and على عيني ('gladly').

عيّن.etymology: From Classical Arabic عَيَّنَ (ʿayyana, 'to specify, designate, appoint to an office, hire'), Form II denominative verb from عَيْن (ʿayn, 'eye; the exact thing itself, specific individual').

history.meaning: to single out by eye, specify, appoint, hire

morphemes.meaning: denominative: to single out specifically or appoint

عَجْن.etymology: Vocalized verbal noun (maṣdar) عَجْن (ʿajn, 'kneading, working dough'), from عَجَنَ (ʿajana, 'to knead dough with the hands').

عَزَف.etymology: From Classical Arabic عَزَفَ (ʿazafa, 'to play a musical instrument, make music'), from the root ع-ز-ف (ʿ-z-f).

morphemes.meaning: playing music, making a resonant sound

عَقَد.etymology: From Classical Arabic عَقَدَ (ʿaqada, 'to tie a knot, bind, knit or furrow [one's eyebrows: عقد حواجبه], conclude a pact, thicken a sauce'), from the root ع-ق-د (ʿ-q-d).

history.meaning: to tie, knot, knit together (including the brows)

عِرق.etymology: From Classical Arabic عِرْق (ʿirq, 'vein, root, wood grain, streak in stone or timber'), vocalized with kasra to distinguish it from عَرَق (ʿaraq, 'sweat; arak').

history.meaning: vein, root, grain of wood, streak in marble

morphemes.meaning: root, vein, branching line or grain

غابة.etymology: Noun غَابَة ('forest, dense woodland', plural غَابَات) from the hollow root غ-ي-ب ('be hidden, disappear from sight'), originally naming a thicket of trees or reeds dense enough to conceal whoever enters it.

غاز.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th–20th centuries from French gaz ('gas; gas stove, gas burner'), coined in 1648 by Flemish chemist Jan Baptist van Helmont after Ancient Greek χάος (kháos, 'chaos, primordial expanse of air'). In Levantine Arabic, غاز commonly denotes the kitchen stove or burner itself.

غازي.etymology: Nisba adjective غَازِيّ (ḡāziyy, 'gaseous; carbonated, sparkling [as in مياه غازية sparkling water]') formed from غَاز (ḡāz, 'gas') with the Arabic relational suffix -ī (ـِيّ).

غالي.etymology: From Classical Arabic غَالٍ / الغَالِي (ḡālin / al-ḡālī, 'expensive, high-priced; precious, dear, beloved'), active participle of غَلَا (ḡalā, 'to rise in price, be dear or precious, exceed bounds').

morphemes.meaning: rising high in price or value, exceeding bounds
having high value or cost; beloved

غامض.etymology: From Classical Arabic غَامِض (ḡāmiḍ, 'obscure, mysterious, enigmatic, Subtle, unapparent'), active participle of غَمَضَ / غَمُضَ (ḡamuḍa, 'to be low-lying, hidden, obscure, hard to fathom; to close the eyelids').

morphemes.meaning: being hidden, obscure; closing the eyelids
in an obscure or mysterious state

غامق.etymology: Levantine and Egyptian adjective غَامِق (ḡāmiq, 'dark-coloured, deep in shade [e.g. أخضر غامق dark green]'), developed as a phonetic and semantic blend of Classical عَمِيق (ʿamīq, 'deep [in colour]') and غَامِض (ḡāmiḍ, 'obscure, dark') / root غ-م-ق (ḡ-m-q, 'deep moisture, rich dark soil').

غباش.etymology: Colloquial Levantine noun غَبَاش (ġabāš, 'blurriness, mist, dim haze') from the root غ-ب-ش (ġ-b-š, 'pre-dawn darkness, dim light, indistinctness'). Related to Classical غَبَش (ġabaš, 'dimness just before dawn'), shifting in spoken Arabic to hazy sight or blurred print.

غبرة.etymology: From Classical Arabic غَبْرَة / غَبَرَة (ḡabra / ḡabara, 'dust, cloud of fine dust'), singulative/noun from غَبَرَ (ḡabara, 'to raise dust, be dust-coloured'), from the root غ-ب-ر (ḡ-b-r, 'dust').

غدا.etymology: Spoken Arabic reflex of Classical Arabic غَدَاء (ḡadāʾ, 'lunch, midday meal; in Classical Arabic originally the morning meal eaten after daybreak'), from غَدَا (ḡadā, 'to go forth in the early morning') and غَدْوَة (ḡadwa, 'early morning'), with a semantic shift from 'morning meal' to 'midday meal / lunch'.
غدا.notes: The same semantic shift from 'morning meal' to 'midday meal' occurred in French dîner and Spanish almuerzo.

غرا.etymology: Spoken Arabic reflex of Classical Arabic غِرَاء (ḡirāʾ, 'glue, mucilage, wood glue, hide or fish glue'), from غَرَا (ḡarā, 'to glue, adhere, stick fast'), with regular vernacular loss of final hamza.

غرام.etymology: Metric weight unit borrowed from French gramme (Greek gramma), homophonous with poetic love from غ-ر-م.

غرب.etymology: Geographic noun from the root غ-ر-ب meaning to set (of the sun) or go away, marking the western horizon.

غربي.etymology: Nisba adjective suffixing -i to غرب (west) to qualify things located toward or coming from the western side.

غرض.etymology: Masculine noun غَرَض (ġaraḍ, 'aim, purpose; needed item, errand'; plural أَغْرَاض) from غَرِضَ (ġariḍa), root غ-ر-ض (ġ-r-ḍ, 'target, aim, wish'). In everyday Levantine speech, the plural أغراض ('things, belongings, groceries') is far more frequent than the abstract singular.

غرفة.etymology: Classical noun غُرْفَة (upper chamber, room, from root غ-ر-ف meaning hollowed or scooped space).

غروب.etymology: From Classical Arabic غُرُوب (ġurūb, 'setting of the sun or stars'), verbal noun of غَرَبَ (ġaraba, 'to go away, sink, set in the west'), from the root غ-ر-ب (ġ-r-b, 'west, departure, strangeness'). Cognate with Akkadian erēbu ('to enter, set [of the sun]') and Hebrew עֶרֶב (ʿerev, 'evening').

غريب.etymology: From Classical Arabic غَرِيب (ḡarīb, 'strange, unfamiliar, foreign, unusual; stranger, foreigner'), on the adjectival pattern فَعِيل (faʿīl) from غَرُبَ (ḡaruba, 'to depart far from home, be foreign or strange'), from the root غ-ر-ب (ḡ-r-b, 'departing, setting of the sun, west').

morphemes.meaning: departing far away, setting of the sun, strangeness

غزير.etymology: From Classical Arabic غَزِير (ḡazīr, 'abundant, copious, plentiful, heavy [of rain, water, tears, or knowledge]'), on the adjectival pattern فَعِيل (faʿīl) from غَزُرَ (ḡazura, 'to be abundant, flow copiously').

history.meaning: abundant, copious, heavy (of rain or flow)

morphemes.meaning: abundance, copiousness of water or milk

غسل.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *rḫṣ / Arabic root غ-س-ل (gh-s-l, 'to wash with water'), one of the core everyday domestic verbs across all varieties of Arabic.

غسيل.etymology: From Classical Arabic غَسِيل (ḡasīl, 'washed; clothes to be washed or freshly washed, laundry'), on the pattern فَعِيل (faʿīl, passive sense 'that which is washed') from غَسَلَ (ḡasala, 'to wash').

غصن.etymology: From Classical Arabic غُصْن (ḡuṣn, 'branch, bough, twig of a tree'), from the root غ-ص-ن (ḡ-ṣ-n).

history.meaning: branch, bough, shoot of a tree

غطا.etymology: Colloquial shortening of Classical غِطَاء (cover, lid, root غ-ط-و) via loss of final hamza.

غطّس.etymology: From Classical Arabic غَطَّسَ (ḡaṭṭasa, 'to dip, plunge, dunk, immerse in liquid'), Form II causative of غَطَسَ (ḡaṭasa, 'to dive, plunge, submerge in water').

history.meaning: to dip, dunk, plunge into liquid

morphemes.meaning: causative: to immerse or dunk something

غلاف.etymology: Covering noun patterned on fi'aal from the root غ-ل-ف meaning to encase, sheath, or wrap securely.

غلب.etymology: Form I verb rooted in غ-ل-ب signifying gaining the upper hand, overcoming, or winning in contest.

غلبة.etymology: From Classical Arabic غَلَبَة (ḡalaba, 'overcoming, mastery; [in Levantine Arabic] trouble, bother, fuss, hassle, imposition'), verbal noun of غَلَبَ (ḡalaba, 'to overcome, prevail over').

غلط.etymology: From Classical Arabic غَلَط (ḡalaṭ, 'mistake, error, slip, wrong'), verbal noun of غَلِطَ (ḡaliṭa, 'to make a mistake, err in speech or calculation').

غلطان.etymology: From Classical and post-Classical Arabic غَلْطَان (ḡalṭān, 'mistaken, in error, in the wrong'), stative adjective on the pattern فَعْلَان (faʿlān) from غَلِطَ (ḡaliṭa, 'to make a mistake, err').

morphemes.meaning: in a state of having erred

غلطة.etymology: From Classical Arabic غَلْطَة (ḡalṭa, 'a single mistake, slip-up, blunder'), noun of instance (ism marra) from غَلِطَ (ḡaliṭa, 'to make a mistake').

غلى.etymology: Defective Form I verb (فَعَلَ) from the root غ-ل-ي (ġ-l-y, boiling, seething, bubbling up, rising in price). In everyday Jordanian kitchens, غلى is used both intransitively ('water boils') and transitively ('to boil coffee or tea').

غلّب.etymology: From Classical Arabic غَلَّبَ (ḡallaba, 'to make prevail'), which in Levantine Arabic developed the everyday polite sense 'to trouble someone, put someone to trouble or inconvenience' (as in رح أغلّبك معي 'I'm going to trouble you with me').

history.meaning: to trouble, inconvenience, put to effort

morphemes.meaning: causative: to cause trouble or effort to someone

غلّف.etymology: Form II verb غَلَّفَ (ghallafa, 'to wrap, put in a sheath or cover') from Arabic root غ-ل-ف (gh-l-f), cf. غِلَاف ('cover').

غموض.etymology: From Classical Arabic غُمُوض (ḡumūḍ, 'obscurity, mystery, ambiguity, impenetrability'), verbal noun (on pattern فُعُول fuʿūl) of غَمُضَ (ḡamuḍa, 'to be obscure, hidden, mysterious').

morphemes.meaning: being hidden, obscure; closing the eyelids

غمّض.etymology: From Classical Arabic غَمَّضَ (ḡammaḍa, 'to close or shut one's eyes, blink'), Form II intensive/causative from the root غ-م-ض (ḡ-m-ḍ, 'closing the eyelids, being hidden').

history.meaning: to close one's eyes, shut the eyelids

غني.etymology: From Classical Arabic غَنِيّ (ḡaniyy, 'rich, wealthy, self-sufficient, full-bodied [of flavour or colour]'), on the adjectival pattern فَعِيل (faʿīl, *ḡaniw- > ḡaniyy) from غَنِيَ (ḡaniya, 'to be free of need, wealthy, rich').

history.meaning: free from need, rich, wealthy, abundant

غنّى.etymology: From Classical Arabic غَنَّى (ḡannā, 'to sing, chant'), Form II verb from the root غ-ن-ي (ḡ-n-y, 'to sing, warble; sufficiency').

غير.etymology: From Classical Arabic غَيْر (ḡayr, 'other than, different from, except, non-, un-'), noun of difference and exception from the root غ-ي-ر (ḡ-y-r, 'alteration, difference, otherness').

غيمة.etymology: Unit noun غَيْمَة (ġayma, 'a single cloud') formed with feminine -a from collective غَيْم (ġaym, 'clouds, mist'), from the root غ-ي-م (ġ-y-m, 'to become cloudy, overcast'). Everyday Levantine prefers غيمة / غيوم over formal سحابة for ordinary clouds in the sky.

غيّر.etymology: From Classical Arabic غَيَّرَ (ḡayyara, 'to change, alter, modify, replace'), Form II denominative/causative verb from غَيْر (ḡayr, 'other, different'), literally 'to make something other than what it was'.

غِلِط.etymology: From Classical Arabic غَلِطَ (ḡaliṭa, 'to make a mistake, err, slip up'), Form I stative/intransitive verb from the root غ-ل-ط (ḡ-l-ṭ), with regular Levantine raising of a-i to i-i (ḡiliṭ).

فإنه.etymology: Formal compound linker uniting causal فَـ (so/then), emphatic إِنَّ (indeed), and 3ms pronoun ـهُ.

فات.etymology: From Classical Arabic فَاتَ (fāta, 'to pass by, slip away, elude'), hollow verb from the root ف-و-ت (f-w-t); in Levantine Arabic, shifted from 'to pass by / pass through a doorway' to the primary everyday verb meaning 'to enter, go in, come inside'.

history.meaning: to pass by, pass through; (Levantine) to enter, go in

فاتورة.etymology: Borrowed from Italian fattura ('invoice, bill, receipt', originally 'making, workmanship'), from Latin factūra ('a making', from facere 'to make, do').

فاز.etymology: Hollow Form I verb (فَعَلَ) from the root ف-و-ز (f-w-z, to attain success, escape peril, triumph, win). Retaining its Classical sense of achieving victory or success (often paired with بـ before the prize), فاز is used across all registers of Jordanian Arabic.

فاصل.etymology: Active participle noun فَاصِل (fāṣil, 'that which separates, interval, partition') from the root ف-ص-ل (f-ṣ-l, 'to divide, cut apart, space out'). Used across physical craft, layout, and time to denote an exact spacing or break between consecutive items.

فاضي.etymology: Active participle from root ف-ض-و (open space, emptiness), used for empty containers and free time.

فاقع.etymology: From Classical Arabic فَاقِع (fāqiʿ, 'bright, vivid, intense, glaring [of colour, classically in Quranic صَفْرَاءُ فَاقِعٌ لَوْنُهَا bright vivid yellow]'), active participle of فَقَعَ (faqaʿa, 'to be intensely bright in colour; to burst, pop').

morphemes.meaning: bursting, popping; intense vividness of colour

فاكر.etymology: Active participle adjective فَاكِر (fākir, 'remembering, keeping in mind') from فَكَرَ (fakara, 'to think, reflect'), root ف-ك-ر (f-k-r). Widespread in Egyptian and Levantine Arabic as a stative predicate meaning 'I/you/she remembers' (matching فاكرة).

فالت.etymology: Active participle فَالت (fālit) of the verb فَلَتَ (falata, 'to slip away, break free, get loose'), from the root ف-ل-ت (f-l-t, 'to escape, slip out of grasp'). In Jordanian colloquial speech it commonly describes a rope, strap, or knot that has come undone.

فالس.etymology: Borrowed from French valse ('waltz'), itself from German Walzer (from walzen 'to roll, revolve, glide in a dance').

history.meaning: waltz (dance and musical metre in triple time)

فانوس.etymology: Borrowed via Byzantine/Medieval Greek φανός (phanós, 'torch, lantern', from φαίνω 'to shine, appear').
فانوس.notes: Takes the broken plural فوانيس, familiar across Amman courtyards and verandas.

فانيليا.etymology: Culinary borrowing entering modern Arabic via Italian vainiglia and French vanille, ultimately from Spanish vainilla.

فايت.etymology: Active participle (فَاعِل, fāʿil) of the Levantine hollow verb فات (fāt, 'to enter, pass into') on the root ف-و-ت (f-w-t, to pass by, slip in). While Classical فَاتَ primarily means 'to pass by or miss', Levantine Arabic developed the primary spatial sense 'to go in / enter'.

فايز.etymology: Levantine colloquial form of فائز from the hollow root ف-و-ز (to triumph, attain), with medial hamza reduced to y.

فتح.etymology: From Classical Arabic فَتَحَ (fataḥa, 'to open, unlock, unfold, conquer, switch on'), inherited from Proto-Semitic *pataḥ- ('to open').

فتحة.etymology: From Classical Arabic فَتْحَة (fatḥa, 'an opening, aperture, slot, keyhole; the short vowel sign a'), noun of instance/concrete noun from فَتَحَ (fataḥa, 'to open').

فتحت.etymology: Past tense 1sg/2ms/3fs verb built on فتح (root ف-ت-ح, to open or unlock).

فترة.etymology: Continues Classical Arabic فَتْرَة (fatra, originally 'an interval of subsidence, lull between two bouts of fever or between two prophets') on the pattern فَعْلَة (faʿla) of فَتَرَ (fatara, 'to abate, subside, grow tepid'), triliteral root ف-ت-ر (f-t-r).

history.meaning: to subside -> lull, interval between events

فترة.notes: In Jordanian speech, هالفترة means 'lately / during this period', and من فترة means 'for a while now / some time ago'.

فتفوتة.etymology: Expressive colloquial feminine diminutive noun built on a reduplicated root ف-ت-ف-ت (f-t-f-t, 'to crumble finely'), itself expanded from the geminate Classical root ف-ت-ت (f-t-t, to crumble into tiny bits). Endearingly idiomatic across Jordan and the Levant, فتفوتة means a tiny crumb or speck.

فجأة.etymology: Continues Classical Arabic noun of sudden occurrence فَجْأَة (fajʾa, adverbial accusative فَجْأَةً fajʾatan, 'suddenly, unexpectedly') on the pattern فَعْلَة (faʿla) from فَجَأَ / فَجِئَ (fajiʾa, 'to come upon unawares, overtake suddenly'), final-hamza root ف-ج-ء (f-j-ʾ).

history.meaning: to overtake suddenly -> unexpectedly, all at once

فجأة.notes: In spoken Jordanian, فجأة is pronounced without accusative -an (فجأة إجت ليان, 'suddenly Layan showed up'), whereas formal MSA reads فَجْأَةً (fajʾatan).

فجر.etymology: Classical Arabic فَجْر ('dawn, daybreak') from the root ف-ج-ر ('cleave open, burst forth'), vividly picturing the first streak of morning light splitting open the darkness of night along the eastern horizon.

فحص.etymology: From Classical Arabic فَحَصَ (faḥaṣa, 'to examine closely, inspect, scrutinize, check', originally 'to scratch and search the ground like a bird'), and its verbal noun فَحْص (faḥṣ, 'examination, inspection, test').

history.meaning: to search, examine closely, inspect; an inspection

morphemes.part: فَعَلَ / فَعْل (Form I verb and verbal noun)

فحم.etymology: From Classical Arabic فَحْم (faḥm, 'charcoal, coal'), Semitic root ف-ح-م (f-ḥ-m, 'to be pitch black').

فخار.etymology: Classical Arabic فُخَّار / فَخَّار (faḫḫār, 'fired pottery, stoneware'), inherited from Aramaic פַּחָרָא (paḥḥārā, 'potter, earthenware'), ultimately from Akkadian paḫāru ('potter').

فخر.etymology: Verbal noun (maṣdar) on the pattern فَعْل (faʿl) from the root ف-خ-ر (f-x-r, pride, glory, boasting, honor), famous in Classical Arabic poetry as the genre of self-praise (فَخْر). Preceded by the preposition بـ (بفخر), it serves in Jordanian speech as the adverbial phrase 'proudly'.

morphemes.meaning: Form I verbal noun (used in بفخر 'proudly')

فخور.etymology: From Classical Arabic فَخُور (faḵūr, 'proud, taking pride in; boastful'), intensive adjective on the pattern فَعُول (faʿūl) from فَخَرَ (faḵara, 'to glory, take pride, boast').

فراولة.etymology: Borrowed via Mediterranean trade from Italian fragola / dialectal fraula ('strawberry'), from Latin frāga ('wild strawberries').

فرج.etymology: From Classical Arabic فَرَجَ / انْفَرَجَ (faraja / infaraja, 'to open up, part, clear away grief, bring relief') and its noun فَرَج (faraj, 'relief from distress, happy resolution, opening'), from the root ف-ر-ج (f-r-j, 'opening, parting, relief'). Often used in the exclamation فَرَجَت! (farajat!, 'relief has come / it's finally sorted out!').

history.meaning: to open up, relieve distress; relief, happy resolution

فرجى.etymology: Levantine causative verb فَرْجَى (farjā, 'to show, let someone see'), back-formed as a transitive counterpart to تَفَرَّجَ (tafarraja, 'to look at, watch, view a spectacle', originally 'to seek relief by gazing out'), blended with Classical أَرَى (ʾarā, 'to show').

morphemes.meaning: opening up to view, relieving, viewing
causative: to cause someone to see

فرح.etymology: From Classical Arabic فَرِحَ (fariḥa, 'to rejoice, be glad, be happy') and its verbal noun فَرَح (faraḥ, 'joy, gladness, wedding celebration'), from the root ف-ر-ح (f-r-ḥ).

history.meaning: to rejoice, be happy; joy, gladness

morphemes.part: فَعِلَ / فَعَل (Form I stative verb and noun)

فرحة.etymology: From Classical Arabic فَرْحَة (farḥa, 'joy, delight, an occasion of happiness'), noun of instance (ism marra) from فَرِحَ (fariḥa, 'to rejoice, be happy').

history.meaning: a feeling or occasion of joy, delight

morphemes.meaning: single experience or occasion of joy

فرد.etymology: From Classical Arabic فَرَدَ (farada, 'to be single, separate; [in post-Classical and spoken Arabic] to spread out flat, unfold, unroll, straighten out [dough, cloth, or a bent wire]'), from the root ف-ر-د (f-r-d).

history.meaning: to spread out flat, unfold, straighten; (also noun فَرْد 'single unit')

فرش.etymology: From Classical Arabic فَرَشَ (faraša, 'to spread out on the ground [a carpet, mat, or bedding], furnish, lay out, pave'), from the Semitic root ف-ر-ش (f-r-š, 'spreading out flat').

history.meaning: to spread out, lay out (bedding, carpets, or a display)

فرشاية.etymology: Levantine singulative noun فُرْشَايَة ('paintbrush, brush', plural فرشايات), adapted from post-classical فُرْشَاة / فُرْشَة and tied in popular usage to the root ف-ر-ش ('spread evenly across a surface').

فرع.etymology: From Classical Arabic فَرْع (farʿ, 'bough, branch, subdivision'), Semitic root ف-ر-ع (f-r-ʿ).

فرق.etymology: Masculine verbal noun on the pattern فَعْل (faʿl) from the root ف-ر-ق (f-r-q, separating, dividing, distinguishing), cognate with Aramaic pəraq. Across both formal and spoken Jordanian Arabic, فرق designates a distinction, discrepancy, or interval in time or distance.

فرم.etymology: From Arabic فَرَمَ (farama, 'to chop finely, mince, dice, shred'), from the Semitic root ف-ر-م (f-r-m, 'cutting into small pieces, chopping'), cognate with Syriac ܦܪܡ (pram, 'to cut up, chop, slice').

فرن.etymology: Early Mediterranean cultural borrowing into Arabic (فُرْن furn) via Aramaic פּוּרְנָא (pūrnā) from Latin furnus ('baking oven, vaulted kiln').
فرن.notes: In Amman and across the Levant, فرن names both a home kitchen oven and the neighbourhood bread bakery.

فرنسي.etymology: Nisba adjective فَرَنْسِيّ (faransiyy, 'French') formed from فَرَنْسَا (faransā, 'France', from French France) with the Arabic relational suffix -ī (ـِيّ).

morphemes.meaning: relating to a country or people

فرني.etymology: Noun فرن (baking oven, ancient Mediterranean loan from Latin furnus / Greek phournos) plus 1sg -i.

فريق.etymology: Masculine collective/group noun on the pattern فَعِيل (faʿīl) from the root ف-ر-ق (f-r-q, dividing into bands or factions). Meaning originally a distinct band or party separated from a larger crowd, فريق became the standard Arabic word for a sports team, work crew, or project squad.

فرّان.etymology: Intensive occupational noun built on the pattern فَعَّال (faʿʿāl) from فُرْن (furn, oven), itself a classical borrowing from Latin furnus ('bakery oven') via Aramaic/Greek. In Levantine cities and villages, فرّان specifically names the artisan operating the neighborhood stone oven.

فستان.etymology: From post-Classical Arabic فُسْتَان (fustān, 'woman's dress, gown'), borrowed via Ottoman Turkish fistan ('skirt, dress, kilt') and Italian fustagno ('fustian cloth'), which Medieval Latin fustāneum had itself named after الفُسْطَاط (al-Fusṭāṭ, Old Cairo, a medieval centre of cotton textile production).

history.meaning: fustian cotton cloth (named after Fustat in Egypt)

فستان.notes: A remarkable linguistic boomerang: named after Old Cairo (al-Fusṭāṭ) in European textile trade, then borrowed back into Arabic via Italian and Turkish as فستان ('dress').

فصل.etymology: Verbal noun from ف-ص-ل meaning division or separation, naturally extending to year seasons, book sections, and classes.

فضح.etymology: Form I verb فَضَحَ (faḍaḥa, 'to expose someone's faults or secrets publicly, disgrace, unmask') from the Classical Arabic triliteral root ف-ض-ح (f-ḍ-ḥ), originally connected to فُضْحَة / الصُّبْح الأَفْضَح ('whitish break of dawn that exposes hidden things to view').

history.meaning: to lay bare in daylight, expose shame
to expose a secret, blow someone's cover, embarrass publicly

rootFamily.gloss: to be exposed / found out (Form VII)

فضح.notes: High-stakes social word in Levantine society: كنتي رح تفضحينا ('you nearly gave us away!') and لا تفضحينا ('don't make a scene / embarrass us!').

فضل.etymology: From Classical Arabic فَضْل (faḍl, 'bounty, kindness, favour, grace; surplus, excellence'), verbal noun of فَضَلَ (faḍala, 'to exceed, remain over, excel in generosity').

فضولي.etymology: From Classical Arabic فُضُولِيّ (fuḍūliyy, 'meddlesome, nosy, overly curious, inquisitive'), nisba adjective from فُضُول (fuḍūl, 'excess, meddling in what does not concern one, curiosity'), plural of فَضْل (faḍl, 'excess, surplus beyond what is needed').

فضي.etymology: Nisba adjective فِضِّيّ (fiḍḍiyy, 'silver, silver-coloured') formed from فِضَّة (fiḍḍa, 'silver'), from the root ف-ض-ض (f-ḍ-ḍ).

morphemes.meaning: made of or coloured like silver

فضّى.etymology: From Classical and spoken Arabic فَضَّى (faḍḍā, 'to empty out, clear, vacate; to free up one's time'), Form II causative of فَضَا (faḍā, 'to be wide, empty, vacant').

history.meaning: to empty out, clear, make vacant

morphemes.meaning: causative: to make empty or free

فطور.etymology: From the root ف-ط-ر (f-t-r, 'to split, break open, break a fast'), naming the morning meal that breaks the night's fast—exact parallel to English 'breakfast'.
فطور.notes: The related Form IV verbal noun إفطار refers especially to breaking the Ramadan fast at sunset, while فطور is everyday morning breakfast in Amman.

فطيرة.etymology: From Classical Arabic فَطِيرَة (faṭīra, 'pastry, pie, tart, unleavened or freshly baked flatbread'), singulative of فَطِير (faṭīr, 'unleavened dough, freshly baked pastry'), from the root ف-ط-ر (f-ṭ-r, 'to split, create freshly, prepare dough without waiting for fermentation').

morphemes.meaning: splitting open, originating freshly, unleavened baking

فظيع.etymology: From Classical Arabic فَظِيع (faẓīʿ, 'repugnant, terrible, awful, atrocious; [colloquially also] tremendous, incredible'), on the adjectival pattern فَعِيل (faʿīl) from فَظُعَ (faẓuʿa, 'to be dreadful, excessively hard or shocking').

فعلا.etymology: Adverb فِعْلًا (fiʿlan, 'actually, in deed, indeed, really'), formed from the indefinite accusative (-an) of فِعْل (fiʿl, 'act, deed'), root ف-ع-ل (f-ʿ-l, 'to do, act'). Literally 'in action / in reality', as opposed to mere appearance.

فقاعة.etymology: From Classical Arabic فُقَّاعَة (fuqqāʿa, 'bubble on water or liquid'), intensive singulative noun on the pattern فُعَّالَة (fuʿʿāla) from فَقَعَ (faqaʿa, 'to burst, pop, crack').

morphemes.meaning: something that swells and pops; a bubble

فقرة.etymology: From Classical Arabic فَقْرَة / فِقْرَة (faqra / fiqra, 'vertebra of the spine; choice verse, clause, or paragraph of a text'), from the root ف-ق-ر (f-ق-r). Classical rhetoricians metaphorically called a distinct section or clause of prose a 'vertebra' (فقرة) because connected clauses form the backbone (فَقَار) of a text.

history.meaning: vertebra of the spine; clause, section, paragraph

فقع.etymology: Form I verb فَقَعَ (faqaʿa, urban Amman fagaʿ / faʾaʿ, 'to burst open, pop loudly; figuratively to burst or die from bottled-up anger or vexation') inherited directly from Classical Arabic فَقَعَ ('to crack, pop, burst from grief or rage'), triliteral root ف-ق-ع (f-q-ʿ).

history.meaning: to pop loudly (like a blister or pod); burst with sorrow/vexation
to burst (balloon); to snap, explode with frustration

rootFamily.gloss: to pop bubbles; drive someone crazy (Form II)

فقع.notes: Already attested in Classical Arabic idioms (فَقَعَ مَرَارَتَهُ, 'burst his gallbladder') and super vivid in Jordanian speech: رح أفقع من القهر! ('I'm about to burst from frustration!').

فك.etymology: From Classical Arabic فَكَّ (fakka, 'to untie, unfasten, loosen, separate, unscrew, release; to break a large coin/note into small change'), geminate verb from the root ف-ك-ك (f-k-k).

history.meaning: to untie, unfasten, detach, unscrew, release

فكة.etymology: Colloquial Arabic فَكَّة (fakka, 'small change, coins'), noun of instance/result from فَكَّ (fakka, 'to separate, break up a large banknote into smaller denominations').

morphemes.meaning: that which is broken into smaller denominations

فكر.etymology: Form II verb فَكَّرَ (fakkara, 'to think deeply, ponder; in Levantine also to suppose or mistakenly think') on the pattern فَعَّلَ (faʿʿala) from the Classical Arabic triliteral root ف-ك-ر (f-k-r, 'thought, mental reflection').

history.meaning: to think (with بـ / في 'about'); in Levantine, 'to think/assume that...'

فكر.notes: In Jordanian conversation, past-tense فكرت... ('I thought [wrongly] that...', replacing MSA ظننت) introduces a mistaken assumption: فكرت ما في حدا هون!

فكرة.etymology: From Classical Arabic فِكْرَة (fikra, 'thought, idea, notion, reflection'), singulative/instance noun of فِكْر (fikr, 'thinking, reflection'), from the root ف-ك-ر (f-k-r).

فكي.etymology: Feminine singular imperative of geminate فكّ (root ف-ك-ك, to unfasten, detach, or untie).

فكّر.etymology: From Classical Arabic فَكَّرَ (fakkara, 'to think deeply, reflect, ponder, consider'), Form II intensive verb from the root ف-ك-ر (f-k-r, 'thought, reflection').

فليفلة.etymology: Diminutive-patterned Levantine plant name derived from فلفل (pepper, ultimately Sanskrit pippali) for sweet bell peppers.

فن.etymology: From Classical Arabic فَنّ (fann, 'variety, branch, craft, art'), from the geminate root ف-ن-ن (f-n-n, 'to diversify, adorn, excel in skill'). Originally meaning a distinct kind or branch of knowledge or decoration, its plural فُنُون (funūn) later became the standard Arabic term for the fine arts.

فنجان.etymology: Borrowed from Persian *pingān / finjān* ('cup, small bowl', originally a water-clock bowl measuring time).
فنجان.notes: In Jordan فنجان (plural فناجين) specifically names a handleless Arabic coffee cup or porcelain teacup, distinct from كاسة ('drinking glass').

فندق.etymology: Borrowed via Aramaic from Ancient Greek πανδοκεῖον (pandokeîon, 'inn welcoming all travellers', from πᾶς 'all' + δέχομαι 'to receive').
فندق.notes: Entered Arabic in the early medieval period for a merchant caravanserai or travellers' inn, and today means 'hotel'.

فني.etymology: Nisba relational adjective (-ī) formed from فَنّ (fann, 'art, craft, technique'). Depending on context across Modern Standard and Levantine Arabic, فَنِّيّ (fanniyy) carries both the aesthetic sense 'artistic' and the craft-derived sense 'technical'.

فهم.etymology: Form I cognitive verb فَهِمَ (fahima, 'to understand, perceive with the mind') on the pattern فَعِلَ (faʿila) from the Classical Arabic triliteral root ف-ه-م (f-h-m, 'comprehension, discernment').

history.meaning: to grasp with the intellect, understand

rootFamily.gloss: understanding (active ptcp.: فاهمة عليّ؟ 'do you get what I mean?')

فهم.notes: Shared across MSA and all spoken dialects; Form II فَهَّم (fahham) means 'to explain / make someone understand'.

فوت.etymology: Levantine Form II causative verb فَوَّت (fawwat, spelled فوت without shadda in unvocalized text, 'to bring inside, let in, usher in, insert'), derived from فَات (fāt, 'to enter, go in'), from the hollow root ف-و-ت (f-w-t).

history.meaning: to cause to pass in, bring inside, admit

morphemes.meaning: causative: to make enter or bring inside

فورا.etymology: From Classical Arabic فَوْرًا (fawran, 'immediately, at once, on the spot'), adverbial accusative of فَوْر (fawr, 'boiling up, sudden gushing forth, immediate instant without delay', as in مِنْ فَوْرِهِ 'straightaway'), from فَارَ (fāra, 'to boil up, gush forth').

history.meaning: at once, immediately, on the boil

فوراً.etymology: Adverbial accusative (-an, -اً) of فَوْر (fawr, boiling up suddenly, instant), from the hollow root ف-و-ر (f-w-r, to gush or boil over rapidly). Evoking the image of liquid boiling up in an instant, فوراً is standard across Jordan for 'immediately' or 'at once'.

history.meaning: at once, on the spot, immediately

فوطة.etymology: From Classical Arabic فُوطَة (fūṭa, 'towel, napkin, waist-cloth, apron'), recorded by medieval Arab geographers and lexicographers as an early Indian Ocean trade borrowing (from Sindhi/Indic fotā 'striped cloth') that became the standard word for 'towel, wiping cloth'.

فوق.etymology: Classical spatial preposition and adverb فَوْقَ (root ف-و-ق) indicating position above or upstairs.

فوقاني.etymology: From post-Classical and Levantine Arabic فَوْقَانِيّ (fawqāniyy, 'upper, top, situated upstairs'), formed from فَوْق (fawq, 'above') with the augmented relational suffix -ānī (ـَانِيّ, paired with تَحْتَانِيّ taḥtāniyy 'lower').

فولاذ.etymology: Classical Arabic borrowing فُولَاذ ('crucible steel, tempered steel') from Middle Persian pōlāwad (modern Persian پولاد pūlād), celebrated historically for Damascus and Khorasan blades and today used for high-tensile steel wire.

في.etymology: Classical locative preposition فِي (in, inside), also grammaticalized across Arabic dialects to mean there is.

فيزيا.etymology: Colloquial feminine academic noun clipped from Modern Standard Arabic فِيزْيَاء (fīzyāʾ), borrowed from Ancient Greek φυσικά / French physique / English physics (ultimately φύσις 'nature'). Spoken Jordanian speech regularly drops the final glottal stop hamza, leaving فيزيا.

فيلم.etymology: 20th-century loanword from English film ('motion picture; originally a thin celluloid strip coated with photographic emulsion', from Old English filmen, 'thin membrane'), integrated into Arabic root-and-pattern morphology with the broken plural أفلام (ʾaflām).

history.meaning: thin skin -> photographic strip -> motion picture

فيلم.notes: Shared across MSA and Levantine speech; in Jordanian Arabic, حضر فيلم means 'to watch a movie', and عالفيلم contracts على + الفيلم ('to the movie').

فيه.etymology: Existential and locative phrase merging preposition في (in) with the third-person masculine singular pronoun -h/-o.

فيها.etymology: Prepositional compound attaching في (in) to the feminine singular pronominal suffix -ha referring to a feminine antecedent.

فيوز.etymology: Borrowed from English fuse ('electrical safety fuse'), ultimately from Latin fūsus ('spindle; melted/poured').

فيّ.etymology: Colloquial Levantine masculine noun فَيّ (fayy, 'shade, shadow'), inherited from Classical فَيْء (fayʾ, 'returning shadow, afternoon shade') from فَاءَ (fāʾa, 'to return'), root ف-ي-أ (f-y-ʾ). Specifically denotes pleasant cooling shade as the sun turns, with normal loss of final glottal stop in spoken speech.

قائمة.etymology: Feminine active participle (فَاعِلَة) of قَامَ (qāma, 'to stand upright'), from root ق-و-م: a vertical column or standing register of items, hence a written 'list' or café 'menu'.

قابل.etymology: From Classical Arabic قَابَلَ (qābala, 'to face, meet face-to-face, encounter, interview'), Form III associative verb from قَبِلَ / قُبُل (qabila / qubul, 'front, facing side').

history.meaning: to stand face-to-face with, meet, encounter

morphemes.meaning: associative: to face or meet someone

قاد.etymology: Hollow Form I verb on the root ق-و-د meaning to lead by a rein or guide someone along a path.

قادر.etymology: Active participle قَادِر (qādir, 'able, capable, possessing power') on the pattern فَاعِل (fāʿil) of قَدَرَ (qadara, 'to measure out, have power or mastery over'), Semitic triliteral root ق-د-ر (q-d-r).

history.meaning: able, capable of (+ subjunctive in speech, + على in MSA)

قادر.notes: In MSA قادر takes على + verbal noun (قادر على الفهم), whereas spoken Jordanian follows قادر / مش قادرة directly with a bare subjunctive verb (مش قادرة أستوعب, 'I can't take it in').

قارب.etymology: From Classical Arabic قَارِب (qārib, 'small boat, skiff'), either from the root ق-ر-ب (q-r-b, 'to be near, approach', referring to a tender boat that stays close to a larger ship or shore) or an early Mediterranean borrowing akin to Ancient Greek κάραβος (kárabos, 'light ship').

قاس.etymology: From Classical Arabic قَاسَ (qāsa, 'to measure, take the dimensions of, compare by analogy'), hollow verb from the root ق-ي-س (q-y-s, 'measuring, comparing').

قاسي.etymology: From Classical Arabic قَاسٍ / القَاسِي (qāsin / al-qāsī, 'hard, unyielding, harsh, stern, cruel, severe'), active participle of قَسَا (qasā, 'to be hard and unyielding [like stone, or of the heart]').

قاضي.etymology: Defective active participle formed on the root ق-ض-ي meaning to decree, decide, or settle a dispute.

قاع.etymology: Masculine hollow-root noun (فَعْل) from ق-و-ع (q-w-ʿ, flat lowland, basin, lowest surface). In Classical Arabic قَاع denoted a level plain or hollow depression, and in everyday Jordanian speech it specifically refers to the bottom of a pot, cup, bag, or valley.

history.meaning: bottom (of a pot, cup, or valley)

قاعة.etymology: From Classical Arabic قَاعَة (qāʿa, 'spacious courtyard, reception hall, auditorium, large room'), feminine/singulative of قَاع (qāʿ, 'flat level ground, open plain'), from the hollow root ق-و-ع (q-w-ʿ).

history.meaning: paved courtyard, large reception hall, auditorium

قاعد.etymology: Active participle from root ق-ع-د (to sit), grammaticalized across Jordanian Arabic as a progressive auxiliary marker.

قاعدة.etymology: From Classical Arabic قَاعِدَة (qāʿida, 'foundation, base, pedestal; fundamental rule, principle, grammar rule'), feminine active participle of قَعَدَ (qaʿada, 'to sit, rest firmly upon a foundation').

morphemes.meaning: sitting, resting on a firm base

قاعدين.etymology: Sound masculine plural active participle of قعد (root ق-ع-د, to sit), serving both literal seating and progressive aspect.

قال.etymology: From Classical Arabic قَالَ (qāla, 'to say, speak, tell'), hollow verb from the root ق-و-ل (q-w-l, 'speaking, saying'), inherited from Proto-Semitic *qawal- ('to speak, call').

قام.etymology: From Classical Arabic قَامَ (qāma, 'to stand up, rise, get up, undertake'), hollow verb from the Proto-Semitic root *q-w-m ('to rise, stand'). In Levantine Arabic, also used transitively ('to remove, take away, lift off') and as an inchoative discourse verb ('then he went and...').

history.meaning: to rise, stand up; (Levantine) to remove, lift away

قانون.etymology: From Classical Arabic قَانُون (qānūn, 'canonical rule, law, statute, tax register; the qanun zither'), borrowed via Syriac ܩܢܘܢܐ (qānōnā) from Ancient Greek κανών (kanṓn, 'straight measuring rod, rule, standard, law'), itself an ancient Semitic loanword into Greek (cognate with Arabic قَنَاة qanāh and Hebrew קָנֶה qāne, 'reed, measuring rod').
قانون.notes: Another famous linguistic boomerang: Greek κανών was borrowed from a Northwest Semitic word for 'reed / measuring cane' (cognate with קָנֶה / قَنَاة), and later returned to Arabic as قَانُون ('law, canon').

قانوني.etymology: Nisba adjective قَانُونِيّ (qānūniyy, 'legal, lawful, statutory') formed from قَانُون (qānūn, 'law') with the relational suffix -ī (ـِيّ).

قبال.etymology: Spatial preposition contracted colloquially from Classical قُبَالَة (directly facing, root ق-ب-ل denoting front or opposite).

قبعة.etymology: Feminine noun قُبَّعَة (qubbaʿa, 'hat, cap, hood'), derived from the root ق-ب-ع (q-b-ʿ, 'to draw one's head in, dome/cup shape'), related to قُبَّة ('dome'). Standard modern Arabic for any brimmed hat or cap.

history.meaning: to tuck head in -> hood, lark crest, hat

قبل.etymology: Ancient Semitic temporal and spatial preposition قَبْلَ derived from the root ق-ب-ل meaning front, prior, or preceding.

قبو.etymology: From Classical Arabic قَبْو (qabw, 'vault, arched ceiling, vaulted cellar or basement room'), from قَبَا (qabā, 'to arch, curve, vault a building with stone'), from the root ق-ب-و (q-b-w, 'curving, arching, vaulting').
قبو.notes: Related to قُبَّة (qubba, 'dome, cupola', source of Spanish alcoba and English 'alcove').

قد.etymology: Spoken Arabic preposition/noun قَدّ (qadd, 'as much as, the size of, equal in measure to, up to [قد هالمسؤولية up to this responsibility]'), from Classical قَدّ (qadd, 'stature, size, figure, proportion') and contracted قَدْر (qadr, 'amount, measure, extent').

history.meaning: size, stature, measure, amount; as much as

قدام.etymology: From Classical Arabic قُدَّامَ (quddāma, 'in front of, before, ahead of'), locative preposition from the root ق-د-م (q-d-m, 'preceding, going before, front').

history.meaning: in front of, ahead of, before

قدر.etymology: From Classical Arabic قَدَرَ / قَدِرَ (qadara / qadira, 'to have power over, be able to, can; to measure, decree'), from the root ق-د-ر (q-d-r, 'power, ability, measure').

history.meaning: to be able, have the power or capacity to do

قديش.etymology: Levantine interrogative adverb fusing قَدّ (measure, extent, root ق-د-د) with إيش (from أَيُّ شَيْءٍ, what thing).

قديم.etymology: From Classical Arabic قَدِيم (qadīm, 'old, ancient, antique, former, historic'), on the adjectival pattern فَعِيل (faʿīl) from قَدُمَ (qaduma, 'to precede in time, be old or ancient'), from Proto-Semitic *qadīm- ('ancient, former').

morphemes.meaning: going before in time or space, antiquity
having the quality of antiquity or precedence

قديمة.etymology: Feminine adjective formed on fa'iila from root ق-د-م (antiquity, precedence), describing objects, buildings, or traditions.

قديه.etymology: Fused Levantine interrogative and exclamative adverb derived from قَدْر إِيه / قَدّ إِيه (qadd ʾēh, literally 'what amount/measure?'), combining قَدّ ('measure, extent', root ق-د-د) with Levantine إيه ('what'). Jordanian speakers use قديه daily for both prices/quantities ('how much?') and exclamations ('how very...!').

history.meaning: how much, how many, how very

قدّم.etymology: From Classical Arabic قَدَّمَ (qaddama, 'to bring forward, present, offer, serve [food or drink], submit [an application], advance'), Form II causative of قَدِمَ / قَدَمَ (qadama, 'to go before, precede').

history.meaning: to put forward, present, offer, serve

morphemes.meaning: causative: to bring forward or offer

قرأ.etymology: From Classical Arabic قَرَأَ (qaraʾa, 'to read, recite aloud'), from the Semitic root ق-ر-ء (q-r-ʾ, 'to call out, proclaim, recite, read').
قرأ.notes: The same root gives القُرْآن (al-Qurʾān, 'the Recitation').

قرا.etymology: Colloquial defective reflex of Classical hamzated قَرَأَ (qaraʾa, 'to read, recite') on the root ق-ر-أ (q-r-ʾ). Because final glottal stops regularly drop in spoken Levantine Arabic, قرا conjugates cleanly like a final-ā weak verb in everyday Jordanian speech.

morphemes.meaning: Form I verb with dropped final hamza

قراءة.etymology: From Classical Arabic قِرَاءَة (qirāʾa, 'reading, recitation'), verbal noun (on the pattern فِعَالَة fiʿāla) of قَرَأَ (qaraʾa, 'to read, recite').

قرار.etymology: From Classical Arabic قَرَار (qarār, 'stability, settledness,resting place, bottom; [modern] decision, resolution; [in Arab music] the lower tonic octave'), verbal noun of قَرَّ (qarra, 'to settle down, become fixed, rest firmly').

morphemes.meaning: settling down, remaining fixed and stable
state of stability or settled decision

قراية.etymology: Colloquial Jordanian verbal noun corresponding to Classical قِرَاءَة (reading, root ق-ر-أ), replacing the glottal stop with glide -y-.

قرش.etymology: From Ottoman-era Arabic قِرْش / غِرْش (qirš / ḡirš, 'piastre, minor coin denomination'), borrowed via Ottoman Turkish kuruş ('piastre') from German Groschen and Medieval Latin denarius grossus ('thick penny').

history.meaning: piastre (one-hundredth of a pound or lira); coin, money

قرفة.etymology: From the Arabic root ق-ر-ف (q-r-f, 'to peel off bark or rind'), naming cinnamon directly as fragrant peeled tree bark.
قرفة.notes: Warm cinnamon rolls and spiced tea are winter favourites in Amman.

قريب.etymology: Adjective and temporal adverb on fa'iil from the root ق-ر-ب (nearness in space or time), inherited directly from Classical Arabic.

قريبا.etymology: From Classical Arabic قَرِيبًا (qarīban, 'soon, shortly, in the near future'), adverbial accusative of قَرِيب (qarīb, 'near').

history.meaning: at a near time, soon, shortly

قرّب.etymology: From Classical Arabic قَرَّبَ (qarraba, 'to bring near, move closer; [in spoken usage also intransitive] to come closer, be nearly there'), Form II intensive/causative of قَرُبَ (qaruba, 'to be near').

history.meaning: to bring closer, draw near, approach

morphemes.meaning: causative: to bring or come closer

قزاز.etymology: Levantine collective noun evolved from Classical زُجَاج (glass) through consonantal metathesis and emphatic assimilation into قزاز.

قسم.etymology: From Classical Arabic قَسَمَ (qasama, 'to divide, split up, distribute, apportion') and قِسْم (qism, 'part, section, department'), from the root ق-س-م (q-s-m, 'dividing, apportioning').

history.meaning: to divide, split into parts; a division or section

morphemes.part: فَعَلَ / فِعْل (Form I verb and noun)

قش.etymology: Collective masculine noun قَشّ (qašš, 'straw, dry stalks, chaff') from قَشَّ (qašša, 'to gather dry scraps, sweep'), geminate root ق-ش-ش (q-š-š). Used across Arabic for straw hats, woven baskets, and dried stalks.

history.meaning: to gather dry scraps -> straw, stubble

قشر.etymology: Collective noun derived from the triliteral root ق-ش-ر signifying the outer skin, rind, bark, or husk.

قشرة.etymology: Singulative noun قِشْرَة (qišra, 'peel, rind, skin of a fruit, bark, shell, flake, veneer') from the collective قِشْر (qišr, 'outer covering, peel, bark, shell'), from the root ق-ش-ر (q-š-r, 'to peel, strip off the outer skin').

history.meaning: a single peel, rind, crust, outer layer

قص.etymology: From Classical Arabic قَصَّ (qaṣṣa, 'to cut with scissors, clip, shear, trim; to follow tracks, relate a story'), geminate verb from the root ق-ص-ص (q-ṣ-ṣ).

history.meaning: to cut, clip, shear, trim; to narrate

morphemes.meaning: cutting, clipping; following tracks step by step, narrating

قصة.etymology: From Classical Arabic قِصَّة (qiṣṣa, 'story, narrative, tale, affair'), from قَصَّ (qaṣṣa, 'to follow someone's tracks step by step, recount events in sequence').

morphemes.meaning: following tracks step by step, recounting in order; cutting

قصد.etymology: From the root ق-ص-د (q-s-d), whose core sense is heading straight toward an aim or target, and by extension intending or meaning something.
قصد.notes: In Jordanian speech قصد with possessive suffixes (قصدي 'I mean', قصدك 'you mean') clarifies a speaker's point.

قصير.etymology: Descriptive adjective on fa'iil built on the root ق-ص-ر denoting shortness in length, stature, or duration.

قضى.etymology: From Classical Arabic قَضَى (qaḍā, 'to decree, accomplish, spend time'), Semitic root ق-ض-ي (q-ḍ-y).

قطار.etymology: Classical Arabic قِطَار originally named a 'single-file caravan of camels linked head-to-tail' (from the root ق-ط-ر 'line up in file, drip in sequence'); in the 19th century, coupled railway carriages were naturally given the same vivid name: 'train'.

history.meaning: file of camels strung one behind another

قطرة.etymology: Noun of unity with ta marbuta from the root ق-ط-ر meaning to drip or trickle down drop by drop.

قطع.etymology: Core Form I triliteral verb (فَعَلَ) built on the root ق-ط-ع (q-ṭ-ʿ, to cut, sever, cross, interrupt). Beyond physical cutting, Jordanian Arabic uses قطع constantly for utility outages ('power/water cut off'), crossing streets, and interrupting someone mid-sentence.

قطعة.etymology: Unit noun patterned on fi'la from the triliteral root ق-ط-ع (to sever or cut), naming a single slice or fragment.

قطن.etymology: Agricultural and textile noun قُطْن from root ق-ط-ن, the direct medieval source of English cotton and Italian cotone.

قطّع.etymology: From Classical Arabic قَطَّعَ (qaṭṭaʿa, 'to cut up into many pieces, slice, chop, dice'), Form II intensive/pluractional of قَطَعَ (qaṭaʿa, 'to cut').

history.meaning: to cut into pieces, slice up, chop

morphemes.meaning: intensive/pluractional: to cut repeatedly into pieces

قعد.etymology: Form I verb rooted in ق-ع-د (to sit down, stay seated), serving as the primary everyday verb for sitting in Jordan.

قعدة.etymology: From Classical Arabic قَعْدَة (qaʿda, 'an act of sitting; a sitting session, social gathering, seating area'), noun of instance (ism marra) from قَعَدَ (qaʿada, 'to sit').

history.meaning: a sitting, social gathering, seating spot

morphemes.meaning: session of sitting together or seating spot

قفل.etymology: From Classical Arabic قُفْل (qufl, 'lock, padlock, bolt'), from the root ق-ف-ل (q-ف-l, 'locking, fastening shut'), with parallels in Aramaic קוּפְלָא / ܩܘܦܠܐ (qūp̄lā, 'lock, bolt, fetter').

قلب.etymology: From the Semitic root ق-ل-ب (q-l-b, 'to turn, invert, change'), naming the heart as the ever-turning centre of feeling and thought.

قلق.etymology: From Classical Arabic قَلِقَ (qaliqa, 'to be uneasy, agitated, restless, worried, anxious') and its verbal noun قَلَق (qalaq, 'anxiety, worry, restlessness', originally 'being loose and unsettled in its socket, like a stone or tooth').

history.meaning: to be restless, uneasy, worried; anxiety, worry

morphemes.part: فَعِلَ / فَعَل (Form I stative verb and noun)

قلقان.etymology: Levantine adjectival pattern فَعْلَان (faʿlān) from Classical Arabic root ق-ل-ق (qaliqa, 'to be restless or anxious').

قلم.etymology: Early borrowing (via Aramaic or Ethiopic) from Ancient Greek κάλαμος (kálamos, 'reed, reed pen').
قلم.notes: Combines in compounds such as قلم رصاص ('pencil', literally 'lead pen') and قلم حبر ('ink pen').

قماش.etymology: From Classical and post-Classical Arabic قُمَاش (qumāš, 'woven cloth, fabric, textile; originally household goods or gleanings gathered together'), from قَمَشَ (qamaša, 'to gather up small things'). In Mamluk and Ottoman usage, قُمَاش specialized to mean fine woven fabric and cloth in general.

morphemes.meaning: gathering things together; woven goods, cloth

قماش.notes: Borrowed from Arabic into Ottoman Turkish as kumaş ('fabric, cloth').

قماشة.etymology: Singulative noun قُمَاشَة (qumāša, 'a piece of cloth, rag, duster, or specific type of fabric') formed from the collective قُمَاش (qumāš, 'cloth, fabric').

history.meaning: a single piece of cloth, wiping cloth, fabric

قمر.etymology: From Classical Arabic قَمَر (qamar, 'moon'), from the root ق-م-ر (q-m-r, 'to be pale-white, moonlit, shine with silvery light'). Unlike solar/lunar pairs in some languages, قَمَر is grammatically masculine in Arabic and belongs to the core inherited vocabulary.

قميص.etymology: Classical Arabic قَمِيص ('shirt, tunic', plural قُمْصَان), borrowed in Late Antiquity from Late Latin camisia ('linen shirt, nightshirt') via Greek καμίσιον, and later re-exported from Andalusi Arabic into Iberian Romance.

قنب.etymology: From Classical Arabic قِنَّب / قُنَّب (qinnab / qunnab, 'hemp, hemp cord'), an ancient Mediterranean/West Asian cultural loan shared with Ancient Greek κάνναβις (kánnabis) and Latin cannabis. In everyday Jordanian hardware and craft vocabulary, خيط قنب specifically denotes brown rough hemp twine.

قنديل.etymology: From Classical Arabic قِنْدِيل (qindīl, 'hanging lamp, oil lamp'), borrowed in Late Antiquity from Late Greek κανδήλα (kandḗla) / Latin candēla ('wax light, candle, hanging lamp'). Long embedded in Levantine Arabic heritage and proverbs, with the broken plural قَنَادِيل (qanādīl).

قنينة.etymology: From Classical Arabic قِنِّينَة (qinnīna, 'glass bottle, flask, phial'), an early Mediterranean/Aramaic vessel term (compare Syriac ܩܢܝܢܬܐ qanīnṯā 'flask, bottle') fully integrated into Arabic with broken plural قَنَانِي (qanānī).

قهوة.etymology: Cultural noun قَهْوَة from root ق-ه-و, shifting historically from an antique word for wine to the roasted coffee brew via Yemen.

قوار.etymology: Levantine Arabic قَوَّار (qawwār, 'flowerpot, terracotta plant pot'), from the root ق-و-ر (q-w-r, 'to hollow out in the round, scoop out a circular cavity'), originally referring to a hollowed-out vessel or broken jar bottom used for planting seedlings.

قوام.etymology: Derived from the hollow root ق-و-م (to stand upright, hold together), denoting structure, consistency, or stature.

قوة.etymology: Continues Classical Arabic قُوَّة (quwwa, 'strength, power, force; originally a single twisted strand giving strength to a rope') from the doubly weak root ق-و-ي (q-w-y, verb قَوِيَ qawiya, 'to be strong, vigorous').

history.meaning: to be strong -> strand of a rope; physical or moral strength

قوة.notes: Watch the two conversational senses of بالقوة in Jordanian: 'by coercion/force' (أخدتها بالقوة) and 'barely / with great difficulty' (بالقوة لحقت الباص, 'I barely caught the bus').

قوس.etymology: From Classical Arabic قَوْس (qaws, 'bow [weapon or violin bow], arch, archway, arc'), inherited from Proto-Semitic *qawš- / *qašt- ('bow, arch').

morphemes.meaning: curving in an arc, bow, arch

قوي.etymology: From Classical Arabic قَوِيّ (qawiyy, 'strong, powerful, sturdy, intense'), on the adjectival pattern فَعِيل (faʿīl, *qawiy-) from قَوِيَ (qawiya, 'to be strong, vigorous').

قياس.etymology: From Classical Arabic قِيَاس (qiyās, 'measurement, measuring, size, comparison, analogy'), verbal noun of قَاسَ (qāsa, 'to measure, compare').

قيمة.etymology: Continues Classical Arabic قِيمَة (qīma, 'standing worth, price, value', phonologically from *qiwma with regular shift of -iw- to long -ī-) from the hollow triliteral root ق-و-م (q-w-m, 'to stand upright, rise, hold equivalent standing').

history.meaning: value, worth; (pl. قِيَم) moral principles, values

قيمة.notes: Plural قِيَم (qiyam) is key in formal school speeches ('moral values': أهم القيم), while colloquial ما إله قيمة means 'it is worthless / counts for nothing'.

قَفَل.etymology: From Classical Arabic قَفَلَ (qafala, 'to lock, bolt shut, close up'), vocalized verb from the root ق-ف-ل (q-f-l, 'locking, fastening shut').

history.meaning: to lock, fasten with a lock, close

قَلَب.etymology: From Classical Arabic قَلَبَ (qalaba, 'to turn over, flip, invert, turn upside down or inside out'), vocalized verb from the root ق-ل-ب (q-l-b, 'turning, inverting; heart').

history.meaning: to turn over, flip, invert, reverse

قِبِل.etymology: From Classical Arabic قَبِلَ (qabila, 'to accept, receive willingly, agree to, consent'), Form I verb from the root ق-ب-ل (q-b-l), with regular Levantine vowel harmony raising a-i to i-i (qibil).

كأن.etymology: From Classical Arabic كَأَنَّ (ka-ʾanna, 'as if, as though, it seems that'), a compound conjunction formed from the proclitic preposition of comparison كَـ (ka-, 'like, as') and the complementizer أَنَّ (ʾanna, 'that').

كأنه.etymology: From Classical Arabic كَأَنَّهُ (ka-ʾannahu, 'as if it/he, it seems as though'), formed from the compound conjunction كَأَنَّ (ka-ʾanna, 'as if') plus the third-person masculine singular pronoun suffix ـهُ (-hu, 'it/he', often functioning as a clause-level expletive pronoun 'it seems that').

history.meaning: as if he/it [were]; it seems as though

كابتن.etymology: Modern loanword borrowed from English captain (ultimately Latin caput 'head') across nautical, aviation, and sports registers.
