كابوس.etymology: Continues Classical Arabic medical and folkloric noun كَابُوس (kābūs, 'incubus, night-terror pressing upon a sleeper's chest, nightmare') on the agentive pattern فَاعُول (fāʿūl) from the Semitic root ك-ب-س (k-b-s, verb كَبَسَ kabasa, 'to press down heavily, squeeze, raid'; cognate with Syriac kāḇūsā).

history.meaning: nightmare (literal bad dream or living ordeal)

cognates.meaning: to press down, subdue (same Semitic root)

rootFamily.gloss: button press; raid; spiced pressed-rice dish

كابوس.notes: Just like English nightmare and Latin incubus ('one who lies upon'), كابوس originally named the terrifying sensation of a heavy weight pressing down on one's chest in sleep.

كاحل.etymology: Classical anatomical noun كَاحِل ('ankle', plural كَوَاحِل) on the pattern فَاعِل from the root ك-ح-ل, designating the joint between the foot and the lower leg.

كاسة.etymology: Singulative noun كَاسَة (kāsa, 'a drinking glass, tumbler, cup, goblet') formed from Classical كَأْس (kaʾs, 'cup, goblet, drinking glass') with regular loss of medial hamza (كَاس kās) and addition of the singulative suffix -a (ـة), inherited from Proto-Semitic *kaʾs- ('cup, goblet').

morphemes.meaning: a single drinking glass or cup

كاش.etymology: Modern commercial borrowing from English cash ('ready money, banknotes and coins', ultimately from Old Italian cassa / Middle French casse 'money box', from Latin capsa 'box, case').

كافيه.etymology: Borrowed from French café ('coffeehouse, café; coffee'), which itself entered European languages via Italian caffè and Ottoman Turkish kahve from Arabic قَهْوَة (qahwa, 'coffee').
كافيه.notes: Another famous linguistic boomerang: Arabic قَهْوَة (qahwa) was borrowed into Turkish (kahve), Italian (caffè), and French (café), and then returned to modern Arabic as كافيه ('café').

كامل.etymology: From Classical Arabic كَامِل (kāmil, 'complete, whole, full, perfect, full-time'), active participle of كَمَلَ / كَمُلَ (kamala / kamula, 'to be whole, complete, perfected').

morphemes.meaning: in a complete or whole state

كان.etymology: Hollow auxiliary verb كَانَ on the root ك-و-ن (to exist, come to be), expressing past tense and past habitual states.

كانت.etymology: Third-person feminine singular past conjugation of كان (root ك-و-ن) with the Classical feminine suffix -at.

كانه.etymology: Subordinating particle uniting comparative كَـ (like), emphatic أَنَّ (that), and 3ms pronoun -hu (Classical كَأَنَّهُ).

كانوا.etymology: Plural past form of the hollow copula كان (root ك-و-ن) carrying the masculine plural suffix -uu.

كب.etymology: From Classical Arabic كَبَّ (kabba, 'to overturn, pour out, spill, throw down face-first'), geminate verb from the root ك-ب-ب (k-b-b). In Levantine Arabic, means 'to spill, pour out, throw away (in the rubbish)'.

morphemes.meaning: pouring out, overturning; rolling into a ball

كبت.etymology: Form I verb كَبَتَ (kabata, 'to throw face down, subdue, choke back rage or grief') from the Classical Arabic triliteral root ك-ب-ت (k-b-t, 'crushing down, holding inward'), adopted in 20th-century Arabic psychology for emotional repression.

history.meaning: to prostrate, humble, hold anger in one's chest
to suppress, bottle up (feelings or hurt)

كبت.notes: Shared across MSA and educated Levantine speech (يكبت بقلبه, 'bottles it up inside his heart').

كبر.etymology: From Classical Arabic كَبِرَ (kabira, 'to grow up, advance in age') and كَبُرَ (kabura, 'to become big, large, great'), from the Semitic root ك-ب-ر (k-b-r, 'greatness, largeness, age').

history.meaning: to grow old, grow up; to become large or great

morphemes.meaning: to become big or grow up

كبس.etymology: From Classical Arabic كَبَسَ (kabasa, 'to press down, squeeze, ram earth, pickle/preserve under pressure; [modern] to press a button or switch'), from the Semitic root ك-ب-س (k-b-s, 'pressing down, treading upon').

history.meaning: to press down firmly, compress, squeeze

كبسة.etymology: From Classical Arabic كَبْسَة (kabsa, 'a single press, push, or click of a button/switch; a sudden raid'), noun of instance (ism marra) from كَبَسَ (kabasa, 'to press down').

history.meaning: a single press, push, or click

كبسولة.etymology: Scientific and medical loanword adopted from French/English capsule, tracing back to Latin capsula (little box).

كبير.etymology: From Classical Arabic كَبِير (kabīr, 'big, large, great, elder, older'), on the adjectival pattern فَعِيل (faʿīl) from كَبُرَ / كَبِرَ (kabura / kabira, 'to be large, great, old').

كتاب.etymology: From the Semitic triliteral root ك-ت-ب (k-t-b, 'to write'), formed on the verbal-noun/object pattern فِعال (fiʿāl) denoting 'that which is written together' — hence a letter, document, or book.

كتابنا.etymology: Noun كتاب (written book, root ك-ت-ب) placed in construct with the first-person plural possessive suffix -na.

كتان.etymology: From Classical Arabic كَتَّان (kattān, 'flax, linen cloth'), cognate with Aramaic כִּתָּנָא (kittānā) and Hebrew כֻּתֹּנֶת (kuttōneṯ, 'linen tunic'), one of the oldest textile terms of the ancient Near East. Denotes both the flax fibre and crisp woven linen cloth.

كتب.etymology: Form I verb كَتَبَ on the Semitic root ك-ت-ب (to inscribe, write); the same unpointed spelling also represents broken plural books.

كتف.etymology: From Classical Arabic كَتِف / كَتْف (katif / katf, 'shoulder, shoulder blade'), inherited from Proto-Semitic *katip- ('shoulder').

كتير.etymology: Levantine and Egyptian reflex of Classical Arabic كَثِير (kaṯīr, 'much, many, a lot, very'), with the regular urban vernacular shift of interdental ث (ṯ) to dental stop ت (t), from كَثُرَ (kaṯura, 'to be numerous, abundant').

history.meaning: much, many, abundant; (adverbially) very, a lot

morphemes.meaning: possessing abundance; to a high degree

كثير.etymology: Quantifier and adjective كَثِير from root ك-ث-ر (abundance), used colloquially as both much/many and the intensifier very.

كذاب.etymology: Intensive agent noun and adjective كَذَّاب (kaḏḏāb, urban Levantine kazzāb / kaḏḏāb, 'habitual liar, deceitful') built on the Classical intensive pattern فَعَّال (faʿʿāl) from the Semitic triliteral root ك-ذ-ب (k-ḏ-b, 'lying, untruth').

cognates.meaning: liar (from the same Semitic root k-ḏ-b)

كذاب.notes: Stronger and more idiomatic in conversation than MSA active participle كاذب; feminine كذابة! ('she's a liar!') is a sharp accusation in school arguments.

كذب.etymology: Form I verb كَذَبَ (kaḏaba, urban Levantine kazab / kaḏab, 'to speak falsely, tell a lie') inherited from Proto-Semitic root ك-ذ-ب (k-ḏ-b, 'falsehood, failing to hold true, deception').

history.meaning: to lie (with على, 'to lie to someone')

cognates.meaning: to lie, fail (like a dry stream)

كذب.notes: In urban Amman and Damascus speech, interdental ذ is often pronounced /z/ (عم بكزبوا عليكي), though standard spelling retains ذ; note that Form II كذّب means 'to accuse someone of lying / disbelieve'.

كراسي.etymology: Quadriliteral-patterned broken plural كَرَاسِيّ derived from singular كرسي (chair, throne, root ك-ر-س).

كرافة.etymology: Levantine feminine clothing loanword borrowed from French cravate ('necktie', itself named after seventeenth-century Croatian horsemen, Cravates) or Italian cravatta. Adapted with a feminine -a ending like other Western garment loans, كرافة (also كرافتة) is standard in Jordan alongside ربطة عنق.

كرافتة.etymology: Borrowed from French cravate / Italian cravatta ('necktie, cravat', originally named in 17th-century France after Croatian mercenaries—Croates / Cravates—who wore distinctive linen neck scarves).

كرامة.etymology: From Classical Arabic كَرَامَة (karāma, 'nobility, generosity, high esteem, dignity, honour'), verbal noun of كَرُمَ (karuma, 'to be noble, generous, honourable, precious').

كرت.etymology: Borrowed from French carte and English card ('card, postcard, ticket, visiting card'), ultimately from Ancient Greek χάρτης (khártēs, 'sheet of papyrus').

كرتونة.etymology: Singulative noun كَرْتُونَة (kartūna, 'a cardboard box, carton') formed with the Arabic singulative suffix -a (ـة) from كَرْتُون (kartūn, 'cardboard, pasteboard'), borrowed from Italian cartone / French carton ('heavy paper, pasteboard, carton', augmentative of carta 'paper').

كرسي.etymology: Ancient Semitic cultural noun كُرْسِيّ borrowed early via Aramaic kursyā (ultimately Akkadian kussû, throne or chair).

كره.etymology: From Classical Arabic كَرِهَ (kariha, 'to dislike, detest, hate, feel aversion toward'), Form I stative verb from the root ك-ر-ه (k-r-h, 'aversion, dislike, repugnance').

كريم.etymology: From Classical Arabic كَرِيم (karīm, 'generous, noble, gracious, munificent, precious'), on the adjectival pattern فَعِيل (faʿīl) from كَرُمَ (karuma, 'to be noble, generous').

كريمة.etymology: Culinary borrowing from French crème / Italian crema / English cream ('dairy cream, pastry cream, custard, frosting'), adapted with the Arabic feminine ending -a (ـة).

كريمي.etymology: Hybrid nisba adjective attaching Arabic -i to كريمة (cream), itself borrowed from European crème/crema.

كسب.etymology: From Classical Arabic كَسَبَ (kasaba, 'to earn, acquire, win'), Semitic root ك-س-ب (k-s-b).

كسر.etymology: From Classical Arabic كَسَرَ (kasara, 'to break, fracture, snap, shatter'), from the Proto-Semitic root *k-s-r ('to break').

كشاف.etymology: From Classical and Modern Standard Arabic كَشَّاف (kaššāf, 'discoverer, scout; searchlight, floodlight, flashlight/torch'), intensive agent/instrument noun on the pattern فَعَّال (faʿʿāl) from كَشَفَ (kašafa, 'to uncover, reveal, illuminate, explore').

كشرة.etymology: Colloquial noun from the root ك-ش-ر (to bare the teeth, grimace), naming a scowl or displeased frown.

كشف.etymology: Triliteral Form I verb on the root ك-ش-ف meaning to lift a veil, uncover something hidden, or inspect closely.

كشك.etymology: From Ottoman-era Arabic كُشْك / كِشْك (kušk / kišk, 'kiosk, wooden booth, garden pavilion, newsstand'), borrowed via Ottoman Turkish köşk ('pavilion, summerhouse, kiosk') from Persian کوشک (kūšk, 'palace, portico, pavilion').

كشّر.etymology: From Classical Arabic كَشَّرَ (kaššara, Form II of كَشَرَ kašara, 'to bare the teeth, grimace, scowl, frown'). While Classical كَشَرَ could mean baring the teeth either in a fierce grimace or a grin, in Levantine and Egyptian Arabic كشّر specialized to mean 'to frown, scowl, look grumpy'.

morphemes.meaning: intensive: to pull a scowl or frown

كعب.etymology: Classical Arabic noun كَعْب ('heel, anklebone; cube', plural كِعَاب / كُعُوب) from the Semitic root ك-ع-ب ('protrude squarely, form a knuckle/joint'). Its square die-bone shape also gave rise to مُكَعَّب ('cube') and الكَعْبَة ('the Cube / Kaaba').

history.meaning: heel of the foot or shoe

كف.etymology: Traditionally feminine geminate noun كَفّ (kaff, 'palm of the hand, flat hand; glove'), inherited from Proto-Semitic *kapp- ('palm, hollow of hand, sole'). The same Semitic root gave Hebrew/Phoenician the letter name kaph ('palm') and via Greek kappa the Latin letter K.

كفّ.etymology: Geminate noun (فَعْل) from the pan-Semitic root ك-ف-ف (k-f-f, palm of the hand, hollow, to hold back), cognate with Hebrew כַּף (kaf). Extending metonymically from 'palm of the hand', كفّ (pl. كفوف) denotes a glove or kitchen oven mitt in everyday Jordanian Arabic.

morphemes.meaning: palm of the hand, flat surface

كفّى.etymology: Intensive Form II defective verb (فَعَّلَ) from the root ك-ف-ي (k-f-y, to suffice, be adequate, satisfy). Alongside Form I كفى, Levantine Arabic heavily favors Form II كفّى / بكفّي to mean 'to be sufficient for' or 'that's enough!' (بكفي!).

كل.etymology: Universal quantifier كُلّ derived from the geminate root ك-ل-ل signifying totality, wholeness, every, or all.

كلاسيكي.etymology: International nisba adjective pairing the Arabic suffix -i with كلاسيك (classic, from Latin classicus).

كلام.etymology: From Classical Arabic كَلَام (kalām, 'speech, talk, words, utterance, discourse'), collective/verbal noun associated with كَلَّمَ (kallama, 'to speak to, address') and تَكَلَّمَ (takallama, 'to speak').

morphemes.meaning: speaking, uttering words; making an impression

كلمات.etymology: Sound feminine plural كَلِمَات from singular كلمة (word, utterance, root ك-ل-م meaning speech).

كلمة.etymology: From Classical Arabic كَلِمَة (kalima, 'word, utterance, short speech'), singulative of كَلِم (kalim, 'words, speech'), from the root ك-ل-م (k-l-m).

كليا.etymology: Adverbial accusative formed from the nisba adjective كلي (total) on the root ك-ل-ل meaning entirety.

كلّف.etymology: Form II verb كَلَّفَ (kallafa, 'to burden, charge with a task, cost') from the root ك-ل-ف (k-l-f, 'to take pains, impose a duty'). In modern Arabic, the sense of imposing an expense evolved naturally into the everyday verb 'to cost'.

history.meaning: to charge with, impose cost upon

كم.etymology: From Classical Arabic كَمْ (kam, 'how much?, how many?; several, a few'), interrogative and exclamative quantifier related to the enclitic indefinite pronoun مَا (mā, 'what') prefixed with كَـ (ka-, 'like, as much as').

history.meaning: how much?, how many?; a few

كمان.etymology: Additive particle widely traced to a fusion of كَمَا (just as) and أَنَّ (that), meaning also, too, or more in dialect.

كمانجة.etymology: Everyday Arabic feminine noun كَمَنْجَة / كَمَانْجَة (kamanja / kamānja, 'violin, fiddle'), borrowed from Persian کمانچه (kamānče, 'little bow'), a diminutive of کمان (kamān, 'bow, arc') + -če ('little'). Originally referring to the spike fiddle played with a bow, it became the common spoken word for the modern violin alongside كمان.

كمانجته.etymology: Combines كمانجة (violin, borrowed from Persian kamānche, bowed lute) with the 3ms possessive pronoun -o/-hu.

كمبيوتر.etymology: Borrowed in the late 20th century from English computer (from Latin computāre, 'to reckon, calculate together').

كمل.etymology: From Classical Arabic كَمَلَ / كَمُلَ (kamala / kamula, 'to be completed, finished, whole') and Form II كَمَّلَ (kammala, 'to complete, finish, continue'), from the root ك-م-ل (k-m-l, 'wholeness, completion').

history.meaning: to be complete; to complete, finish, continue

morphemes.part: فَعَلَ / فَعَّلَ (Form I and Form II verb)

كمنجة.etymology: Musical loanword entering Arabic from Persian کمانچه (kamānče, literally 'little bow', diminutive of kamān 'bow') via Ottoman Turkish kemençe, adapted as a feminine noun with -a. Across Jordan and the Levant, كمنجة (and كمان) denotes the classical and Arabic violin.

morphemes.meaning: from Persian kamānče ('little bow') via Turkish kemençe

كمية.etymology: From Classical Arabic كَمِّيَّة (kammiyya, 'quantity, amount'), abstract noun coined by medieval Arab philosophers and translators (such as al-Kindī) by adding the abstract suffix -iyya (ـِيَّة) to the interrogative quantifier كَمّ (kamm, 'how much?') as a calque of Ancient Greek ποσότης (posótēs) / Latin quantitās.
كمية.notes: Formed in the exact same way as كَيْفِيَّة (kayfiyya, 'quality, manner' from كَيْفَ 'how?') and مَاهِيَّة (māhiyya, 'essence, quiddity' from مَا هِيَ 'what is it?').

كندرة.etymology: Levantine feminine noun for a pair of dress shoes, borrowed via Ottoman Turkish kundura from Medieval Greek κόντουρα (kóntoura, 'short-tailed/low shoe'). In Jordanian Arabic, كندرة behaves as feminine singular even though it refers to a matched pair of shoes (pl. كنادر).

morphemes.meaning: from Ottoman Turkish kundura < Greek kóntoura (shoe)

كنز.etymology: Classical noun كَنْز on the root ك-ن-ز (to bury or store away wealth), possibly influenced in antiquity by Iranian ganj.

كنزة.etymology: Levantine Arabic كَنْزَة (kanza, 'sweater, jumper, pullover, cardigan, knitted top'), from كَنَزَ (kanaza, 'to pack tightly, press close together, compact') and مَكْنُوز (maknūz, 'firmly compacted, close-fitting'), originally describing a closely knitted woollen garment that hugs the body.

history.meaning: closely knitted garment; sweater, jumper, cardigan

كنس.etymology: From Classical Arabic كَنَسَ (kanasa, 'to sweep, broom away dust and dirt'), from the Semitic root ك-ن-س (k-n-s, 'sweeping, gathering together').

كهربا.etymology: Levantine colloquial form of كَهْرَباء (kahrabāʾ, 'electricity'), borrowed from Persian کهربا (kahrubā, literally 'straw-attractor', i.e. amber, from kāh 'straw' + rubā 'attracting'), mirroring Greek ἤλεκτρον ('amber' -> 'electricity').

كورد.etymology: Musical borrowing from English chord ('simultaneous combination of musical notes', shortened from accord, ultimately from Latin chorda / Ancient Greek χορδή 'string of a musical instrument').

كيس.etymology: From Classical Arabic كِيس (kīs, 'bag, sack, pouch, purse'), an ancient pan-Semitic cultural word attested in Aramaic כִּיסָא / ܟܝܣܐ (kīsā), Hebrew כִּיס (kīs, 'bag, purse'), and Akkadian kīsu ('leather money-bag, pouch'), ultimately from Sumerian kuš ('leather bag').

كيف.etymology: Interrogative adverb descended from Classical كَيْفَ via monophthongization of the diphthong ay to long ii.

كيك.etymology: Collective culinary loanword borrowed directly from English cake and treated grammatically as masculine singular.

كيكة.etymology: Singulative feminine noun formed by adding the Arabic unit marker -a (ta marbuta) to the English loanword كيك.

كيلو.etymology: Borrowed from French kilo, clipped from kilogramme ('kilogram, one thousand grams') and kilomètre ('kilometre'), from Ancient Greek χίλιοι (khílioi, 'one thousand').

كَسْر.etymology: From Classical Arabic كَسْر (kasr, 'breaking, fracturing; a break, fracture, crack; mathematical fraction'), vocalized verbal noun (maṣdar) of كَسَرَ (kasara, 'to break').

history.meaning: act of breaking; a break, crack, fracture

كُمّ.etymology: From Classical Arabic كُمّ (kumm, 'sleeve of a garment; calyx or spathe covering a flower bud'), vocalized with ḍamma and shadda to distinguish it from كَمْ (kam, 'how many?'), from the geminate root ك-م-م (k-m-m, 'to cover, envelop, muzzle').

ل.etymology: From Classical Arabic لِـ / لَـ (li- / la-, 'to, for, belonging to, in order to'), proclitic dative, benefactive, and possessive preposition inherited from Proto-Semitic *la- / *li- ('to, for').

لأربعة.etymology: Prepositional phrase uniting directional لـ (to, into) with the cardinal numeral أربعة (four, root ر-ب-ع).

لأن.etymology: From Classical Arabic لِأَنَّ (li-ʾanna, 'because, for the reason that'), compound causal conjunction formed from the preposition لِـ (li-, 'for') and the complementizer أَنَّ (ʾanna, 'that').

لأنه.etymology: Causal conjunction compounding preposition لـ (for), complementizer أَنَّ (that), and 3ms suffix -o/-hu.

لإن.etymology: Spoken Levantine causal conjunction stem (لِإِنّ- liʾinn- / laʾinn-, 'because'), continuing Classical Arabic compound conjunction لِأَنَّ (li-ʾanna, literally 'for [the fact] that'), formed from the causal preposition لِـ (li-, 'for') + the nominalizing complementizer أَنَّ (ʾanna, 'that'), with colloquial vowel raising to إِنّ.

morphemes.meaning: for, on account of (< Classical لِـ)

history.meaning: because (always hosting a pronoun or default -ه suffix)

لإن.notes: Like MSA لأنّ, Levantine لإنّ cannot stand bare before a verb: it either attaches the subject pronoun (لإني تعبانة 'because I'm tired', لإنها غايبة) or adds default -ه before a full clause (لإنه المس عرفت).

لا.etymology: Pan-Semitic negative particle لَا descended from Proto-Semitic *lā, used for prohibitions and negative answers.

لابس.etymology: From Classical Arabic لَابِس (lābis, 'wearing, dressed in, clothed'), active participle of لَبِسَ (labisa, 'to wear, put on clothing'). In Arabic grammar, the active participle of verbs of dressing expresses the resultant state ('currently wearing').

لاحظ.etymology: Form III verb from Classical Arabic لَاحَظَ (lāḥaẓa, 'to watch closely, observe, notice'), root ل-ح-ظ (l-ḥ-ẓ).

لازم.etymology: From Classical Arabic لَازِم (lāzim, 'necessary, obligatory, inseparable, adhering closely'), active participle of لَزِمَ (lazima, 'to cling to, be necessary or obligatory for'); in spoken Arabic, grammaticalized as an invariant modal particle meaning 'must, have to, need to'.

history.meaning: clinging, necessary, obligatory; (modal) must, have to

morphemes.meaning: clinging to, being necessary or obligatory

لافتة.etymology: Feminine active participle (فَاعِلَة, fāʿila) of لَفَتَ ('to turn someone's gaze, attract attention') on the root ل-ف-ت (l-f-t, turning, glancing). Literally meaning 'that which catches the eye', لافتة became the standard Arabic noun for a shop signboard, street sign, or banner.

morphemes.meaning: feminine active participle used as noun

لاقى.etymology: Form III defective verb from the root ل-ق-ي (to encounter), displacing Form I لقي in much of urban Levantine speech.

لام.etymology: From Classical Arabic لَامَ (lāma, 'to blame, reproach, censure'), hollow verb from the root ل-و-م (l-w-m, 'blaming, reproaching').

history.meaning: to blame, reproach, find fault with

لامبة.etymology: Variant spelling of لَمْبَة (lamba, 'desk lamp, table lamp, lightbulb'), borrowed via Italian lampa / lampada and French lampe from Ancient Greek λαμπάς (lampás, 'torch, oil lamp', from λάμπω lámpō 'to shine').

لامع.etymology: From Classical Arabic لَامِع (lāmiʿ, 'shining, glossy, gleaming, polished, brilliant'), active participle of لَمَعَ (lamaʿa, 'to shine, flash, gleam').

morphemes.meaning: having a shiny or gleaming quality

لان.etymology: From Classical Arabic لَانَ (lāna, 'to become soft, supple, tender, gentle, yield'), hollow verb from the root ل-ي-ن (l-y-n, 'softness, suppleness, gentleness').

history.meaning: to become soft, pliable, tender, gentle

لانه.etymology: Unpointed spelling of لأنه uniting لـ (for), أن (that), and 3ms pronominal suffix -o/-hu.

لباد.etymology: From Classical Arabic لُبَّاد / لِبْد (lubbād / libd, 'wool felt, matted wool'), from لَبَدَ (labada, 'to mat together, press and compact wool into felt, stick fast to the ground'), from the root ل-ب-د (l-b-d).

morphemes.meaning: matting wool together, compacting, sticking fast

لبرية.etymology: Combines directional لـ (to) with برية (wilderness, open countryside, derived from root ب-ر-ر meaning open land).

لبس.etymology: From Classical Arabic لَبِسَ (labisa, 'to wear, put on a garment') and لِبْس / لُبْس (libs / lubs, 'clothing, dress, act of wearing'), inherited from Proto-Semitic *labiš- ('to put on clothes, wear').

لبلاب.etymology: From Classical Arabic لَبْلَاب (lablāb, 'ivy, bindweed, climbing vine [Hedera helix or Convolvulus]'), a reduplicated quadriliteral botanical noun shared with Syriac ܠܒܠܒܐ (laḇlāḇā, 'ivy, bindweed'), evoking the plant's twining and wrapping tendrils.

لبن.etymology: From Classical Arabic لَبَن (laban, 'milk; soured milk, yoghurt'), from the Proto-Semitic root *l-b-n ('white', because of the whiteness of milk). In the Levant, لَبَن means specifically 'yoghurt / cultured dairy' (while fresh milk is حَلِيب), whereas in Egypt لبن retains the Classical sense 'milk'.
لبن.notes: The same Semitic root *l-b-n ('white') gave rise to لُبْنَان (Lubnān, 'Mount Lebanon', from its snow-capped white peaks) and لُبَان (lubān, 'frankincense', from its milky-white resin).

لتحت.etymology: Directional adverb pairing لـ (toward) with تحت (below, under, root ت-ح-ت); antonym of لفوق.

لجوا.etymology: Spatial adverb combining directional لـ (toward) with جوا (inside, from Classical جو meaning interior).

لحتى.etymology: Compound Levantine subordinating conjunction merging the dative/purposive preposition لِـ (li-, 'for, in order to') with the Classical temporal particle حَتَّى (ḥattā, 'until'). Across Jordan and the Levant, لحتى introduces both temporal ('until') and purposive ('so that / in order to') clauses.

history.meaning: until, so that, in order to

لحد.etymology: Temporal and spatial preposition fusing لـ (up to) with حد (boundary, limit, geminate root ح-د-د).

لحظة.etymology: From Classical Arabic لَحْظَة (laḥẓa, 'a quick glance of the eye from the outer corner; a moment, instant, blink of an eye'), noun of instance (ism marra) from لَحَظَ (laḥaẓa, 'to glance at, observe').

history.meaning: a single glance of the eye; a brief moment, instant

morphemes.meaning: glancing sideways with the eye, observing
a single glance or fleeting moment

لحظة.notes: Compare English 'in the twinkling of an eye' or German Augenblick ('moment', literally 'eye-glance').

لحق.etymology: From Classical Arabic لَحِقَ (laḥiqa, 'to catch up with, overtake, reach in time, follow closely'), Form I verb from the root ل-ح-ق (l-ḥ-q, 'following closely, overtaking, joining').

history.meaning: to overtake, catch up with, reach in time, follow

morphemes.meaning: catching up with, following closely, joining

لحن.etymology: Classical Arabic لَحْن (laḥn, 'melody, musical mode, cadence of voice'), from root ل-ح-ن denoting modulated intonation and song.

لخبطة.etymology: Verbal noun لَخْبَطَة (laḵbaṭa, 'mix-up, confusion, mess, jumble') of the quadriliteral verb لَخْبَطَ (laḵbaṭa, 'to mix up, muddle, confuse'), formed as an expressive consonantal blend of Classical خَلَطَ (ḵalaṭa, 'to mix') and خَبَطَ (ḵabaṭa, 'to strike at random, knock about blindly').

لزاق.etymology: From Arabic لَزَّاق / لِزَاق (lazzāq / lizāq, 'adhesive tape, sticky tape, glue, cement'), on the intensive instrument pattern فَعَّال (faʿʿāl) from لَزِقَ (laziqa, 'to stick, adhere, cling'), a classic phonetic variant of لَصِقَ (laṣiqa).

history.meaning: that which sticks fast; adhesive tape, glue

morphemes.meaning: substance or strip that sticks strongly

لزق.etymology: From Classical Arabic لَزِقَ (laziqa, 'to stick, cling, adhere') and Form II لَزَّقَ (lazzaqa, 'to stick, paste, tape'), recorded by classical Arab philologists as a dialectal and phonological variant of لَصِقَ (laṣiqa, 'to adhere').

morphemes.part: فَعِلَ / فَعَّلَ (Form I and Form II verb)
morphemes.meaning: to adhere or cause to adhere

لسا.etymology: Colloquial temporal adverb contracted historically from Classical لِلسَّاعَةِ (up to this hour, root س-و-ع).

لسان.etymology: Inherited across Classical and colloquial Arabic from Proto-Semitic anatomical noun *lišān- ('tongue; spoken language'), triliteral root ل-س-ن (l-s-n).
لسان.notes: Masculine in everyday Jordanian (لسانك طويل, 'you have a sharp mouth'), though Classical Arabic allowed both masculine and feminine gender.

لسه.etymology: Orthographic variant of لسا contracted from لِلسَّاعَةِ (to the hour), pronounced lissa across Jordan.

لصبح.etymology: Colloquial temporal expression combining لـ (until) with صبح (morning, root ص-ب-ح) with elided article.

لطف.etymology: Form II causative verb لَطَّفَ (laṭṭafa, 'to make gentle, soften, soothe, lighten [a tense mood]') on the pattern فَعَّلَ (faʿʿala) from لَطُفَ (laṭufa, 'to be delicate, subtle, kind'), triliteral root ل-ط-ف (l-ṭ-f).

history.meaning: to be subtle/kind -> to soften, mitigate
to soften, lighten (especially ألطف الجو, 'lighten the mood')

لطف.notes: Classic social collocation across MSA and Levantine: لطّف الجو ('break the ice / ease the tension in the room').

لطيف.etymology: From Classical Arabic لَطِيف (laṭīf, 'kind, gentle, pleasant, gracious, delicate, subtle'), on the adjectival pattern فَعِيل (faʿīl) from لَطُفَ (laṭufa, 'to be fine, delicate, gentle, kind').

لعاد.etymology: Characteristic Jordanian and southern Levantine discourse particle fused from لَـ + عَاد (ʿād, 'then, still', from root ع-و-د 'to return'), cognate with Syrian لكن / لكان. Functioning as an inferential marker, لعاد translates naturally as 'then', 'well then', or 'in that case'.

history.meaning: then, well then, in that case

لعب.etymology: Form I verb لَعِبَ (laʿiba, 'to play, sport, jest') on the pattern فَعِلَ (faʿila) from the Semitic triliteral root ل-ع-ب (l-ʿ-b, 'playfulness, jesting').

history.meaning: to play, amuse oneself, toy with
to play; with مع in colloquial warnings, 'to mess with'

لعب.notes: Literally 'play', and in Jordanian street/school warnings ما حدا بيلعب معي ('nobody messes with me!') or عم تلعبي بالنار ('you're playing with fire').

لغرفة.etymology: Prepositional phrase uniting لـ (to) with indefinite غرفة (room, chamber, from root غ-ر-ف).

لغز.etymology: Masculine noun on the pattern فُعْل (fuʿl) from the root ل-غ-ز (l-ġ-z, to wind obliquely, burrow like a jerboa, speak obscurely in riddles). Originally evoking twisting underground burrows whose entrance is hidden, لغز (pl. ألغاز) means 'riddle', 'puzzle', or 'mystery' in Jordanian Arabic.

لـ.etymology: Primary Semitic dative and benefactive proclitic preposition لِـ (li- / la-, 'to, for'), cognate with Hebrew לְ־ (lə-) and Aramaic lə-. In spoken Jordanian Arabic, لـ attaches directly to verbs as an indirect-object marker (جبتلنا 'brought for us') or precedes nouns and pronouns.

لف.etymology: From Classical Arabic لَفَّ (laffa, 'to wrap, roll up, wind, fold around; [in spoken Arabic also] to turn a corner, go around'), geminate verb from the root ل-ف-ف (l-f-f, 'wrapping, winding, turning').

history.meaning: to wrap, roll up, wind; to turn around

لفافة.etymology: Feminine noun on the pattern فَعَالَة (faʿāla) from the geminate root ل-ف-ف (l-f-f, to wrap, wind, roll up). Denoting anything rolled or wrapped around itself, لفافة (pl. لفائف / لفافات) serves in Jordanian Arabic for rolled pastries like cinnamon rolls as well as paper scrolls.

لفة.etymology: Noun of instance from geminate لفّ (root ل-ف-ف, to turn or wrap), denoting a turn, walk around, or wrapped flatbread.

لفت.etymology: Form I verb لَفَتَ (lafata, 'to turn, twist, bend aside; to turn someone's gaze or mind toward something') inherited from Classical Arabic triliteral root ل-ف-ت (l-f-t, 'turning round, twisting').

history.meaning: to twist, turn someone's face toward or away

rootFamily.gloss: to turn around, look back (Form VIII)
thoughtful gesture, turn of the head

لفت.notes: Almost always appears in the fixed collocations لفت انتباهي ('caught my attention') and لفت نظرهم ('drew their eyes/notice').

لفوق.etymology: Directional adverbial compound merging the preposition لـ (toward) with فوق (above, root ف-و-ق).

لفيفة.etymology: From Classical Arabic لَفِيفَة (lafīfa, 'rolled scroll, bundle, wrapped pastry roll'), on the pattern فَعِيلَة (faʿīla, passive sense 'that which is rolled or wrapped up') from لَفَّ (laffa, 'to roll up, wrap').

history.meaning: something rolled or wrapped up; scroll, pastry roll

لفّ.etymology: Geminate Form I verb (فَعَّ) built on the root ل-ف-ف (l-f-f, to wrap, twist, fold around, turn). Across everyday Jordanian speech, لفّ covers wrapping food or gifts, turning a corner while driving, and strolling around town (بيلفّ بالبلد).

history.meaning: to wrap up, roll, turn around

لقاء.etymology: From Classical Arabic لِقَاء (liqāʾ, 'meeting, encounter, reunion, interview'), verbal noun of لَقِيَ (laqiya, 'to meet, encounter') and Form III لَاقَى (lāqā).

لقطة.etymology: Feminine instance noun on the pattern فَعْلَة / فُعْلَة from the root ل-ق-ط (l-q-ṭ, to pick up from the ground, glean, catch). In Jordanian slang and market talk, لقطة describes an unbeatable bargain ('a real catch'), alongside its standard sense of a camera shot.

لقمة.etymology: From Classical Arabic لُقْمَة (luqma, 'mouthful, bite of food, morsel'), from لَقِمَ (laqima, 'to swallow hurriedly, take a mouthful of food').

morphemes.meaning: taking a mouthful, swallowing a morsel
amount taken in a single bite

لقمة.notes: Borrowed into Turkish as lokma and lokum ('Turkish delight', from راحة الحلقوم / لقمة), and Greek λουκουμάς.

لقى.etymology: From Classical Arabic لَقِيَ (laqiya, 'to meet, encounter, find') and Form III لَاقَى (lāqā, 'to meet, find'), from the root ل-ق-ي (l-q-y).

morphemes.part: فَعِلَ / فَاعَلَ (Form I and III verb)

لقي.etymology: Form I defective verb rooted in ل-ق-ي (to meet or come upon), retaining the stative fa'ila vocalic pattern in dialect.

لكان.etymology: Levantine inferential discourse adverb derived from Classical لَكِنْ / لَا كَانَ or لَـ + كَانَ ('it would then be'). Widespread in Syrian, Lebanese, and northern Jordanian speech (often alternating with لعاد), لكان introduces a logical consequence ('then / well then / in that case').

history.meaning: then, well then, in that case

للأسبوع.etymology: Fuses preposition لـ (for), definite article الـ, and أسبوع (week, built on root س-ب-ع meaning seven).

للاسف.etymology: From Classical Arabic لِلْأَسَفِ (li-l-ʾasafi, 'unfortunately, regrettably, to [one's] regret'), prepositional phrase composed of لِـ (li-, 'to, for') + الـ (al-, 'the') + أَسَف (ʾasaf, 'grief, sorrow, regret'), from أَسِفَ (ʾasifa, 'to grieve, feel regret').

للخمسة.etymology: Temporal phrase merging لـ (until), الـ (the), and خمسة (five, root خ-م-س) for telling clock time.

للرسمة.etymology: Links directional لـ (to, for) to the definite feminine noun الرسمة (drawing, from root ر-س-م).

للشرق.etymology: Directional phrase attaching لـ (toward) to definite الشرق (east, from root ش-ر-ق meaning sunrise).

للشمال.etymology: Combines لـ (toward) and الشمال (north or left, root ش-م-ل, because facing east puts north on the left).

للفطور.etymology: Attaches لـ (for) to definite الفطور (breakfast, derived from root ف-ط-ر meaning breaking a fast).

للمدير.etymology: Unites dative لـ (to, for) with definite المدير (director, Form IV active participle from أدار, root د-و-ر).

لله.etymology: Classic contraction fusing preposition لـ (for) with الله (God), dropping the initial alif orthographically.

لما.etymology: Temporal subordinating conjunction descended directly from Classical Arabic لَمَّا (when, once).

لمبة.etymology: From post-Classical Arabic لَمْبَة (lamba, 'lightbulb, lamp, lantern'), borrowed via Italian lampa and Ottoman Turkish lamba from Ancient Greek λαμπάς (lampás, 'torch, oil lamp', from λάμπω lámpō 'to shine').

لمس.etymology: From Classical Arabic لَمَسَ (lamasa, 'to touch, feel with the hand') and its verbal noun لَمْس (lams, 'touch, touching'), from the root ل-م-س (l-m-s).

history.meaning: to touch, feel with the hand

لمع.etymology: From Classical Arabic لَمَعَ (lamaʿa, 'to flash, gleam, glisten'), Semitic root ل-م-ع (l-m-ʿ).

لمعلم.etymology: Colloquial fusion of definite الـ and معلم (master craftsman or boss, Form II participle from root ع-ل-م).

لمكانه.etymology: Combines directional لـ (to), مكان (place, root ك-و-ن), and the 3ms possessive clitic -o/-hu.

لمّع.etymology: From Classical Arabic لَمَّعَ (lammaʿa, 'to polish, burnish, make shine or gleam'), Form II causative of لَمَعَ (lamaʿa, 'to shine, flash, gleam').

history.meaning: to cause to shine, polish, burnish

morphemes.meaning: causative: to make shiny or polish

لنصين.etymology: Pairs directional لـ (into) with نصين, the dual of نص (half, shortened from Classical نِصْف, root ن-ص-ف).

لهون.etymology: Levantine spatial adverb joining the directional prefix لـ to هون (here), itself derived from Classical هاهنا.

لو.etymology: Ancient Semitic hypothetical conditional particle لَوْ used in Arabic for counterfactual or polite requests.

لوح.etymology: From Classical Arabic لَوْح (lawḥ, 'flat board, plank of wood, slate, tablet, sheet or pane of glass/metal'), inherited from Proto-Semitic *lūḥ- ('wooden or stone tablet, plank, board').

history.meaning: board, plank, tablet, flat sheet or pane

لوحة.etymology: Singulative noun لَوْحَة (lawḥa, 'a single board, painting, canvas, signboard, brass nameplate, control panel') formed from لَوْح (lawḥ, 'board, tablet, flat panel').

history.meaning: a single board, plaque, sign, painting

لورا.etymology: Directional adverb merging لـ (toward) with ورا (behind, shortened from Classical وَرَاءَ, root و-ر-ي).

لوز.etymology: Ancient Near Eastern botanical noun لَوْز attested in Classical Arabic, Aramaic, and Akkadian for almonds.

لون.etymology: From Classical Arabic لَوْن (lawn, 'colour, hue, tint; kind, sort, dish of food'), from the root ل-و-ن (l-w-n).

لوية.etymology: From Classical Arabic لَوْيَة (lawya, 'a twist, bend, turn, sprain [e.g. of the ankle or wrist]'), noun of instance (ism marra) from لَوَى (lawā, 'to twist, bend, wrench, turn aside').

history.meaning: a single twist, wrench, bend, or sprain

morphemes.meaning: single act or result of twisting

لوين.etymology: Levantine interrogative adverb لَوَيْن (la-wēn, 'where to?, whither?'), compounded from the directional preposition لَـ (la- < إِلَى / لِـ, 'to') and وَيْن (wēn, 'where?', from وَأَيْنَ wa-ʾayna).

ليرات.etymology: Sound feminine plural of ليرة (from Ottoman Turkish lira and Latin libra), colloquially meaning Jordanian dinars.

ليش.etymology: Interrogative adverb contracted across Levantine Arabic from Classical لِأَيِّ شَيْءٍ (for what thing?).

ليف.etymology: Botanical collective noun from the root ل-ي-ف signifying fibrous palm bark or plant fibres used for cordage and scrubbing.

ليل.etymology: From Classical Arabic لَيْل (layl, 'night, nighttime' as a collective/generic), inherited from Proto-Semitic *layliy- ('night').

ليلة.etymology: Singulative noun لَيْلَة (layla, 'a single night; tonight [الليلة]'), formed from the generic/collective لَيْل (layl, 'nighttime').

ليمون.etymology: Entered Arabic from Persian *līmūn* (ultimately of Indo-Aryan/Austronesian citrus origin), and travelled from Arabic into medieval Mediterranean Europe as English 'lemon'.
ليمون.notes: Collective noun in Jordanian Arabic; a single whole lemon is counted as حبة ليمون.

لَمَع.etymology: From Classical Arabic لَمَعَ (lamaʿa, 'to shine, gleam, flash, sparkle'), vocalized Form I verb from the root ل-م-ع (l-m-ʿ, 'flashing, shining, gleaming').

لُطف.etymology: Masculine abstract noun لُطْف (luṭf, 'gentleness, kindness, delicacy, courtesy') from لَطُفَ (laṭufa, 'to be gentle, fine, gracious'), root ل-ط-ف (l-ṭ-f). Contrasts in pattern with the verb لَطَفَ ('to soften').

مألوف.etymology: From Classical Arabic مَأْلُوف (maʾlūf, 'familiar, customary, accustomed, well-known'), Form I passive participle (on pattern مَفْعُول mafʿūl) of أَلِفَ (ʾalifa, 'to become accustomed to, be familiar or friendly with').

morphemes.meaning: that which one is accustomed to

مؤدب.etymology: Form II passive participle adjective مُؤَدَّب (muʾaddab, 'polite, well-bred, courteous') from أَدَّبَ (ʾaddaba, 'to teach good manners, educate'), root أ-د-ب (ʾ-d-b, 'manners, literature, etiquette'). Literally 'one who has been cultured in good manners'.

مؤقت.etymology: From Classical and Modern Standard Arabic مُؤَقِّت (muʾaqqit, 'timer, timekeeper') and مُؤَقَّت (muʾaqqat, 'temporary, timed, provisional'), Form II active/passive participle of وَقَّتَ (waqqata, 'to fix a time, set a timer'), denominative from وَقْت (waqt, 'time'), with shift of initial wāw after ḍamma (*muwaqqit > muʾaqqit).

history.meaning: timekeeper, timer; fixed to a set time, temporary

مؤلف.etymology: From Classical Arabic مُؤَلِّف (muʾallif, 'author, writer, musical composer'), Form II active participle of أَلَّفَ (ʾallafa, 'to join together, unite harmoniously, compile or compose a book or musical work'), from the root ء-ل-ف (ʾ-l-f, 'joining together, familiarity').

history.meaning: one who joins elements into a whole; author, composer

ما.etymology: Inherited Semitic particle مَا functioning both as a verbal negator and an indefinite or relative pronoun.

مائي.etymology: Nisba adjective formed by attaching -i to ماء (water, root م-و-ه), describing watercolours or aquatic things.

ماخد.etymology: Colloquial Levantine active participle of أخد ('to take', Classical أَخَذَ on root أ-خ-ذ ʾ-x-ð), formed by lengthening the initial vowel to mā- (analogous to hollow/initial-hamza participles like ماكل 'eating') and shifting interdental /ð/ to /d/. Used in Jordan for both ongoing and planned near-future actions.

مارق.etymology: Colloquial active participle built on the Levantine verb مرق (to pass by), from the root م-ر-ق.

مازن.etymology: Pre-Islamic Arabic masculine given name on the active participle pattern فَاعِل (fāʿil) from the root م-ز-ن (m-z-n, rainclouds, swiftness, gleaming). Meaning originally 'raincloud' (مُزْن) or 'moving briskly', مازن was borne by an ancient Arab tribe and remains popular across Jordan.

morphemes.meaning: active participle used as proper name

مازورة.etymology: Borrowed into Arabic musical terminology from Italian misura ('measure, bar of sheet music'), from Latin mēnsūra ('measuring, measure').

ماسك.etymology: Active participle built on the triliteral root م-س-ك (to hold, grasp, grip), functioning like a progressive verb.

ماسورة.etymology: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish ماصوره (masura, 'reed bobbin, water spout, pipe'), itself from Persian ماسوره (māsūra, 'reed tube, spool, pipe').

ماشي.etymology: Active participle مَاشٍ / مَاشِي (māšī, 'walking, going') from مَشَى (mašā, 'to walk, go, proceed') on the root م-ش-ي (m-š-y); in Levantine speech also used to mean 'working smoothly; alright, okay'.

ماضي.etymology: Active participle مَاضٍ / مَاضِي (māḍī, 'passing, bygone, past, last') from the verb مَضَى (maḍā, 'to pass, elapse, go by') on the root م-ض-ي (m-ḍ-y).

ماكن.etymology: Participial adjective مَاكِن (mākin, 'firm, solid, sturdy, well-established') from مَكُنَ (makuna, 'to be firm, strong, solidly fixed') on the root م-ك-ن (m-k-n).

ماكينة.etymology: Borrowed into Levantine and Egyptian Arabic from Italian macchina ('machine, engine, mechanism'), from Latin māchina, from Doric Greek μᾱχᾰνᾱ (mākhanā).

مال.etymology: Form I hollow verb مَالَ (māla, 'to incline, lean, tilt, bend') from the triliteral root م-ي-ل (m-y-l).

مالح.etymology: Participial adjective مَالِح (māliḥ, 'salty, salted, saline') derived from مِلْح (milḥ, 'salt') via مَلَحَ (malaḥa, 'to salt, be salty') on the Proto-Semitic root م-ل-ح (m-l-ḥ).

مبارح.etymology: Levantine adverb مْبَارِح (mbāriḥ, 'yesterday'), evolved from Classical Arabic البَارِحَة (al-bāriḥa, 'yesterday, last night') with labial assimilation of the definite article al- to m- before b-, from بَرِحَ (bariḥa, 'to pass away, depart'), root ب-ر-ح (b-r-ḥ).

مباشرة.etymology: Adverb مُبَاشَرَةً (mubāšaratan, 'directly, immediately, straight away, live') formed from the feminine Form III participle of بَاشَرَ (bāšara, 'to touch directly, undertake in person'), root ب-ش-ر (b-š-r, 'skin, direct contact'). Literally 'skin-to-skin / without intermediary', hence 'directly'.

history.meaning: to handle directly -> directly, at once

مبتسم.etymology: Form VIII active participle مُبْتَسِم (mubtasim, 'smiling, beaming') from اِبْتَسَمَ (ibtasama, 'to smile'), derived from بَسَمَ (basama, 'to smile gently') on the root ب-س-م (b-s-m).

مبحوح.etymology: Passive participle (مَفْعُول) of Classical Arabic بَحَّ (baḥḥa, 'to be hoarse'), root ب-ح-ح (b-ḥ-ḥ).

مبروز.etymology: Passive participle of Levantine quadriliteral verb بَرْوَز (barwaz, 'to frame'), from برواز (birwāz, 'frame', Persian parvāz).

مبروش.etymology: Passive participle constructed on the maf'uul pattern from the verb برش (root ب-ر-ش, meaning to grate or shred).

مبروك.etymology: Passive participle (مَفْعُول, mafʿūl) of بَرَكَ on the Semitic root ب-ر-ك (b-r-k, blessing, abundance, kneeling), literally meaning 'blessed'. Across Jordan and the Arab world, مبروك (often intensified as ألف مبروك) is the universal expression for 'congratulations!' on any happy occasion.

مبسوط.etymology: Form I passive participle مَبْسُوط (mabsūṭ, literally 'spread out, expanded, at ease', whence 'happy, glad, pleased, content') from بَسَطَ (basaṭa, 'to spread out, expand, gladden') on the root ب-س-ط (b-s-ṭ).

مبطّن.etymology: Form II passive participle of Arabic بَطَّنَ (baṭṭana, 'to line the inside of'), root ب-ط-ن (b-ṭ-n, 'belly, interior').

مبكر.etymology: Form II active participle adjective مُبَكِّر (mubakkir, 'early, ahead of the usual time') from بَكَّرَ (bakkara, 'to rise or act early in the morning'), root ب-ك-ر (b-k-r, 'firstborn, dawn, early'). Used in formal and literary phrases like الموعد المبكر ('the early appointment').

مبلول.etymology: Form I passive participle مَبْلُول (mablūl, 'wetted, moistened, wet') from the geminate verb بَلَّ (balla, 'to wet, moisten') on the root ب-ل-ل (b-l-l).

مبلولة.etymology: Feminine passive participle of geminate بلّ (root ب-ل-ل, to moisten or wet) carrying feminine -a.

مبنى.etymology: Noun of place مَبْنًى / مَبْنَى (mabnā, 'building, structure, edifice') derived from the verb بَنَى (banā, 'to build, construct') on the Proto-Semitic root ب-ن-ي (b-n-y).

مبين.etymology: Levantine active participle مْبَيِّن (mbayyin, 'appearing, looking, obvious'), from Form II مُبَيِّن (mubayyin) of بَيَّنَ (bayyana, 'to make clear; [Levantine] to appear, show, be evident') on the root ب-ي-ن (b-y-n).

مبيّن.etymology: Form II active participle (مُفَعِّل, mufaʿʿil) of بيّن ('to become clear, appear, show') from the hollow root ب-ي-ن (b-y-n, clarity, distinctness). In spoken Jordanian Arabic, مبيّن functions impersonally ('it seems / looks like') or predicatively ('looking/appearing').

متأخر.etymology: Form V active participle مُتَأَخِّر (mutaʾaḫḫir, 'lagging behind, delayed, late') on the pattern مُتَفَعِّل (mutafaʿʿil) of تَأَخَّرَ (taʾaḫḫara, 'to stay back, fall behind, be late'), from the Semitic root ء-خ-ر (ʾ-ḫ-r, 'back, behind, after').

history.meaning: to hang back -> coming late, subsequent
late (in arriving or in the hour of the day)

cognates.meaning: late, tardy (from the same Semitic root ʾ-ḫ-r)

متأخر.notes: Works both as an adjective (الوقت متأخر, 'it's late'; أنا متأخرة, 'I'm running late') and uninflected adverbially in Levantine (نمت متأخر, 'I went to sleep late').

متأكد.etymology: Form V active participle مُتَأَكِّد (mutaʾakkid, 'certain, assured, sure') from تَأَكَّدَ (taʾakkada, 'to become certain, ascertain, verify') on the root ء-ك-د (ʾ-k-d, 'firmness, assurance').

متبدّل.etymology: Form V participle of Arabic تَبَدَّلَ (tabaddala, 'to be exchanged or altered'), Semitic root ب-د-ل (b-d-l).

متجوّل.etymology: Form V active participle noun/adjective مُتَجَوِّل (mutajawwil, 'roamer, stroller, hiker, itinerant walker') from تَجَوَّلَ (tajawwala, 'to wander about, tour'), hollow root ج-و-ل (j-w-l, 'to go round, roam'). Used for hikers out on trails or wandering visitors.

history.meaning: to roam -> to stroll around -> wanderer, hiker

متحمس.etymology: Form V active participle مُتَحَمِّس (mutaḥammis, 'zealous, fired up, enthusiastic, excited') on the pattern مُتَفَعِّل (mutafaʿʿil) of تَحَمَّسَ (taḥammasa, 'to show ardor or zeal'), from Classical حَمَاسَة / حَمَاس ('bravery, fiery ardor'), triliteral root ح-م-س (ḥ-m-s).

morphemes.meaning: Form V active participle ('filled with enthusiasm')

rootFamily.gloss: to excite, fire someone up (Form II)

متحمس.notes: Standard way in both MSA and Jordanian speech to say 'I am excited!' (أنا كتير متحمسة للرحلة).

متدرّب.etymology: Form V active participle (مُتَفَعِّل, mutafaʿʿil) of تدرّب ('to train or practice') on the triliteral root د-ر-ب (d-r-b, path, habituation, training). Used as a masculine noun (pl. متدرّبين), it refers to an intern, trainee, or workshop apprentice across Jordan.

متذكر.etymology: Form V active participle مُتَذَكِّر (mutaḏakkir, 'remembering, mindful of') from تَذَكَّرَ (taḏakkara, 'to remember, recall, call to mind') on the Semitic root ذ-ك-ر (ḏ-k-r).

متذكّر.etymology: Form V active participle of Arabic تَذَكَّرَ (tadhakkara, 'to recall, remember'), Semitic root ذ-ك-ر (dh-k-r).

متر.etymology: International metric unit مِتْر ('metre', plural أَمْتَار), borrowed in the 19th century from French mètre, itself from Ancient Greek μέτρον (métron, 'measure, rule')—fully naturalized into Arabic broken-plural morphology (متر -> أمتار).

متساوي.etymology: Form VI active participle مُتَسَاوٍ / مُتَسَاوِي (mutasāwī, 'equal, even, uniform, level') from تَسَاوَى (tasāwā, 'to be equal, be level with one another') on the root س-و-ي (s-w-y).

متشابك.etymology: Form VI reciprocal active participle مُتَشَابِك (mutašābik, 'interlacing with one another, tangled') from the root ش-ب-ك (š-b-k, 'to weave, net, interlock'). Literally describes strands or lines crossing over and hooking into each other.

متصل.etymology: Form VIII active participle مُتَّصِل (muttaṣil, 'connected, continuous; caller [by telephone]') from اِتَّصَلَ (ittaṣala, 'to be connected, reach, contact, call') on the root و-ص-ل (w-ṣ-l).

متفاجئ.etymology: Form VI active participle from تفاجأ (root ف-ج-أ, unexpected event), meaning caught by surprise.

متل.etymology: Spoken Levantine preposition مِتِل (mitil, 'like, just as'), reflecting the regular urban Levantine shift *ṯ > t from Classical Arabic مِثْل (miṯl, 'likeness, similar; like'), root م-ث-ل (m-ṯ-l).

متوازي.etymology: Form VI active participle مُتَوَازٍ / مُتَوَازِي (mutawāzī, 'running parallel to one another') from the root و-ز-ي (w-z-y, 'to be opposite, equal, abreast of'). Standard geometric and everyday term across Arabic for lines, streets, or ropes running side by side.

متواصل.etymology: Form VI active participle (مُتَفَاعِل, mutafāʿil) of تَوَاصَلَ ('to link together without break') from the root و-ص-ل (w-ṣ-l, joining, connecting, reaching). Describing unbroken continuity in time or space, متواصل is common across educated and everyday Jordanian Arabic.

متوتر.etymology: Form V active participle مُتَوَتِّر (mutawattir, 'drawn taut; tense, nervous') from تَوَتَّرَ (tawattara, 'to be stretched tight, become tense'), denominal from وَتَر (watar, 'bowstring, string, tendon') on the root و-ت-ر (w-t-r).

متين.etymology: From Classical Arabic مَتِين (matīn, 'firm, solid, tough, durable'), verbal adjective from the root م-ت-ن (m-t-n, 'to be strong, firm, back/ridge'). Retained across Levantine Arabic to praise materials, knots, furniture, and ropes that hold up under stress.

مثالي.etymology: Adjective suffixed with nisba -i on مثال (example, pattern, root م-ث-ل meaning likeness or model).

مثقوب.etymology: Passive participle مَثْقُوب (maṯqūb, 'pierced, perforated') from the root ث-ق-ب (ṯ-q-b, 'to bore, pierce, penetrate'), cognate with Hebrew נָקַב (nāqav, via metathesis) and Aramaic תְּקַב. Standard across craft, carpentry, and everyday description for anything punched or holed.

مثيل.etymology: Adjective and noun مَثِيل (maṯīl, 'like, peer, equal, match') derived on the pattern فَعِيل (faʿīl) from مَثَلَ (maṯala, 'to resemble, be like') on the Semitic root م-ث-ل (m-ṯ-l).

مجاني.etymology: Relational adjective (nisba) مَجَّانِيّ (majjāniyy, 'free of charge, complimentary, gratis') formed from مَجَّانًا (majjānan, 'for free, gratis'), borrowed from Classical Syriac ܡܓܢ (maggān, 'freely, gratis').

مجفّف.etymology: Form II passive participle of Arabic جَفَّفَ (jaffafa, 'to dry out, dehydrate'), root ج-ف-ف (j-f-f).

مجهول.etymology: Formed on the passive participle pattern مَفْعُول (mafʿūl) of جَهِلَ ('to be ignorant of, not know') on the root ج-ه-ل (j-h-l, ignorance, lack of knowledge). Across both Classical grammar and daily Jordanian life, مجهول describes anything unidentified, anonymous, or mysterious.

مجوز.etymology: Levantine colloquial passive participle مُجَوَّز / مجوّز (mjawwaz, 'doubled, paired'), derived from جَوْز (jōz, 'pair'), itself via phonetic shift from Classical Arabic زَوْج (zawj, 'pair, couple'). Used widely in Jordanian craft and everyday speech for doubled knots, double glass, or paired items.

محاضرة.etymology: Form III verbal noun مُحَاضَرَة (muḥāḍara, 'lecture, talk, academic class') from حَاضَرَ (ḥāḍara, 'to address an audience present before one'), root ح-ض-ر (ḥ-ḍ-r, 'be present, attend'). Literally 'presenting knowledge face-to-face to those present'.

history.meaning: to be present -> to lecture -> lecture

محافظ.etymology: Form III active participle built on the root ح-ف-ظ (to guard, preserve), meaning protective or maintaining.

محامي.etymology: Form III active participle مُحَامٍ / مُحَامِي (muḥāmī, 'defender, advocate, lawyer') from حَامَى (ḥāmā, 'to defend, protect, plead on behalf of') on the root ح-م-ي (ḥ-m-y).

محبس.etymology: Noun of instrument/place مِحْبَس / مَحْبِس (miḥbas / maḥbis, 'device that holds back or shuts off flow; shutoff tap, main valve') from حَبَسَ (ḥabasa, 'to hold back, confine, shut off [water]') on the root ح-ب-س (ḥ-b-s).

محتاج.etymology: Form VIII active participle مُحْتَاج (muḥtāj, 'needing, in need of') from اِحْتَاجَ (iḥtāja, 'to need, require, be in want of') on the hollow root ح-و-ج (ḥ-w-j).

محترم.etymology: Form VIII passive participle مُحْتَرَم (muḥtaram, 'respected, honored, respectable, polite') from اِحْتَرَمَ (iḥtarama, 'to respect, honor, revere') on the root ح-ر-م (ḥ-r-m).

محجوز.etymology: Form I passive participle adjective مَحْجُوز (maḥjūz, 'reserved, booked, set aside, scheduled') from حَجَزَ (ḥajaza, 'to hold back, partition off, reserve'), root ح-ج-ز (ḥ-j-z). Setting a seat or room apart from general access yields 'booked / reserved'.

محدش.etymology: Fused negative pronoun contracting ما (not), أحد (anyone, root أ-ح-د), and the enclitic negative marker -sh.

محرك.etymology: Form II active participle مُحَرِّك (muḥarrik, 'mover, agitator; motor, engine') from حَرَّكَ (ḥarraka, 'to move, set in motion') on the root ح-ر-ك (ḥ-r-k).

history.meaning: that which sets in motion; motor; engine

محروق.etymology: Everyday adjective محروق is the Form I passive participle (مَفْعُول) of حَرَقَ ('to burn') from the root ح-ر-ق (ḥ-r-q, fire, burning, scorching). Beyond scorched food or wood, everyday Jordanian speech uses محروق for a burnt-out lightbulb or blown electrical fuse.

محشور.etymology: Passive participle built on the maf'uul pattern from حشر (root ح-ش-ر, to cram, crowd, or wedge tightly).

محطة.etymology: Noun of place مَحَطَّة (maḥaṭṭa, 'halting place, stopping point, station') from the geminate verb حَطَّ (ḥaṭṭa, 'to put down [loads], alight, halt') on the root ح-ط-ط (ḥ-ṭ-ṭ).

محطوط.etymology: Colloquial passive participle formed on maf'uul from the geminate root ح-ط-ط (to put or set down).

محفظة.etymology: Noun of instrument/container on the maf'ala pattern from the root ح-ف-ظ (to preserve or safeguard).

محفور.etymology: Form I passive participle مَحْفُور (maḥfūr, 'dug, carved, engraved') from the verb حَفَرَ (ḥafara, 'to dig, carve, engrave, hollow out') on the Semitic root ح-ف-ر (ḥ-f-r).

محفورة.etymology: Feminine passive participle from حفر (root ح-ف-ر, to dig or engrave), describing carved inscriptions.

محكم.etymology: Form IV passive participle derived from أحكم (root ح-ك-م, to fasten securely or perfect).

محل.etymology: From Classical Arabic مَحَلّ (maḥall, 'place, halting spot, establishment'), noun of place from حَلَّ (ḥalla, 'to alight, settle').

محلى.etymology: Serves both as Form II passive participle of حلّى (sweetened, root ح-ل-و) and colloquial exclamative contracted from ما أحلى.

محلي.etymology: Nisba adjective formed from محل (place, location, root ح-ل-ل meaning to settle or alight).

محمي.etymology: Form I passive participle مَحْمِيّ (maḥmiyy, 'protected, guarded, sheltered') from the verb حَمَى (ḥamā, 'to protect, defend, shield') on the root ح-م-ي (ḥ-m-y).

محمّص.etymology: Form II passive participle adjective مُحَمَّص (muḥammaṣ, 'toasted, roasted') from حَمَّصَ (ḥammaṣa, 'to roast nuts, coffee beans, or chickpeas in a dry pan'), root ح-م-ص (ḥ-m-ṣ). Related to حمّص ('chickpeas'), originally named for their roasted or hard-seeded nature.

مخبز.etymology: Masculine noun of place (اسم مكان) on the pattern مَفْعَل (mafʿal) derived from the root خ-ب-ز (x-b-z, baking bread). Literally meaning 'place where baking occurs', مخبز (pl. مخابز) is the universal Jordanian word for a bakery.

مخبى.etymology: Levantine Form II passive participle مْخَبَّى (mḫabbā, 'hidden, tucked away') from خَبَّى (ḫabbā, 'to hide'), reflecting the regular Levantine loss of final hamza from Classical Arabic مُخَبَّأ (muḫabbaʾ) of خَبَّأَ (ḫabbaʾa, 'to hide, conceal'), root خ-ب-ء (ḫ-b-ʾ).

مخبي.etymology: Passive participle of Form II خبّى (from Classical خبّأ, root خ-ب-أ meaning to conceal or tuck away).

مخبّى.etymology: Colloquial passive participle مخبّى (pattern مُفَعَّل) stems from خبّى ('to hide, conceal') from the root خ-ب-أ / خ-ب-ي (x-b-ʾ, concealing, storing away), with historical loss of final hamza into a weak -ā stem. In Jordanian Arabic, مخبّى (f. مخبّاة) means 'hidden' or 'tucked out of sight'.

مخبّي.etymology: Form II active participle (مُفَعِّل, mufaʿʿil) of خبّى ('to hide or keep secret'), built on the root خ-ب-أ / خ-ب-ي (x-b-ʾ) with the Levantine shift to a final-weak stem. Contrasting in vowel with passive مخبّى (mxabba), مخبّي (mxabbi) means 'actively hiding or keeping something secret'.

مختبر.etymology: Place noun identical to the Form VIII passive participle of اختبر (root خ-ب-ر), naming a room where trials are conducted.

مختلف.etymology: Form VIII active participle from the root خ-ل-ف (to differ, come behind), used adjectivally across all registers.

مختوم.etymology: Administrative term مختوم comes from the passive participle مَفْعُول of خَتَمَ ('to seal, stamp, conclude') from the Semitic root خ-ت-م (x-t-m, seal, signet ring), cognate with Hebrew חָתַם. In modern Jordanian bureaucracy and mail, مختوم indicates that a document or envelope bears an official seal or stamp.

مخدة.etymology: Instrumental noun مِخَدَّة ('pillow, cushion', plural مَخَدَّات) built with prefix مِـ on خَدّ ('cheek', geminate root خ-د-د): literally 'a cheek-rest' on which a sleeper lays their cheek.

مخطط.etymology: Passive participle مُخَطَّط ('floor plan, blueprint, layout; striped') from Form II خَطَّطَ ('draw lines, map out'), built on the geminate root خ-ط-ط ('carve or draw a line, خط').

مخفوق.etymology: Form I passive participle adjective مَخْفُوق (maḵfūq, 'whisked, whipped, beaten') from خَفَقَ (ḵafaqa, 'to beat rapidly, flutter, whip'), root خ-ف-ق (ḵ-f-q, 'flutter, throb, beat'). Widely used in recipes for whipped cream and beaten eggs.

مخفي.etymology: Form I passive participle مَخْفِيّ (maḫfiyy, 'hidden, concealed, kept out of sight') from خَفَى (ḫafā) / خَفِيَ (ḫafiya, 'to hide, be hidden') on the root خ-ف-ي (ḫ-f-y).

مخمل.etymology: Textile noun derived on the maf'al template from root خ-م-ل (soft nap or pile of a woven cloth).

مدام.etymology: Borrowed from French madame ('madam, Mrs., ma'am'), originally the phrase ma dame ('my lady'), from Latin mea domina.

مدة.etymology: Noun مُدَّة (mudda, 'stretch of time, period, duration') derived from the geminate verb مَدَّ (madda, 'to stretch, extend, prolong') on the root م-د-د (m-d-d).

مدح.etymology: From Classical Arabic مَدَحَ (madaḥa, 'to praise, commend, eulogize'), root م-د-ح (m-d-ḥ).

مدخل.etymology: Noun of place مَدْخَل (madḫal, 'place of entry, entrance, doorway, lobby') derived from دَخَلَ (daḫala, 'to enter, go in') on the root د-خ-ل (d-ḫ-l).

مدرسة.etymology: Noun of place مَدْرَسَة (madrasa, 'place of study, school') derived from دَرَسَ (darasa, 'to study, learn, read repeatedly') on the Semitic root د-ر-س (d-r-s).

مدفوع.etymology: Form I passive participle مَدْفُوع (madfūʿ, 'pushed, handed over; paid') from دَفَعَ (dafaʿa, 'to push, hand over, pay [a sum]') on the root د-ف-ع (d-f-ʿ).

مدفون.etymology: Passive participle patterned on maf'uul from the pan-Semitic root د-ف-ن (to bury or inter).

مدهون.etymology: Workshop and household adjective مدهون derives as passive participle مَفْعُول of دَهَنَ ('to anoint, grease, coat with oil or paint') on the root د-ه-ن (d-h-n, oil, grease, paint). Shifting from oiling wood or skin in Classical Arabic, مدهون is the standard Jordanian adjective for painted walls, doors, and signs.

مدور.etymology: Form II passive participle مُدَوَّر (mudawwar, 'made round, circular, round') from دَوَّرَ (dawwara, 'to make round, turn around') on the hollow root د-و-ر (d-w-r).

مدوّر.etymology: Circular-shape adjective مدوّر follows the Form II passive participle (مُفَعَّل) of دوّر ('to make round, turn around') from the hollow root د-و-ر (d-w-r, circle, turning). While Formal Arabic prefers مستدير, everyday Jordanian speech uses مدوّر for round tables, faces, windows, and loaves.

مدير.etymology: Form IV active participle مُدِير (mudīr, 'one who turns, runs, or directs; director, manager') from أَدَارَ (ʾadāra, 'to turn, revolve, manage, direct') on the root د-و-ر (d-w-r).

مديرة.etymology: Feminine (-ة) of Form IV active participle مُدِير (mudīr, 'director, manager, principal', literally 'one who makes affairs revolve and run') of أَدَارَ (ʾadāra, 'to turn round, administer, manage'), from the hollow root د-و-ر (d-w-r, 'to revolve, turn in a circle').

history.meaning: to cause to revolve -> overseer, governor

مديرة.notes: Standard across MSA and spoken Jordanian for a female school principal (مديرة المدرسة) or company director.

مدينة.etymology: Inherited from Classical Arabic مَدِينَة (madīna, 'city, town'), borrowed from or cognate with Aramaic ܡܕܝܢܬܐ (məḏīntā, 'jurisdiction, province, city'), from the Semitic root د-ي-ن (d-y-n, 'to judge, govern').

مدّد.etymology: Intensive Form II verb (فَعَّلَ, faʿʿala) built from the geminate root م-د-د (m-d-d, to stretch, lengthen, extend). Commonly used in both formal and colloquial Jordanian Arabic, مدّد means extending a stay, contract, lease, or deadline.

history.meaning: to extend (a stay, deadline, or pipe)

مر.etymology: Form I geminate verb مَرَّ (marra, 'to pass, go by, cross') from the Semitic root م-ر-ر (m-r-r).

مراجعة.etymology: Feminine Form III verbal noun (مُفَاعَلَة, mufāʿala) of رَاجَعَ ('to go back over, review, consult') on the root ر-ج-ع (r-j-ʿ, returning). In Jordanian administrative and everyday speech, مراجعة denotes reviewing files, medical checkups, or municipal follow-up visits.

مراية.etymology: Levantine noun مْرَايَة (mrāye, 'mirror, looking-glass'), reshaped from Classical Arabic مِرْآة (mirʾāh, 'mirror'), a noun of instrument derived from رَأَى (raʾā, 'to see') on the root ر-ء-ي (r-ʾ-y).

مربع.etymology: Form II passive participle of ربّع (root ر-ب-ع, four), substantivized as the geometric noun for a four-sided square.

مربعة.etymology: Feminine form of مربع (root ر-ب-ع, four) agreeing with feminine nouns like علبة or طاولة.

مربوط.etymology: Form I passive participle مَرْبُوط (marbūṭ, 'tied, bound, fastened, attached') from رَبَطَ (rabaṭa, 'to tie, bind, fasten') on the root ر-ب-ط (r-b-ṭ).

مربوطة.etymology: Feminine passive participle from ربط (root ر-ب-ط, to bind, tie, or fasten together).

مربى.etymology: Passive participle of Form II رَبَّى (rabbā, 'to nurture, cure, preserve in syrup'), from root ر-ب-و: fruit preserved slowly in sugar.

history.meaning: fruit preserve; confection cured in honey or sugar

مرة.etymology: Noun of single occurrence from root م-ر-ر (to pass by, an occasion); distinct from homophonous مرّة meaning woman (< امرأة).

مرتاح.etymology: Form VIII active participle مُرْتَاح (murtāḥ, 'resting, at ease, relaxed, comfortable') from اِرْتَاحَ (irtāḥa, 'to rest, find relief, feel at ease') on the hollow root ر-و-ح (r-w-ḥ).

مرتب.etymology: Form II passive participle of رتّب (root ر-ت-ب, to arrange or put in order), meaning tidy, smart, or well-organized.

مرتبان.etymology: Beloved Levantine pantry word مَرْتَبَان (also spelled مَرْطَبَان, 'glass or glazed storage jar'), named after the historic Burmese port city of Martaban (Mottama), whose glazed stoneware jars carried spices, preserves, sugar, and pickles across Indian Ocean and Ottoman trade routes into Syrian and Jordanian kitchens.

history.meaning: glazed spice and preserve jar from Martaban

مرتبة.etymology: Feminine passive participle of رتّب (root ر-ت-ب) meaning neat/tidy, and in another vocalization a bed mattress.

مرجاني.etymology: Nisba colour adjective derived from مَرْجَان (marjān, 'coral, small pearls'), a pre-Islamic cultural loan in Arabic connected with Aramaic מַרְגָּנִיתָא (margānīṯā) and Ancient Greek μαργαρίτης (margarítēs, 'pearl'). In modern Jordanian colour usage, مرجاني names the warm pinkish-orange shade of Red Sea coral.

مرحبا.etymology: Adverbial accusative greeting مَرْحَبًا (marḥaban, 'welcome!, hello!'), elliptical for صَادَفْتَ أَهْلًا وَسَهْلًا وَمَرْحَبًا ('you have found welcoming kin, smooth ground, and ample room'), from مَرْحَب (marḥab, 'wide, spacious place') on the root ر-ح-ب (r-ḥ-b, 'to be wide, roomy, welcoming').

مرحلة.etymology: Continues Classical Arabic noun of place and distance مَرْحَلَة (marḥala, originally 'a single day's journey between two caravan halting-stations') on the pattern مَفْعَلَة (mafʿala) from the triliteral root ر-ح-ل (r-ḥ-l, 'to saddle a camel, set out on a journey').

history.meaning: stage, phase, educational level, breaking point

مرحلة.notes: Links directly to رحلة ('school trip'): every مرحلة ('phase, stage') was originally one leg of a desert journey.

مرخي.etymology: Passive participle مَرْخِيّ (marḫiyy) of the weak-final verb رَخَى / أرخى ('to slacken, loosen, let hang down'), from the root ر-خ-و (r-ḫ-w, 'to be soft, loose, slack'). Directly contrasts with مشدود ('pulled tight') in Levantine speech.

مرسل.etymology: Substantivized Form IV active participle from أرسل (root ر-س-ل, to send a messenger or dispatch).

مرسوم.etymology: Form I passive participle مَرْسُوم (marsūm, 'traced, drawn, sketched, painted') from رَسَمَ (rasama, 'to trace, draw, sketch, mark out') on the root ر-س-م (r-s-m).

مرطبان.etymology: From post-classical Arabic مَرْطَبَان (marṭabān, 'glazed storage vessel, jar'), named after the Mon port city of Martaban (Mottama) in Lower Burma (Myanmar), a major Indian Ocean export center for glazed storage jars that entered Levantine and Ottoman usage for any glass or ceramic food jar.

مرفوع.etymology: Form I passive participle مَرْفُوع (marfūʿ, 'raised, lifted, elevated, propped up') from رَفَعَ (rafaʿa, 'to raise, lift, elevate') on the root ر-ف-ع (r-f-ʿ).

مرق.etymology: Form I verb مَرَقَ (maraqa, 'to pass rapidly through, pierce through'), which in Levantine Arabic (presumably reinforced by Aramaic substrate usage) became the everyday verb meaning 'to pass by, walk past, go through, drop by' on the root م-ر-ق (m-r-q).

history.meaning: to pass by; walk past; drop by

مرقة.etymology: Feminine culinary noun derived from مَرَق (maraq, broth, gravy, stock) on the root م-ر-ق (m-r-q, thin liquid, sauce, passing through). Across Jordan and the Levant, the feminine form مرقة (maraqa) is the everyday kitchen term for meat or vegetable broth and stew sauce.

مرقم.etymology: Form II passive participle مُرَقَّم (muraqqam, 'numbered, striped, marked with figures') from the root ر-ق-م (r-q-m, 'to mark, write, number'). Used across both formal Arabic and colloquial Levantine for sequentially numbered pages, tickets, or lantern frames.

مرقمين.etymology: Sound masculine plural Form II passive participle of رقّم (root ر-ق-م, to mark with numerals).

مرقّم.etymology: Form II passive participle of Arabic رَقَّمَ (raqqama, 'to mark with numbers'), from رَقْم (raqm, 'numeral'), root ر-ق-م.

مركزي.etymology: Relative (nisba) adjective مَرْكَزِيّ (markaziyy, 'central, main, focal') derived from مَرْكَز (markaz, 'centre, station, post'), noun of place from رَكَزَ (rakaza, 'to plant firmly in the ground'), root ر-ك-ز (r-k-z). Originally 'the spot where a banner or pole is planted', hence 'centre'.

مروحة.etymology: Instrumental noun مِرْوَحَة ('fan, ventilator') formed on the pattern مِفْعَلَة from the hollow root ر-و-ح ('blow gently, breeze, refresh'), originally naming a woven palm-leaf hand fan and in modern Arabic any electric cooling fan.

مريح.etymology: Form IV active participle مُرِيح (murīḥ, 'giving rest, restful, comfortable, soothing') from أَرَاحَ (ʾarāḥa, 'to give rest, relieve, comfort') on the hollow root ر-و-ح (r-w-ḥ).

مريول.etymology: Traditional Levantine noun مَرْيُول (maryūl, 'apron, pinafore, school smock'), considered either an old Mediterranean borrowing linked to Italian/Romance mariola or an expressive colloquial formation for a front-covering garment. Widely used in Jordan for both art/kitchen aprons and classic school pinafores.

مزاح.etymology: Form III verbal noun مُزَاح (muzāḥ, 'joking, banter, playful teasing') from مَازَحَ (māzaḥa, 'to joke with someone'), root م-ز-ح (m-z-ḥ, 'jest, banter'). Denotes friendly, good-natured humour among peers.

مزبوط.etymology: Colloquial Levantine reflex of Classical مَضْبُوط (maḍbūṭ, 'accurately recorded, exact, firm'), the passive participle of ضَبَطَ on the root ض-ب-ط (ḍ-b-ṭ, to hold firmly, regulate, make exact), with urban dissimilation of emphatic /ḍ/ to /z/. Ubiquitous in Jordan, مزبوط means 'right', 'straight', or 'exact'.

مزح.etymology: Verbal noun of Classical Arabic مَزَحَ (mazaḥa, 'to jest, joke'), Semitic root م-ز-ح (m-z-ḥ).

مزدوج.etymology: Form VIII participle (مُفْتَعِل, muftaʿil) from the root ز-و-ج (z-w-j, pair, couple, mate, itself an early Semitic/Greek-contact cultural root cf. zeugos), where the Form VIII infix -t- voices to -d- after /z/ (مُزْدَوِج). Standard across modern Jordanian Arabic, it means 'double' or 'twofold'.

morphemes.meaning: Form VIII participle (t > d after z)

مزع.etymology: Form I sound verb rooted in م-ز-ع (a dialectal shift/variant related to م-ز-ق, to tear or rip apart).

مزعج.etymology: Form IV active participle مُزْعِج (muzʿij, 'disturbing, unsettling, annoying, noisy') from أَزْعَجَ (ʾazʿaja, 'to disturb, unsettle, trouble, bother') on the root ز-ع-ج (z-ʿ-j).

مزهرية.etymology: Feminine instrumental/locative noun formed on the pattern مَفْعَلِيَّة (mafʿaliyya) from زَهْر (zahr, blossoms, flowers) on the root ز-ه-ر (z-h-r, to bloom, shine). Coined in modern Arabic to designate a vessel for cut flowers, مزهرية is standard across Jordan alongside فازه.

مزيّت.etymology: Kitchen and mechanical term مزيّت is the Form II passive participle (مُفَعَّل) of زيّت ('to oil, lubricate, grease') derived from زَيْت (zayt, olive oil) on the pan-Semitic root ز-ي-ت (z-y-t). In Jordanian workshops and kitchens, مزيّت describes anything lubricated with oil or greased for baking.

مس.etymology: Borrowed in Jordanian and Levantine school usage from English Miss (originally clipped in 17th-century English from mistress), generalized in Amman schools as the respectful everyday title for any female teacher or principal regardless of marital status.

morphemes.meaning: Miss / Ms., female teacher (< English Miss)

history.meaning: polite form of address for a woman or female schoolteacher
female teacher, headmistress (title and common noun)

cognates.meaning: title for a female teacher (source word)

rootFamily.gloss: the female teacher (definite noun in Jordanian student talk)

مس.notes: Colloquial Jordanian school register (contrasting with formal MSA أستاذة or معلمة): takes the Arabic vocative particle (يا مس!), definite article (إجت المس, 'the teacher came'), and precedes first names (مس فاتن).

مسؤولية.etymology: Abstract noun formed in 19th-century Nahda Arabic with the productive suffix -يَّة (-iyya) on Classical passive participle مَسْؤُول (masʾūl, 'questioned, answerable, accountable', pattern مَفْعُول of سَأَلَ saʾala, 'to ask, call to account', root س-ء-ل), calquing French responsabilité.

history.meaning: asked, answerable (cf. Qurʾan 17:36 كَانَ عَنْهُ مَسْؤُولًا)

مسؤولية.notes: Spelled مسؤولية (with hamza on و, Jordanian/Gulf/Levant standard) or مسئولية (Egyptian orthography, hamza on ي carrier).

مسا.etymology: Spoken Levantine form مَسَا (masā, 'evening'), with regular drop of word-final hamza after a long vowel from Classical Arabic مَسَاء (masāʾ, 'evening'), root م-س-و (m-s-w).

مساء.etymology: Masculine noun on the pattern مَفْعَل / فَعَال from the root م-س-و (m-s-w, evening, dusk), related to أَمْسَى ('to enter the evening'). Anchoring the universal Arabic greeting مساء الخير ('good evening'), مساء also serves adverbially as مساءً ('p.m. / in the evening').

مسائي.etymology: Nisba relational adjective formed by suffixing -ī (-ي) to مَسَاء (masāʾ, evening) on the root م-س-و (m-s-w), with the Classical final hamza preserved or simplified in speech. Jordanian Arabic uses مسائي for evening classes, shifts, newspapers, and gatherings.

مساحة.etymology: Nouns on mif'aala/maf'aala from root م-س-ح (originally wiping or surveying land with a cord).

مسافة.etymology: From Classical Arabic مَسَافَة (masāfa, 'distance, stretch of journey'), noun of place from the hollow root س-و-ف (s-w-f, originally 'to smell/scent the trail', hence the stretch of desert a guide covers by scenting landmarks). Today it is the universal Arabic word for distance and spacing.

مسافر.etymology: Form III active participle of Arabic سَافَرَ (sāfara, 'to travel'), root س-ف-ر (s-f-r, 'to set out on a journey').

مستحيل.etymology: Form X active participle مُسْتَحِيل (mustaḥīl, 'altered from its nature, absurd, impossible') from اِسْتَحَالَ (istaḥāla, 'to change state, become impossible or inconceivable') on the hollow root ح-و-ل (ḥ-w-l).

مستعجل.etymology: Form X active participle مُسْتَعْجِل (mustaʿjil, 'hastening, in a hurry, rushing') from اِسْتَعْجَلَ (istaʿjala, 'to hasten, urge speed, be in a hurry') on the root ع-ج-ل (ʿ-j-l).

مستعمل.etymology: Form X passive participle derived from استعمل (to put to use, root ع-م-ل), meaning previously used or second-hand.

مستقبل.etymology: Form X passive participle of Arabic اِسْتَقْبَلَ (istaqbala, 'to face, receive what is coming'), root ق-ب-ل (q-b-l).

مستقيم.etymology: Form X active participle of Arabic اِسْتَقَامَ (istaqāma, 'to stand straight, be upright'), root ق-و-م (q-w-m).

مستوي.etymology: Form VIII participle of Arabic اِسْتَوَى (istawā, 'to become even, level, or mature'), root س-و-ي (s-w-y).

مسجل.etymology: Form II passive participle مُسَجَّل (musajjal, 'registered, recorded, entered in a register') from سَجَّلَ (sajjala, 'to register, record'), denominal from سِجِلّ (sijill, 'scroll, register'), root س-ج-ل (s-j-l).

مسح.etymology: Form I verb مَسَحَ (masaḥa, 'to wipe, rub off, stroke, anoint') from the Proto-Semitic root م-س-ح (m-s-ḥ).

مسطح.etymology: Form II passive participle of سطّح (root س-ط-ح, to spread out flat or level a roof).

مسطحة.etymology: Feminine Form II passive participle derived from سطّح on the root س-ط-ح (plane, flat surface).

مسطرة.etymology: Instrumental noun مِسْطَرَة ('ruler, straightedge', plural مَسَاطِر) formed with prefix مِـ from the root س-ط-ر ('rule straight lines, write in neat rows').

مسطّح.etymology: Descriptive adjective مسطّح represents the Form II passive participle (مُفَعَّل) of سطّح ('to level out, flatten') on the root س-ط-ح (s-ṭ-ḥ, surface, roof, flat expanse). Used across formal and colloquial Jordanian Arabic, مسطّح describes level ground, flat stones, and shallow platters.

مسك.etymology: Form I verb مَسَكَ (masaka, 'to take hold of, grasp, hold, seize') on the triliteral Semitic root م-س-ك (m-s-k).

مسكة.etymology: Noun مَسْكَة (maska, 'grip, hold; handle, knob, catch [of a door, window, or drawer]') derived from مَسَكَ (masaka, 'to hold, grasp') on the root م-س-ك (m-s-k).

مسكر.etymology: Form II passive participle from سكّر (root س-ك-ر, to bolt or shut), the standard Jordanian adjective for closed.

مسكون.etymology: Form I passive participle مَسْكُون (maskūn, 'inhabited, occupied, dwelt in') from سَكَنَ (sakana, 'to dwell, reside, inhabit') on the Semitic root س-ك-ن (s-k-n).

مسكين.etymology: Inherited from Classical Arabic مِسْكِين (miskīn, 'poor, needy, humble, unfortunate'), an ancient Semitic cultural word borrowed via Aramaic ܡܣܟܢܐ (miskēnā) from Akkadian muškēnum ('subject, commoner, poor person'), later aligned by folk and grammatical analysis with the Arabic root س-ك-ن (s-k-n, 'to be still, humble').

مسمار.etymology: Instrumental noun مِسْمَار ('nail, metal pin, peg', plural مَسَامِير) formed on the pattern مِفْعَال from the Semitic root س-م-ر ('fasten tightly with nails').

مسند.etymology: Form IV passive participle مُسْنَد (musnad, 'propped up, leaned against, supported') from أَسْنَدَ (ʾasnada, 'to prop up, lean [something] against, support') on the root س-ن-د (s-n-d).

مش.etymology: Ubiquitous Levantine and Egyptian negator contracted from مَا شَيْءَ (not a thing) before nouns, adjectives, and participles.

مشاركة.etymology: Form III verbal noun مُشَارَكَة (mušāraka, 'sharing, participation, partnership') from شَارَكَ (šāraka, 'to share with, take part in, participate') on the root ش-ر-ك (š-r-k).

مشبك.etymology: Noun of instrument مِشْبَك (mišbak, 'clasp, clip, catch, fastener') derived from شَبَكَ (šabaka, 'to entwine, fasten, hook together') on the root ش-ب-ك (š-b-k).

مشبوك.etymology: Form I passive participle مَشْبُوك (mašbūk, 'fastened, clipped, hooked together, plugged in') from شَبَكَ (šabaka, 'to intertwine, fasten, connect') on the root ش-ب-ك (š-b-k).

مشبّك.etymology: Form II passive participle مُشَبَّك (mušabbak, 'fastened with a clip, lattice-worked, clipped') from شَبَّكَ (šabbaka, 'to interlace, fasten together, clip') on the root ش-ب-ك (š-b-k).

مشتر.etymology: Form VIII active participle مُشْتَرٍ (muštarin, construct/definite مُشْتَرِي muštarī, 'buyer, purchaser, customer') from اِشْتَرَى (ištarā, 'to buy, purchase') on the root ش-ر-ي (š-r-y).

مشدود.etymology: Passive participle مَشْدُود (mašdūd, 'pulled tight, fastened, taut') from the geminate root ش-د-د (š-d-d, 'to bind firmly, pull tight, strengthen'). Used in Levantine Arabic both literally for stretched ropes/wires and figuratively for someone tense or deeply absorbed.

مشرق.etymology: Form IV active participle مُشْرِق (mušriq, 'shining, radiant, bright, sunlit') from أَشْرَقَ (ʾašraqa, 'to rise and shine [of the sun], radiate light') on the root ش-ر-ق (š-r-q).

مشروخ.etymology: Form I passive participle (مَفْعُول, mafʿūl) of شَرَخَ ('to split slightly, crack') on the root ش-ر-خ (š-r-x, crack, split, shoot). In everyday Jordanian households, مشروخ specifically distinguishes a chipped or hairline-cracked cup, plate, or glass pane from one completely shattered (مكسور).

مشغول.etymology: Form I passive participle مَشْغُول (mašġūl, 'busied, occupied, engaged, taken') from شَغَلَ (šaġala, 'to occupy, keep busy, engage') on the root ش-غ-ل (š-ġ-l).

مشقوق.etymology: Form I passive participle مَشْقُوق (mašqūq, 'split, cleft, cracked, slit') from the geminate verb شَقَّ (šaqqa, 'to split, cleave, crack open') on the root ش-ق-ق (š-q-q).

مشكلة.etymology: Noun مُشْكِلَة (muškila, 'difficulty, dubious matter, problem'), originally the feminine active participle of Form IV أَشْكَلَ (ʾaškala, 'to be ambiguous, intricate, or difficult to resolve') on the root ش-ك-ل (š-k-l).

مشمس.etymology: Form IV active participle from أشمس (root ش-م-س, sun), describing clear, sunlit days or rooms.

مشهور.etymology: Passive participle مَشْهُور (mašhūr, 'widely known, famous, celebrated') on the pattern مَفْعُول (mafʿūl) of شَهَرَ (šahara, 'to make conspicuous, proclaim publicly, unsheathe a sword'), from the Semitic root ش-ه-ر (š-h-r, also yielding شَهْر 'new moon, month', named for its public visibility).

history.meaning: to make publicly known -> renowned, notorious

مشهور.notes: Covers both public celebrity fame and high-school popularity (البنت المشهورة بالمدرسة).

مشوي.etymology: Form I passive participle مَشْوِيّ (mašwiyy, 'roasted, grilled, broiled') from شَوَى (šawā, 'to roast, grill [meat or vegetables]') on the Semitic root ش-و-ي (š-w-y).

مشى.etymology: Form I defective verb مَشَى (mašā, 'to walk, go on foot, proceed, function smoothly') on the triliteral root م-ش-ي (m-š-y).

مشي.etymology: Form I defective verb rooted in م-ش-ي (to walk on foot), inherited directly from Classical مَشَى.

مشية.etymology: Manner and instance noun shaped on fi'la/fa'la from the defective root م-ش-ي (to walk on foot).

مصاري.etymology: Levantine plural noun مَصَارِي (maṣārī, 'money, cash'), historically the broken plural of مِصْرِيَّة (miṣriyya, 'Egyptian [coin]'), denoting the Ottoman silver para coins minted in Cairo (مِصْر Miṣr) that served as everyday currency across Syria, Lebanon, Palestine, and Jordan.
