مصب.etymology: Noun of place patterned on maf'al from the geminate root ص-ب-ب (to pour out liquid), naming a spout or river mouth.

مصدق.etymology: Form II active participle مُصَدِّق / مْصَدِّق (mṣaddiq, 'believing, holding to be true') from صَدَّقَ (ṣaddaqa, 'to believe, deem true, confirm') on the Semitic root ص-د-ق (ṣ-d-q).

مصروف.etymology: Passive participle of ص-ر-ف (s-r-f) on the pattern مفعول, literally 'that which is spent or disbursed', used as a noun for everyday expenses or pocket money.
مصروف.notes: The root ص-ر-ف covers turning, exchanging currency, and spending money.

مصفوف.etymology: Form I passive participle adjective مَصْفُوف (maṣfūf, 'arranged in rows, lined up, neatly parked') from صَفَّ (ṣaffa, 'to line up in a row, park'), geminate root ص-ف-ف (ṣ-f-f, 'row, rank, line'). Used for parked buses and coaches as well as pastries on a tray.

history.meaning: to arrange in rows -> lined up, parked

مصفى.etymology: Form II passive participle مُصَفًّى / مْصَفَّى (mṣaffā, 'strained, filtered, drained, clarified') from صَفَّى (ṣaffā, 'to strain, filter, purify, drain') on the root ص-ف-و (ṣ-f-w).

مصقول.etymology: Form I passive participle adjective مَصْقُول (maṣqūl, 'polished, burnished, smooth and gleaming') from صَقَلَ (ṣaqala, 'to polish stone, metal, or wood'), root ص-ق-ل (ṣ-q-l). Describes polished courtyard tiles, glazed ceramics, and smooth prose.

مصنفر.etymology: Quadriliteral passive participle (مُفَعْلَل) derived from صَنْفَرَ ('to sand with sandpaper, frost glass'), a verb coined from صَنْفَرَة (sandpaper/emery), widely linked to Persian sunbāda ('emery stone') or Ottoman zımpara. In Jordan, مصنفر means both 'sanded smooth' (wood) and 'frosted/sandblasted' (glass).

مصيبة.etymology: Noun مُصِيبَة (muṣība, 'calamity, misfortune, disaster'), originally the feminine active participle of Form IV أَصَابَ (ʾaṣāba, 'to hit the mark [of an arrow], strike, befall, afflict someone') on the hollow root ص-و-ب (ṣ-w-b).

مصيدة.etymology: Noun of instrument مِصْيَدَة (miṣyada, 'trap, snare, net, hunting device') derived from صَادَ (ṣāda, 'to hunt, catch, trap') on the hollow Semitic root ص-ي-د (ṣ-y-d).

مضبوط.etymology: Form I passive participle مَضْبُوط (maḍbūṭ, pronounced mazbūṭ in urban Levantine with sibilant voicing of ḍ > z via Ottoman Turkish pronunciation, 'held firm, regulated, accurate, exact; properly, right') from ضَبَطَ (ḍabaṭa, 'to hold fast, regulate, render exact') on the root ض-ب-ط (ḍ-b-ṭ).

مضحك.etymology: Form IV active participle from أضحك built on the root ض-ح-ك (to laugh), meaning causing laughter.

مضغ.etymology: Form I triliteral verb on the root م-ض-غ denoting the mechanical act of chewing food.

مضغوط.etymology: Passive participle (مَفْعُول) of Classical Arabic ضَغَطَ (ḍaghaṭa, 'to press, compress, squeeze'), root ض-غ-ط (ḍ-gh-ṭ).

مطابق.etymology: Form III active participle of Arabic طَابَقَ (ṭābaqa, 'to fit closely, match, correspond'), root ط-ب-ق (ṭ-b-q).

مطبخ.etymology: Noun of place on the pattern مَفْعَل (maf'al) from the Semitic root ط-ب-خ (t-b-kh, 'to cook'), literally 'place of cooking'.
مطبخ.notes: Regular place-noun formation alongside مدخل ('entrance') and مكتب ('office/desk').

مطبوع.etymology: Print-culture adjective مطبوع is the passive participle (مَفْعُول, mafʿūl) of طَبَعَ ('to stamp, impress, print') on the Semitic root ط-ب-ع (ṭ-b-ʿ, seal, imprint, nature), cognate with Hebrew טָבַע. Moving from stamping clay or wax seals in Classical Arabic, مطبوع became the standard word for printed books, menus, and documents.

مطحون.etymology: Passive participle patterned on maf'uul from the triliteral root ط-ح-ن (to mill, grind grain or spices).

مطر.etymology: Pan-Semitic weather noun مَطَر from root م-ط-ر denoting rain, attested across Classical and spoken Arabic.

مطرقة.etymology: Instrumental noun مِطْرَقَة ('hammer') formed with the tool prefix مِـ (mi-) on the root ط-ر-ق ('to strike, knock, forge metal'). In a piano, the same word names each felt-covered wooden hammer striking the strings.

مطروق.etymology: Passive participle on the maf'uul pattern from the root ط-ر-ق meaning to strike with a hammer or beat a path.

مطلق.etymology: Form IV passive participle from أطلق (root ط-ل-ق, to set free, release), signifying unrestricted or absolute.

مطوي.etymology: Form I passive participle مَطْوِيّ (maṭwiyy, 'folded, rolled up, tucked') from طَوَى (ṭawā, 'to fold, roll up') on the root ط-و-ي (ṭ-w-y).

مطّر.etymology: Form II denominal verb مَطَّرَ (maṭṭara, 'to rain, pour down rain'), corresponding to Classical Arabic أَمْطَرَ (ʾamṭara) and مَطَرَ (maṭara), derived from مَطَر (maṭar, 'rain') on the Proto-Semitic root م-ط-ر (m-ṭ-r).

مع.etymology: Inherited from Classical Arabic مَعَ / مَعْ (maʿa / maʿ, 'with, together with, in the company of'), from Proto-Semitic *maʿ- / *ʿim- ('with').

معبّي.etymology: Levantine Form II active participle (مُفَعِّل, mufaʿʿil) of عبّى ('to fill up, pack') from the root ع-ب-أ / ع-ب-ي (ʿ-b-ʾ, packing, loading). Functioning like a vivid present verb in Jordanian speech, معبّي describes both people packing containers and scents or crowds filling a space.

معتم.etymology: Form IV active participle مُعْتِم (muʿtim, 'darkening, dim, dark, unlit') from أَعْتَمَ (ʾaʿtama, 'to enter into nightfall, become dark'), related to عَتَمَة (ʿatama, 'darkness of night') on the root ع-ت-م (ʿ-t-m).

معجزة.etymology: Feminine Form IV active participle (مُفْعِلَة, mufʿila) of أَعْجَزَ ('to render incapable, surpass human power') from the root ع-ج-ز (ʿ-j-z, inability, wondrousness). Literally 'that which leaves onlookers astounded and unable to imitate', معجزة (pl. معجزات) means 'miracle' across all Arabic registers.

معجنات.etymology: Feminine sound plural (-āt, -ات) of مُعَجَّن (muʿajjan, 'kneaded dough product'), Form II passive participle on the root ع-ج-ن (ʿ-j-n, kneading flour). Used collectively in the feminine plural across Jordan and the Levant, معجنات covers savory baked pies, fatayer, and bakery pastries.

معدن.etymology: Noun of place/origin on maf'il from root ع-د-ن (originally a mine or ore vein), generalized to mean metal or mineral.

معدني.etymology: Nisba adjective suffixing -i to معدن (mine, ore, metal), itself a noun of place from the root ع-د-ن.

معرش.etymology: Form II active/passive participle مُعَرِّش / مْعَرِّش (mʿarriš, 'climbing on a trellis, trailing over an arbor [of vines]') from عَرَّشَ (ʿarraša, 'to train a vine upon a trellis, roof over with a bower'), denominal from عَرْش / عَرِيش (ʿarīš, 'trellis, pergola, arbor') on the root ع-ر-ش (ʿ-r-š).

معروض.etymology: Form I passive participle مَعْرُوض (maʿrūḍ, 'presented, exhibited, displayed, offered [for sale]') from عَرَضَ (ʿaraḍa, 'to show, present, offer, display') on the root ع-ر-ض (ʿ-r-ḍ).

معصب.etymology: Levantine Form II active participle مْعَصِّب (mʿaṣṣib, 'angry, cross, worked up'), from عَصَّبَ (ʿaṣṣaba, 'to bind tightly; [Levantine, denominal from أَعْصَاب ʾaʿṣāb "nerves"] to get tense, lose one's temper, become angry') on the root ع-ص-ب (ʿ-ṣ-b).

معطف.etymology: Instrumental garment noun مِعْطَف ('coat, overcoat', plural مَعَاطِف) formed with prefix مِـ from the root ع-ط-ف ('bend around, fold over affectionately'), literally 'a garment wrapped warmly around the shoulders'.

معطي.etymology: Form IV active participle مُعْطٍ / مَعْطِي (muʿṭī / maʿṭī, 'giving, having given') from أَعْطَى (ʾaʿṭā, 'to give, grant, hand over') on the root ع-ط-و (ʿ-ṭ-w).

معقول.etymology: Form I passive participle مَعْقُول (maʿqūl, 'comprehended by the mind, reasonable, sensible, plausible; [interjection] really?!, can it be?!') from عَقَلَ (ʿaqala, 'to bind; understand, reason') on the root ع-ق-ل (ʿ-q-l).

معك.etymology: Comitative preposition مع (with, root م-ع) combined with the 2ms pronominal suffix -ak (with you).

معلق.etymology: Form II passive participle مُعَلَّق (muʿallaq, 'hung, suspended, hanging, attached') from عَلَّقَ (ʿallaqa, 'to hang up, suspend, attach') on the root ع-ل-ق (ʿ-l-q).

معلقة.etymology: Colloquial Levantine metathesis of Classical مِلْعَقَة (milʿaqa, 'spoon', instrument noun from ل-ع-ق l-ʿ-q 'to lick'), swapping /l/ and /ʿ/ into معلقة (maʿlaqa). Note that its feminine homograph مُعَلَّقَة means 'hanging'; as a kitchen utensil, معلقة is universally feminine in Jordan.

معلم.etymology: Form II active participle مُعَلِّم (muʿallim, 'teacher, instructor; master craftsman, boss') from عَلَّمَ (ʿallama, 'to teach, instruct, train in a craft') on the Semitic root ع-ل-م (ʿ-l-m).

معلّق.etymology: Passive participle of Form II علّق ('to hang, suspend') built on the triliteral root ع-ل-ق (ʿ-l-q, clinging, attaching, suspending). Across Jordan and the Levant, معلّق describes framed pictures, coats, lights, or signs hanging in place, as well as unresolved matters.

معلّم.etymology: Form II active participle (مُفَعِّل, muʿallim) of عَلَّمَ ('to teach, instruct') on the root ع-ل-م (ʿ-l-m, knowledge, mark). Beyond 'schoolteacher', everyday Jordanian speech uses يا معلّم as a warm, respectful title for a skilled craftsman, tradesman, or 'boss'.

معماري.etymology: Relational adjective (nisba) مِعْمَارِيّ (miʿmāriyy, 'architectural; architect') formed from مِعْمَار (miʿmār, 'master builder, mason, architect'), an intensive instrument/agent formation from عَمَرَ (ʿamara, 'to build, construct, inhabit') on the root ع-م-ر (ʿ-m-r).

معنى.etymology: Noun on the maf'al template from the defective root ع-ن-ي (to mean, intend), universally used for meaning or sense.

معين.etymology: Form II passive participle مُعَيَّن (muʿayyan, 'specified, pinpointed, particular') on the pattern مُفَعَّل (mufaʿʿal) of عَيَّنَ (ʿayyana, 'to fix with the eye, individuate, appoint'), denominative from عَيْن (ʿayn, 'eye; exact self'), hollow root ع-ي-ن (ʿ-y-n).

history.meaning: to specify, appoint -> specified, designated; rhombus

معين.notes: Follows an indefinite noun to render English 'a certain...' (شخص معين 'a certain person', لمرحلة معينة 'up to a certain point').

مغامرة.etymology: Form III verbal noun derived from غامر on the root غ-م-ر (to plunge into deep water or risk bravely).

مغبر.etymology: Form II participle adjective مُغَبَّر (muġabbar, 'covered with dust, dusty') derived from غُبَار / غَبْرَة (ġubār / ġabra, 'dust'), from the root غ-ب-ر (ġ-b-r, 'to be dust-coloured, remain behind'). Common everyday Levantine word after windy days.

مغبش.etymology: Levantine Form II participle مْغَبِّش / مُغَبَّش (mġabbiš, 'blurred, misty, fogged up, frosted [of glass]') from غَبَّشَ (ġabbaša, 'to dim, blur, cloud over'), derived from Classical Arabic غَبَش (ġabaš, 'dimness of twilight before dawn, haziness') on the root غ-ب-ش (ġ-b-š).

مغبّش.etymology: Form II participle (مُفَعِّل) of غبّش ('to grow dim, hazy, fogged up') on the root غ-ب-ش (ġ-b-š, pre-dawn dimness, obscurity, haze). Extending from twilight haze in Classical Arabic, مغبّش in Jordan describes misty glass, cloudy weather, or blurry camera shots.

مغرفة.etymology: Noun of instrument from Classical Arabic غَرَفَ (gharafa, 'to scoop water or soup with the hand or a spoon'), root غ-ر-ف.

مغسلة.etymology: Noun of place مَغْسَلَة (maġsala, 'washing place, washbasin, sink, laundry') derived from غَسَلَ (ġasala, 'to wash') on the root غ-س-ل (ġ-s-l).

مغلف.etymology: Form II passive participle of غلّف (root غ-ل-ف, to encase or wrap), used substantively for an envelope or wrapper.

مغلّف.etymology: Form II passive participle (مُفَعَّل, mufaʿʿal) of غلّف ('to encase, wrap, laminate') from the root غ-ل-ف (ġ-l-f, sheath, husk, cover). In modern Jordanian usage, مغلّف (as an adjective) describes gift-wrapped parcels as well as plastic-laminated menus or documents.

مفتاح.etymology: Instrumental noun on the pattern مِفْعال (mif'āl) from the root ف-ت-ح (f-t-h, 'to open'), literally 'an instrument for opening'.
مفتاح.notes: In Jordanian Arabic مفتاح covers both a door key and a mechanic's spanner or wrench.

مفتش.etymology: Form II active participle مُفَتِّش (mufattiš, 'examiner, searcher, inspector') from فَتَّشَ (fattaša, 'to search carefully, examine, inspect') on the root ف-ت-ش (f-t-š).

مفتوح.etymology: Form I passive participle مَفْتُوح (maftūḥ, 'opened, open') from فَتَحَ (fataḥa, 'to open') on the Proto-Semitic root ف-ت-ح (f-t-ḥ).

مفرش.etymology: Masculine noun of instrument/object on the pattern مِفْعَل (mifʿal) from the root ف-ر-ش (f-r-š, to spread out, lay flat, furnish). Denoting a cloth or mat spread over a surface, مفرش (pl. مفارش) is the standard everyday word across Jordan for a tablecloth or table runner.

مفرود.etymology: Passive participle of Arabic فَرَدَ (farada, 'to spread out, unfold, flatten'), root ف-ر-د (f-r-d).

مفروض.etymology: Form I passive participle مَفْرُوض (mafrūḍ, 'ordained, imposed, obligatory; supposed [to], expected') from فَرَضَ (faraḍa, 'to notch, appoint, impose as an obligation, suppose') on the root ف-ر-ض (f-r-ḍ).

مفصلة.etymology: Noun of instrument/place مِفْصَلَة / مَفْصَلَة (mifṣala / mafṣala, 'hinge, articulated joint [of a door or shutter]') derived from فَصَلَ (faṣala, 'to separate, divide at a joint'; compare مَفْصِل mafṣil 'anatomical joint') on the root ف-ص-ل (f-ṣ-l).

مفضل.etymology: Form II passive participle مُفَضَّل (mufaḍḍal, 'preferred, favored, favorite') from فَضَّلَ (faḍḍala, 'to prefer, favor, deem superior') on the root ف-ض-ل (f-ḍ-l).

مفقودات.etymology: Feminine sound plural مَفْقُودَات (mafqūdāt, 'lost items, lost property') of the Form I passive participle مَفْقُود (mafqūd, 'lost, missing') from فَقَدَ (faqada, 'to lose, miss') on the root ف-ق-د (f-q-d).

مفك.etymology: Noun of instrument مِفَكّ (mifakk, 'tool for loosening or unscrewing; screwdriver') derived from the geminate verb فَكَّ (fakka, 'to untie, loosen, unfasten, unscrew') on the root ف-ك-ك (f-k-k).

مفكر.etymology: Form II active participle مُفَكِّر / مْفَكِّر (mfakkir, 'thinking, pondering; [Levantine] thinking, supposing') from فَكَّرَ (fakkara, 'to think, reflect, suppose') on the root ف-ك-ر (f-k-r).

مفيد.etymology: Form IV active participle مُفِيد (mufīd, 'beneficial, useful, informative') of أَفَادَ (ʾafāda, 'to confer benefit, profit, or meaning'), built on the hollow triliteral root ف-ي-د (f-y-d, 'benefit, utility').

history.meaning: to impart benefit or complete meaning -> useful, instructive

rootFamily.gloss: benefit, point/use (ما في فايدة = 'it's no use')

مفيد.notes: Fun grammar trivia: in medieval Arabic grammar, جملة مفيدة ('a useful/complete sentence') is the technical term for an independent clause that conveys a complete thought!

مقابل.etymology: Form III active participle مُقَابِل (muqābil, 'facing, opposite, across from, in return for') from قَابَلَ (qābala, 'to face, stand opposite, meet face to face') on the Semitic root ق-ب-ل (q-b-l).

مقاس.etymology: Noun of measure مَقَاس (maqās, 'measurement, dimension, size') derived from the hollow verb قَاسَ (qāsa, 'to measure, gauge, compare') on the root ق-ي-س (q-y-s).

مقام.etymology: Noun of place/standing مَقَام ('standing place, station, musical mode/key') built with prefix مَـ on the hollow root ق-و-م ('stand, rise'). In Arab musical theory since the medieval treatises, مقام names the tonal scale/mode (and by extension a piece's key) on which a melody rests.

مقرمش.etymology: Quadriliteral active participle مُقَرْمِش / مْقَرْمِش (mqarmiš, 'crunchy, crispy, crusty') from قَرْمَشَ (qarmaša, 'to crunch, nibble crisp food'), an expressive quadriliteral expansion of Semitic roots ق-ر-م (q-r-m, 'to gnaw, nibble') and ق-ر-ش (q-r-š, 'to crunch').

مقسومة.etymology: Feminine passive participle from قسم (root ق-س-م, to split, share, or partition into parts).

مقطع.etymology: Masculine noun مَقْطَع (maqṭaʿ, 'cut place, passage, section, musical bridge, syllable') from قَطَعَ (qaṭaʿa, 'to cut, divide'), root ق-ط-ع (q-ṭ-ʿ). A clean 'cut' in a song or text naturally names a distinct section or verse.

مقعد.etymology: Noun of place (مَفْعَد) from root ق-ع-د (q-ʿ-d, 'to sit down'): literally 'a place for sitting', hence a chair seat or garden bench.

مقفول.etymology: Form I passive participle (مَفْعُول, mafʿūl) of قَفَلَ ('to lock, fasten') on the root ق-ف-ل (q-f-l, lock, bolt, caravan returning). Contrasting with مسكّر ('closed/shut'), مقفول specifically emphasizes that a door, box, or room is secured with a lock.

مقلوب.etymology: Form I passive participle adjective مَقْلُوب (maqlūb, 'flipped, upside down, inverted') from قَلَبَ (qalaba, 'to turn upside down, flip'), root ق-ل-ب (q-l-b, 'turn over, invert, heart'). The same root names the famous Levantine dish مقلوبة ('upside-down' rice pot).

مقلي.etymology: Form I passive participle مَقْلِيّ (maqliyy, 'fried, roasted in a pan') from قَلَى (qalā, 'to fry, roast') on the Semitic root ق-ل-ي (q-l-y).

مقلّم.etymology: Form II passive participle adjective مُقَلَّم (muqallam, 'striped, ruled with lines, trimmed') from قَلَّمَ (qallama, 'to stripe, cut with a reed pen, trim'), root ق-ل-م (q-l-m, 'reed pen, stripe'). Drawing parallel pen-lines gave the sense 'striped' for fabrics and bags.

مقنطر.etymology: Quadriliteral passive participle (مُفَعْلَل) derived from قَنْطَرَة (qanṭara, 'stone arch, vaulted bridge'), itself an early borrowing into Classical Arabic from Greek/Byzantine κέντρον or Aramaic qanṭrā ('arch/bridge', cf. Alcantara). In Levantine architecture, مقنطر describes classic arched doorways and windows.

مقهى.etymology: Noun of place مَقْهًى ('coffeehouse, café', plural مَقَاهٍ / مقاهي) formed with the locative prefix مَـ from قَهْوَة ('coffee'), literally 'the place where coffee is brewed and shared'.

مقوس.etymology: Form II passive participle مُقَوَّس (muqawwas, 'curved like a bow, arched, vaulted') from قَوَّسَ (qawwasa, 'to bend into an arch or bow'), denominal from قَوْس (qaws, 'bow, arch, arc') on the Proto-Semitic root ق-و-س (q-w-s).

مقوّس.etymology: Form II passive participle (مُفَعَّل, mufaʿʿal) of قَوَّسَ ('to curve like a bow') from the hollow root ق-و-س (q-w-s, bow, arc, arch), cognate with Hebrew קֶשֶׁת and Aramaic qeštā. Across Jordan, مقوّس describes curved furniture, mirrors, eyebrows, and arched windows.

مكالمة.etymology: Form III verbal noun مُكَالَمَة (mukālama, 'speaking with someone, conversation; telephone call') from كَالَمَ (kālama, 'to speak with, address, converse') on the root ك-ل-م (k-l-m).

مكان.etymology: Noun of place مَكَان (makān, 'place, spot, location, site'), formed with the locative prefix ma- from كَانَ (kāna, 'to be, exist, stand') on the root ك-و-ن (k-w-n), and secondarily reanalyzed as root م-ك-ن (m-k-n) in its plural أَمَاكِن (ʾamākin).

مكتب.etymology: Noun of place patterned on maf'al from the root ك-ت-ب (to write), naming a desk, study, or office.

مكتبة.etymology: Noun of place مَكْتَبَة (maktaba, 'place of books; library, bookshop, bookcase') formed on the pattern مَفْعَلَة (mafʿala) from كَتَبَ (kataba, 'to write') and كِتَاب (kitāb, 'book'), root ك-ت-ب (k-t-b).

مكتوب.etymology: Passive participle on maf'uul from كتب (root ك-ت-ب, to write); also serves as a noun for a written letter.

مكتوبة.etymology: Feminine passive participle of كتب (root ك-ت-ب, to write) agreeing with feminine nouns like رسالة or وصفة.

مكرم.etymology: Form II passive participle مُكَرَّم (mukarram, 'honoured, revered, treated generously') from the root ك-ر-م (k-r-m, 'nobility, generosity, honour'). Classic polite hospitality expression across Arabic when welcoming guests.

مكرّم.etymology: Form II passive participle adjective مُكَرَّم (mukarram, 'honoured, revered, esteemed') from كَرَّمَ (karrama, 'to honour, treat generously'), root ك-ر-م (k-r-m, 'nobility, generosity, honour'). Used for guests of honour and respected elders.

history.meaning: to be noble -> to honour -> honoured

مكسرات.etymology: Feminine plural noun formed from مكسّر (cracked open, root ك-س-ر), naming nuts whose shells are cracked to eat.

مكسور.etymology: Form I passive participle مَكْسُور (maksūr, 'broken, fractured, shattered') from كَسَرَ (kasara, 'to break, fracture') on the Semitic root ك-س-ر (k-s-r).

مكشوف.etymology: Form I passive participle مَكْشُوف (makšūf, 'uncovered, exposed, bare, open to the air') from كَشَفَ (kašafa, 'to uncover, reveal, expose') on the root ك-ش-ف (k-š-f).

مكعب.etymology: Form II passive participle and noun مُكَعب (mukaʿʿab, 'cube-shaped; cube, die') from كَعَّبَ (kaʿʿaba, 'to make cubic'), denominal from كَعْب (kaʿb, 'anklebone, knucklebone die, cube') on the root ك-ع-ب (k-ʿ-b).

مكون.etymology: Substantivized Form II passive participle of كوّن (root ك-و-ن, to form or bring into being), naming a constituent part.

مكوي.etymology: Defective Form I passive participle (مَفْعُول → مَفْعِيّ) of كَوَى ('to press with hot iron, cauterize') on the root ك-و-ي (k-w-y, branding, burning, ironing). Narrowing in domestic life from hot metal cautery to pressing cloth, مكوي is the everyday Jordanian word for 'ironed'.

ملاحظة.etymology: Form III verbal noun derived from لاحظ (root ل-ح-ظ, originally to glance out of the corner of the eye, hence observe).

ملاقي.etymology: Form III active participle مُلَاقٍ / مْلَاقِي (mlāqī, 'meeting, encountering; [Levantine] finding') from لَاقَى (lāqā, 'to encounter, meet; [Levantine] to find') on the root ل-ق-ي (l-q-y).

ملح.etymology: Inherited Proto-Semitic primary noun مِلْح ('salt') from `*milḥ-`, conserved unchanged for millennia across Arabic, Hebrew, and Aramaic—and central to the Arab ethic of hospitality (عيش وملح, 'bread and salt').

ملحن.etymology: Form II active participle مُلَحِّن (mulaḥḥin, 'melodist, musical composer') from لَحَّنَ (laḥḥana, 'to chant, set to music, compose a melody'), denominal from لَحْن (laḥn, 'melody, tune, tone') on the root ل-ح-ن (l-ḥ-n).

ملزق.etymology: Levantine Form II passive participle مْلَزَّق (mlazzaq, 'stuck on, glued, taped') from لَزَّقَ (lazzaqa, 'to stick, glue, tape'), from Classical Arabic لَزِقَ (laziqa, variant of لَصِقَ laṣiqa, 'to adhere, cling, stick') on the root ل-ز-ق (l-z-q).

ملصق.etymology: Form IV passive participle and noun مُلْصَق (mulṣaq, 'affixed, pasted on; sticker, label, poster') from أَلْصَقَ (ʾalṣaqa, 'to stick, affix, paste') on the root ل-ص-ق (l-ṣ-q).

ملطخ.etymology: Form II passive participle built from لطّخ on the root ل-ط-خ meaning to besmirch, stain, or daub with liquid.

ملعقة.etymology: Instrumental noun مِلْعَقَة ('spoon') formed with prefix مِـ on the root ل-ع-ق ('lick, sip honey or soup'). In spoken Jordanian and Palestinian Arabic, harmless metathesis shifts مِلْعَقَة to مَعْلَقَة (ma'laqa).

ملف.etymology: Noun مِلَفّ / مَلَفّ (milaff / malaff, 'wrapper, folder, binder, file, dossier') derived from the geminate verb لَفَّ (laffa, 'to wrap, fold, roll up') on the root ل-ف-ف (l-f-f).

ملفوف.etymology: Form I passive participle مَلْفُوف (malfūf, 'wrapped, rolled up, folded') from the geminate verb لَفَّ (laffa, 'to wrap, roll, fold') on the root ل-ف-ف (l-f-f).

ملقط.etymology: Instrumental noun مِلْقَط ('tweezers, tongs') formed with the tool pattern مِفْعَل on the root ل-ق-ط ('pick up, glean tiny things from the ground').

ملكي.etymology: Nisba relational adjective مَلَكِيّ (malakiyy, 'royal, kingly') derived from مَلِك (malik, 'king'), from the pan-Semitic root م-ل-ك (m-l-k, 'to reign, possess, advise'). In modern colour naming it translates 'royal' in shades such as أزرق ملكي ('royal blue').

ملكية.etymology: Abstract noun مِلْكِيَّة (milkiyya, 'ownership, property right, title') formed with the abstract suffix ـِيَّة (-iyya) from مِلْك (milk, 'possession, property, ownership') on the Proto-Semitic root م-ل-ك (m-l-k).

ملمع.etymology: Form II passive participle مُلَمَّع (mulammaʿ, 'polished, burnished, made glossy or shiny') from لَمَّعَ (lammaʿa, 'to polish, burnish, cause to shine') on the root ل-م-ع (l-m-ʿ).

ملى.etymology: Levantine verb مَلَى (malā, 'to fill, fill up'), reflecting the regular Levantine merger of final-hamza verbs into final-yāʾ from Classical Arabic مَلَأَ (malaʾa, 'to fill') on the Proto-Semitic root م-ل-ء (m-l-ʾ).

ملي.etymology: Colloquial clipped form مِلِّي (millī, 'millimetre') of مِلِّيمِتْر (millīmitr, 'millimetre'), borrowed from French millimètre (from Latin mille 'thousand' + Greek μέτρον métron 'measure').

مليان.etymology: Levantine adjective مَلْيَان (malyān, 'full, filled'), reshaped with the glide -y- from Classical Arabic مَلْآن (malʾān, 'full') on the stative pattern فَعْلَان (faʿlān) from مَلَأَ (malaʾa, 'to fill'), root م-ل-ء (m-l-ʾ).

مليسة.etymology: Herbal name entering Levantine Arabic from Ancient Greek melissa (bee-balm, literally honeybee) via Aramaic and Mediterranean botany.

مليمتر.etymology: International metric unit loanword adapted from French millimètre (Latin mille 'thousand' + Greek metron).

ممتاز.etymology: Form VIII active participle of امتاز (hollow root م-ي-ز, to stand apart or be distinguished).

ممثّل.etymology: Form II active participle (مُفَعِّل, mufaʿʿil) of مَثَّلَ ('to represent, impersonate, stand in for') on the root م-ث-ل (m-θ-l, likeness, image, example). Both formal and colloquial Jordanian Arabic use ممثّل for an official delegate/representative as well as a stage or film actor.

ممر.etymology: Noun of place (ism makān) on the pattern مَفْعَل (mafʿal) from the geminate root م-ر-ر (m-r-r, 'to pass, go through'), literally 'a place of passing' — a corridor, hallway, or walkway.

ممزوع.etymology: Levantine passive participle مَمْزُوع (mamzūʿ, 'torn, ripped') from colloquial مَزَعَ (mazaʿ, 'to tear cloth or paper'), itself from Classical Arabic مَزَعَ (mazaʿa, 'to pluck apart cotton/wool, rush') blending semantically with مَزَّقَ (mazzaqa, 'to tear to shreds').

ممطر.etymology: Form IV active participle مُمْطِر (mumṭir, 'rainy, bringing rain') from أَمْطَرَ (ʾamṭara, 'to rain, send down rain'), derived from مَطَر (maṭar, 'rain') on the Proto-Semitic root م-ط-ر (m-ṭ-r).

ممكن.etymology: Form IV active participle from أمكن (root م-ك-ن, capability/possibility), used adjectivally and for polite requests.

ممل.etymology: Form IV active participle مُمِلّ (mumill, 'wearisome, tedious, boring, dull') from أَمَلَّ (ʾamalla, 'to weary, tire, bore') on the geminate root م-ل-ل (m-l-l).

ممم.etymology: Onomatopoeic humming interjection shared across languages, written in Arabic with repeated mim to reflect savouring or pondering.

ممنوع.etymology: Passive participle patterned on maf'uul from منع (root م-ن-ع, to prevent, bar, or forbid).

مميز.etymology: Form II passive/active participle مُمَيَّز / مُمَيِّز (mumayyaz, 'distinguished, distinctive, special, signature') from مَيَّزَ (mayyaza, 'to distinguish, single out, set apart') on the hollow root م-ي-ز (m-y-z).

من.etymology: Foundational Semitic preposition مِنْ expressing source, separation, material, or partitive relation.

مناخير.etymology: Plural of Classical Arabic مِنْخَار / مَنْخَر (minkhār, 'nostril'), root ن-خ-ر, generalized in Levantine and Egyptian Arabic to mean 'nose'.

مناسب.etymology: Form III active participle مُنَاسِب (munāsib, 'corresponding, fitting, suitable, appropriate') from نَاسَبَ (nāsaba, 'to correspond to, suit, be proportionate to') on the root ن-س-ب (n-s-b).

منبه.etymology: Form II active participle and noun مُنَبِّه (munabbih, 'awakener, warner; alarm clock') from نَبَّهَ (nabbaha, 'to awaken, rouse from sleep, alert') on the root ن-ب-ه (n-b-h).

منحوت.etymology: Passive participle shaped on maf'uul from the triliteral root ن-ح-ت meaning to chisel, carve, or sculpt stone and wood.

منخار.etymology: Colloquial Levantine noun related to Classical منخر (nostril, from root ن-خ-ر meaning to snort or breathe through the nose), generalized to the whole nose.

مندهش.etymology: Form VII active participle مُنْدَهِش (mundahiš, 'astonished, amazed, surprised') from اِنْدَهَشَ (indahaša, 'to be astonished, taken aback'), derived from دَهِشَ (dahiša, 'to be bewildered, amazed') on the root د-ه-ش (d-h-š).

منديل.etymology: Inherited from Classical Arabic مِنْدِيل / مَنْدِيل (mindīl / mandīl, 'kerchief, napkin, hand towel'), borrowed via Byzantine Greek μανδήλιον (mandḗlion) from Late Latin mantēle / mantēlium ('hand towel, napkin', derived from manus 'hand').

منذ.etymology: Classical temporal preposition مُنْذُ (munðu, 'since, for [duration]'), historically derived from the fusion of مِن ('from') and ذُو ('that which / time'). While everyday Jordanian speech favors من ('since'), منذ marks formal, literary, or stiffly official phrasing.

منشفة.etymology: Instrumental noun on the feminine pattern مِفْعَلَة (mif'ala) from ن-ش-ف (n-sh-f, 'to dry, absorb moisture'), literally 'a drying cloth, towel'.
منشفة.notes: Plural مناشف; directly transparent alongside the adjective ناشف ('dry').

منشور.etymology: Form I passive participle (مَفْعُول, mafʿūl) of نَشَرَ ('to spread out, unfold, publish') on the root ن-ش-ر (n-š-r). Beyond meaning 'published' in print, modern Jordanian Arabic uses منشور constantly as a noun for a social-media post or official leaflet.

منطقة.etymology: Inherited from Classical Arabic مِنْطَقَة / مَنْطِقَة (minṭaqa / manṭiqa, originally 'girdle, belt, waist-zone', then geographical 'zone, region, area, district'), derived from نَطَقَ (naṭaqa, 'to gird, encircle') on the root ن-ط-ق (n-ṭ-q).

منظر.etymology: From Classical Arabic مَنْظَر (manẓar, 'sight, view, aspect, scenic vista'), a noun of place (مَفْعَل) from the root ن-ظ-ر (n-ẓ-r, 'to look, gaze, behold'). Used across all Arabic varieties for both natural panoramas and striking sights.

منعش.etymology: Form IV active participle (مُفْعِل, mufʿil) of أَنْعَشَ ('to revive, invigorate, refresh') from the root ن-ع-ش (n-ʿ-š, lifting up, reviving spirits). Standard across Jordan, منعش describes crisp breezes, cold citrus drinks, and invigorating scents.

منقذ.etymology: Form IV active participle derived from أنقذ on the root ن-ق-ذ signifying saving or delivering from danger.

منور.etymology: Form II participle مُنَوَّر / مْنَوِّر (mnawwir, 'illuminated, lit up, bright, shining') from نَوَّرَ (nawwara, 'to illuminate, light up, shine'), denominal from نُور (nūr, 'light') on the Semitic root ن-و-ر (n-w-r).

منوّر.etymology: Form II active participle of Arabic نَوَّرَ (nawwara, 'to shine, light up'), from نُور (nūr, 'light'), root ن-و-ر (n-w-r).

منيح.etymology: Levantine adjective مْنِيح (mnīḥ, 'good, fine, well'), formed by liquid-nasal dissimilation (l > n before Labial m-) from Classical Arabic مَلِيح (malīḥ, 'pleasant, comely, good, winsome'), originally 'savory, well-salted' from مِلْح (milḥ, 'salt') on the root م-ل-ح (m-l-ḥ).

منيحة.etymology: Signature Levantine feminine adjective derived from root م-ن-ح (to bestow or favour), meaning good or fine.

مهذب.etymology: Form II passive participle formed from هذّب (root ه-ذ-ب, originally to prune a tree), figuratively meaning refined and well-behaved.

مهرجان.etymology: Early borrowing into Arabic مِهْرَجَان (mihrajān) from Middle Persian Mihragān (the autumn festival of Mithra), now meaning any festival.

مهل.etymology: Verbal noun مَهْل (mahl, 'gentle pace, slowness, deliberation, ease'), used especially in عَلَى مَهْل (ʿalā mahl, 'slowly, gently, take your time'), from مَهَلَ (mahala, 'to proceed gently and without haste') on the root م-ه-ل (m-h-l).

مهم.etymology: Form IV active participle مُهِمّ (muhimm, 'causing concern, momentous, important') from أَهَمَّ (ʾahamma, 'to concern, occupy the mind, matter to') on the geminate root ه-م-م (h-m-m).

مهملات.etymology: Feminine sound plural مُهْمَلَات (muhmalāt, 'discarded things, rubbish, trash') of the Form IV passive participle مُهْمَل (muhmal, 'neglected, left unused, discarded') from أَهْمَلَ (ʾahmala, 'to neglect, leave alone, discard') on the root ه-م-ل (h-m-l).

history.meaning: neglected or discarded items; waste; rubbish

مهندس.etymology: Quadriliteral active participle مُهَنْدِس (muhandis, 'surveyor, geometrician, architect, engineer') from هَنْدَسَ (handasa, 'to measure, lay out water channels or buildings, engineer'), denominal from هَنْدَسَة (handasa, 'geometry, architecture, engineering'), Arabicized from Middle Persian handāzag / Persian اندازه (andāza, 'measure, proportion, plan').

مو.etymology: Levantine nominal negative particle contracted from Classical مَا هُوَ (mā huwa, 'it is not') through rapid fusion into mū. Widely used across Jordan and Syria alongside مش (mā šayʾ) to negate nouns, adjectives, prepositional phrases, and participles.

موافق.etymology: Form III active participle of Arabic وَافَقَ (wāfaqa, 'to agree, accord with'), root و-ف-ق (w-f-q).

موافقة.etymology: Form III verbal noun مُوَافَقَة (muwāfaqa, 'agreement, consent, approval, accord') from وَافَقَ (wāfaqa, 'to agree with, suit, consent to') on the root و-ف-ق (w-f-q).

موجود.etymology: Form I passive participle مَوْجُود (mawjūd, 'found, existing, present, available') from وَجَدَ (wajada, 'to find') on the Semitic root و-ج-د (w-j-d).

مورّد.etymology: Form II passive participle adjective مُوَرَّد (muwarrad, 'floral, rose-patterned, rosy') from وَرَّدَ (warrada, 'to tint rose-pink or pattern with flowers'), derived from وَرْد (ward, 'roses, blossoms'), root و-ر-د (w-r-d).

موزونة.etymology: Feminine passive participle from the assimilated root و-ز-ن (to weigh or balance evenly).

موسيقى.etymology: Borrowed into Classical Arabic مُوسِيقَى (mūsīqā, 'music') from Ancient Greek μουσική [τέχνη] (mousikḗ [tékhnē], 'art of the Muses, music'), from Μοῦσα (Moûsa, 'Muse').

موسيقي.etymology: Relational adjective (nisba) مُوسِيقِيّ (mūsīqiyy, 'musical; musician') formed with the suffix ـِيّ (-iyy) from مُوسِيقَى (mūsīqā, 'music'), from Ancient Greek μουσική (mousikḗ).

موصول.etymology: Form I passive participle مَوْصُول (mawṣūl, 'joined, connected, linked, wired') from وَصَلَ (waṣala, 'to join, connect, link, reach') on the Semitic root و-ص-ل (w-ṣ-l).

موضة.etymology: Borrowed into Arabic from Italian moda / French mode ('fashion, manner'), ultimately from Latin modus ('measure, manner').

موضوع.etymology: Passive participle مَوْضُوع (mawḍūʿ, literally 'placed, laid down') on the pattern مَفْعُول (mafʿūl) of وَضَعَ (waḍaʿa, 'to lay down, set in place'), from the initial-weak root و-ض-ع (w-ḍ-ʿ); already used in medieval Arabic logic and rhetoric for a 'subject or proposition laid down for discussion' (parallel to Greek hupokeímenon and Latin subiectum).

history.meaning: to lay down -> laid down; logical subject, fabricated Tradition

موضوع.notes: Equally natural in formal MSA and casual Jordanian talk (شو الموضوع؟ 'what's going on / what's the matter?', انسى الموضوع 'forget about it').

موظف.etymology: Form II passive participle and noun مُوَظَّف (muwaẓẓaf, 'appointed to an office or post; employee, clerk, official') from وَظَّفَ (waẓẓafa, 'to assign a daily allowance or post, employ'), related to وَظِيفَة (waẓīfa, 'assigned duty, office, job') on the root و-ظ-ف (w-ẓ-f).

history.meaning: appointed to a post; official; employee

morphemes.meaning: assigning a task or post; employment

موظفة.etymology: Feminine Form II passive participle (مُفَعَّلَة, mufaʿʿala) of وَظَّفَ ('to appoint to an office, employ') from the root و-ظ-ف (w-ẓ-f, assigned duty, post, allowance). Across Jordanian offices and municipalities, موظفة denotes a female employee, clerk, or civil servant.

موعد.etymology: Noun of time and place مَوْعِد (mawʿid, 'appointed time or place, promise, appointment, schedule') derived from وَعَدَ (waʿada, 'to promise, appoint a time') on the Semitic root و-ع-د (w-ʿ-d).

موقّع.etymology: Form II passive participle of Arabic وَقَّعَ (waqqaʿa, 'to affix a signature, stamp'), root و-ق-ع (w-q-ʿ).

مونة.etymology: Levantine contraction of Classical مؤونة (provisions, sustenance) from the root م-و-ن denoting storing up food for winter.

موهبة.etymology: Noun مَوْهِبَة (mawhiba, 'gift, natural endowment, talent') derived from وَهَبَ (wahaba, 'to give, grant, bestow freely') on the Proto-Semitic root و-ه-ب (w-h-b).

مي.etymology: Levantine noun مَيّ / مَيَّة (mayy / mayye, 'water'), evolved from the Classical Arabic diminutive مُوَيْه / مُوَيْهَة (muwayh / muwayha, 'little water') of مَاء (māʾ, 'water') via glide assimilation, from Proto-Semitic *may- ('water'), root م-و-ه (m-w-h).

مية.etymology: Spoken Levantine numeral مِيَّة (miyye, 'one hundred'), reflecting regular medial hamza loss and glide resolution (-iʾa > -iyye) from Classical Arabic مِائَة / مِئَة (miʾa, 'hundred'), from Proto-Semitic *miʾat-.

ميتين.etymology: Oblique dual of مية (hundred, Classical مِائَة), contracting the medial glottal stop to long ii.

ميدالية.etymology: European loanword traced to Italian medaglia and French médaille, adapted to the Arabic feminine ending -iyya/-a.

ميزانية.etymology: Abstract noun in -iyya built on مِيزَان (mīzān, 'pair of scales, balance'), itself an instrument noun (مِفْعَال) from root و-ز-ن (w-z-n, 'to weigh'): weighing income against expenditure ('budget').

مين.etymology: Levantine interrogative pronoun evolved from Classical مَنْ (who) with vowel lengthening to miiin.

مينا.etymology: Colloquial Levantine pronunciation مِينا (mīnā) of Classical Arabic مِينَاء (mīnāʾ, 'harbour, port'), borrowed in late antiquity from Ancient Greek λιμένας / λιμήν (liménas / limḗn, 'harbour') via Coptic or Syriac intermediaries with dissimilation of l-m to m-n (or reanalyzed under root و-ن-ي).

ميّز.etymology: Form II hollow-root verb (فَعَّلَ, faʿʿala) from م-ي-ز (m-y-z, to separate, set apart, distinguish). Retaining its Classical Arabic force of discerning subtle differences, ميّز is used daily in Jordanian Arabic for telling two things apart or recognizing someone.

مَنَع.etymology: Form I verb مَنَعَ (manaʿa, 'to prevent, block, keep out, withhold, forbid') on the triliteral Semitic root م-ن-ع (m-n-ʿ).

مِشِي.etymology: Levantine Form I verb مِشِي (mišī, 'to walk, go, flow, move along'), reflecting the regular Levantine shift of active intransitive defective verbs to the faʿil vocalism from Classical Arabic مَشَى (mašā, 'to walk, go on foot') on the root م-ش-ي (m-š-y).

نادى.etymology: Form III verb نَادَى (nādā, 'to call out to, summon, call by name') on the root ن-د-و (n-d-w) / ن-د-ي (n-d-y, 'calling out, assembly').

history.meaning: to call out to; summon; call by name

نار.etymology: From Classical Arabic نَار (nār, 'fire'), root ن-و-ر ('light/fire'), cognate with Aramaic נוּרָא (nūrā).

نازل.etymology: Form I active participle نَازِل (nāzil, 'descending, going down; alighting, staying [at an inn or hotel]') from نَزَلَ (nazala, 'to descend, alight, lodge') on the Semitic root ن-ز-ل (n-z-l).

ناس.etymology: Collective noun نَاس (nās, 'people, folk, humankind'), formed by apheresis of initial hamza from أُنَاس (ʾunās, 'people'), on the Proto-Semitic root ء-ن-س (ʾ-n-s, 'human, sociable, companion').

ناشف.etymology: Active participle built on root ن-ش-ف (to absorb moisture, dry up), the everyday word for dry in Jordan.

ناشفة.etymology: Feminine active participle of نشف (root ن-ش-ف, to dry out) taking the feminine suffix -a.

ناعم.etymology: Form I active participle نَاعِم (nāʿim, 'soft, smooth, tender, finely powdered') from نَعُمَ (naʿuma) / نَعِمَ (naʿima, 'to be soft, smooth, delicate') on the Semitic root ن-ع-م (n-ʿ-m).

نافورة.etymology: Intensive noun derived from root ن-ف-ر (to spurt, spring forth, or gush) naming a water fountain.

ناقص.etymology: Form I active participle نَاقِص (nāqiṣ, 'diminished, lacking, missing, incomplete') from نَقَصَ (naqaṣa, 'to decrease, fall short, lack') on the root ن-ق-ص (n-q-ṣ).

نام.etymology: Form I hollow verb نَامَ (nāma, 'to sleep, fall asleep, lie dormant'), inherited from Proto-Semitic *nawām- ('to slumber, doze'), on the root ن-و-م (n-w-m).

ناول.etymology: Form III verb نَاوَلَ (nāwala, 'to hand over, reach out and pass [something to someone]') from نَالَ (nāla, 'to reach, obtain, give') on the hollow root ن-و-ل (n-w-l).

history.meaning: to hand over; pass to someone

ناوي.etymology: Form I active participle نَاوٍ / نَاوِي (nāwī, 'intending, resolving, planning to') from نَوَى (nawā, 'to intend, purpose, resolve upon') on the root ن-و-ي (n-w-y).

نايم.etymology: Spoken Levantine active participle نَايِم (nāyim, 'sleeping, asleep'), reflecting the regular vernacular shift of medial hamza to y in hollow active participles from Classical Arabic نَائِم (nāʾim, 'sleeping'), from نَامَ (nāma, 'to sleep'), root ن-و-م (n-w-m).

نبات.etymology: Verbal noun from the root ن-ب-ت (to sprout, grow out of the soil), serving as the collective term for plants.

نبروز.etymology: Denominative quadriliteral verb (1pl imperfect) coined from برواز (picture frame), itself from Persian parwāz.

نبوءة.etymology: Classical noun نُبُوءَة built on the root ن-ب-أ (to announce or foretell), preserving the glottal stop.

نتبع.etymology: First-person plural imperfect of تبع / Form VIII اتبع (root ت-ب-ع, to follow behind or pursue).

نتحرك.etymology: First-person plural Form V verb derived from تحرّك (root ح-ر-ك, motion, movement).

نتفة.etymology: Noun نُتْفَة / نَتْفَة (nutfa / natfa, 'small tuft plucked with the fingers; tiny bit, pinch, scrap') derived from نَتَفَ (natafa, 'to pluck, pull out [hairs, wool, or a pinch]') on the root ن-ت-ف (n-t-f).

history.meaning: plucked tuft; small pinch or bit

نجار.etymology: Occupational noun نَجَّار (najjār, 'carpenter, joiner, woodworker') on the professional pattern فَعَّال (faʿʿāl) from نَجَرَ (najara, 'to hew, plane, shape wood'), root ن-ج-ر (n-j-r), an ancient Mesopotamian-Semitic craft term cognate with Aramaic ܢܓܪܐ (naggārā) and Akkadian naggārum ('carpenter').

نجح.etymology: Form I verb نَجَحَ (najaḥa, 'to succeed, prosper, turn out well, pass') on the triliteral root ن-ج-ح (n-j-ḥ).

نجرب.etymology: Form II imperfect 1pl verb from جرّب (root ج-ر-ب, to test, sample, or experiment with).

نجرح.etymology: First-person plural imperfect verb built on جرح (root ج-ر-ح, to cut, wound, or injure).

نجمة.etymology: Singulative feminine noun formed from نجم (stars, root ن-ج-م denoting rising celestial bodies).

نحاس.etymology: Inherited metallic noun نُحَاس from the root ن-ح-س denoting copper and brass alloys in Arabic.

نحاسية.etymology: Feminine relational nisba adjective attaching -iyya to نحاس (copper or brass, root ن-ح-س).

نخزة.etymology: Feminine instance noun on the pattern فَعْلَة (faʿla) from the root ن-خ-ز (n-x-z, to prick, poke, prod with something sharp), related to ن-خ-س. In everyday Jordanian speech, نخزة specifically describes a sudden prick, jab, or sharp muscular twinge.

ندور.etymology: Form II 1pl imperfect of دوّر (hollow root د-و-ر, literally to turn around, specialized in Levantine for searching).

نرفع.etymology: First-person plural imperfect verb from رفع (root ر-ف-ع, to lift up, hoist, or raise higher).

نزل.etymology: Noun نُزُل / نُزْل (nuzul / nuzl, 'lodging prepared for a traveler, guesthouse, inn, hospice') derived from نَزَلَ (nazala, 'to alight, dismount, stop for lodging') on the Semitic root ن-ز-ل (n-z-l).

نزلي.etymology: Feminine singular Form II imperative of نزّل (root ن-ز-ل, to bring down, lower) marked by -i.

نزّل.etymology: Form II causative verb نَزَّلَ (nazzala, 'to bring down, lower, send down, unload') from نَزَلَ (nazala, 'to descend, go down') on the root ن-ز-ل (n-z-l).

history.meaning: to send down; bring down; lower

نسبة.etymology: Prepositional phrase element built on نِسْبَة (nisba, 'relation, proportion, attribution') from the root ن-س-ب (n-s-b, lineage, relation). In the fixed compound بالنسبة لـ (bi-n-nisba la-), it functions across Jordanian Arabic as a topicalizing preposition meaning 'regarding' or 'as for'.

history.meaning: in relation to, with respect to

نسخ.etymology: From Classical Arabic نَسَخَ (nasaḫa, 'to copy out, transcribe, replace'), from the root ن-س-خ (n-s-ḫ, 'to remove, transcribe, supersede'). Historically the core verb for manuscript scribes, it remains the everyday word for copying drawings, keys, and digital files.

نسخة.etymology: From Classical Arabic نُسْخَة (nuskha, 'transcript, copy'), root ن-س-خ (n-s-kh, 'to copy, transcribe').

نسمة.etymology: Singulative noun نَسَمَة / نَسْمَة (nasama / nasma, 'gentle breath of air, breeze') from نَسَمَ (nasama, 'to blow gently [of the wind], breathe softly') on the Proto-Semitic root ن-س-م (n-s-m, 'breath, breeze').

نسي.etymology: Form I defective verb نَسِيَ (nasiya, 'to forget, leave out of mind'), inherited from Proto-Semitic *našay- ('to forget'), on the root ن-س-ي (n-s-y).

نسيم.etymology: From Classical Arabic نَسِيم (nasīm, 'gentle breeze, soft breath of wind'), derived from the root ن-س-م (n-s-m, 'to blow gently, breathe'), cognate with Hebrew נְשָׁמָה (nəšāmā, 'breath, soul'). Beloved in Arabic poetry and everyday conversation for Amman's cool summer evening air.

نشارة.etymology: Craft noun on the fi'aala residue pattern from نشر (root ن-ش-ر, to saw timber), meaning sawdust shavings.

نشافة.etymology: Instrument noun built on the fa''aala pattern from the root ن-ش-ف meaning to dry up or absorb moisture.

نشر.etymology: From Classical Arabic نَشَرَ (našara, 'to spread out, unfold, scatter, diffuse'), from the root ن-ش-ر (n-š-r, 'to unfold, unroll, saw'). In Levantine household speech, نَشَرَ is the everyday verb for stringing laundry or banners out across a rooftop line, alongside modern 'to publish/post'.

نشرة.etymology: Noun نَشْرَة (našra, 'spreading out, announcement, bulletin, broadcast, weather forecast') derived from نَشَرَ (našara, 'to spread out, unfold, publish, broadcast') on the root ن-ش-ر (n-š-r).

نشط.etymology: Adjective on the fa'il pattern derived from the root ن-ش-ط denoting briskness, liveliness, and readiness for action.

نشف.etymology: Form I intransitive verb نَشِفَ (našifa, 'to dry, become dry, absorb water') on the Semitic root ن-ش-ف (n-š-f).

history.meaning: to absorb water; dry up; become dry

نشّف.etymology: Form II transitive verb نَشَّفَ (naššafa, 'to dry something, wipe dry, drain') from Form I نَشِفَ (našifa, 'to dry out, absorb moisture'), root ن-ش-ف (n-š-f, 'absorb, dry'). Doubling the middle consonant turns intransitive 'become dry' into transitive 'dry something off'.

نص.etymology: Colloquial Levantine contraction of Classical Arabic نِصْف (half, root ن-ص-ف) by consonant cluster reduction.

نصاني.etymology: Levantine relational adjective نُصَّانِيّ (nuṣṣānī, 'middle, central, situated in the middle'), formed with the augmented relational suffix ـَانِيّ (-āniyy) from نُصّ (nuṣṣ, 'half, middle') < Classical Arabic نِصْف (niṣf), root ن-ص-ف (n-ṣ-f).

نصها.etymology: Combines نص (half, from نِصْف, root ن-ص-ف) with the third-person feminine singular pronominal suffix -ha.

نضارة.etymology: Colloquial Levantine reflex of نَظَّارَة (naẓẓāra, 'eyeglasses, binoculars'), an instrumental noun on the intensive pattern فَعَّالَة (faʿʿāla) from the root ن-ظ-ر (n-ẓ-r, looking, gazing), with urban merger of /ẓ/ to emphatic /ḍ/. Treated as feminine singular in Jordan, نضارة denotes a pair of glasses.

نضافة.etymology: Urban Jordanian/Levantine realization نَضَافَة (naḍāfa) of Classical Arabic نَظَافَة (naẓāfa, 'cleanliness, purity'), verbal noun from the root ن-ظ-ف (n-ẓ-f, 'to be clean, spotless'). Reflects the regular urban Levantine merger of interdental ظ with emphatic stop ض.

نضيف.etymology: Spoken Levantine adjective نْضِيف (nḍīf, 'clean, spotless'), reflecting the regular urban Levantine merger of interdental *ẓ into emphatic stop ḍ from Classical Arabic نَظِيف (naẓīf, 'clean'), root ن-ظ-ف (n-ẓ-f).

نط.etymology: Form I geminate verb نَطَّ (naṭṭa, 'to jump, leap, hop, bound') on the triliteral root ن-ط-ط (n-ṭ-ṭ).

نطعج.etymology: First-person plural imperfect of the Levantine verb طعج (root ط-ع-ج, to crease, bend, or dent).

نظاراتك.etymology: Sound feminine plural نظارات (eyeglasses, from root ن-ظ-ر meaning looking) plus 2ms suffix -ak.

نظاراتي.etymology: Plural optical noun نظارات (eyeglasses, root ن-ظ-ر) suffixed with the 1sg possessive -i.

نظارة.etymology: Intensive instrumental feminine noun نَظَّارَة ('eyeglasses, spectacles') coined on the pattern فَعَّالَة from the Semitic root ن-ظ-ر ('look, observe, gaze attentively').

نظام.etymology: Verbal noun on fi'aal from root ن-ظ-م (originally stringing pearls onto a thread), hence order and system.

نظر.etymology: Continues Classical Arabic verbal noun نَظَر (naẓar, 'looking, gaze, eyesight, consideration') on the pattern فَعَل (faʿal) of نَظَرَ (naẓara, 'to look at, observe'), inherited from Proto-Semitic root ن-ظ-ر (n-ẓ-r, 'to watch, guard').

history.meaning: sight, gaze, attention, point of view

نظر.notes: Appears in everyday expressions like لفت نظرهم ('draw their attention'), بغض النظر ('regardless'), and بنظري ('in my view').

نظرة.etymology: Noun of single instance (ism marra) نَظْرَة (naẓra, 'a single look, glance, gaze') from نَظَرَ (naẓara, 'to look at, gaze, observe') on the Proto-Semitic root ن-ظ-ر (n-ẓ-r).

نظف.etymology: Form II verb from the root ن-ظ-ف (to be clean, pure), intensifying the sense into actively cleaning something.

نظيف.etymology: Adjective patterned on fa'iil from the root ن-ظ-ف (to be clean, pure, spotless), retained across registers.

نعم.etymology: Inherited from Classical Arabic affirmative particle نَعَمْ (naʿam, 'yes, indeed'), traditionally derived from the Semitic root ن-ع-م (n-ʿ-m, 'pleasantness, ease, favor', compare نِعْمَ niʿma 'how good is...').

نعناع.etymology: Reduplicated botanical noun نَعْنَاع from the root ن-ع-ن-ع, native to Classical Arabic herbology and ubiquitous across the Levant.

نعنع.etymology: Levantine dialectal variant of Classical نَعْنَاع (mint, quadriliteral root ن-ع-ن-ع) with shortened final vowel.

نعومة.etymology: From Classical Arabic نُعُومَة (nuʿūma, 'softness, smoothness, tenderness'), abstract verbal noun from the root ن-ع-م (n-ʿ-m, 'to be soft, comfortable, pleasant'), cognate with Hebrew נֹעַם (nōʿam, 'pleasantness'). Preceded by بـ (bi-nʿūme), it serves as an adverb meaning 'gently, smoothly'.

نغمة.etymology: Singulative noun نَغْمَة (naġma, 'musical note, tone, melody, inflection') derived from نَغَمَ (naġama, 'to hum, sing softly, intone') on the root ن-غ-م (n-ġ-m).

نفخ.etymology: Form I verb نَفَخَ (nafaḫa, 'to blow, inflate, puff up, swell'), inherited from Proto-Semitic *napāḫ- ('to blow, breathe upon'), on the root ن-ف-خ (n-f-ḫ).

نفس.etymology: Classical Semitic noun نَفْس (breath, soul, self, root ن-ف-س), widely used before definite nouns to mean the same.

نفسها.etymology: Emphatic reflexive pronoun uniting نفس (self, root ن-ف-س) with the third-person feminine singular suffix -ha.

نقطة.etymology: Unit noun from root ن-ق-ط (to dot or spot), naming a geometric point, punctuation dot, or small liquid drop.

نقل.etymology: Form I verbal noun (maṣdar) نَقْل (naql, 'carrying across, transfer, transport, relocation, copying') from نَقَلَ (naqala, 'to move, carry from one place to another') on the root ن-ق-ل (n-q-l).

نقّط.etymology: Form II verb نَقَّطَ (naqqaṭa, 'to drip, fall in drops, dot') from نَقَطَ (naqaṭa) and نُقْطَة (nuqṭa, 'drop, dot') on the root ن-ق-ط (n-q-ṭ).

نكهة.etymology: Derived from the Classical root ن-ك-ه meaning breath or aromatic scent, shifting in modern usage to culinary flavour.

نلاقي.etymology: First-person plural imperfect of Form III لاقى (defective root ل-ق-ي, to meet or find), replacing Form I in urban speech.

نلتقي.etymology: Form VIII first-person plural imperfect verb from the defective root ل-ق-ي (l-q-y, 'to encounter, meet'), al-taqā -> naltaqī reflects reciprocal engagement. In spoken Jordanian Arabic niltiʾī/naltaqī carries a slightly warmer or semi-formal tone alongside colloquial ntʾābal.

نلف.etymology: First-person plural imperfect verb from the geminate root ل-ف-ف (l-f-f, 'to wrap, fold, turn around'). Across Jordan nliff serves effortlessly for turning a vehicle at an intersection, rolling stuffed grape leaves, or wrapping parcels.

نهار.etymology: Inherited from Classical Arabic نَهَار (nahār, 'daytime, daylight, day from dawn to dusk'), cognate with Aramaic ܢܗܪܐ / נהورא (nəhōrā, 'light'), from the Semitic root ن-ه-ر (n-h-r, 'to shine brightly, flow abundantly').

نهاية.etymology: Verbal noun نِهَايَة (nihāya, 'end, limit, extremity, conclusion') derived on the pattern فِعَالَة (fiʿāla) from نَهَى (nahā) / اِنْتَهَى (intahā, 'to reach the end, come to a stop') on the root ن-ه-ي (n-h-y).

نهر.etymology: Directly inheriting Proto-Semitic *nahar- ('river, stream'), cognate with Hebrew nāhār, Aramaic nahrā, and Akkadian nāru, Arabic nahr derives from the root ن-ه-ر (n-h-r, 'to flow abundantly'). Modern Jordanian speech keeps nahar virtually unchanged.

نوتة.etymology: Borrowed into Arabic from Italian nota ('musical note, written score, memorandum, pocket notebook'), from Latin nota ('mark, sign, musical character, note').

history.meaning: sheet music; musical score; pocket notepad

نور.etymology: From the hollow root ن-و-ر (n-w-r, 'light, illumination, blossom'), related to نار ('fire') and منارة ('lighthouse, minaret').
نور.notes: Appears both as a beloved Arabic given name (نور) and in the classic morning reply صباح النور ('morning of light').

نوع.etymology: From Classical Arabic نَوْع (nawʿ, 'kind, sort, species, manner'), from the hollow root ن-و-ع (n-w-ʿ, 'to sway, branch out into varieties'). Adopted into philosophical, scientific, and everyday Arabic alike as the standard word for 'type' or 'kind'.

نوم.etymology: Masculine verbal noun (maṣdar) on the pattern فَعْل (faʿl) from the hollow root ن-و-م (n-w-m, sleep, slumber), cognate with Aramaic nəwām and Hebrew נָם. In spoken Jordanian households, the contracted call عالنوم ('to bed / to sleep!') briskly sends everyone off to rest.

نومة.etymology: Noun of single instance (ism marra) نَوْمَة (nawma, 'a sleep, nap, night's rest') from نَامَ (nāma, 'to sleep') on the hollow root ن-و-م (n-w-m).

history.meaning: a single sleep; nap; night's rest

ني.etymology: Levantine shortening of Classical نِيء (raw, uncooked) from the root ن-ي-أ with elision of the final glottal stop.

نَقَل.etymology: Form I verb نَقَلَ (naqala, 'to move, carry from one place to another, transfer, copy') on the triliteral Semitic root ن-ق-ل (n-q-l).

history.meaning: to carry across; move; transfer; copy

نِزِل.etymology: Levantine Form I verb نِزِل (nizil, 'to go down, come down, descend, get off, stay [at a hotel]'), from Classical Arabic نَزَلَ (nazala, 'to descend, alight, lodge') on the Semitic root ن-ز-ل (n-z-l).

history.meaning: to go down; come down; stay at

ها.etymology: Inherited from Classical Arabic presentative and attentional particle هَا (hā, 'lo!, behold!, here!, ha!'), from Proto-Semitic *hā-.

هات.etymology: Inherited from Classical Arabic suppletive imperative verb هَاتِ (hāti, 'give!, bring!, hand over!'), historically an old causative imperative formation (with h- for ʾ-) related to آتَى (ʾātā, 'to bring, give') from أَتَى (ʾatā, 'to come') on the Proto-Semitic root ء-ت-ي (ʾ-t-y).

هاد.etymology: Colloquial masculine singular demonstrative pronoun evolved from Classical Arabic hādhā ('this') by dropping the final long vowel and stopping the interdental dh to d in urban speech. Alongside rural hāḏa, hād is ubiquitous across Jordanian cities.

morphemes.meaning: masculine demonstrative element from Classical ذا (dhā)

هادا.etymology: Spoken Levantine masculine singular proximal demonstrative pronoun descended from Classical هٰذَا (hāðā, 'this'), combining the attention prefix hā- with demonstrative ðā and exhibiting the urban Levantine shift of interdental /ð/ to stop /d/ (hāda).

هادي.etymology: Levantine active participle هَادِي (hādī, 'quiet, calm, gentle'), reflecting the regular loss of word-final hamza after -ī from Classical Arabic هَادِئ (hādiʾ, 'calm, quiet, still'), from هَدَأَ (hadaʾa, 'to be still, subside, calm down') on the root ه-د-ء (h-d-ʾ).

هاديك.etymology: Levantine feminine distal demonstrative formed from ها- (ha-) + ذِيك (dhīk, 'that fem.') with colloquial d/dh shift.

هالألوان.etymology: Demonstrative clitic phrase fusing Levantine ha- ('this/these', clipped from hādhā) onto the definite broken plural al-alwān ('the colors', root ل-و-ن). Dropping the glottal stop yields hal-alwān in fluent Jordanian conversation.

هالاربع.etymology: Colloquial compound attaching the demonstrative proclitic ha- and definite article al- to the cardinal arbaʿ ('four', root ر-ب-ع). Written unhamzated as هالاربع, this Jordanian construction introduces definite groups of four items immediately before a counted noun.

هالبورتريه.etymology: Integrating the French/English art term portrait (borrowed via French portrait, ultimately Latin prōtrahere, 'to draw forth') into Levantine morphosyntax, this phrase prefixes ha-l- ('this the'). Jordanian artists and galleries smoothly inflect European loans with native demonstratives.

هالبوصلة.etymology: Joining the dialectal demonstrative ha- + al- to būṣala ('compass'), this phrase incorporates an Ottoman-era Mediterranean loan from Italian bussola ('small box', originally housing a magnetic needle). In Jordan hikers and scouts pronounce it hal-būṣale.

هالجورة.etymology: Attaching the Levantine demonstrative clitic hal- ('this') to jōra ('pit, hole'), derived from the hollow root ج-و-ر (j-w-r, 'to hollow out, sink'). Everyday Jordanian Arabic relies on jōra constantly for road potholes, drainage pits, and garden holes.

هالحجر.etymology: Binding colloquial ha- and the definite article al- to ḥajar ('stone', Proto-Semitic *ḥigr-, root ح-ج-ر), this phrase points out a specific rock nearby. Speakers pronounce it hal-ḥajar cleanly without sun-letter assimilation since ḥ is a moon consonant.

هالحكي.etymology: Fusing the demonstrative hal- with ḥakī ('speech, talk', verbal noun of ḥakā, root ح-ك-ي), this iconic Levantine expression evolved from Classical 'to recount, imitate'. Jordanians regularly use hal-ḥakī to dismiss gossip, excuses, or idle chatter.

هالريحة.etymology: Prefixing ha- + al- onto rīḥa ('scent, odor', clipped from Classical rāʾiḥa under root ر-و-ح), this demonstrative phrase exhibits sun-letter assimilation to har-rīḥa. In Jordanian speech it works equally well for enticing food aromas and unpleasant odors.

هالصدى.etymology: Uniting the Levantine demonstrative ha-l- with ṣadā ('echo', root ص-د-ي, 'to resound'), this phrase assimilates the article's l into emphatic ṣ, yielding haṣ-ṣada. Classical lexicons already documented ṣadā for reverberating canyon sounds.

هالعلبة.etymology: Combining the demonstrative proclitic ha-l- with ʿilbe ('box, tin, carton', from Classical ʿulba, root ع-ل-ب), this everyday phrase points out containers of all kinds. Note the characteristic Levantine vowel raising from -a to -e in the feminine suffix.

هالكتاب.etymology: Merging demonstrative ha- + al- with kitāb ('book', root ك-ت-ب, 'to write'), spoken Jordanian Arabic elides the unstressed first vowel to produce hal-ktāb. It demonstrates the tight prosodic bonding between demonstratives and definite nouns in Levantine.

هالنص.etymology: Contracted demonstrative phrase joining ha-l- with naṣṣ ('text, wording', root ن-ص-ص, 'to stipulate clearly'). In speech the article's l assimilates completely to initial n, yielding han-naṣṣ across classrooms and editing rooms in Jordan.

هاي.etymology: Urban Levantine feminine singular demonstrative pronoun hāy, derived by palatalizing and shortening Classical Arabic hādhihī ('this', f.) or combining presentative hā- with the feminine deictic element -y. It pairs with masculine hād and also modifies non-human plurals.

هب.etymology: From Classical Arabic هَبَّ (habba, 'to blow [of wind], wake up suddenly, flare up'), geminate verb from the root ه-ب-ب (h-b-b, 'blowing wind, sudden rising'). When conjugated with consonant-initial endings in Levantine, the doubled b resolves with -ē- (habbēt 'I/you blew', habb 'it blew').

هبة.etymology: Noun of single instance (اسم مرة) هَبَّة (habba, 'a single gust, sudden puff') formed with -a from the geminate verb هَبَّ (habba, 'to blow'). Very frequent in Jordanian speech in the phrase هبة هوا ('a sudden gust of wind').

هبطاقة.etymology: Informal spelling omitting the silent alif of the definite article (normally هالبطاقة, hal-bṭāqa), combining demonstrative ha- with biṭāqa ('card, tag', borrowed in medieval Arabic from Greek pittákion, 'writing tablet'). Notice the initial cluster bṭ in Jordanian speech.

هدا.etymology: Levantine noun هَدَا (hadā, 'calm, quietness, gentleness', used especially in عَالهَدَا ʿa-l-hadā 'gently, slowly, quietly'), evolved with loss of final hamza from Classical Arabic هَدْء (hadʾ) / هُدُوء (hudūʾ, 'stillness, calm') from هَدَأَ (hadaʾa, 'to be still, quiet'), root ه-د-ء (h-d-ʾ).

هداك.etymology: Spoken Levantine masculine distal demonstrative هَدَاك (hadāk, 'that [over there]'), from Classical Arabic هٰذَاكَ (hāḏāka, 'that'), compounded of presentative هَا (hā) + demonstrative ذَا (ḏā, with urban Levantine *ḏ > d) + distal suffix ـكَ (-ka).

هداوة.etymology: Colloquial Levantine feminine abstract noun هَدَاوَة (hadāwa, 'calmness, gentleness, unhurried pace') from the root ه-د-أ (h-d-ʾ, 'to be quiet, calm down'), adapted to a final-weak pattern analogously to طراوة / حلاوة. Widely heard in بهداوة ('gently, take it easy').

هدوء.etymology: Form I verbal noun (maṣdar) هُدُوء (hudūʾ, 'stillness, quietness, calm, peace') on the pattern فُعُول (fuʿūl) from هَدَأَ (hadaʾa, 'to be still, subside, grow quiet') on the root ه-د-ء (h-d-ʾ).

هدول.etymology: Spoken Levantine plural demonstrative هَدُول (hadōl, 'these, those'), compounded of presentative هَا (hā) + plural demonstrative stem ذُول (ḏōl, related to Classical أُولَىٰ ʾulā / هٰؤُلَاءِ hāʾulāʾi, with urban Levantine *ḏ > d).

هدي.etymology: Intransitive Levantine Form I verb evolved from Classical hamzated هَدَأَ (hadaʾa, 'to grow calm, subside, quiet down') on the root ه-د-أ (h-d-ʾ). Dropping the final glottal stop, Jordanian speech treats هدي as a final-weak stative verb (f. هِدْيَتْ / هَدَتْ) for rooms, streets, storms, or tempers settling down.

morphemes.meaning: Form I intransitive stative verb (ʾ > y)

هدية.etymology: Feminine noun on the pattern فَعِيلَة (faʿīla) from the defective root ه-د-ي (h-d-y, to guide, lead, offer a gift). Related to أَهْدَى ('to present a gift'), هدية (pl. هدايا) is the universal Arabic word for a present or keepsake.

هدّى.etymology: Levantine Form II verb هَدَّى (haddā, 'to calm, quiet down, slow down'), reflecting the regular merger of final-hamza verbs into final-yāʾ from Classical Arabic هَدَّأَ (haddaʾa, 'to calm, soothe, quiet') from هَدَأَ (hadaʾa, 'to be still') on the root ه-د-ء (h-d-ʾ).

هذه.etymology: Classical and Modern Standard Arabic feminine singular proximal demonstrative pronoun هٰذِهِ (hāðihi, 'this'), formed from the presentative prefix hā- and feminine demonstrative element ðihi. While spoken Jordanian prefers هاي, هذه appears when speakers adopt formal or written prose.

هذي.etymology: Continuing Classical hādhihī ('this', f.) with retention of the interdental fricative dh/ḏ and elision of the medial syllable, hāḏī/haḏī remains active across Bedouin and rural Jordanian dialects alongside urban hāy.

هرب.etymology: Form I verb هَرَبَ (haraba, 'to flee, run away, escape') on the triliteral Semitic root ه-ر-ب (h-r-b).

هز.etymology: Form I geminate verb هَزَّ (hazza, 'to shake, rock, nod [the head], vibrate') on the triliteral root ه-ز-ز (h-z-z).

هسا.etymology: Signature Jordanian and Palestinian temporal adverb meaning 'now', fused from Classical hādhihi s-sāʿa ('this very hour'). Progressive phonetic erosion reduced the demonstrative and noun to a single crisp adverb, hassa, distinct from Syrian hallaʾ.

هش.etymology: Geminate adjective from the root ه-ش-ش originally meaning brittle, friable, or soft, used appreciatively for light cake crumbs.

هل.etymology: Ancient Semitic interrogative particle هَلْ introducing polar yes-or-no questions in formal and elevated speech.

هلأ.etymology: Urban Levantine colloquial adverb (hallaʾ, 'now, right now'), evolved by rapid allegro contraction of هَالْوَقْت (hal-waqt) < Classical Arabic هٰذَا الْوَقْت (hāḏā l-waqt, 'this time'), with assimilation and loss of -w- plus the urban Levantine shift of uvular ق (/q/) to glottal stop أ (/ʾ/).

rootFamily.gloss: now (Syrian/Lebanese orthographic variant keeping etymological ق)
now (parallel Egyptian contraction of ذا الوقت!)

هلأ.notes: Replaces MSA الآن (al-ʾān) in Amman, Damascus, and Beirut speech; at the start of a sentence (هلأ شوفي...), it also works as a conversational discourse marker ('Look / Well, now...').

هلا.etymology: Levantine temporal adverb هَلَّأ / هَلَّق (hallaʾ / hallaq, 'now, right now'), contracted from the phrase هٰذَا الوَقْت (hāḏā l-waqt, 'this time') via هَالْوَقْت (hal-waqt > hallaq).

هلق.etymology: Signature Levantine temporal adverb contracted from هذا الوقت (this time), parallel to Jordanian هلا.

هم.etymology: Form I geminate verb هَمَّ (hamma, 'to concern, matter to, worry, occupy the mind') on the triliteral root ه-م-م (h-m-m).

همس.etymology: From Classical Arabic هَمَسَ (hamasa, 'to whisper, murmur, tread softly'), root ه-م-س (h-m-s).

همه.etymology: Spoken Jordanian and Palestinian third-person plural pronoun هُمِّه (humme, 'they'), developed with gemination and final vowel from Classical Arabic هُمْ / هُمُ (hum / humu, 'they'), from Proto-Semitic *humū.

هنا.etymology: Spoken Levantine noun هَنَا (hanā, 'happiness, wholesome pleasure, enjoyment of food and drink', especially in صَحْتَيْن وَهَنَا ṣaḥtēn w-hanā), apocopated without final hamza from Classical Arabic هَنَاء (hanāʾ, 'wholesomeness, felicity, pleasure') from هَنِئَ (haniʾa, 'to be wholesome and pleasant') on the root ه-ن-ء (h-n-ʾ).

هناك.etymology: Inherited from Classical Arabic locative adverb هُنَاكَ (hunāka, 'there, over there'), formed from proximal هُنَا (hunā, 'here') + distal suffix ـكَ (-ka).

هندسة.etymology: Adapted in early Abbasid scholarship from Middle Persian handāzag ('measure, proportion, geometry'), the noun handasa was back-formed into the quadriliteral Arabic root ه-ن-د-س (h-n-d-s). Originally naming geometry, it now covers all branches of modern engineering in Jordan.

هنيك.etymology: Colloquial demonstrative adverb corresponding to Classical هناك (there), with vowel raising (imala) typical of Levantine dialects.

هو.etymology: Going straight back to Proto-Semitic *huʾa ('he'), cognate with Hebrew hū and Akkadian shū, Classical huwa develops final consonant gemination in Levantine Arabic, typically pronounced huwwe. It serves both as subject pronoun and pronominal copula.

هوا.etymology: Spoken Levantine noun هَوَا (hawā, 'air, breeze, wind, weather'), with regular loss of word-final hamza after a long vowel from Classical Arabic هَوَاء (hawāʾ, 'air, atmosphere, breeze') on the root ه-و-ي (h-w-y).

هواية.etymology: From Arabic هِوَايَة (hiwāya, 'hobby, amateur pursuit, fondness'), derived from the root ه-و-ي (h-w-y, 'to desire, love, incline toward'). Alongside هاوٍ ('amateur, hobbyist'), it became the universal Arabic word for a recreational pastime.

هوف.etymology: Expressive onomatopoeic interjection (hūf / hōf) imitating the rushing breath of wind or a relieved exhale, parallel to Levantine أُوف / أفّ. Used conversationally in storytelling to dramatize a sudden gust sweeping across an open terrace.

هون.etymology: Levantine spatial adverb hōn ('here'), corresponding to Classical hāhunā / hunā ('here') through contraction of the medial vowel sequence into long ō. Along with hōna in some dialects, hōn is the universal Jordanian word for 'here'.

هي.etymology: Inherited from Classical Arabic third-person feminine singular pronoun هِيَ (hiya, 'she, it'), from Proto-Semitic *šiʾa / *hiʾa.

هيك.etymology: Manner adverb hēk ('like this, thus') characteristic of Levantine Arabic, widely traced to a fusion of the demonstrative hā- with the preposition/comparative element *k- (cf. Classical hākadhā or Aramaic hēḵ / hāḵ). Jordanian speakers also use it as a filler meaning 'and so on'.

هيكلي.etymology: Nisba adjective formed by adding -i to هيكل (frame, temple, structure), itself a Semitic borrowing from Sumerian e-gal.

هيه.etymology: Expressive colloquial interjection used across Levantine Arabic to call attention, parallel to Classical Arabic هَيَّا / هَيْ.

هيهم.etymology: Presentative compound combining the Levantine attention-drawing particle hayy- (related to Classical hāʾa / hiyya, 'behold, here is') with the third-person plural clitic pronoun -hum ('them'). Pronounced hayyhum in Jordan, it introduces people or things in immediate view.

هَيّ.etymology: Spoken Levantine presentative particle هَيّ (hayy, 'here is!, look!'), formed by fusing the presentative particle هَا (hā, 'lo!, behold!') with the third-person pronoun هِيَ / هُوَ (hiya / huwa) or demonstrative element.

و.etymology: Tracing directly to Proto-Semitic *wa- ('and'), cognate with Hebrew wə-, Aramaic wə-, and Geʿez wa-, the coordinating conjunction wa connects words and clauses across every variety of Arabic. In Jordanian speech it surfaces proclitically as w- or syllabic u-.

وإبرة.etymology: Conjoined phrase pairing proclitic w- ('and') with ibra ('needle', Classical ibra from root أ-ب-ر, 'to prick, sting'). In Jordanian Arabic the final vowel undergoes imāla to w-ibre while preserving the initial glottal stop in careful spelling.

وإحنا.etymology: Joining coordinating/circumstantial w- ('and/while') to the Levantine first-person plural pronoun iḥna ('we'), derived via metathesis and vowel shift from Classical naḥnu. In Jordanian Arabic w-iḥna frequently introduces background circumstantial clauses ('while we were...').

وإلا.etymology: Compound conjunction وَإِلَّا (wa-ʾillā, 'and if not; otherwise, or else'), composed of coordinating وَ (wa-, 'and') + conditional إِنْ (ʾin, 'if') + negative لَا (lā, 'not').

history.meaning: and if not; otherwise; or else

واجهة.etymology: Indefinite feminine noun formed on the fāʿila template from the root و-ج-ه (w-j-h, 'face, front side'). Traditionally naming the front elevation of a building, wājha in modern Jordan just as commonly means a shop display window or digital user interface.

واحد.etymology: Derived from the Proto-Semitic numeral stem *waḥid- ('one'), cognate with Hebrew ʾeḥāḏ and Aramaic ḥaḏ, wāḥid comes from و-ح-د (w-ḥ-d, 'singularity, unity'). Spoken Jordanian lowers the second vowel to wāḥad and also uses it substantively for 'someone'.

وارفعي.etymology: Constructed from the conjunction w- ('and') and the second-person feminine singular imperative irfaʿī ('lift, raise') from ر-ف-ع (r-f-ʿ, 'to elevate, raise'). Jordanian speech retains both the prosthetic i- and the feminine -ī ending cleanly.

وارم.etymology: Form I active participle وَارِم (wārim, 'swollen, puffed up') from وَرِمَ (warima, 'to swell, become swollen') on the Semitic root و-ر-م (w-r-m).

وازن.etymology: Form III verb derived from the assimilated root و-ز-ن (to weigh), expressing holding two weights or tastes in equilibrium.

واسع.etymology: Form I active participle وَاسِع (wāsiʿ, 'wide, broad, spacious, roomy') from وَسِعَ (wasiʿa) / وَسُعَ (wasuʿa, 'to be wide, spacious, ample') on the Semitic root و-س-ع (w-s-ʿ).

واصل.etymology: Form I active participle وَاصِل (wāṣil, 'arriving, reaching, connected') from وَصَلَ (waṣala, 'to arrive, reach, join') on the Semitic root و-ص-ل (w-ṣ-l).

واضح.etymology: Form I active participle وَاضِح (wāḍiḥ, 'clear, plain, evident, distinct') from وَضَحَ (waḍaḥa, 'to be clear, become plain or visible') on the root و-ض-ح (w-ḍ-ḥ).

واضحة.etymology: Feminine active participle of waḍaḥa ('to be clear, visible'), built on the root و-ض-ح (w-ḍ-ḥ). Syncope of the unstressed short vowel shifts Classical wāḍiḥa into Levantine wāḍḥa, used for clear speech, sharp photos, and legible handwriting.

واضغطي.etymology: Conjunction w- ('and') prefixed to the feminine singular imperative iḍghaṭī ('press, squeeze') from ض-غ-ط (ḍ-gh-ṭ). Originally meaning physical compression, it expanded in digital Jordanian usage to pressing buttons or tapping touchscreen icons.

واطولها.etymology: Compound verb phrase uniting conjunction w- ('and'), the hollow subjunctive aṭūl ('I reach/fetch', root ط-و-ل, 'length, reach'), and the feminine object clitic -ha. Jordanian speakers constantly employ ṭāl/yaṭūl for reaching down items from shelves or pockets.

واطوي.etymology: Pairing w- ('and') with the defective Form I imperative iṭwī ('fold, roll up') from ط-و-ي (ṭ-w-y, 'to fold, traverse'), this verb form merges masculine and feminine singular imperatives colloquially into a final -ī when addressing a woman in Jordan.

واطي.etymology: Levantine active participle وَاطِي (wāṭī, 'low [in height, level, or volume]'), reflecting the regular loss of word-final hamza after -ī from Classical Arabic وَاطِئ (wāṭiʾ, 'treading; low-lying, depressed [ground]'), from وَطِئَ (waṭiʾa, 'to tread underfoot, level') on the root و-ط-ء (w-ṭ-ʾ).

وافق.etymology: Form III verb وَافَقَ (wāfaqa, 'to agree with, approve, consent to, suit') on the triliteral root و-ف-ق (w-f-q).

واقف.etymology: Form I active participle وَاقِف (wāqif, 'standing, stopped, stationary, parked') from وَقَفَ (waqafa, 'to stand, stop, halt') on the root و-ق-ف (w-q-f).

واقي.etymology: Active participle from the doubly weak root و-ق-ي (to guard, shield), functioning as both modifier and protective gear noun.

والبطاقة.etymology: Combining proclitic w- ('and'), definite al-, and biṭāqa ('card, tag'), this phrase rests on an early Arabic borrowing from Ancient Greek pittákion ('small tablet, slip'). Colloquial Jordanian Arabic drops the unstressed first vowel, pronouncing it w-il-bṭāqa.

والتغطية.etymology: Conjoining w- ('and') with al-taghṭiya, the Form II verbal noun (maṣdar) of ghaṭṭā ('to cover', root غ-ط-ي). With sun-letter assimilation and Levantine imāla, w-it-taghṭiye covers blankets, media reporting, and mobile signal coverage.

والذهبية.etymology: Uniting w- ('and') with the feminine definite nisba adjective al-dhahabiyya ('the golden', from Proto-Semitic *ḏahab-, root ذ-ه-ب). Jordanian urban speech frequently shifts dh to d or z (w-id-dahabiyye), while formal sports commentary preserves the interdental.

والشمال.etymology: Attaching conjunction w- ('and') to al-shamāl ('the north / the left', from Proto-Semitic *śimʾāl-, root ش-م-ل). Spoken Jordanian Arabic maintains a neat vowel distinction between w-ish-shamāl ('and the north') and w-ish-shmāl ('and the left').

history.meaning: and the north / and the left

والفطور.etymology: Built from w- ('and') plus al-fuṭūr ('the breakfast', root ف-ط-ر, 'to break a fast, split open'). Syncope of the short u leaves a crisp initial consonant cluster in Jordanian Arabic, pronounced w-il-fṭūr at morning tables.

history.meaning: and the breakfast, breaking of fast

والله.etymology: Univerbation of the Classical Arabic oath phrase وَٱللّٰهِ (wa-llāhi, 'by God!'), combining the jurative preposition وَ- (wa-, 'by [in oaths]', governing the genitive) + ٱللّٰه (Allāh, 'God', from root ء-ل-ه).

rootFamily.gloss: oh God! (also source of يلا, 'let's go!')

والله.notes: Ubiquitous across registers: uttered earnestly to vouch for the truth (والله ما حكيت إشي, 'honestly I didn't say anything') or with rising pitch (والله؟, 'oh really?').

واللوز.etymology: Conjoining w- ('and') with al-lawz ('the almonds', collective noun from root ل-و-ز, cognate with Aramaic lūzā and Hebrew lūz). Jordanian speech contracts the diphthong into w-il-lōz for both roasted nuts and positive slang.

واو.etymology: Modern English loan exclamation adopted widely in urban Jordanian speech to express immediate wonder or excitement.

وبيرفوف.etymology: Representing a dialectal pronunciation or informal spelling of w-birafref ('and it flutters'), this verb joins w- ('and'), Levantine progressive prefix b-, and the reduplicated quadriliteral root ر-ف-ر-ف (r-f-r-f, from geminate ر-ف-ف, 'to flap, flutter').

وتد.etymology: From Classical Arabic وَتِد / وَتَد (watid / watad, 'peg, tent-pin, stake'), cognate with Hebrew יָתֵד (yāṯēḏ, 'peg, tent-pin') and Aramaic יַתְדָא. Reflecting shared West Semitic nomadic and architectural vocabulary, it applies to any wooden or iron peg used to anchor cords.

وتر.etymology: Ancient Semitic noun وَتَر ('bowstring; musical string', plural أَوْتَار) from the root و-ت-ر ('draw taut'). From early lutes and qanuns to modern pianos, أوتار names the stretched strings whose vibration produces musical pitch.

وتوت.etymology: Pairing conjunction w- ('and') with the collective fruit noun tūt ('mulberries, berries'), an ancient Near Eastern term shared with Syriac tūṯā and Persian tūt (from root ت-و-ت). Across Jordan w-tūt commonly refers to dark mulberries and seasonal berries.

وثق.etymology: Assimilated Form I verb rooted in و-ث-ق (to be firm, bound, trustworthy), governing its complement with بـ.

وجع.etymology: Verbal noun وَجَع (wajaʿ, 'pain, ache, soreness') from وَجِعَ (wajiʿa, 'to ache, feel pain') on the Proto-Semitic root و-ج-ع (w-j-ʿ).

وجنبه.etymology: Fusing w- ('and') with janb ('side, flank', root ج-ن-ب) and the masculine singular suffix -o/-uh ('it/him'), this noun-preposition links spatial descriptions cleanly. In Jordanian Arabic w-janbo introduces adjacent landmarks or seated companions.

وجه.etymology: Inherited from Classical Arabic وَجْه (wajh, 'face, countenance, front, top surface, side') on the triliteral Semitic root و-ج-ه (w-j-h).

وجود.etymology: Classical Arabic verbal noun (maṣdar) وُجُود (wujūd, 'being found, presence, existence') on the pattern فُعُول (fuʿūl) of وَجَدَ / passive وُجِدَ (wujida, 'to be found, exist'), initial-weak Semitic root و-ج-د (w-j-d).

history.meaning: to be found -> presence, philosophical existence

وجود.notes: Equally common in philosophical MSA and warm everyday Jordanian phrases like وجودك مريح ('having you around is comforting').

وجّه.etymology: Form II denominal/causative verb وَجَّهَ (wajjaha, 'to turn [something] toward, point, aim, direct') derived from وَجْه (wajh, 'face, front, direction') on the root و-ج-ه (w-j-h).

history.meaning: to turn toward; direct; aim; point

وحدة.etymology: Spoken Levantine feminine singular of واحد ('one'), pronounced وَحْدَة (waḥde), contracted by unstressed vowel syncope from Classical Arabic وَاحِدَة (wāḥida), built on the Semitic initial-weak root و-ح-د (w-ḥ-d, 'oneness, being single').

history.meaning: one (f.); a girl/woman; with الـ (الوَحْدَة), generic 'one / a girl'

rootFamily.gloss: (MSA wuḥda / waḥda) unity; loneliness; curriculum unit

وحدة.notes: Do not confuse colloquial وَحْدَة (waḥde, 'one [female] / a girl', as in ولا وحدة 'not a single one' or لازم الوحدة تنتبه 'a girl must be careful') with MSA وَحْدَة (waḥda, 'loneliness / unity') spelled identically without vowels!

وختم.etymology: Proclitic w- ('and') attached to khatama ('he stamped, sealed') from the Semitic root خ-ت-م (kh-t-m, 'seal, signet, conclude'), cognate with Hebrew ḥāṯam and Akkadian ḫatāmu. Jordanian office and bureaucratic speech keeps w-khatam intact.

وخذوا.etymology: Conjunction w- ('and') joined to the plural imperative khudhū ('take!'), from the initial-hamza root أ-خ-ذ (ʾ-kh-dh). Both Classical and Levantine Arabic drop the initial glottal stop in the imperative, shifting dh to d in urban Jordanian w-khudū.

وخفيفة.etymology: Coordinating w- ('and') prefixed to khafīfa ('light', feminine singular faʿīla adjective from geminate خ-ف-ف, 'to be light, brisk'). Across Jordan w-khafīfe describes lightweight bags, gentle breezes, easy-to-digest meals, and witty personalities.

ودفتر.etymology: Combining w- ('and') with daftar ('notebook, ledger'), which entered early Arabic via Middle Persian daftar, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek diphthéra ('prepared leather hide, scroll'). Today w-daftar is an everyday school-supply pairing across Jordan.

morphemes.meaning: from Middle Persian daftar < Ancient Greek διφθέρα (diphthéra)
