ورا.etymology: Spatial preposition warā ('behind, beyond'), descending from Classical Arabic warāʾa (root و-ر-ي, 'to conceal, be behind') after regular loss of the final glottal stop. Jordanian speakers also use wara metaphorically for chasing or backing someone.

وراه.etymology: Suffixed prepositional form attaching the third-person masculine singular pronoun -h ('him/it') onto warā ('behind', Classical warāʾahu, root و-ر-ي). In Jordan warāh conveys both static location behind someone and pursuit after them.

ورد.etymology: Collective noun وَرْد (ward, 'roses, blossoms, flowers'), an ancient borrowing via Aramaic ܘܪܕܐ (wardā) from Old Iranian *wrda- / Middle Persian *ward ('rose, flower').

وردة.etymology: Singulative feminine noun from collective ward ('roses, blossoms'), which was borrowed into ancient Semitic and Arabic from Old Iranian *warda- (cf. Persian gol, Avestan varəda-, related to English 'rose'). In Jordan warde designates a single rose or any individual flower.

ورشة.etymology: Borrowed into Egyptian and Levantine Arabic وَرْشَة (warša, 'workshop, repair shop, construction site') in the nineteenth century from English workshop.

ورق.etymology: Collective noun waraq from the Semitic root و-ر-ق (w-r-q, 'foliage, green leaf'), cognate with Hebrew yereq ('greenery'). Beyond tree leaves and writing paper, Jordanian households immediately associate waraq with stuffed vine leaves and card games.

ورقة.etymology: Singulative noun وَرَقَة (waraqa, 'a single leaf; a sheet of paper, slip, note') formed with the singulative suffix ـَة (-a) from the collective وَرَق (waraq, 'leaves, paper') on the Proto-Semitic root و-ر-ق (w-r-q).

history.meaning: a leaf; a sheet of paper

ورقي.etymology: Nisba material adjective formed by adding -ī (-ي) to وَرَق (waraq, leaves, foliage, paper) on the root و-ر-ق (w-r-q). Shifting from tree leaves to sheets of writing paper in medieval Arabic, ورقي describes paper bags, printed books, and paperwork across Jordan.

ورم.etymology: Masculine verbal noun (maṣdar) on the pattern فَعَل (faʿal) from the initial-weak root و-ر-م (w-r-m, to swell, puff up, bulge). Preserved continuously from classical Arabic medical terminology into everyday Jordanian speech, ورم refers to a bump or bodily swelling.

ورنيش.etymology: Technical craft loanword entering Levantine Arabic from French vernis / Italian vernice ('varnish', ultimately from Medieval Latin veronix and Ancient Greek Berenikē). Treated as a masculine noun in Jordanian carpentry and restoration workshops, ورنيش refers to wood lacquer and gloss finish.

وريحة.etymology: Linking conjunction w- ('and') to rīḥa ('scent, aroma', simplified from Classical rāʾiḥa under the hollow root ر-و-ح, 'wind, breath'). Jordanians pronounce the pair w-rīḥa (or w-rīḥet in construct phrases) cleanly in daily speech.

وزع.etymology: Form II verb وَزَّعَ (wazzaʿa, 'to divide into shares, distribute, hand out, assign') from وَزَعَ (wazaʿa, 'to restrain, apportion') on the root و-ز-ع (w-z-ʿ).

وزن.etymology: Form I verbal noun (maṣdar) وَزْن (wazn, 'weighing, weight, measure, meter') from وَزَنَ (wazana, 'to weigh') on the Semitic root و-ز-ن (w-z-n).

وزّع.etymology: Causative/distributive Form II verb (فَعَّلَ, faʿʿala) built on the initial-weak root و-ز-ع (w-z-ʿ, to divide, distribute, hold back, apportion). Standard in both Classical and colloquial Jordanian Arabic, وزّع means 'to hand out', 'distribute', or 'apportion evenly'.

وسط.etymology: Inherited from Classical Arabic وَسَط / وَسْط (wasaṭ / wasṭ, 'middle, center, midst') on the triliteral root و-س-ط (w-s-ṭ, 'to be in the middle').

وسطاني.etymology: Levantine relational adjective وَسْطَانِيّ (wasṭānī, 'middle, central'), formed with the augmented positional suffix ـَانِيّ (-āniyy) from وَسَط (wasaṭ, 'middle, center') on the root و-س-ط (w-s-ṭ).

وسع.etymology: Form I verb وَسِعَ (wasiʿa, 'to be wide enough for, hold, contain, have room for') on the Proto-Semitic root و-س-ع (w-s-ʿ).

history.meaning: to hold; accommodate; have room for

وسيم.etymology: From Classical Arabic وَسِيم (wasīm, 'handsome, having goodly features'), root و-س-م (w-s-m, 'mark, comeliness').

وش.etymology: Levantine phonological reduction of Classical Arabic وَجْه (wajh, 'face'), via assimilation wajh to wihh and wishsh.

وشمس.etymology: Compound of proclitic w- ('and') and shams ('sun', grammatically feminine without a suffix), inheriting Proto-Semitic *śamš-, cognate with Hebrew shemesh and Akkadian shamash. Jordanian speech keeps the form identical as w-shams.

وشوشوا.etymology: Third-person plural past verb from the onomatopoeic quadriliteral root و-ش-و-ش (w-sh-w-sh, 'to whisper softly, murmur'), imitating gentle rustling or hushed speech. In Jordanian Arabic washwashū describes whispering conspiratorially in someone's ear.

وصفة.etymology: Feminine unit noun waṣfa built on the initial-weak root و-ص-ف (w-ṣ-f, 'to describe, specify, prescribe'), contrasting with the verbal noun ṣifa. Across Jordan waṣfe does double duty in pharmacies as a doctor's prescription and in kitchens as a recipe.

وصل.etymology: Form I verb وَصَلَ (waṣala, 'to arrive, reach, join, connect') on the Semitic root و-ص-ل (w-ṣ-l).

وصلة.etymology: Noun وَصْلَة (waṣla, 'link, joint, connection, pipe fitting, short musical piece') derived from وَصَلَ (waṣala, 'to join, connect') on the root و-ص-ل (w-ṣ-l).

وصلت.etymology: Third-person feminine singular past verb from و-ص-ل (w-ṣ-l, 'to reach, join, arrive'). Standard waṣalat shortens colloquially to wiṣlat or waṣlat in Jordanian Arabic, where it also idiomatically confirms understanding ('got it!').

وصول.etymology: From Classical Arabic وُصُول (wuṣūl, 'arrival, reaching, joining'), the standard فُعُول verbal noun of وَصَلَ (waṣala, 'to join, reach, arrive'), from the root و-ص-ل (w-ṣ-l, 'connection, arrival'). Used across all registers for the arrival of guests, trains, or packages.

وضع.etymology: Continues Classical Arabic verbal noun وَضْع (waḍʿ, 'placing, laying down, posture') on the pattern فَعْل (faʿl) of وَضَعَ (waḍaʿa, 'to put down, set'), initial-weak root و-ض-ع (w-ḍ-ʿ), extended in modern MSA and colloquial Arabic to 'state of affairs, situation'.
وضع.notes: Everyday Jordanian greeting/check-in: كيف الوضع؟ ('how are things / what's the situation?'), or هاد الوضع مو طبيعي ('this situation isn't normal').

وضوح.etymology: Form I verbal noun (maṣdar) وُضُوح (wuḍūḥ, 'clarity, plainness, distinctness') on the pattern فُعُول (fuʿūl) from وَضَحَ (waḍaḥa, 'to be clear, plain, evident') on the root و-ض-ح (w-ḍ-ḥ).

وطلعتوا.etymology: Attaching w- ('and') to the second-person plural past verb ṭliʿtū ('you went out / up', root ط-ل-ع), formed by dropping the final -m of Classical ṭalaʿtum and raising the stem vowel. In Jordan ṭiliʿ covers going outside, ascending stairs, and heading out.

وطّى.etymology: Form II verb from Arabic root و-ط-أ (waṭuʾa, 'to be low'), meaning to make low, lower, or turn down.

وظيفة.etymology: Continues Classical Arabic وَظِيفَة (waẓīfa, 'fixed daily ration, allotted duty, official post') on the nominal pattern فَعِيلَة (faʿīla) from the triliteral root و-ظ-ف (w-ẓ-f, 'to assign a regular share or task').

morphemes.meaning: assign a regular duty or ration

وظيفة.notes: Crucial register split: in MSA and Gulf/Egyptian Arabic وظيفة primarily means 'job / employment' (while homework is واجب), whereas in Jordanian, Syrian, and Lebanese schools وظيفة is the everyday word for 'homework'.

وعد.etymology: Form I verbal noun وَعْد (waʿd, 'promise, pledge, word') from وَعَدَ (waʿada, 'to promise') on the Semitic root و-ع-د (w-ʿ-d).

وعشرين.etymology: Conjoining w- ('and') with the oblique numeral ʿishrīn ('twenty', dual/plural derivative of Proto-Semitic *ʿaśar-, 'ten', root ع-ش-ر). Levantine Arabic generalized the oblique -īn ending across all syntactic cases in compound numbers.

وعلى.etymology: Linking the coordinating conjunction w- ('and') with the preposition ʿalā ('on, upon, over', from root ع-ل-و, 'height, elevation'). While standalone ʿalā often contracts to ʿa- before definite nouns in Jordan, the full form w-ʿala remains frequent in coordinated phrases.

وغرفة.etymology: Pairing conjunction w- ('and') with ghurfa ('room', root غ-ر-ف, originally an elevated chamber or loft). In Jordanian real-estate and household speech w-ghurfe routinely lists rooms alongside salons and kitchens.

وفى.etymology: Doubly weak verb from the root و-ف-ي (to be complete, pay in full, keep a vow), preserved across formal and colloquial registers.

وفي.etymology: Joining coordinating w- ('and') with the preposition fī ('in, within', historically developed from Classical fū/fī, 'mouth, inside'). In Jordanian Arabic w-fī functions both prepositively ('and in') and existentially ('and there is/are').

وفيه.etymology: Fusing w- ('and'), preposition fī ('in'), and the third-person masculine singular suffix -h ('him/it'), Classical wa-fīhi loses its final short vowel to become w-fīh (or w-fīyo) in Levantine dialects. Jordanians often use it existentially to mean 'and inside it there is'.

history.meaning: and in it / and there is in it

وفّر.etymology: Form II verb وَفَّرَ (waffara, 'to make abundant, spare, save [money, time, or effort], economize') from وَفَرَ (wafara, 'to be abundant, ample, complete') on the root و-ف-ر (w-f-r).

وقار.etymology: Noun وَقَار (waqār, 'dignity, gravity, calm composure') from وَقُرَ (waqura, 'to be grave, dignified, staid, heavy') on the Proto-Semitic root و-ق-ر (w-q-r, 'to be heavy, honored').

وقت.etymology: Stemming from the root و-ق-ت (w-q-t, 'to fix a time, appoint an hour'), waqt names an interval, moment, or period across Classical and modern Arabic. In Jordanian usage waʾit/waqt also works as a temporal subordinator meaning 'when' or 'at the time of'.

وقتك.etymology: Possessive noun combining waqt ('time', root و-ق-ت) with the second-person masculine singular clitic -ak ('your'). Spoken Jordanian retains the full consonant cluster in waʾtak/wagtak, famously appearing in friendly phrases like khud waʾtak ('take your time').

وقع.etymology: Form I verb وَقَعَ (waqaʿa, 'to fall, drop, tumble, happen, occur') on the triliteral root و-ق-ع (w-q-ʿ).

وقف.etymology: Form I verb وَقَفَ (waqafa, 'to stand, stop, come to a halt') on the triliteral root و-ق-ف (w-q-f).

وقفتي.etymology: Second-person feminine singular past verb from و-ق-ف (w-q-f, 'to stop, stand'), functioning either as Form I waʾaftī ('you stood/stopped') or Form II waʾʾaftī ('you parked/halted'). Both forms share identical unvoweled orthography in Jordanian writing.

وقور.etymology: From Classical Arabic وَقُور (waqūr, 'sedate, dignified, composed'), root و-ق-ر (w-q-r, 'gravity, reverence').

وقّع.etymology: Form II verb (فَعَّلَ, faʿʿala) from the root و-ق-ع (w-q-ʿ, falling, landing, affixing a mark). Evolving from the medieval chancery practice of inscribing a ruler's formal endorsement (توقيع) onto a petition, وقّع became the universal Arabic verb for signing contracts, letters, and leases.

history.meaning: to sign (a contract, check, or letter)

وقّف.etymology: Form II causative verb وَقَّفَ (waqqafa, 'to cause to stand or stop, halt, park') from وَقَفَ (waqafa, 'to stand, stop') on the root و-ق-ف (w-q-f).

ول.etymology: Traditional Jordanian and Levantine exclamation of astonishment, related to Classical ويل or vocalic emphatic calls of amazement.

ولا.etymology: Compound negative particle uniting conjunction w- ('and') with negator lā ('no, not'). Across Jordan wala serves in 'neither...nor' coordination, emphatic negations like wala shī ('nothing at all'), and conversational tag questions meaning 'or what?'.

ولد.etymology: Inherited from Classical Arabic وَلَد (walad, 'child, boy, son, offspring') from وَلَدَ (walada, 'to give birth, bear, beget') on the Proto-Semitic root و-ل-د (w-l-d).

وماسكين.etymology: Joining coordinating/circumstantial w- ('and') to the masculine plural active participle māskīn ('holding', from مسك m-s-k, 'to grasp, hold'). Jordanian Arabic syncopates the short i of Classical māsikīn to māskīn to express continuous simultaneous action.

ومعها.etymology: Prepositional phrase combining w- ('and'), preposition maʿ ('with', root م-ع), and the third-person feminine singular pronoun -ha ('her/it'). Pronounced w-maʿha in Jordan, it commonly marks accompaniment or items someone brought along.

ومغلفة.etymology: Conjoining w- ('and') with mughallafa, the feminine Form II passive participle of ghallafa ('to wrap, encase', from غ-ل-ف gh-l-f, 'sheath, wrapper'). Both Standard and Jordanian Arabic use w-mghallafe for gift-wrapped parcels and sealed food.

ومكتب.etymology: Conjoining proclitic w- ('and') with maktab, a mafʿal noun of place built on the root ك-ت-ب (k-t-b, 'to write'). Originally meaning an elementary writing school, maktab evolved in Modern Arabic to denote both a wooden writing desk and a professional office.

history.meaning: and a place of writing, school

وناشف.etymology: Joining w- ('and') to nāshif, the Form I active participle of nashifa ('to dry up, absorb moisture', root ن-ش-ف). Throughout Jordan w-nāshif is the everyday word for dry clothes, dry soil, or stale bread.

ونص.etymology: Fusing coordinating w- ('and') with nuṣṣ, the Levantine contraction of Classical niṣf ('half', root ن-ص-ف) via elision of final f and gemination of ṣ. Essential in Jordanian shopping and clock time, w-nuṣṣ handles weights, hours, and quantities.

ونصها.etymology: Compound attaching w- ('and') and the feminine possessive suffix -ha ('of it') to colloquial nuṣṣ ('half', from Classical niṣf, root ن-ص-ف). Pronounced w-nuṣṣha in Jordan, it partitions any feminine singular noun into halves.

وهاذ.etymology: Pairing w- ('and') with the rural/Jordanian masculine demonstrative hāḏ ('this'), evolved from Classical hādhā by dropping the final vowel while retaining the interdental fricative dh. It contrasts with urban hād in Jordanian dialect geography.

وورق.etymology: Attaching proclitic w- ('and') to collective waraq ('leaves, paper', root و-ر-ق), producing a double-waw onset written وورق. Pronounced w-waraʾ or u-waraq in Jordanian speech, it pairs naturally with pens, notebooks, or kitchen ingredients.

ويكند.etymology: Urban Arabic borrowing directly from English weekend, integrated with sound feminine plural -aat.

ويل.etymology: Continues Classical Arabic exclamatory noun of calamity وَيْل (wayl, 'woe, ruin, affliction'), expanded from the primary Semitic lamentation interjection وَيْ (way, 'alas!, woe!').
ويل.notes: In Jordanian speech, يا ويلك مني! ('you're in big trouble with me!') and يا ويل البنت اللي... ('heaven help the girl who...') are vivid dramatic warnings.

وين.etymology: Universal colloquial Arabic interrogative adverb wēn ('where?'), evolved via fusion of the interrogative/conjoining element wa- with Classical ayna ('where?'). Across Jordan wēn replaces ayna completely in both direct questions and indirect clauses.

morphemes.meaning: prefixed element fused onto interrogative base

وييجي.etymology: Combining w- ('and') with yījī, the Levantine third-person masculine singular imperfect of jāʾa ('to come', root ج-ي-ء). Dropping the final hamza and lengthening the imperfect vowel yields w-yījī in Jordanian Arabic for sequential motion.

وَعَد.etymology: Form I verb وَعَدَ (waʿada, 'to promise, give one's word') on the Proto-Semitic root و-ع-د (w-ʿ-d).

يا.etymology: Ancient Semitic vocative particle yā, cognate with Syriac and Ugaritic vocative markers, used identically from pre-Islamic poetry to modern street speech. In Jordan yā introduces names, kinship terms, polite titles, and exclamations of surprise.

ياخذنا.etymology: Third-person masculine singular subjunctive verb yākhudh ('he takes') with the first-person plural object suffix -na ('us'), from أ-خ-ذ (ʾ-kh-dh). Levantine dialects replace the glottal stop with compensatory vowel lengthening (yākhudna / yākhidna).

ياسمين.etymology: Borrowed from Middle Persian *yāsamīn* ('jasmine flower'), fragrant climbing shrub cultivated across Levantine courtyards for centuries.
ياسمين.notes: From Arabic and Persian the word entered medieval Latin and French *jasmin*, giving English 'jasmine'.

ياقوت.etymology: Collective masculine noun يَاقُوت (yāqūt, 'ruby, sapphire, corundum'), borrowed in early Arabic via Aramaic יָקוּנְתָּא / Syriac ܝܩܘܢܕܐ from Ancient Greek ὑάκινθος (huákinthos, 'hyacinth stone / blue-red gem'). Arabic mineralogists classified rubies as 'red corundum' (ياقوت أحمر), giving modern 'ruby'.

يبطل.etymology: Form II imperfect verb yibaṭṭil (from baṭṭala, root ب-ط-ل, 'to render void, cease'). While Classical baṭala meant 'to become invalid or idle', Levantine Arabic shifted Form II into the everyday transitive verb for quitting a habit or canceling a plan.

يتركها.etymology: Imperfect verb yatruk ('he leaves, abandons', root ت-ر-ك) carrying the third-person feminine singular object clitic -ha ('her/it'). In Jordanian speech syncope drops the stem vowel in favor of yitrukha or yitrakha, keeping the classical root intact.

يتفركش.etymology: Colloquial Levantine quadriliteral medio-passive verb yitfarkash ('to trip, stumble'), built on tafaʿlala from the expressive root ف-ر-ك-ش (likely blending ف-ر-ك 'to rub, scramble' with expressive -sh). Jordanians use it daily for tripping over steps or tangling feet.

يد.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *yad- ('hand, arm, handle'), grammatically feminine because body parts in pairs are feminine in Arabic.
يد.notes: In spoken Jordanian, 'hand' is pronounced إيد (īd, plural إيدين), while يد (yadd) also names a door handle or tool grip.

يدخل.etymology: Built on the triconsonantal root د-خ-ل (d-kh-l, 'to enter, go inside'), Classical yadkhulu becomes yidkhul or yudkhul in Jordanian Arabic. While casual speech often prefers yfūt for entering rooms, yidkhul stays common in polite invitations and set phrases.

يدوي.etymology: Nisba adjective formed from Arabic يَد (yad, 'hand') with the historical glide -aw- (يَدَوِيّ), Semitic root ي-د-ي.

يروح.etymology: Hollow imperfect verb yrūḥ ('he goes') from ر-و-ح (r-w-ḥ). In Classical Arabic rāḥa meant specifically 'to depart in the evening', yet across Levantine and Egyptian dialects it generalized to become the primary everyday verb for 'to go' at any hour.

يس.etymology: Borrowed exclamation from English yes used colloquially in playful celebration of success.

يسار.etymology: Inherited Semitic directional noun from the root ي-س-ر (originally denoting ease or auspiciousness as well as the left hand).

يسلموا.etymology: Levantine gratitude expression يِسْلَمُوا (yislamū, 'thank you!', literally 'may they [your hands] be kept safe and well!'), elliptical for يِسْلَمُوا إِيدَيْك (yislamū ʾīdēk), third-person plural optative imperfect of سَلِمَ (salima, 'to be safe, sound, unharmed') on the Proto-Semitic root س-ل-م (s-l-m).

history.meaning: may they be safe and sound

يعني.etymology: Originally the third-person masculine singular imperfect of عنى ('to mean, intend', root ع-ن-ي), literally 'it means'. In spoken Levantine Arabic it grammaticalized into a versatile discourse marker ('so, that is, I mean').
يعني.notes: Learners hear يعني both as a literal verb ('that means') and as a natural conversational bridge.

history.meaning: so, I mean, that is to say

يلا.etymology: Pan-Arabic hortative interjection yalla, fused from the pious invocation yā Allāh ('O God!'). Desemanticized from a call for divine help into a lively prompt meaning 'come on, hurry up, let's go', it peppers Jordanian conversation constantly.

يلمس.etymology: Imperfect verb from the root ل-م-س (l-m-s, 'to touch lightly, feel by hand'), shifting Classical yalmisu to Levantine yilmis. Beyond physical touch, Jordanian speakers use the same root for gentle requests or tangible results.

يمكن.etymology: Impersonal third-person masculine singular imperfect verb يُمْكِن (yumkin, literally 'it is possible', used adverbially as 'maybe, perhaps') from Form IV أَمْكَنَ (ʾamkana, 'to be possible, enable') on the root م-ك-ن (m-k-n).

يمنع.etymology: Form I imperfect verb yimnaʿ/yamnaʿ built on م-ن-ع (m-n-ʿ, 'to withhold, forbid, bar'), cognate with Hebrew mānaʿ ('to hold back'). Jordanian legal, civic, and everyday speech retains both the consonant skeleton and meaning identically.

يمين.etymology: Inherited from Classical Arabic يَمِين (yamīn, 'right hand, right side; oath'), from Proto-Semitic *yamīn- ('right hand, right side') on the root ي-م-ن (y-m-n).

ينقطع.etymology: Form VII medio-passive imperfect verb from ق-ط-ع (q-ṭ-ʿ, 'to cut, sever'), Classical yanqaṭiʿu -> Jordanian yinʾiṭiʿ / yingiṭiʿ. Across Jordan it describes snapped cords, power outages, dropped phone calls, and discontinued supplies.

history.meaning: it gets cut off, drops out

يوقع.etymology: Levantine imperfect verb yūqaʿ/yūgaʿ ('he falls') from the initial-weak root و-ق-ع (w-q-ʿ). Whereas Classical Arabic deletes the initial w in yaqaʿu, Jordanian dialects level the stem across the paradigm, restoring ū from underlying w.

يوكل.etymology: Jordanian subjunctive/imperfect verb yōkil ('he eats') from the Proto-Semitic root أ-ك-ل (ʾ-k-l, cognate with Hebrew ʾāḵal). Dropping the initial hamza of Classical yaʾkulu yielded compensatory long ō in Levantine speech, reflected directly in the spelling يوكل.

يوم.etymology: Continuing Proto-Semitic *yawm- ('day'), cognate with Hebrew yōm, Aramaic yōmā, and Akkadian ūmu, Arabic yawm contracts to yōm in spoken Levantine dialects. Across Jordan it denotes a 24-hour day, a calendar date, or a memorable occasion.

يوميا.etymology: Adverbial accusative يَوْمِيًّا (yawmiyyan, 'daily, every day') formed from the relational adjective يَوْمِيّ (yawmiyy, 'daily'), itself from يَوْم (yawm, 'day') + nisba suffix ـِيّ (-iyy) + adverbial accusative ending ـًا (-an), root ي-و-م (y-w-m).
